UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L644] OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY
SECTION: Practical Training Periods
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/618

Practical Training Periods The Bachelor's Degree Program in Occupational Therapy, like all three-year health-related courses, has a strong practical focus that is expressed through the practical training activity. Practical training is a form of educational activity that allows the acquisition of professional competencies through the execution of practical activities with varying degrees of autonomy that gradually increase as the student's experience grows.

Three-year health-related degrees require 60 credits of practical training (professional training in a clinical setting) to be completed from the first to the third year. The Occupational Therapy Degree Program organizes these activities across all relevant areas for the training of an Occupational Therapist, based on the competencies outlined in the professional profile. All practical training activities are carried out at specialized health and rehabilitation services, as well as other scientifically significant institutions, which meet the specific educational objectives for the professional figure for each academic year. The progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy acquired during the course enables students to develop the correct ability to observe, assess, and intervene in various rehabilitation issues related to pediatric and adult age groups.

Internship agreements are established after thorough collection of information to verify the quality of the facility and, if necessary, a preparatory visit to the host site. All practical training activities are conducted within accredited facilities and supervised by clinical/professional tutors, specifically designated by each facility in agreement with the Course's responsible body, who assist students in acquiring professional competencies. Tutors work closely with the Occupational Therapist Coordinator for Internships.

The primary point of reference for students within the Course is represented by the Course's Internal Training Tutors, who support the tutors present in the facilities to enhance the educational experiences.

The Director of Professional Training, Dr. Christian Parone, in collaboration with the appointed Tutors, identifies the accredited internship sites necessary for students to acquire the competencies outlined in the professional profile. For each activated internship, a specific training project and an internship agreement are established in collaboration with the host site, respecting the prerequisites useful for educational purposes.

During the periods of professional training in a clinical setting, the internship tutors conduct periodic formative evaluations to verify progress toward the established goals, as well as a certificative evaluation at the conclusion of the training period. Throughout the training process, to facilitate the acquisition of professional competencies in the domains of knowledge, being, and doing, the Tutors or Course instructors conduct tutoring activities to support the learning process with individual students (if necessary) and the class group.

At the end of each academic year, a committee composed of the Course's Tutors conducts a verification of the professional competencies acquired by the student during the reference year.

The Occupational Therapy Degree Program, through the Training Tutors, maintains constant communication with public and private specialized institutions that host students across the territory.

Starting from the 2022/2023 academic year, the revision of the curriculum and consequently the training offer plan, aimed at meeting the requests of stakeholders in the workplace, as well as the continuous feedback before and during the internship, will involve administering evaluation questionnaires to both the facility tutors and the students completing the internship, in order to assess the quality of the professional training experiences and to understand the opinions of the host institutions and students regarding the strengths and weaknesses of the facilities on one hand and each student on the other.

The student evaluation criteria consider the level of preparation and training, accuracy in performing assigned tasks, consistency in personal engagement, engagement in observation activities, interest in deepening knowledge of work tools, ability to reflect on work experience, ability to link theoretical aspects with practical activities, and willingness to interact with the tutor.

The professional training experiences offered by the accredited host facilities are monitored by evaluating: the significance of the activities and the type of activities carried out, the welcome from the tutor, the relationship with the tutor and their working method according to the Course's operational guidelines, the theoretical-practical correspondence of the Occupational Therapy content, the stimulation received in the facility, and the evaluation of the experience for career orientation in the workplace.

All students enrolled in the Course, starting from the second semester of the first year, must compulsorily complete practical training activities at facilities outside the Course. The number of students varies depending on enrollments in different academic years. For the 2022/2023 academic year, 60 students completed their experience at facilities of various types, addressing different Occupational Therapy themes. Over 95% of these students reported satisfaction with the experience, thanks also to the presence of an occupational therapist tutor in all selected facilities, unlike previous years.

International Mobility Office The Department of Neuroscience, Imaging and Clinical Sciences, with the support of the International Relations Office (URI), manages student mobility within bilateral agreements that provide for incoming and outgoing student exchanges within community-funded programs such as the Erasmus+ program. Mobility is encouraged and promoted through the provision of scholarships and support in administrative procedures: from contacting the foreign institution, to preparing the study plan for international mobility, to the recognition of exams taken abroad.
The Department maintains various collaboration agreements with foreign universities and research laboratories. The primary goal is to acquaint students of the CdS with the importance of international training. This involves sensitizing students to an international perspective on occupational therapy.
Currently, three agreements are active with the University of Coimbra (School of Health Technology, Coimbra, Portugal), the University of Cracow (University of Physical Education in Krakow, Poland), and the University of Plzeň in the Czech Republic (University of West Bohemia in Plzeň).
Within the call issued during the 2022/2023 academic year, valid for the Erasmus+ Student project for the 2023/2024 academic year, four female students were selected, with destinations at the three different partner institutions.
Calls for international mobility for internship activities are also available: Emasmus+ for Traineeship call. This call aims to promote the activation of internships at companies or training and research centers in one of the European countries participating in the Program. Erasmus students have the opportunity to acquire specific skills and a better understanding of the socio-economic culture of the host country, with support from preparatory or updating courses in the language of the host country (or the working language), with the ultimate goal of facilitating the mobility of young workers across Europe.
Within the call issued during the 2022/2023 academic year, valid for the Erasmus+ for Traineeship project for the 2023/2024 academic year, two applications were submitted, but the rankings are not yet known.
The Department responsible for the CdS, represented by the Erasmus coordinator, in collaboration with the Erasmus contact person for the CdS, organizes annual presentation days for both Erasmus+ pathways following the call release, to facilitate students in submitting applications. During these meetings, students who previously completed a study period abroad are also present to share their experience and assist students in choosing the destination and study methods abroad.

Student opinions The Bachelor's Degree Course is subject to annual evaluation to monitor overall satisfaction, satisfaction regarding organizational and logistical aspects, and satisfaction with teaching effectiveness.
Specifically, the assessment of perceived educational process effectiveness by students is presented by considering some questions from the mandatory evaluation questionnaire under Law 370/99, particularly: interest in the topics covered (D0), adequacy of prior knowledge (D1), adequacy of study load to credits assigned to the course of interest (D3), adequacy of teaching materials (D9), coherence of the teaching delivered (D13), respect for teaching schedule (D14), examination procedures (D16), satisfaction with professors (D20), their clarity of exposition (D21), and their availability to provide clarifications (D22). These questionnaires do not investigate the quality of clinical internship training, which represents 1/3 of the total teaching activity of the entire course. The average score in the student opinion survey indicates that the Degree Course maintains a rating above the average over the years, reaching a score of 3.49 for the 2022/23 academic year. Specifically, all evaluated macro-indicators show a score above the university average and even more so above the entire Health Area average, particularly regarding organizational and logistical aspects, confirming that the new internal organization of the Degree Course and the new educational offer plan are effective. The Degree Course has improved from a rating of 3.25 to 3.49 over the last 8 years. The percentage of professors rated in grade A (3.5 to 4 inclusive) remains high, while the percentage in the lowest grade is below 2%. The assessment of professor opinions over the last three cohorts has significantly increased, especially regarding: professors' preparation on the actual role of occupational therapists; full availability of professors from different courses to clarify topics covered in lectures; competence and ability of individual professors to deliver their courses as indicated on the Course website, stimulating adequate student interest. Better also the evaluation of the study load required based on the credits assigned to the course, the organization of lectures and exercises, as well as the definition of examination procedures, confirming the validity of the new Degree Course organization following the modification of the educational offer plan. Over the years, professors have aligned their courses with what is presented on institutional websites, encouraging students to follow a training path aligned with their expectations, as reflected in the evaluation of question D21, which scores 3.54, significantly exceeding the university averages for health professions.
The assessment of professors' effort and teaching activities is communicated to individual professors, discussed in the Teaching Committee and the Degree Course Council, and considered for resource allocation. In this regard, the Degree Course Council meeting of September 20, 2022, was dedicated to discussing evaluations received from the University Quality Assurance Office and individual professor evaluations for the latest cohort, as well as discussing and resolving criticalities emerging during the compilation of annual evaluation documents for the Degree Course to meet required parameters and ensure students an adequate training path. Each year, the Degree Course allocates an agenda item in the Degree Course Council meeting for discussing and approving the SUA-CdS tables dedicated to student opinions.
During the compilation of the annual report of the Joint Teaching-Student Committee (CPDS), some criticalities emerged and were reported and discussed. Some have been resolved, others are still under evaluation. A methodological limitation in collecting information/evaluations regarding individual courses was identified, but this issue was successfully resolved by the University Quality Assurance Office during the year.
The collected and analyzed data unfortunately reveal the presence of some chronic criticalities mainly related to logistical and infrastructural issues. Criticalities resulting in scores below the university average concern: a) perceived low adequacy of computer workstations and equipment for non-frontal teaching activities; b) presence of classrooms and laboratories that are not functional and insufficiently equipped; c) inadequacy of libraries available to students. These criticalities stem from the fact that the Occupational Therapy Degree Course is based at CUMS, which is far from the Campus and thus from the services it provides (library, computer classrooms, etc.).
Some criticalities identified in the previous academic year have significantly improved, but others, which fall outside the Degree Course's responsibility, will be managed at the university level.
Over the years, the University has activated a service (i.e., Parla con noi per crescere insieme) aimed at improving the quality of services offered, allowing various categories (such as: prospective student, student, families, graduate, professor, administrative staff, companies, others) to submit complaints, suggestions, or praise in different areas (teaching, facilities, services, and internationalization) via an online form.

GRADUATE OPINIONS The survey of graduates' opinions is continuously and significantly growing. The analysis of graduates' opinions, conducted by the University Quality Assurance Office for the year 2023, reveals an improvement in the performance of the course of study in all three areas defined by the macro-indicators: logistical-organizational aspects, teaching facilities, and overall satisfaction. The areas of greatest concern, which have nonetheless seen a significant improvement even from the latest cohort, relate to the course organization in terms of class and exam schedules and the secretariat service. A clearly positive judgment, exceeding even the university's average for the health area, was obtained for the support provided to carry out the internship activity. The absence of evaluation for potential study abroad experiences is due to the recent activation of agreements with foreign universities for Erasmus Plus projects. It is hoped that evaluations will improve in future academic years following the implemented changes and the new reorganization of the Course of Study itself.

A decidedly positive response was given by graduates regarding the courses and the overall study load relative to the course duration (3.47 and 3.53 respectively vs. 3.33 and 3.21 university averages in the Health Area), as it has been steadily improving over time.

Finally, the overall judgment on internship experiences and the course of study itself confirm the adequacy of the work carried out by the Course of Study in improving the quality of the educational offer in recent years. The internship experience received a graduate evaluation of 3.58 (vs 3.48 university average in the Health Area), while the overall course of study evaluation was 3.42 (vs 3.31 university average in the Health Area).

The analysis of results from the AlmaLaurea survey on the graduate profile and the survey on the perceived effectiveness of the educational process by students further confirms that the Course of Study continues to improve its educational offer over the last three cohorts, with a course organization more aligned with student needs. The training received is extremely well-suited for applying acquired competencies in the workplace: over 93% of students are highly satisfied, and the number of students who consider the professional training and degree obtained highly effective for their current work has increased (60%).

The AlmaLaurea data regarding the graduate profile (referring to all satisfaction evaluations for the completed course of study, for the latest cohort considered, i.e., students graduating during the calendar year 2022) reveals that the main reasons for choosing the Course of Study are cultural and professional factors. Almost 80% of enrolled students graduate on time with an average graduation grade of 104.6, and over 83% of graduates are employed and not enrolled in a second-level degree.

Over 90% of students (more than 20% above the university average) regularly attend more than 75% of the required courses.

Some concerns remain regarding the perceived adequacy of computer workstations and teaching equipment (laboratories, practical experiences).

Over 85% of graduates would re-enroll in the same course of study at the university.

Graduates' opinions, as well as those of students, were widely discussed in the Course of Study Council meeting on September 20, 2022, for the latest cohort considered last year, using suggestions and criticisms raised during evaluation to improve the Course of Study organization and educational offer. The results of the annual discussion are evident in the continuous growth in the Course of Study's evaluation. Each year, the Course of Study dedicates an item to the agenda in the Course of Study Council meeting in September/October for the discussion and approval of the SUA-Course of Study tables related to graduates' opinions.

Applying Knowledge and Understanding
Apply knowledge and understanding to demonstrate a professional approach to work, devising and supporting arguments to solve problems in basic and characteristic disciplines. Teaching tools: classroom activities, teaching laboratories, practical lessons in laboratories and/or equipped classrooms, internship, reading and interpretation of international literature, interactive teaching with tools and e-learning methodology.

The evaluation of such knowledge and understanding capabilities will be carried out through the following verification methods (which can be conducted in person or exceptionally in virtual form): theoretical/practical exams, written reports on technical aspects (compilation of functional diagnosis and rehabilitation program and project verification of the rehabilitation file), oral and written presentation of projects and practical tests.

Learning Skills
Upon completion of the study path, the graduate will be able to know and independently apply the appropriate therapeutic rehabilitation intervention using clinical reasoning as a guiding tool for decision-making within the various options composing the different phases of the rehabilitation process. This autonomy will be achieved through the ability to effectively respond to individual and/or collective health needs as a single operator or within a multidisciplinary team, opting for the best therapeutic strategies, identifying appropriate approaches and tools, collecting data (including social context analysis), functional assessment and diagnosis, defining prognosis and therapeutic goals in the short, medium, and long term, developing the therapeutic program, selecting and applying appropriate methodologies for the clinical case (including intensity, timing, and type of therapeutic approach) according to the best available scientific evidence, international guidelines, and best practices; ethically, it will manifest through respect for relevant regulations, professional, legal, health, and ethical standards.

Upon completion of the study path, the Occupational Therapy graduate will:
- be aware of the need for continuous knowledge updating,
- be able to design self-training paths and plan the updating of their knowledge through Continuing Medical Education,
- have acquired an effective study methodology enabling further university education with a high degree of autonomy,
- be able to consult databases and online information on specific topics, as well as scientific literature, even in English.

This capability will be developed and verified through exam preparation, internship attendance and evaluation, which combines theory with practice, and through critical use of scientific literature and bibliography for final exam preparation.

Teaching tools: classroom activities, seminars, simulation laboratories (also in e-learning), internship.

The evaluation of learning skills will be carried out through the following verification methods (which can be conducted in person or exceptionally in virtual form): theoretical-practical exams, written and oral reports on technical/professional aspects, clinical case discussions, development of the Rehabilitation Plan/Program and compilation of the clinical file for their area of responsibility.

Knowledge and Understanding
Occupational Therapy graduates, upon completion of the training path, will have acquired a solid mastery of knowledge in both basic and characteristic disciplines, as well as in social/relational and professional practice aspects.

In particular, they will have acquired the necessary cultural and scientific foundations to:
- understand biological phenomena, organ and apparatus functioning mechanisms, motor and psychomotor development, and correlate them with psychological, social, and environmental aspects of health;
- know and understand the principles of elementary physics and their applications in healthcare, biomechanics, and assistive devices;
- know the biochemical bases and regulatory mechanisms of pathophysiological processes, with particular attention to muscles and the Central and Peripheral Nervous Systems;
- know and understand the functioning and structure of the cell, the specificity of eukaryotic cellular structures, bacteria, and viruses, and basic concepts of current biological topics of scientific interest;
- know the essential morphological characteristics and functional mechanisms of systems, organs, and apparatus in humans and their interactions, particularly regarding sensory organs, Central and Peripheral Nervous Systems, skeletal, muscular, visual, auditory, and respiratory systems in pediatric and adult age;
- know the histological characteristics of tissues: bone, striated muscle, and nervous tissue;
- know the main causes of disease and their pathogenetic mechanisms, fundamental pathophysiological mechanisms of major systems and apparatus, main pathogenic microorganisms for humans, and host defense mechanisms;
- know the basics of general sociology with particular attention to socio-cultural aspects, including interculturalism;
- understand the physio-pathological elements of different clinical situations;
- understand the elements underlying the rehabilitation intervention process;
- know the meaning of occupation, its influence on a person's health status, the relationship between occupation and human development throughout life, including the conceptual components of the ICF;
- know the main models underlying Occupational Therapy practice;
- know the relationship between occupation and environment understood as sociocultural context, environmental resources, urbanistic environment, and institutional environment to promote the elimination of physical and human barriers and foster participation;
- recognize and understand how changes, psychophysical alterations in development, socio-cultural disorders, and the personal meaning attributed to occupation can affect quality of life;
- know the characteristics of the therapeutic relationship and elements of interpersonal communication;
- know the scientific foundations of general and specific rehabilitation methodologies guiding the Occupational Therapist's actions in various intervention areas defined by the professional profile;
- know the regulations governing the practice of Occupational Therapy, civil and criminal responsibilities, and related medical-legal implications;
- know the correct methods for consulting international scientific literature;
- know the principles of evidence-based medicine;
- know the statistical tools useful for planning research and professional management processes;
- know the organizational characteristics of rehabilitation activities respecting appropriateness criteria, effectiveness, and efficiency;
- know at least one European Union language besides Italian, within their specific area of competence, for general information exchange.

The teaching methods provided to achieve this specific training objective (application of knowledge) include lectures (in person or virtual), conferences, seminars, working groups, and discussions. The teaching process will utilize modern teaching tools.

The ability to apply acquired knowledge will be developed through guided activities in university laboratories, in agreement with internship sites, and in the territory, especially through multiprofessional and multidisciplinary approaches.

The evaluation of such knowledge and understanding capabilities will be carried out through the following verification methods: oral, written exams, simulated practical tests, written reports, and rehabilitation file compilations.

Organization and Responsibility of Quality Assurance at the Course of Study Level
The bodies and organizations involved in the Course of Study's quality assurance process in Occupational Therapy are:
- Course of Study Chair: coordinates the Course of Study's quality assurance system and oversees compliance with obligations set by regulations, collaborating with the Parity Commission and Review Group, in line with the central university bodies' guidelines on quality assurance. Members: Prof. Cecilia Paolini.
- Parity Commission of the School of Medicine and Health Sciences: specifically monitors the educational offer and teaching quality and services provided to students by faculty and structures. Course of Study members: Dr. Alberto Granzotto and the student representative.
- Quality Assurance/Review Group: prepares the review report, analyzing the current Course of Study situation, highlighting strengths and improvement opportunities, and proposing corresponding objectives, indicators, and target values. Members: Prof. Stefania Della Penna, Dr. Alberto Granzotto, Prof. Angelo di Iorio, and Prof. Valentina Tomassini, coordinated and supported by the Course of Study Chair, Prof. Cecilia Paolini.
- Course of Study Council: discusses and approves the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA); collaborates with the smooth operation of the Course of Study's quality assurance. Members: all faculty members responsible for teaching for the reference cohorts.
- Quality Assurance Course of Study Reference Teachers: supports and monitors the quality assurance processes related to the Course of Study. Members: Prof. Stefania Della Penna, Dr. Alberto Granzotto, Prof. Angelo di Iorio, Prof. Cecilia Paolini, and Prof. Valentina Tomassini.

At the beginning of each academic year and at the end of each semester, the Course of Study's Quality Assurance Commission consults with the Course of Study's Teaching Commission to identify improvement actions.

The Department's Quality Assurance Commission: carries out monitoring and support actions for AVA processes related to the Course of Study and serves as a liaison with central bodies (PQA and Evaluation Unit), particularly regarding orientation and placement aspects and teaching aspects.

Department Quality Assurance Representative (ReAQD): The ReAQD ensures the connection between PQA and peripheral structures (Department, Course of Study, CPDS) and provides support and consultation to the Department Director regarding quality assurance in Teaching, Research, and Third Mission. Members: Prof. Maria Addolorata Mariggiò.

The ReAQD has the following tasks:
- carry out training and information activities on quality assurance for Department staff;
- monitor and provide consultation for the correct execution of AVA-related activities related to Teaching, Research, and Third Mission;
- support the Department Director to ensure coordination of activities across different sectors, both within the Department and with central university bodies.

Each academic year, the examination programs of various modules within Integrated Courses are reviewed, and general comparisons are made between different Integrated Courses, promoting meetings among faculty within Integrated Courses and among their Coordinators.

Department Quality Assurance Representative for Teaching (ReAQD-Teaching): The ReAQD-Teaching ensures the connection between PQA and peripheral structures (Department, Course of Study, CPDS) and provides support and consultation to the Department Director regarding quality assurance in Teaching. Member: Prof. Mirco Fasolo.

Brief Description of Related and Complementary Activities
The training cycle focuses on knowledge and understanding of the main criteria for accessibility and full usability of public and private facilities and environments by an expanded user base. It will also deepen basic knowledge related to architecture, both in historical, logical-formal, compositional, typological-distributive, structural, construction, and technological aspects, as well as their relationships with historical, physical, and environmental contexts.

The general training objectives aim at acquiring specific competencies related to:
- universal design,
- design for need,
- correct interaction between humans and the environment.

The main knowledge will be provided to enable actions to improve living at home, school, workplace, and primary leisure places to implement all daily activities, productive activities, and social and relational life.

Frontal teaching is also dedicated to social structures, meaning environments for healthcare and assistance activities, such as hospitals, care homes, rehabilitation centers, nursing homes, etc.; environments for cultural activities, such as libraries, museums, temporary exhibition halls; environments for any other social activity; finally, all public buildings, including judicial (courts, police stations, police headquarters) and administrative (previdential, assistance, etc.) facilities.

The training process is structured around frontal teaching hours, where discussion of internship experiences related to specific teaching knowledge becomes central.

Brief Course Description
The Occupational Therapy Bachelor's Degree Course falls under the Class of Degrees in Rehabilitation Health Professions (L/SNT2) as defined by the Ministry of University and Research Decree of March 16, 2007. It is structured over three years and is established within the School of Medicine and Health Sciences. The Occupational Therapy Bachelor's Degree Course is qualifying and allows registration in the Professional Register.

Pursuant to Law 10 August 2000, No. 251, Article 2, Paragraph 1, Occupational Therapy graduates are identified as health professionals in the rehabilitation area who, in professional autonomy, perform prevention, care, and rehabilitation tasks, as well as functional assessment procedures to fulfill the competencies specified in the professional profile for subjects affected by physical, mental, temporary, or permanent disabilities.

The graduate identifies the health needs of the patient, with particular attention to the subject's, family's, and socio-environmental situation; assesses difficulties and resources regarding functionality, autonomy, and integration into the living environment; selects appropriate interventions to help the patient achieve the maximum possible recovery of abilities and competencies in motor, cognitive, motivational, and occupational areas. They also implement specific interventions and educate families and caregivers to promote the person's autonomy and propose the selection and implementation of aids and environmental modifications to facilitate occupations. They verify the achievement of predefined goals for the best possible quality of life in the patient's daily life, at home, school/work, and social environments, and evaluate the quality of results and rehabilitation paths.

Graduates in this class must acquire adequate preparation in basic disciplines, aimed at the best understanding of fundamental physiological and pathological phenomena related to their preventive and curative activities, as well as the maximum capacity for integration with other health professions.

It is also necessary to know, besides Italian, at least one additional European Union language, aimed at both the specific area of competence and the possibility of exchanging general information.

The academic year is organized into annual courses starting in October and ending in the first week of June.

The Occupational Therapy graduate is a Health Area Professional who provides services under a dependent regime:
- in rehabilitation services within the National and Regional Health Services,
- in accredited and contracted private facilities,
- in clinical facilities,
- in rehabilitation centers,
- in assisted healthcare residences,
- at the patient's home,
- in medical and/or multispecialty clinics.

Occupational Therapists work in various medical fields, addressing all life stages whenever autonomy is needed.

Occupational Therapy graduates can also provide self-employed activities:
- in prevention,
- in social settings in schools and nurseries, laboratories, and disability residences, as rehabilitation consultants, specialists in therapeutic materials and aids, and in consulting services.

External Effectiveness
Confirmation that the Course of Study's objectives provide training that offers employment prospects comes from the National Conference of Health Professions Courses of Study and AlmaLaurea surveys. The external effectiveness data elaborated by AlmaLaurea report an average employment rate of over 83% for the latest cohort, in line with national averages for the same class. All graduates work as professionals in healthcare facilities, predominantly in the private sector, and found employment shortly after graduation. 11% of students chose to enroll in a second-level degree. Nearly 6% are not working but have not pursued further education and are seeking employment. Over 93% of employed graduates consider the competencies acquired during the study course extremely useful and adequate for professional training and are satisfied with their current job, a value close to national averages for the same class. The rating given to job satisfaction reflects the national average (7.5/10).

Specific Course Objectives and Training Path Description
The training path aims at acquiring competencies related to the professional profile through the development of knowledge (knowing), practical skills (knowing how to do), and attitude (knowing how to be).

The Occupational Therapy graduate, as required by current legislation, must possess:
- a good knowledge of the foundations of preparatory disciplines [Basic Biological Sciences (human anatomy, applied biology, histology); Basic Preparatory Sciences (biochemistry, physics applied to biomechanics and aids, informatics and information processing); Morpho-Genetic Sciences for Occupational Therapy Prevention (physiology, medical genetics, neurophysiology, pharmacology); Neuropsychiatric Sciences in Occupational Therapy (neurology, fundamentals of neuroimaging, psychiatry)];
- a deep knowledge of the disciplines characteristic of the occupational profession [Basic Principles of Occupational Therapy I (theoretical foundations of occupational therapy, preparatory elements for occupational therapy); Basic Principles of Occupational Therapy II (tools in occupational therapy, assessments in occupational therapy, approaches in occupational therapy: application of models, nursing sciences, assistive sciences)];
- understanding and relationship capabilities with the clientele [Psychology and Sociology (clinical psychology, general psychology, disability psychology, sociology of cultural and communication processes); Occupational Therapy in Developmental Age (pediatrics, occupational therapy in pediatric age, speech therapy and cognitive processes, occupational therapy in childhood, child neuropsychiatry); Accessibility and Assistive Technologies in Occupational Therapy (autonomy aids, electronic and computer bioengineering, architecture and accessibility); Occupational Therapy in Adult Age (diseases of the locomotor apparatus, physical medicine and rehabilitation and spinal cord injuries, occupational therapy in neurological conditions in adults); Occupational Therapy in School Setting (therapeutic aids in developmental age, occupational therapy in school age, developmental psychology and educational psychology, general and social pedagogy); Occupational Therapy in Work Setting (work organization and ergonomics in occupational therapy, general and applied hygiene, occupational medicine, business organization, legal medicine, work psychology and organizational psychology); Applied Medical and Surgical Sciences in Occupational Therapy (oncology, internal medicine, rheumatology, occupational therapy in clinical settings, diseases of the visual apparatus, otorhinolaryngology and diseases of the auditory apparatus); Occupational Therapy in Geriatric Age (fundamentals of neuropsychiatry in geriatric age, geriatrics, prevention, care, and rehabilitation for chronic conditions, occupational therapy in geriatric age)];
- practical application of Occupational Science (Professional Internship in neuro-cognitive, psychosocial, and rehabilitation settings; Professional Laboratories; Seminars);
- competencies to participate in various forms of professional development and to engage in research activities in different application areas [Scientific English; Research Methodology (research methodology, medical statistics, psychometrics, research methodology in occupational therapy)].

In formulating the Training Project, priority is given to the theoretical/practical study of Occupational Science, carried out through lectures and teaching laboratories that serve as a bridge to the Professional Internship in the qualifying areas of Occupational Therapy. Courses are structured into modules delivered through lectures and laboratory activities.

Learning outcomes are evaluated through in-process self-assessment tests for students and a final oral, practical, or written exam (evaluation expressed as pass/fail or out of thirty), aimed at verifying the achievement of the set objectives for each course and necessary for acquiring credit points. For professional and internship activities, objectives refer to the Professional Profile and are reported on the Internship Sheet and approved by the Course of Study Council.

The final exam of the Course allows the acquisition of 6 credit points.

Professional Responsibility
This area refers to the Occupational Therapist professional assuming responsibility in all professional actions through the achievement of the following competencies:
- in professional conduct, learns to act in accordance with the professional profile, code of ethics, regulations, and laws related to the profession, developing specific competencies regarding the person and their caregivers.
- acts in the interest of the clientele, recognizing their abilities, resources, interests, and reference contexts.
- develops a careful awareness of their internal setting, making it available to the clientele.
- exercises professional autonomy in clinical practice while respecting the user's interests.

Care and Rehabilitation
This area refers to the competencies the student must possess to define the therapeutic-occupational project based on the emotional, cognitive, motor, and functional abilities of the clientele. The student develops competencies to identify strategies in the context of care and rehabilitation for temporary or permanent physical and psychological disorders, considering individual resources, specific occupations, and living environments to improve quality of life, autonomy, and occupational performance.

Therapeutic Education
This area refers to the competencies the student must possess to define educational projects for both the clientele and caregivers.

Prevention
This area refers to the competencies the student must possess to define occupational projects aimed at primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.

Management
This area includes all essential management tools for the correct daily implementation of the Occupational Therapist's actions through the following actions:
- identify the nature of the problem
- analyze
- choose and interpret
- identify the problem resolution, possibly through collaboration.

Training/Self-Training
This area encompasses the context in which the Occupational Therapist develops and consolidates their knowledge and competencies:
- identify learning and training objectives with the coordinator and tutor
- evaluate the achievement of objectives
- assume responsibility for their own training and professional development
- self-evaluate the achievement of objectives
- reflect and self-evaluate in implementing their knowledge and skills.

Communication and Relationship
This area defines the relational substrate through which the Occupational Therapy graduate will apply their professional practice within the overall context through:
- professional communication and relationship skills with the clientele
- knowledge and management of relational dynamics with other professionals, coordinators, and tutors
- acquisition of the ability to interact with colleagues in a multidisciplinary team and with operators from other structures
- negotiate objectives with other professionals
- recognize the need for support.

Training Path
The training path constitutes the necessary cultural, scientific, and relational background to acquire full professional competence and to understand, address, and manage pathological events requiring rehabilitation and/or therapeutic intervention. These competencies will be acquired through participation in the entire training path. In particular, through preparatory disciplines, the student will achieve a solid foundation of knowledge of bodily functions and structures. The professional construct will be guaranteed by the characteristic disciplines of Occupational Therapy. Practical courses will ensure the translation of Occupational Science into clinical practice, experienced through the professional internships related to the aforementioned areas. Training in research methodology will enable the acquisition of competencies for professional updating and participation in research activities in various application areas.

The teaching methods provided include lectures, seminars, working groups, and discussions on relevant topics and simulations aimed at achieving the training path objectives. Traditional teaching activities are complemented by guided internship activities at specialized healthcare services and other scientifically significant structures, located in Italy or abroad and linked by specific agreements. This training allows for a progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy, within which students acquire the ability to observe, assess, and intervene in various rehabilitation-related issues across all life stages, with particular attention to ensuring the person's autonomy and supporting integration and participation, while working in a team and cooperating with the various figures involved in the rehabilitation project.

Laboratory and internship activities are carried out under the supervision and guidance of professional tutors specifically designated based on communication skills, specifically trained for this role, and assigned for each class.

The learning assessment is evaluated through exam tests, which, beyond traditional oral or written exams, include a sequence of in-process tests (self-assessment tests and intermediate interviews) to verify acquired knowledge and competencies.

The training path is structured, monitored, validated, and optimized in a continuous manner to acquire the competencies, knowledge, and skills specified in the curriculum profile established by current regulations and the specific objectives of the Course. These specific training objectives are supported by a faculty aware of the need to use all institutional tools activated by competent bodies for the accreditation of teaching quality. Through these tools, it is possible to measure the improvement of teaching performance in all different phases contributing to the achievement of the first-level degree, in terms of training path, exams, perceived quality evaluation by students, and acquisition of professional competencies specified in the specific training objectives.

Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Practicum Agreements
The structuring of the professional internship, even for the previous academic year, remains a complex issue due to the number of Occupational Therapists available to facilitate student rotation across various sites. However, the situation compared to previous academic years has significantly improved, as many professionals have been hired and immediately available to serve as tutors. We anticipate further improvement in the future, as recent competitive procedures have been conducted in one of the four ASLs in the region.

Internship activities are safeguarded and improved thanks to the consolidated structure of the Internship Service. The presence of the Course of Study Internship Office, supporting tutors in the structures, greatly enhances the training experiences. A tutor supports the Teaching Director each year to personalize solutions for the needs of different career paths. In synergy with AITO Abruzzo, suppliers of materials related to the profession (wheelchairs and aids), and other sector associations, training events and practical workshops are regularly organized at the Course of Study. New agreements have been established with high-quality structures in the Abruzzo region, expanding the internship experiential offer, and existing agreements with national excellence structures have been renewed, allowing students to complete internship periods when not engaged in teaching activities or in preparation for specific thesis projects.

All internship activities carried out at specialized healthcare services and other scientifically significant structures meet the specific educational objectives for the professional figure. This training allows for a progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy, within which students acquire the ability to observe, assess, and intervene in various rehabilitation-related issues in pediatric and adult age, to develop the rehabilitation project and individualized rehabilitation program in a team. Students learn to integrate into a work group, cooperating with the various figures involved in the rehabilitation project. Laboratory and internship activities are carried out under the supervision and guidance of professional tutors specifically designated by each structure in agreement with the university. Tutors work closely with the Course of Study Internship Office representatives.

During the 2022/2023 academic year, with the improvement of the COVID-19 pandemic situation, students from all three cohorts were able to complete their internships regularly.

Regular comparison with hosting structures, which numbered 24 in the previous academic year, is maintained.

We have structured a questionnaire regarding the structure's experience, which was sent to structure managers and tutors, and the results are available at the following link: https://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-studio/terapia-occupazionale-l644/tesi

The questionnaire includes closed-answer questions and space for observations. The structure's experience with the internship program was rated positively, with particular attention to the interaction with the facility, the team, and the professional knowledge provided. The support for the internship activity was rated highly, with over 93% of students reporting satisfaction with the support provided.

The analysis of the questionnaire results shows that the main areas for improvement are the scheduling of classes and exams and the secretariat service. The areas of greatest concern, which have nonetheless seen a significant improvement even from the latest cohort, relate to the course organization in terms of class and exam schedules and the secretariat service.

The overall judgment on internship experiences and the course of study itself confirm the adequacy of the work carried out by the Course of Study in improving the quality of the educational offer in recent years. The internship experience received a graduate evaluation of 3.58 (vs 3.48 university average in the Health Area), while the overall course of study evaluation was 3.42 (vs 3.31 university average in the Health Area).

The analysis of results from the AlmaLaurea survey on the graduate profile and the survey on the perceived effectiveness of the educational process by students further confirms that the Course of Study continues to improve its educational offer over the last three cohorts, with a course organization more aligned with student needs. The training received is extremely well-suited for applying acquired competencies in the workplace: over 93% of students are highly satisfied, and the number of students who consider the professional training and degree obtained highly effective for their current work has increased (60%).

The AlmaLaurea data regarding the graduate profile (referring to all satisfaction evaluations for the completed course of study, for the latest cohort considered, i.e., students graduating during the calendar year 2022) reveals that the main reasons for choosing the Course of Study are cultural and professional factors. Almost 80% of enrolled students graduate on time with an average graduation grade of 104.6, and over 83% of graduates are employed and not enrolled in a second-level degree.

Over 90% of students (more than 20% above the university average) regularly attend more than 75% of the required courses.

Some concerns remain regarding the perceived adequacy of computer workstations and teaching equipment (laboratories, practical experiences).

Over 85% of graduates would re-enroll in the same course of study at the university.

Graduates' opinions, as well as those of students, were widely discussed in the Course of Study Council meeting on September 20, 2022, for the latest cohort considered last year, using suggestions and criticisms raised during evaluation to improve the Course of Study organization and educational offer. The results of the annual discussion are evident in the continuous growth in the Course of Study's evaluation. Each year, the Course of Study dedicates an item to the agenda in the Course of Study Council meeting in September/October for the discussion and approval of the SUA-Course of Study tables related to graduates' opinions.

The Course of Study has at its disposal teaching and structural resources commensurate with the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The course covers an area of certain professional relevance. The proposed structure appears significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness and contributes to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the university's educational offer.

Admission procedures Candidates may be admitted to the Medical Radiology, Imaging and Radiotherapy Techniques Degree Course if they hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent.
The required prerequisites for students wishing to enroll in the course should include good interpersonal skills, good teamwork abilities, and problem analysis and resolution skills.
Access to the Degree Course is quota-controlled in accordance with Law 264/99 and requires an admission exam consisting of a multiple-choice test.
Adequate preparation in physics and mathematics is required for admission to the Medical Radiology, Imaging and Radiotherapy Techniques Degree Course.
Students admitted to the Degree Course who score below 25% of the maximum score in Mathematics, Physics, Biology and Chemistry will be assigned Additional Educational Requirements (OFA).
For students admitted with OFA, who have been duly informed of the identified deficiencies, attendance at the additional training activities specifically provided is mandatory, with the aim of enabling recovery within the first year of the course.
OFA will be considered fulfilled upon passing the exams related to the disciplinary areas subject to OFA.
Students who fail to fulfill the Additional Educational Requirements, as per Article 28 of the University Regulations, by the date set by the University Bodies and within the first year of the course, may enroll in the second year but will not be permitted to take second-year exams until the individually assigned OFA have been fulfilled.

Programme, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate in Medical Radiology, Imaging and Radiotherapy Techniques:
- communicates effectively and understandably, ideas, information, problems and solutions to the public and specialist interlocutors, justifying their actions and decisions;
- demonstrates listening and understanding skills with users, colleagues, doctors and other professionals;
- communicates with users while fully respecting cultural or ethnic differences;
- adapts language, using English when necessary, and verifies the understanding of the information provided;
- uses various information and computer technologies specific to their professional field.
Teaching tools, methodologies and training activities to develop expected outcomes:
- Videos and critical analysis of films, simulations, narratives and testimonies;
- Discussion of cases and paradigmatic relational situations in small groups with presentations in plenary sessions;
- Group and individual computer lab exercises on specific applications;
- Internship with supervised experiences by tutors in various contexts with debriefing sessions to reflect and reprocess relational experiences with users and the team.
Assessment tools to verify achievement of expected outcomes
- Observation of film or written frames, dialogues with structured grids;
- Evaluation feedback during internship (through portfolio, structured evaluation sheets and clinical reports);

Autonomy of Judgment
The graduate in Medical Radiology Techniques, Imaging and Radiation Therapy has the ability to:
- collect and interpret data and situations characterizing their professional activity in order to develop an autonomy of thought and judgment that includes reflection on relevant practices and issues, social, scientific or ethical;
- use critical thinking skills to provide effective technical-diagnostic and therapeutic services;
- assume responsibility for their actions in relation to the goals and priorities of the work activity;
- identify criticalities in the organizational context or in diagnostic/therapeutic techniques, proposing solutions with the application of the best evidence, fully respecting the ethical and professional norms.
Teaching tools, methodologies and training activities to develop the expected outcomes:
- Discussion of cases in subgroups with presentations in plenary sessions;
- Internship with supervised experiences by tutors in different contexts and with a progressive assumption of autonomy and responsibility;
- Debriefing sessions to reflect and re-elaborate professional practice experiences.
Assessment tools to verify the achievement of the expected outcomes:
- Written and oral exams, step-by-step case tests;
- Evaluation feedback during the internship (through structured evaluation forms and clinical reports on professional practice);
- Structured objective station exam.

Analyzing student satisfaction for questions D0, D1, D9, D14, and D20, the average scores are always above 3, albeit slightly below the university and health area averages.
For question D3 (is the required study load proportional to the assigned credits?), the average score for the Course of Study was slightly higher than the health area average (3.29 vs 3.28, respectively).
The same result is observed for question D13 (was the teaching delivered consistently with what was declared on the Course of Study website?) with a score of 3.47 vs 3.44 for the health area.
A higher score than the university and health area averages was found for question D16 (were the exam modalities clearly defined?). In particular, the Course of Study score was 3.51 vs 3.42 for the university and 3.46 for the health area.
For question D21 (does the instructor present topics appropriately according to the complexity of the subject?), the average score for the Course of Study was slightly higher than the health area average (3.41 vs 3.40, respectively).
Finally, a score equal to the university average and higher than the health area average was found for question D22 (is the instructor available during lectures and/or office hours to provide clarifications on the topics covered?). In particular, the Course of Study score was 3.57 vs 3.57 for the university and 3.50 for the health area.
During the Course of Study meetings on February 8, 2023, and May 16, 2023, the most critical points raised by students were addressed. In particular, following the report of the Joint Faculty-Student Commission (CPDS), presented at the Course of Study meeting on February 8, 2023. Student questionnaires revealed several critical issues, such as the possibility of evaluating overseas experience, continued presence after graduation, study load, and secretariat services.
Another point raised by students at the university level concerns the possibility of removing certain horizontal barriers for exams, not related to prerequisite criteria but to the acquisition of training credits during the academic year. In this regard, a commission has been established, in line with the university's suggestion, to analyze individual cases and adjust training credits to remove specific barriers.
Proposals: as suggested by the CPDS, a sensitization action is proposed towards faculty to improve less appreciated areas through the remodulation of study programs and learning methods. For first-year faculty, it is proposed to consider students' basic knowledge and focus more on fundamental concepts of basic scientific courses.
Additionally, further proposals from the CPDS for improving the delivery and scheduling of exam sessions, teaching activities (CI, ADO modules, etc.), in general and specifically for gaps in subjects such as radiographic anatomy, were reported and discussed at the February 8, 2023 Course of Study meeting.

Learning Skills
The graduate in Medical Radiology Techniques, Imaging, and Radiotherapy has developed abilities, strategies, learning methods, and practical skills necessary to continue pursuing further studies with a high degree of autonomy.
In particular:
- demonstrates the ability to self-assess their competencies and outline their development and update needs;
- demonstrates the ability for independent study;
- demonstrates autonomy in seeking necessary information to resolve problems or uncertainties in professional practice by critically selecting literature;
- promotes their knowledge in academic and professional contexts.
Teaching tools, methodologies, and training activities to develop expected outcomes:
- Problem-Based Learning (PBL);
- Use of contracts and self-learning plans to empower students in planning their internship path and self-assessment;
- Laboratories on bibliographic research methodology, both paper and online;
- Guided reading for critical evaluation of scientific and professional literature in both Italian and English.
Assessment tools to verify the achievement of expected outcomes
- Project work, report on specific research mandates;
- Tutorial supervision on the internship path;
- Active participation in work sessions and debriefings;
- Punctuality and quality in the presentation of reports.

Brief Course Description. The Bachelor's Degree Course in Medical Radiology Techniques, Imaging, and Radiotherapy aims to train healthcare operators (in accordance with Article 3, paragraph 1 of Law 10 August 2000, No. 251) responsible for their own actions and authorized to perform radiological investigations and procedures, respecting European Union radiation protection standards. Graduates are authorized to perform (in accordance with Law 31 January 1983, No. 25) independently or in collaboration with other healthcare figures, based on medical prescription, all interventions requiring the use of ionizing radiation sources, artificial and natural, thermal, ultrasonic, and nuclear magnetic resonance, as well as physical or dosimetric protection interventions, to fulfill the competencies specified in their professional profile (Ministry of Health Decree 26 September 1994, No. 746 and subsequent amendments). Additionally, graduates are responsible for controlling the correct operation of assigned equipment, resolving minor issues, and implementing verification and control programs to ensure quality according to predefined indicators and standards; they perform their activities in public or private healthcare facilities, either under employment or as independent professionals; contribute to the training of support staff and directly participate in updating their professional profile and research.
Graduates in Medical Radiology Techniques, Imaging, and Radiotherapy must have acquired knowledge, skills, and attitudes to practice the profession of Medical Radiology Healthcare Technician.
To achieve this goal, the graduate in Medical Radiology Techniques, Imaging, and Radiotherapy must demonstrate the ability to:
- manage technical-diagnostic procedures for acquisition and processing of imaging according to scientific evidence and guidelines, including functional imaging procedures in Nuclear Medicine;
- evaluate the quality of the produced iconographic document and whether it meets the specifications in the investigation proposal;
- manage technical diagnostic procedures for transmission and storage of imaging;
- deliver radiotherapy treatments;
- use methodologies and tools for quality control, evaluation, and review;
- implement radiation protection and safety regulations and use individual protection devices;
- establish professional communication with users and colleagues;
- ensure comfort, safety, and privacy of users during diagnostic investigations and radiotherapy treatments;
- act responsibly towards users and the Service by adopting professional behaviors in line with ethical and deontological principles;
- receive and manage patient preparation for diagnostic investigations or radiotherapy treatments, obtaining informed consent where applicable;
- collaborate with doctors, colleagues, and all staff to ensure optimal Service operation and contribute to solving organizational problems;
- use information systems for data collection, analysis, and information management;
- seek the best scientific evidence to explore areas of uncertainty or improvement in their professional practice;
- know English for exchanging instructions and information within their specific field of competence;
- acquire skills in Health Physics for supporting the Physics Director in quality control of radiological, radiotherapy, and nuclear medicine equipment, as well as supporting the Physics Director in developing radiotherapy treatment plans.
Therefore, the prerequisites required for students enrolling in the course should include good interpersonal skills, good teamwork ability, and the ability to analyze and solve problems.
To be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree Course in Medical Radiology Techniques, Imaging, and Radiotherapy, a sufficient preparation in physics and mathematics is required.
External Effectiveness: From Alma Laurea data, out of 11 graduates, 6 were interviewed, with a collective examined of 4. 'Data is not provided for groups smaller than 5 units.'

TRAINING PATH. The development of the training path aims to involve three aspects of the Medical Radiology Healthcare Technician professional considered essential:
- motivation and aptitude;
- professional skills;
- scientific culture.
1st Year. Focused on providing a good understanding of essential theoretical disciplines derived from basic sciences, with a view to their subsequent professional application. Students will also learn the foundations of disciplines characterizing the Medical Radiology Healthcare Technician profession and concepts of radiation protection and safety as prerequisites for the first internship experience, aimed at orienting students to relevant professional fields and acquiring basic competencies.
2nd Year. Focused on deepening specific sectors, procedures, and techniques of Imaging Diagnostics, such as the Senology field, Computed Tomography, and Magnetic Resonance, as well as Oncology and Radiotherapy.
Additionally, relational and communication skills will be acquired.
Multiple internship experiences are planned in contexts where students can apply the acquired knowledge, methodologies, and techniques.
3rd Year. Specialized deepening with particular reference to Interventional Radiology, Neuroradiology, Nuclear Medicine, and Radiotherapy.
The second semester focuses on acquiring knowledge and methodologies related to professional practice, healthcare legislation, and Service organization, as well as legal, bioethical, and deontological principles inspiring the profession.
The importance assigned to internship experiences increases, where students can gradually assume autonomy and responsibility under expert supervision. This curricular logic is also reflected in the selection of credits assigned to internship experiences, which gradually increase from the 1st to the 3rd year.

Final Exam Characteristics. In accordance with Article 7 of the Interministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, the final exam consists of:
a) a practical test during which the student must demonstrate having acquired the theoretical-practical and technical-professional knowledge and skills specific to the specific professional profile;
b) preparation of a thesis and its defense.
The final exam is organized, by decree of the Minister of Education, University, and Research in concert with the Minister of Health, in two sessions defined at the national level.
Final Exam Execution. The student has access to 6 CFU (Training Activity 'Final Exam') for preparing the Thesis at facilities designated for training. This student activity is defined as 'Graduation Internship'. The student intending to complete the Graduation Internship must, after contacting the Supervisor Professor, submit a formal request to the Course of Study Council President within 12 months for the experimental thesis and 6 months for the compilation thesis from the period in which they intend to obtain the final degree, accompanied by their curriculum (list of exams taken and ADO followed with respective grades, list of laboratories where the mandatory internship was performed, any other activity completed for training purposes) and indicating the Supervisor Professor, the discipline within the Integrated Course for developing the thesis, and the period they intend to take the final exam. The Course of Study Council President, after consulting the relevant professors and confirming their availability, assigns the student to the Supervisor, who will be responsible for controlling and certifying the activities performed by the student in preparing the thesis. It is the student's responsibility to fulfill the obligations imposed by the University's General Student Secretariat for the graduation exam.
The student, upon completing their training path, accesses the final exam prepared by the Course of Study Council in accordance with Ministerial Decree/MURST No. 136 of June 5, 2001, Article 6.
The graduation exam, consisting of practical skill demonstration (Practical Test – Simulation of radiological investigations) and preparation of a report (Thesis), is organized in two sessions, typically in March and October. The graduation exam commission is composed of at least 7 and no more than 11 members, appointed by the Rector on the proposal of the Course of Study Council.
To be admitted to take the graduation exam, the student must:
a. have attended all Integrated Courses and passed the respective exams;
b. have obtained, in total, 180 CFU distributed over the three years of the Course of Study;
c. have passed (minimum grade 18/30) the mandatory professionalizing training internship, evaluated with an exam and certified annually through a written report;
d. have submitted to the Student Secretariat the request to the Rector 90 days before the graduation exam, and a copy of the thesis at least 30 days before the graduation exam.
e. have passed (minimum grade 18/30), the Practical Test scheduled in the same session as the thesis defense.
The graduation exam grade, expressed in centesimal, is determined by the sum of the following parameters:
a. the average in thirtieths (then converted to centesimal) obtained by summing the thirtieths grades achieved in Integrated Course exams and the evaluation of the mandatory professionalizing training internship;
b. points assigned by the Commission to the Practical Test (18/30 to 21/30 = 1 point; 22/30 to 24/30 = 2 points; 25/30 to 27/30 = 3 points; 28/30 to 29/30 = 4 points; 30/30 to 30/30 with honors = 5);
c. The Commission has a maximum of 3 points for the compilation thesis and 4 points for the experimental thesis in evaluating the method, presentation, and discussion. Honors (Lode) can be awarded with the Commission's unanimous opinion to candidates who achieve a final score of 112 or higher. The Academic Mention, in addition to Honors, can only be awarded with the Commission's unanimous consent and exclusively to candidates who graduate on time with a base score of at least 106/110 and have completed an experimental thesis of particular scientific relevance.
Bonus Scores: A maximum of 4 points total, with the following criteria: 1 point for study duration (1 point for students in course); 1 point for number of honors (0.2 points per honor in profit exams, up to 1 point); 1 point for participation in the Erasmus project with at least 3 months' stay; 1 point for completing the thesis in English.

The course covers a clearly relevant professional area. The proposed curriculum appears significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, contributing to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the university's educational offer.

Access Requirements Required knowledge for access Candidates who hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as suitable may be admitted to the Biomedical Laboratory Techniques Study Program.
The prerequisites required for students enrolling in the course should include good interpersonal skills, teamwork abilities, and the capacity to analyze and solve problems.
An adequate preparation in biology and chemistry is required to be admitted to the Biomedical Laboratory Techniques Study Program. Students admitted to the course with a level below the predefined minimum grade will be required to attend preparatory teaching activities during the first semester of the first year, which must be compulsorily followed by students in debt. The assessment of results achieved in the preparatory teaching activities will be conducted within the evaluation of the corresponding courses.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L605] BIOMEDICAL LABORATORY TECHNIQUES
SECTION: Admission Procedures
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/612

Admission Procedures Candidates with a Five-Year Upper Secondary School Diploma or an equivalent foreign qualification may be admitted to the Course of Study in Biomedical Laboratory Techniques. Admission to the first year is regulated and requires passing a multiple-choice admission test on topics specified by the Ministry. The test is held only if the number of applications exceeds available places. Admission to subsequent years for students from the same Course of Study at other universities is subject to available places within the previously approved regulated number by the Course of Study Council. Admitted students must demonstrate competence in Biology, Chemistry, and Physics. Any additional educational obligations (OFA) will be assigned based on the admission test results. In particular, candidates who score below 25% of the maximum score in Biology, Chemistry, and Physics on the entrance test will be enrolled with OFA. Students enrolled in the Course of Study in Biomedical Laboratory Techniques with OFA will be informed via email or direct meetings. Fulfilling OFA involves individual seminar-style training activities assigned for each discipline in which the student has a deficiency. OFA must be completed by the end of the first semester of the first year, and completion will be certified by the relevant discipline instructors through an oral verification test. Fulfilling OFA is required to take second-year exams. While enrollment in the second year is permitted, it will not be possible to take second-year exams before fulfilling the assigned OFA.

Program, texts and objectives Note regarding the selected sectors and credits for characteristic activities The VET/06 sector has been included among the characteristic disciplines Communication skills
The graduate in Biomedical Laboratory Techniques must be able to:
- demonstrate communication and listening skills towards users and various healthcare professionals with whom they interact in the workplace or occasionally come into contact, using both written and verbal communication forms. In particular, they must demonstrate the ability to complete dedicated forms, communicating clearly, concisely, and professionally in both verbal and written form, technically and grammatically accurate, in order to convey ideas, pose problems and find appropriate solutions.
- establish effective and collaborative relationships with other healthcare professionals, being aware of the specificities of different professional roles;
- demonstrate the ability to use information and computer technologies in their work environment.
Teaching tools: frontal lectures in the classroom, internship, reading and interpretation of international literature.
Assessment methods: oral reports on communication aspects; periodic meetings with tutors and the coordinator; oral and written presentation of projects.

SECTION: Critical Judgment (making judgements)
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/612

Critical Judgment (making judgements)
The biomedical laboratory techniques graduate must:
- demonstrate responsibility for their area of competence, performing technical-professional tasks autonomously in direct collaboration with other laboratory-qualified personnel responsible for various operational duties;
- exercise critical thinking to deliver effective technical diagnostic services;
- be responsible, in laboratory settings, for the correct execution of analytical procedures and their own work within specific functions, in accordance with protocols defined by responsible managers, and verify that delivered services meet predefined indicators and standards set by the facility manager;
- demonstrate the ability to consider other operators in the exercise of their actions;
- participate in the planning and organization of work within the facility where they operate.
- apply ethical principles in their professional conduct.
Teaching Methods: lectures, teaching laboratories, practical laboratory and/or equipped room lessons, internship, reading and interpretation of international literature.
Assessment Methods: written and oral reports on technical/professional aspects, discussion of clinically relevant practical cases.
