UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [0659] LANGUAGE MEDIATION AND INTERCULTURAL COMMUNICATION
SECTION: Opinions of graduates
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/563

Opinions of graduates The University of Chieti-Pescara documents on the Quality Assurance Unit website the teaching development as well as the opinions of graduates made available, for each academic year, through the University databases based on the AlmaLaurea surveys.
The information regarding the 2022 graduates of the L-12 Study Course in Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication, based on the AlmaLaurea survey, is accessible from the University Quality Assurance Unit website through the external link below. The data in the attachment also includes the opinions of graduates from equivalent courses and are compared with the University total for the same course type.
For the purpose of monitoring the Study Course development and potential improvement interventions, the data regarding satisfaction with the completed Study Course are first considered, compared with the University data for 2022, AlmaLaurea data updated to April 2023.
Analysis of the pdf satisfaction for the completed course - AlmaLaurea Data (updated to April 2023):
In 2022, 149 students obtained the degree in Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication (compared to 183 in 2021), of whom 143 were interviewed. The percentage of students who regularly attended more than 75% of the required courses decreased to 65.7%, compared to 71.7% in 2021 and 80.3% in 2020; this is a slightly lower value than the University average of 67.5%.
In evaluating the adequacy of the course workload relative to the course duration, both items (definitely yes and mostly yes) show good stability, with a total of 81.9%, slightly below the University trend (88.7%). The data regarding students who would enroll again in the same Study Course at the same University decreased slightly from 47.5% in 2021 to 43.4% in 2022.
The evaluation of the exam organization of the Study Course is considered adequate by 21.7% of the interviewed students; this is a significant increase compared to the previous four years: 16.7% in 2021, 13.4% in 2020, and 7.8% in 2019. However, these values are lower than the University average (30.6%).
There is an improvement in the evaluation of classrooms, which are considered always, almost always, or often adequate by 64% of the interviewed students, compared to 50% in 2021. The same improvement applies to the evaluation of computer workstations, which decreased from 72% of inadequate responses in 2021 to 54.5% in 2022. However, these values are still slightly below the University average (43.7%).
Equipment for other teaching activities is considered always, almost always, or often adequate by 56.3% of the interviewed students in 2022, an increase from 48.1% in 2021. However, these data are significantly lower than the University average (73.2%). The library services evaluation remains good (the evaluation of definitely and quite positive reaches 87.9%). Considering approximately 200 students enrolled in the L-12 Study Course, the low satisfaction percentages regarding infrastructure and equipment use should be carefully analyzed by the University to implement synergistic improvement interventions.
Regarding satisfaction expressed by the interviewed students on relationships with professors in general, summing the first two items (definitely yes and mostly yes) yields a satisfaction rate of 85.3%, slightly below the University data (90.3%). The same items for overall Study Course satisfaction, summed together, reach 81.1%, also slightly below the University trend (89.8%).
Useful is also the analysis of some data reported in the graduates' profile, as per the attached pdf.
Regarding the graduates' profile, the following points emerge:
- The average age at graduation in 2022 is 24.4, in line with the previous year;
- The number of foreign citizens increased (4% in 2022 compared to 3.3% in 2021);
- It is significant that, in the selected group, regarding the social origin, 81.8% of graduates have no parent with a degree; 14% have at least one parent with a degree;
- Data on student origin show a decrease in graduates from other regions, dropping from 36.3% in 2021 to 32.2% in 2022; 40.9% of students come from another province in the same region, while 26.8% reside in the same province as the study location. Therefore, revitalization of communication and promotion through orientation activities is necessary.
- Regarding secondary education, there is a prevalence of students from high schools (linguistic, scientific, classical, human sciences, and artistic-musical-coreutic), totaling 69.1%; this figure is lower than the previous year (73.1%). The percentage of students from technical and professional institutes increases (29.6% in 2022 compared to 24.7% in 2021). It is significant that the L-12 Study Course attracts students from diverse backgrounds. Only 1.3% hold a foreign degree.
Regarding academic success, the average exam score is 25.5 out of 30, and the graduation grade is 97.6 out of 110. Both values are in line with previous years. However, the percentage of students still enrolled decreased significantly to 36.2%, compared to 47.8% last year. Regarding study conditions, 37.1% of graduates used the scholarship service, and only 17.5% completed recognized study periods abroad. These data are influenced by the pandemic conditions that slowed student careers and made international mobility with Erasmus or Conventions more complex.
The pandemic also reduced the percentage of students who completed curricular or recognized work placements; this figure stands at 34.3%, an increase from 28% in 2021. In substitution of placements, the Study Course has activated professional seminars to allow students to acquire the necessary CFU. Despite the pandemic, the Study Course has implemented agreements with entities, institutions, and companies to promote placement and internship activities. These are training opportunities that will be further encouraged to better prepare graduates for the job market.
Ability to apply knowledge and understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
Graduates of the Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication Study Course have developed the ability to professionally apply acquired knowledge and address issues, identifying appropriate solutions, in relation to their field of study and in diverse work contexts, with particular emphasis on environments requiring communication skills. They are able to interact with texts, people, and institutions of other cultures and civilizations in various daily and professional contexts, including migration, and have acquired interdisciplinary knowledge integration skills. They can collect, classify, and synthesize data and information typical of their field, as well as transmit them orally and in writing, in the study languages, also using new technologies. They are also able to read, listen, interpret, and translate texts of various types, including specialized texts, in Italian and the foreign study languages, using linguistic, translation, and communication methods and tools. They can use multimedia and telematic tools in specific areas and competencies, i.e., for research and processing of information materials. They can also apply the acquired interdisciplinary knowledge, particularly economic-legal, to written and oral mediation.
These abilities are developed, in addition to theoretical- descriptive lectures and seminar activities, through debate and exercise tools, with the support of laboratories and multimedia tools, through exchange with native speakers of the study languages carried out both in collaboration with CEL/Readers from the University Language Center and through international agreements (Erasmus, University agreements, etc.), as well as through internship and placement experiences.
The acquisition of these abilities is assessed through oral and/or written checks, during and at the end of each course, evaluating disciplinary knowledge, understanding abilities, argumentation, and correct exposition of content. Regarding the study languages, lexical and morphosyntactic knowledge, comprehension and production abilities of oral and written texts, as well as the ability to perform linguistic and intercultural mediation, are evaluated. The final exam assesses the ability to analyze and synthesize materials related to the chosen topic.
Learning skills (learning skills)
Graduates of the Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication Study Course must demonstrate they have acquired adequate learning abilities and methodologies to address subsequent in-depth study and expansion, as well as the progressive updating required by the job market. In particular, they must demonstrate: acquisition of a study method, ability to work towards goals, and ability for autonomous and group work; acquisition and development of linguistic abilities and mediation strategies adequate for performing the professional activities provided by the Course and for continuing studies. These abilities are developed through lectures and seminars, debates and classroom exercises, and in-course tutoring activities. The acquisition of these abilities is assessed through oral and/or written checks, during and at the end of each course, as well as through the preparation of the final exam.
Knowledge and understanding (knowledge and understanding)
To obtain the degree, students must demonstrate they have acquired and consolidated linguistic-communicative competencies in two foreign languages, adequate cultural and interdisciplinary knowledge, and understanding abilities regarding the issues and epistemological horizon of at least two foreign languages besides Italian. Knowledge and understanding extend to linguistic and intercultural mediation in various contexts, based on metalinguistic reasoning. In particular, graduates are able to understand conversations and texts, even specialized, in a foreign language, interpreting them from an adequate cultural and interdisciplinary perspective; they know the historical-cultural contexts of the studied foreign languages, especially regarding traditions and customs, and can compare them with their own reality; they know the methodologies and strategies of linguistic mediation necessary for work environments; they possess economic-legal knowledge useful for the professional context and information technology skills that increasingly accompany language study and its use in the job market; they develop transversal competencies of a communicative-relational, organizational-management, and programming nature.
Acquisition of such knowledge and understanding abilities primarily occurs through the didactic tool of theoretical-descriptive lectures and seminar activities, coordinated with classroom exercises, and integrated with the use of language laboratories and other multimedia tools.
Verification of acquired knowledge and understanding abilities is carried out, in addition to standard end-of-course checks, through ongoing checks of achieved learning levels. Verification forms evaluate knowledge, ability to organize thoughts, argumentative abilities, correctness of oral and/or written exposition, and communication strategies used. Acquired knowledge and understanding are also applied in the preparation of the final exam paper.
Organization and responsibility of AQ at Study Course level The bodies and organizations involved in the Study Course Quality Assurance (AQ) process are as follows:
- The Study Course Chair, Professor Lorella Martinelli, who performs the following duties: coordination of the Study Course AQ system, maintaining direct relations with the University Quality Assurance Unit, the Evaluation Committee, and the Parity Committee of Teachers-Students of the School of Human Studies, monitoring compliance with obligations set by specific regulations.
- Parity Committee that monitors the teaching offer, teaching quality, and services provided to students by teachers and structures. The Parity Committee of Teachers-Students of the School of Human Studies is chaired by Professor Sara Bani and represented by four teachers from the Department of Languages, Literatures, and Modern Cultures: Professors Sara Bani, Mariapia D'Angelo, Barbara Delli Castelli, Donata Di Leo. For the L-12 Study Course in Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication, the teacher representative is Professor Donata Di Leo; the student component is represented by Jessica Mirabilio.
- Departmental AQ Representative (ReAQD) and Departmental Delegate for Research, Professor Paola Partenza
- AQ Group composed of Professor Lorella Martinelli (Responsible) and the Study Course teachers: Professors Anita Trivelli (PO), Emanuela Ettorre (PA), Carmela Perta (PA), Marcella Solinas (RtdB), Paola Partenza (PA), Beatrice Fedi (RU), and Lorena Savini (T/A). The AQ Group evaluates the Study Course quality in various areas: infrastructure (classrooms, laboratories), student opinions on teaching delivery, analysis of results from various knowledge and ability assessments. The Group prepares the review report and monitors the Study Course AQ development, highlighting strengths and improvement opportunities; carrying out monitoring of indicators for continuous process control and improvement; promoting a quality culture within the Study Course; planning and controlling the efficiency of contextual services.
The AQ Group also conducts monitoring and self-assessment of the training path to identify strengths and weaknesses to be reported within the Study Course. These activities are directed at designing corrective and preventive actions for identified weaknesses and implementing improvement strategies to propose to the Study Course Council.
- Study Course Teaching Committee composed of the Chair and teachers: Paola Brusasco, Eleonora Cianci, Antonio Gurrieri, and Francesca Guazzelli. This Committee (established in the Study Course Council meeting of February 15, 2022), in synergy with the Quality Group, carefully monitors enrollments, student careers, and teaching offer to identify more suitable solutions for Study Course issues and make teaching more functional and effective.
- Study Course Council: discusses and approves the review report; collaborates with the Study Course AQ development and carries out all necessary resolutions.
Planning of work and implementation deadlines To ensure organization aimed at improving the suitability of educational objectives, the Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication Study Course has defined a general planning of main activities based on internal needs and deadlines set by current regulations. This planning provides for periodic meetings of the School Parity Committee, the AQ Management Group, the Teaching Committee, and the Study Course Council. Generally, the Parity Committee and the AQ Management Group meet in view of deadlines set by current regulations. Additionally, the Study Course Chair coordinates with the Department's teaching staff to monitor the proper conduct of Study Course activities, ensuring work is carried out as planned.
The annual or multi-year planning responds to the following scheme:
* Annually, the Study Course reviews or revises educational objectives, evaluates proposed updates, and inserts them in time in the SUA-CdS (March-April).
* Similarly, the Study Course reconsiders, annually, the validity of the training path, always respecting the time needed for inserting any updates in the SUA-CdS (January-February).
* The Study Course proposes to the Department Council the teaching coverage for the next academic year, indicating any shortages and weaknesses (January-February).
* Analysis of data from student, candidate, and graduate opinion surveys is conducted between July and September.
* The survey on training demand, through meetings with social partners, entities, and companies involved in producing goods and services, occurs once a year (February-March).
* Periodic evaluation of Study Course activities in various areas: infrastructure (classrooms and laboratories) and their improvement, student opinions on teaching activities, analysis of results from knowledge and ability assessments, occurs before each Study Course Council meeting, during meetings with other Study Course Chairs of the Department of Languages, and during AQ Group meetings held at least quarterly.
The 2024-2025 academic year teaching offer and related teaching assignments (planned 2024-2025 cohort teaching offer, delivered 2024-2025) were decided in the L-12 Study Course Council meeting held on February 20, 2024, the Department Council on February 20, 2024, and the School of Human Studies Board on February 23, 2022.

Annual review The Study Course, with the review sheet, seeks to capture the sense of self-assessment as an organized process, articulated in problem analysis and identification, as well as planning concrete activities aimed at resolving the weaknesses identified during the current teaching management. The Study Course, through the specifically created Review Group, elaborates the review sheet, which is further approved by the Study Course Council.
Brief description of related and complementary activities The L-12 Study Course allocates 18 credits to related and complementary training activities, distributed within the study plan across three academic years. Below is a brief description of the planned activities to clarify how they contribute to achieving the specific educational objectives of the course:
CRITICAL LITERATURE AND COMPARATIVE LITERATURE (L-FIL-LET/14):
The course aims to provide a synchronic and diachronic orientation on literary theories, literary criticism, and comparatistics within an interdisciplinary framework, referring to studies and research on textuality. The inclusion of this course in the L-12 Study Course is functional both to deepen theoretical-practical knowledge regarding the contextualization of studied languages and their cultures, and to build a solid theoretical foundation, essential for developing advanced communication and written and oral mediation skills.
INTERNATIONAL LAW (IUS/13):
The objective of the course is to acquire fundamental knowledge of international legal order, while also providing tools for learning the correct methodology of the subject. Knowledge of international law is essential for the professionalization of the linguistic mediator figure and responds to the occupational needs of the territory.
BUSINESS ECONOMICS (SECS-P/07):
The course aims to indicate the foundations of company study in its various aspects, presenting at the same time the basic concepts and language of economic-business disciplines. This discipline intends to provide a unified and synthetic vision of phenomena, operational processes, and company functioning, deepening analytical and quantitative determination issues of their equilibrium conditions in relation to technical, economic, and financial aspects. At the end of the training path, students will possess tools to interact, within the various professions they will undertake as linguistic mediators, with different company realities and especially with various types of stakeholders.
PHILOSOPHY OF SCIENCE (M-FIL/02):
The course represents an introduction to fundamental topics of contemporary Philosophy of Science; basic notions of logic, reasoning, problem solving are provided, and main authors and theoretical models are considered. The course aims to lead students to critically reflect on the indicated topics (objectivity, truth, analyticity, realism, theorization, experimentation, innovation, models), linking them to issues of contemporary science and technology, particularly in linguistic, translation, and interpretation fields.
GEOGRAPHY OF LANGUAGES (GGR/01): The purpose of the course is to deepen the connections between culture, cultural geography, and languages. The discipline thus provides an in-depth understanding of the relationship between space and language from a geographical perspective. Initially, the main themes, concepts, and key terms of cultural geography are introduced, followed by highlighting changes in various languages over time and space, acculturation and deculturation processes, and linguistic policies in some European and extra-European contexts.
INTERNATIONAL FILM MOVEMENTS AND AUTHORS (L-ART/06):
The course contributes to achieving the Study Course educational objectives by introducing students to the main concepts of audiovisual language through the exploration of significant practices of international film production. The course aims to enable students to know the general lines of International New Cinema, common elements of the examined film movements, and specificities of the proposed films, in light of the most advanced critical and theoretical reflections on cinema and audiovisuals. The acquired skills can be productively applied in students' participation in the Venice and Pesaro International Film Festivals, valuable opportunities to meet scholars, experts, directors, and actors.
GLOBAL COMMUNICATION HISTORY (M-STO/04):
The course activities and educational objectives aim to provide students with basic knowledge of contemporary world history, with particular attention to forms, modes, and languages of communication processes in the globalized dimension of the last two centuries, believing such knowledge is necessary to achieve the goals of the Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication course.
MODERN EUROPEAN HISTORY (M-STO/02): Among the educational objectives of the discipline, on one hand, is to lead the student to appropriate the keys to reading the past, and on the other, to educate them to critical exercise, placing them in a position to evaluate European historical reality in its specificity and complexity. At the end of preparation, the student will be able to understand, through acquired historical knowledge, the centrality of long-term changes and continuities in European history from the 1500s to the 1800s.
Brief course description The Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication L-12 Study Course presents as a highly specialized course in the linguistic field. Beyond linguistic training, with a special focus on translation and mediation, the student receives qualified training of a linguistic, glottodidactic, and microlinguistic nature, together with knowledge in the field of multietnic and multicultural contexts, including institutional environments. The Study Course aims to create a professional figure of a linguistic expert capable of performing an interlinguistic and intercultural mediation function. The Course provides for the acquisition of linguistic-cultural mediation knowledge and skills that can be applied in numerous areas: public and private entities, companies, and educational and training institutions, both at national and international levels.
The Department of affiliation organizes, in collaboration with public and private entities, internships to familiarize students with the various professional areas provided by the Course.
In the Study Course structure, linguistic courses, which are allocated the majority of training credits, are complemented by disciplines from different fields such as historical-cultural, literary, and economic-legal. Participation in courses, professional seminars, and other training and cultural experiences that aim to expand and deepen the disciplinary specifics of the study path is also encouraged.
The Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication degree allows access to various master's degrees, particularly the LM38 and LM37 Study Courses.
External effectiveness Based on AlmaLaurea surveys, information regarding the 2022 graduates of the L-12 Study Course in Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication is accessible from the University Quality Assurance Unit website at the following link: https://pqa.unich.it/archivio-aq/aq-della-didattica/l-12-mediazione-linguistica-e-comunicazione-interculturale For the purpose of monitoring the Study Course development and potential improvement interventions, the data regarding graduates' employment status are first considered, AlmaLaurea data updated to April 2023 for the 2022 survey year. Of the 182 graduates of 2021, 128 were interviewed one year after graduation. Additionally, a comparison of the L-12 Study Course data (2021) available on the same site under the "AlmaLaurea 2022 (Ud'A Data)" section is made with the University d'Annunzio data and national data.
Analysis of the pdf data (Ud'A Data):
The employment rate of the interviewed individuals (examined group: 44 graduates who did not enroll in another degree course) is 50%. The L-12 Study Course employment rate is lower than the University rate (69.4%) and national data (64.3%).
The monthly salary is €1,139, lower than the University average (€1,333) but in line with national data (€1,157). The percentage of employed individuals who highly utilize the skills acquired with the degree is 22.7%. This is a lower value than the University average (56.8%) and national average (29.7%).
Satisfaction with the job is 8 out of 10, in line with the University average and higher than the national average (7.4).
The number of those enrolling in a master's degree continues to increase, at 63.3%; however, this is a lower figure than the University average (68%) and national data (66%).
The same AlmaLaurea survey on graduates' employment status, updated to June 2023, also provides data on a group of 182 graduates including those who were working at the time of graduation. The survey considers second-level education and post-graduation, employment status, entry into the job market, characteristics of current work, company characteristics, salary, use and demand for the degree in current work, degree effectiveness, and satisfaction with current work, and finally job search. Of a total of 182 graduates (decreasing from the previous year's 212), 128 were interviewed, with an average age of 24.3 years and an average graduation grade of 98.7. Given the moderate percentage of second-level education in the selected group (64.1%), of which 55.6% at the same University, entry into the job market shows 36% employed.
Regarding current work characteristics, most interviewees report performing "other professions" (42.6%). 12.8% perform indefinite-term work (a significant decrease from 30.3% last year). The spread of part-time work is 51.1%, increasing from last year (45.5%). A new data point to consider is the spread of remote work at 8.5%.
Compared to the previous year, there is a slight increase in private sector employment (90.9% in 2021 and 91.5% in 2022) and a consequent decrease in the public sector (6.4% in 2022 compared to 9.1% in 2021). Greater employment is in commerce (46.8%); the education and research sector decreases to 4.3% compared to 12.1% last year. The transport, advertising, and communication sector records 8.5%.
Regarding geographical work area, the south prevails with 70.2%, followed by the north with 19.2% and the center with 4.3%. The foreign sector records 6.4%.
40% of the selected graduates who continue working after graduation report noticing an improvement in their work due to the degree itself; this is a significant increase from 15.4% the previous year. Similarly, 34% of the selected group states that the professional training acquired at university is very suitable, compared to 21.2% the previous year. It is noteworthy that the percentage of degree demand for work activities is only 4.3%, while it is not required but useful for 51.1%. The degree is not required and not useful for 19.1%. These are concerning data to monitor, highlighting a significant gap between training and the job market.
A final data point regarding employment status indicates that 45.3% of the unemployed are engaged in continuing studies.

Specific educational objectives and description of the training path The L-12 Study Course aims to provide adequate knowledge of methods, skills, and cultural and scientific content related to foreign languages, linguistic-cultural mediation, translation, and interpretation. In particular, the Course intends to respond to a dual educational purpose, linguistic and cultural, as the mediator's role, beyond communication and technical-linguistic skills, requires specific intercultural training to facilitate fruitful comparison with the reality of foreign countries, even in migration contexts. This training is also accompanied by knowledge of issues related to the work areas for which the Course aims to form professional figures. More specifically, graduates in Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication must have acquired:
- Solid linguistic skills, oral and written, in two foreign languages, one of which European, as well as in Italian;
- Secure skills in the field of translation and interpretation;
- Specific theoretical knowledge on language structures and usage variations in both synchronic and diachronic dimensions;
- Specific knowledge on Italian as a second language, used in all social and institutional contexts of linguistic-cultural mediation;
- Solid knowledge of the cultural heritage of the study languages, including literary heritage, also in a comparative perspective;
- Basic notions in historical, geographical, logical-communicative, audiovisual-multimedia, and economic-legal fields;
- Ability to use main information technology and telematic tools in communication and technical-linguistic activities;
- Ability to operate with organizational autonomy and integrate into work environments.
Knowledge, skills, and abilities will be acquired through participation in lectures, seminars, and classroom exercises; use of language laboratories and other multimedia tools; linguistic-communicative experiences obtained through international exchanges; training and cultural experiences to facilitate entry into the job market; internships and placements.
The training path is structured into four correlated learning areas:
1. Language Area. This area includes training activities in the two foreign languages (one of which European) chosen by the student from those indicated in the teaching regulations. Language teaching proceeds in parallel throughout the triennium and is organized to foster the formation and progressive consolidation of written and oral, multimedia linguistic-communicative skills, suitable for the context of use and specific cultural reality of the studied languages. The teaching is also aimed at developing technical skills specific to linguistic mediation, i.e., translation and interpretation from and to Italian, in line with the Study Course educational objectives.
2. Linguistic Area. This area includes training activities in linguistic-theoretical, glottodidactic, and philological fields. It aims to develop knowledge and reflection abilities on metalinguistic aspects in synchrony and diachrony, and analysis of language usage variations.
3. Literature and Culture Area. This area includes training activities aimed at developing a good awareness of the cultural and literary contexts of the study languages, in an international dimension and from an intercultural perspective.
4. Interdisciplinary Knowledge Area. This area includes training activities in historical, geographical, logical-communicative, and audiovisual-multimedia fields, forming the basis of interdisciplinary training, as well as economic-legal teachings functional to the training path and linked to the territory's occupational needs.
The path also includes student-selected activities to enrich and complete the interdisciplinary horizon, and the mandatory acquisition of information technology and telematic skills aimed at mediation activities necessary for performing more specific communication and information management activities (internet access, electronic resource consultation, preparation of multimedia texts, etc.). Professional seminars are also organized, aimed at providing useful knowledge for entering the job market (such as European community project design, use of digital tools, international cooperation activities, etc.), as well as internships and placements at companies, entities, and public and private institutions requiring linguistic and intercultural mediation skills.
Opinions of entities and companies with curricular or extracurricular internship agreements As with other Study Courses of the Department of Languages, Literatures, and Modern Cultures, the L-12 Study Course has prepared a survey of opinions from entities, companies, and institutions that have signed curricular or extracurricular internship agreements. The survey activities were conducted by the Study Course Chair, assisted by the Department's Teaching Tutor, Dr. Lorena Savini.
On March 9, 2023, the L-12 Study Course Chair held a meeting with entities and companies that had hosted students for internship or placement activities.
The numerous agreements currently in place by the Department (list available at the inserted link) include companies, entities, and institutions where L-12 Study Course students can complete internships and placements. So far, most companies, entities, and institutions that have previously hosted our interns and trainees have renewed their collaboration, expressing positive opinions on the students' commitment during their internship/placement periods. In some cases, local companies have provided, using government incentives, the hiring of some more capable, professionally qualified graduates, and more available for geographical mobility. The usefulness of the internship/placement experience has been confirmed by all hosting structures.
From the perspective of enhancing the Study Course training offer, the meeting with social partners highlighted the following significant points:
- Social partners' appreciation for this annual working table and active involvement in making university paths increasingly aligned with job market needs;
- Need to complement linguistic skills with some sector-specific knowledge (economic, legal, tourism techniques, company functioning, etc.), as well as acquisition of transversal skills;
- Opportunity to enhance techniques for using foreign language in professional contexts: from customer psychology to public communication techniques;
- Need to enhance practical aspects and spontaneous use of foreign language at all levels;
- Need to enhance information technology (Excel, PowerPoint, cloud usage, etc.) and digital skills (company websites, but also digital teaching modules).
Representatives of entities, companies, and businesses are regularly asked to complete a questionnaire indicating whether they have hosted L-12 Study Course students/graduates for internship/placement activities, and their overall evaluation. They are then asked to identify the Study Course's strengths and areas for improvement, providing suggestions and observations. Social partners are asked which foreign languages are most functional in their sector, and finally, they are asked to evaluate the correspondence between the professional figures the Study Course aims to form and the sector they represent. The questionnaire also focuses on the information technology skills provided by the Study Course, which in the past represented an area to enhance and on which the Study Course is investing. Finally, social partners are asked if, in light of changed work needs caused by the pandemic, new skills are sought in a professional figure within their sector.
The results of questionnaires completed by social partners regarding the Study Courses indicate that:
- Half of the involved parties have hosted L-12 Study Course students/graduates for curricular or extracurricular internships;
- The aforementioned parties are satisfied or very satisfied with the students'/graduates' activities;
- The aforementioned parties have hired L-12 Study Course graduates in half of the cases;
- English and German are indicated as the first and second most important languages in the sector represented by social partners;
- The L-12 Study Course educational objectives are considered fairly or fully adequate in all cases;
- The majority of involved parties consider the professional figures of Linguistic and Intercultural Mediator and Facilitator and Linguistic Expert in the field of international company and business relations that the Study Course aims to form as decidedly or fairly responsive to the needs of the represented sector;
- Among suggestions provided by Social Partners regarding training activities and skills to insert or enhance in the Study Course, information technology and digital skills, knowledge in commercial law and business economics are highlighted;
- Among new skills sought in a professional figure emerging from changed work needs caused by the pandemic, interviewees indicated digital skills, workflow and activity management in remote work, knowledge related to online teaching methodologies;
- Among the Study Course strengths, the development of social communication skills, possession of flexibility and transversality, possession of linguistic knowledge, and students' cultural preparation are indicated.

Consultation with representative organizations - at national and international level - of goods and service production, professions (Subsequent consultations)
The Study Course dialogues with the job market continuously through internships and placements, professional seminars - through which students interact with experienced professionals - and through consultations with social partners. The Study Course Chair, in agreement with the AQ Group, the Teaching Tutor, and interested teachers, periodically organizes meetings with social partners.
Over the last five years, these meetings have been very useful for modifying the L-12 Study Course teaching regulations, making the Study Course more effective educationally and more competitive for the job market. During these meetings, the enhancement of certain linguistic disciplines and teachings providing interdisciplinary knowledge was discussed; the possibility of enhancing activities aimed at conveying knowledge useful for entering the job market, such as professional seminars; and the possibility of transforming the previous four professional profiles of the Study Course into two main figures, namely Linguistic and Intercultural Mediator and Linguistic Expert in the field of international company and business relations. It also emerged the need to strengthen knowledge of the local company reality and information technology means. Finally, the importance of enhancing linguistic study through linguistic certifications issued by the CLA was emphasized.

Entry, progression, and exit data Data available on the University Quality Assurance Unit website are here examined:
Enrollment flow The number of new enrollments for the 2022-2023 academic year is 200; this is a stable figure compared to the previous academic year (198). Total enrolled students are 784, of which 464 are in course and 320 are out of course, 440 regular.
Enrolled students by geographical origin and type of high school diploma From the comparison of data regarding geographical origin, in the 2022-2023 academic year, the figure for new enrollments from other regions remains stable compared to the previous year: 56. However, it is noted that this figure is lower than the 2020-2021 academic year (75) and the 2019-2020 academic year (93). Most students come from another municipality in the province (71); additionally, 32 students come from another province in the same region, and 38 students come from the same municipality. Three students reside abroad.
Regarding the type of high school diploma, it is noted that most new enrollments come from high schools (69), followed by magistral institutes (54), and finally technical and professional institutes (52). Twenty-five new enrollments come from unspecified other training.
New enrollments by high school diploma grade Most new enrollments at the L-12 Study Course achieved a high school diploma grade up to 80 (87) and between 80 and 99 (76). The number of students with a grade of 100 and 100 cum laude is increasing: 29 compared to 27 in the previous academic year, and 25 in the 2020-2021 academic year.
Course progression It should be noted that data for the 2022-2023 academic year are partial as the academic year is not yet completed, so it is not possible to analyze and evaluate the documentation precisely. In the 2021-2022 academic year, the average number of exams passed per student was 4.33, increasing from the 2020-2021 academic year (3.50). Regarding the percentage of CFU acquired, the figure stands at 54% in 2021, also increasing from the previous academic year (43.2%). Additionally, non-renewals of enrollment decreased from 36 in the 2020-2021 academic year to 15 in the 2021-2022 academic year. Regarding explicit withdrawals within the cohort, it decreased from 48 in 2020 to 11 in 2021.
Regarding progression to the second year, analyzing the latest available cohort (2021-2022), the percentage of progression to the second year is 57.21, decreasing from the previous cohort (64.57). A nearly stable figure concerns the percentage of progression to the second year with more than 40 CFU (23.38). The percentage of CFU acquired relative to CFU to be taken is 34.55, a value decreasing from the previous cohort (37.95).
Exit data From the analysis of data regarding 2022 graduates, a total of 149 graduates are recorded, decreasing from the previous year (183). 52 students graduate in course; this is a declining figure compared to the previous year (82). 41 students graduate one year beyond the course duration, decreasing from the previous academic year (53), and 54 students graduate two or more years beyond the course duration; this figure is slightly increasing from the previous academic year (41). These are certainly data to monitor, but it is also necessary to consider that these values stem from the complex period of the pandemic.
Regarding the grade, the total number of graduates who obtained the final grade of 110 and 110 cum laude is 7; 16 students obtained a grade between 105 and 110, and 126 students fall within the grade range up to 105.

Characteristics of the final exam The final exam requires the preparation of a written paper on a topic connected with one of the courses in the Study Course, chosen by the student to verify abilities and competencies acquired during their training path.
Final exam execution The final exam requires 6 CFU and consists of preparing and discussing a written paper on a topic connected with one of the courses in the Study Course.
The student has access to the final exam after acquiring all credits provided by the teaching regulations and after demonstrating to have reached a linguistic competence level of B2+ of the CEFR in both study languages. Verification of this competence occurs simultaneously with the Language, Translation, and Mediation exam of the third year, whose content is structured for achieving the linguistic abilities corresponding to the B2+ level.
The final exam consists of preparing a written paper (minimum 20, maximum 40 pages, each of 2,000-2,500 characters) belonging to one of the following types: specialist article; brief linguistic analysis essay; translation of a short text; review article of recent publications on a specific topic or disciplinary field; reasoned bibliography on a scientific theme/question. The final paper should be recognized as an important individual training opportunity to complete the study path, without requiring particular originality.
A student who wishes to prepare the final paper in a foreign language may request authorization from the Study Course Council. In any case, a written paper in a foreign language must be accompanied by an adequate summary in Italian.
It is possible to write the thesis in a Taf D course (held at another Department) only with prior authorization from the Study Course Council, which will evaluate the congruence of the chosen course with the student's training path.
The choice of topic, consistent with the Study Course educational objectives, must be agreed upon with a teacher who teaches a discipline for which the candidate has taken at least one exam and who will serve as Supervisor. The examining committees, composed of at least five members, evaluate the candidate considering the entire study path. In assigning scores, the Committee starts from the weighted average of the scores acquired by the student in the exams, to which an additional score for the paper evaluation is added. This additional score, ranging from 0 to 5, takes into account the breadth of the paper, precision of writing and analysis, effectiveness of argumentation and/or translation. Additionally, the following additional scores are assigned:
1 additional point for students who are not out of course at the time of the graduation exam;
1 additional point for students who have participated in international mobility;
1 additional point for students who have acquired at least three honors in their study path. Acquisition of more than three honors will not yield additional points.

The Faculty has adequate, appropriate, and effective equipped spaces, and following an advanced program for the deep restructuring of the Pescara Campus, new teaching and scientific spaces will be acquired in the short term, fully commensurate with the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The Faculty can rely on a specific teaching staff for basic and characteristic disciplines, widely adequate to the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The proposed regulations, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the University's teaching offer.

The proposed regulations, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the University's teaching offer.

Department DEPARTMENT OF MODERN LANGUAGES, LITERATURES AND CULTURES Website https://www.lingue.unich.it/didattica  Admission requirements Required knowledge for admission Students with a five-year secondary school diploma or equivalent foreign qualification recognized according to current regulations are admitted to the L11 program.
Admission to the Study Program is regulated by an assessment of knowledge and skills through a verification test.
The methods for verifying such knowledge and skills will be determined in the Teaching Regulations of the Study Program. In case of negative verification results, additional mandatory requirements must be fulfilled during the first year through specific recovery activities established in the Teaching Regulations.
Admission methods All students holding a five-year secondary school diploma or equivalent recognized qualification are admitted to the Program. At enrollment, students must indicate the chosen study languages as LANGUAGE A and LANGUAGE B (one of which must be European) from those available in the Course Offer. The three-year language (both Language A and B) can only be changed at the time of enrollment for the second year.
The Ministry of Education, University and Research (Article 6 of DM 270/2004) requires all universities to verify the initial preparation of new students, to enable first-year students to assess their personal preparation against the basic knowledge required for university study, and to identify, with the help of Tutor teachers, individual paths to address any initial gaps, thus facilitating the student's successful integration into the chosen program. The ministerial provision also clarifies that any academic debts must be recovered during the first year.
For the L11 Study Program, the Verification Test for admission requirements is mandatory for first-year students. Students transferring from other universities and students enrolling in a second degree are exempt from the Test.
The Verification Test is held according to a schedule indicated on the Department of Modern Languages, Literatures and Cultures website. Two sessions are scheduled: September and February.
The Test Committee is appointed by the Department Director. The Committee consists of a minimum of three to a maximum of five permanent faculty members.
The Verification Test, lasting 60 minutes, consists of 30 multiple-choice questions designed to assess an adequate level of text comprehension, knowledge of morphosyntactic structures and vocabulary of the Italian language.
Each correct answer is awarded 1 point, while no points are given for unanswered or incorrect answers. The test is passed if the student achieves a score of at least 20/30.
For students who take and pass the Test, the Additional Mandatory Requirements are considered fulfilled. A negative test result results in the assignment of an Additional Mandatory Requirement (OFA) to be fulfilled during the first year by attending a mandatory 24-hour Italian language course offered by the Department.
At the end of the recovery procedures, the student must retake the Test to verify the required competence levels. The debt must be resolved within the first year. If the debt is not resolved, the Verification Test must be retaken in the following academic year.
As per the University Teaching Regulations, students who have not fulfilled the OFA by October 31 of the year following enrollment cannot register for second-year courses, unless they have acquired at least eighteen CFU in the first-year basic and core courses.
In addition to the Verification Test for admission requirements, a Placement Test is administered to assess the linguistic competence level in one of the following languages: French, English, Spanish or German. This second Test is used to optimize the organization of teaching activities and does not entail Additional Mandatory Requirements.

Program, texts and objectives Note regarding credits for other activities The linguistic competence level of students is verified through in-course assessments and curriculum examinations; students who have not acquired these skills are not admitted to the final examination.
Communication skills
Graduates of the L11 Program must be able to effectively argue and communicate ideas, problems and solutions in the foreign languages studied, as well as in Italian.
In particular, they must possess:
- the ability to present orally and in writing, considering textual types and literary and specialist genres, content, information and ideas related to their field of study, using appropriate communication forms depending on the interlocutors;
- the ability to interact in multilingual and multicultural contexts by selecting specific communication registers;
- the ability to process and present data using basic information technology and multimedia tools.
In addition to the specific linguistic training and support activities provided by native speaker lecturers and CEL on duty at the University Language Center, the acquisition of the above communication skills is provided through various forms within the different training activities, through direct contact with multilingual and multicultural contexts thanks to the extensive international exchange program offerings.
These skills are verified through examinations that include text comprehension, written report and document preparation, and oral presentation of the same.

SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/2

Judgment Autonomy (making judgements)
Graduates of the L11 degree program must develop autonomous judgment capabilities regarding the specific themes of their field of study. In particular, they must have acquired:
- ability to describe and interpret, based on the four linguistic skills, literary, journalistic and specialized texts;
- ability to deepen the socio-cultural relevance of the historical-geographical and cultural contexts related to the studied languages, also from the perspective of interculturality;
- ability to identify and analytically rephrase the issues related to the socio-cultural contexts investigated and to propose autonomous solutions;
- ability to address diverse work areas and themes, as well as to locate and evaluate information sources and data in the linguistic, philological-literary and artistic-historical-cultural fields.
To achieve this autonomy, in addition to frontal lessons and seminars, teaching tools include debate and exercises, support from laboratories and multimedia tools, attendance at professionalizing seminars, and experience through internships and traineeships.
The assessment of acquired judgment autonomy will be carried out through oral and/or written evaluations, during the course and at the end of each disciplinary course, as well as through the preparation of the final exam.

Ass. periodi di formazione Courses, internships or traineeships are mandatory and scheduled in the third year of the Study Course.
For internship or traineeship, it refers to a period of training and work orientation at an institution or company that has established a convention with the Department of Languages, Literatures and Modern Cultures, activated with the aim of connecting school and work.
Students may also identify companies or other organizations known to them or of interest, willing to host them, following the signing of a convention with the Department or the Study Course.
This service allows students to gain their first contact with the world of work and to carry out activities at public and/or private entities, which may eventually serve as the topic for the final thesis.
The duration of an internship is calculated based on the CFU to be acquired as specified in the student's study plan. These CFU are automatically inserted into the student's academic record.
The organization and coordination of internships and traineeships are entrusted to the Department Teaching Tutor, Dr. Lorena Savini, who also manages the evaluation of interns and trainees by host entities.
The list of public and private entities with which conventions for conducting internships and traineeships are in place is available at the external link indicated in this section.
For students with disabilities, the Teaching Tutor is responsible for organizing traineeships at external entities and organizations (preparing the entity for welcoming the student, planning essential support to ensure autonomy during the internship or traineeship activity, etc.).
All students have the opportunity to experience an internationally paid work experience. The Erasmus for Traineeships Call provides an economic contribution to carry out a traineeship abroad for a duration ranging from 2 to 12 months.
The Traineeship can be curricular or extracurricular and can also occur post-graduation.

Student opinions The L-11 Study Course provides a pre-exam online questionnaire to collect student opinions, managed by the university offices responsible for this task. The questionnaire covers the overall organization of the Course of Study, the various courses, teaching activities and study, interest and satisfaction.
Each individual teacher has access, through a restricted area, to the evaluation results of students regarding their own courses, while the Course of Study Chair has access to all evaluations. Some aspects of the evaluations are periodically discussed in the Course of Study Council, to highlight positive aspects, critical elements, and potential improvement actions.
Data analysis Regarding the evaluation of teaching activities by students, collected through pre-exam questionnaires, the average score for the L11 Course of Study for the academic year 2022-23 is in line with the university average but slightly behind the Humanities Area average.
More specifically, the scores for the 3 macro-areas are as follows:
Teaching effectiveness: CdS 3.52; Area 3.60; University average 3.48;
Logistical and organizational aspects: CdS 3.51; Area 3.58; University average 3.35;
Overall satisfaction: CdS 3.37; Area 3.42; University average 3.35.
In the latest survey, the main critical factor remains the inadequacy of preliminary knowledge for understanding the topics covered in the courses (CdS average 3.31. This is the worst score in the entire table).
As strengths, the consistency between information provided on the Department website and the actual delivery of teaching activities (D13, CdS 3.57), respect for office hours and class schedules (D14, CdS 3.61), and teacher availability to provide clarifications during lessons or during office hours (D22, CdS 3.66) are noted.
Among improvement actions, the Department of Languages and the four affiliated Courses of Study are preparing a call for student tutors, aiming to promote, through the introduction of these figures already successfully used in the previous academic year, the acquisition of information, knowledge of departmental structures, and interaction with the teaching organization.
Finally, it is noted that the Quality Assurance Office has established a centralized complaint management system at the university level, accessible at:
https://www.unich.it/parla-con-noi The data regarding student opinions were discussed in a dedicated point in the Course of Study meeting on October 12, 2023.
