Il giorno Venerdì 21.12.18 presso la sala consiliare 'Pietro De Fazio' del Dipartimento di Scienze Mediche, Orali e Biotecnologiche si è tenuta la prima delle due riunioni programmate per incontrare le parti sociali per definire l'opportunità e la necessità di istituire un cds in Logopedia presso l'Università 'G. d'Annunzio' di Chieti-Pescara.
La seconda riunione è già calendarizzata, come riportato nella email di invito, per il 07.01.19
Le riunioni sono state indette dal Prof. Michele D'Attilio, Professore Associato di Ortodonzie e Gnatologia presso il cds di Odontoiatria e Protesi Dentaria, su incarico del Rettore Prof. Sergio Caputi.
Il Professor D'Attilio ha invitato le parti sociali tramite email, allegando un questionario da riempire che favorisse la discussione dell'ordine del giorno , ovvero: ll'opportunità e la necessità di cui sopra e la validità del piano di studi realizzato.
Alla riunione sono state invitate le seguenti parti sociali:
Il Presidente della Federazione Logopedisti Italiani sezione Abruzzo e Molise Il Presidente della Società Italiana di Neurologia sezione Abruzzo Il Presidente della Società Italiana di Neurologia Pediatrica sezione Abruzzo-Marche-Umbria Il Presidente della Società Italiana di Pediatria sezione Abruzzo Il Presidente della Società Italiana di Neonatologia sezione Abruzzo Il Presidente dell'Associazione Nazionale Dentisti Italiani Regione Abruzzo Il Presidente della Commissione Albo Odontoiatri Pescara Il Presidente della Commissione Albo Odontoiatri Chieti Il Presidente della Commissione Albo Odontoiatri L'Aquila Il Presidente della Commissione Albo Odontoiatri Teramo L'Associazione nazionale dei disabili italiani (ANDI)
Il Presidente della Società Italiana di otorinolaringologia pediatrica Il Presidente della Società Italiana di otorinolaringoiatria e chirurgia Cervico-facciale e la Prof.ssa Oriana Trubiani quale delegata dal Rettore all'Orientamento.
La riunione inizia alle 9,30.
Alla riunione erano presenti:
il Prof. Michele D'Attilio, la Prof.ssa Oriana Trubiani, il Presidente Regionale A.N.D.I., la Presidentessa Regione Abruzzo e Molise Federazione Logopedisti Italiani e Il Presidente della Commissione Albo Odontoiatri Chieti.
Questi ultimi due erano presenti mediante collegamento telematico.
Il Prof. D'Attilio ha riferito che tutti i questionari ricevuti, in funzione delle risposte ai quesiti manifestavano pieno apprezzamento all'iniziativa, infatti le risposte alle singole domande erano tutte positive.
Il Professor D'Attilio, quindi, ha spiegato ai presenti la finalità di quella riunione, sottolineando che qualche giorno prima si è riunita la CRUA (Commissione dei Rettori delle Università Abruzzesi), riunione a cui lui era presente e in cui i Rettori di tutti gli Atenei Abruzzesi hanno concordato l'opportunità e la necessità di istituire un secondo cds in Logopedia in Abruzzo.
Il Prof. D'Attilio ha continuato dicendo che la presenza di un cds in Logopedia a L'Aquila ha indotto lui e la Prof.ssa Trubiani a pensare un piano di studi che fosse in linea con le caratteristiche che storicamente caratterizzano un cds in Logopedia personalizzandolo verso l'area Odontoiatrica e le problematica multidisciplinare delle OSAS (Sindrome apnee ostruttive in sonno). Quindi, fornisce il piano di studi ai presenti e lo spedisce via email a chi era collegato telematicamente e lo espone, nel dettaglio.
La motivazione di tale scelta e stata frutto di:
1. la presenza dal 2006 di un servizio di logopedia all'interno della clinica odontoiatrica del Dipartimento di Scienze Mediche, Orali e Biotecnologiche
2. della presenza sul territorio Abruzzese e Molisano di più di 2000 dentisti;
3. della difficoltà riscontrata, in 25 anni di attività nella clinica odontoiatrica universitaria, a riferire pazienti a logopedisti sul territorio Abruzzese e Molisano, costringendo, spesso, i pazienti ad andare fuori regione
4. di poter dare la scelta all'aspirante studente in logopedia di poter scegliere un profilo di studio orientato in tal senso con l'intento di porre il cds in logopedia di Chieti-Pescara attrattivo anche verso le regioni limitrofe all'Abruzzo Il Prof. D'Attilio al termine della sua esposizione apre la discussione e passa la parola alla Presidentessa Regione Abruzzo e Molise Federazione Logopedisti Italiani Quest'ultima, concorda con il fatto che il piano di studi sia in linea con quello degli altri cds presenti in Italia e loda l'iniziativa di aver caratterizzato il programma di studio orientandolo verso la riabilitazione delle problematiche logopediche legate all'odontoiatria e alla riabilitazione delle OSAS.
Inoltre, ritiene corretta questa politica perché il corso di studi in logopedia dell'Università di L'Aquila è caratterizzato in area pediatrica e in particolare sulla terapia delle prassie.
Al termine dell'intervento della Presidentessa, il Prof. D'Attilio passa la parola al Presidente ANDI Regione Abruzzo il quale, profondo conoscitore delle problematiche della categoria odontoiatrica abruzzese, ritiene che potrà essere solo una grande risorsa per l'Abruzzo un altro corso in Logopedia considerata la forte carenza di tale figura sul territorio che obbliga spesso i pazienti ad andare fuori regione con un aggravio di spesa per le risorse sanitarie regionali. Il piano di studi proposto, secondo lui, è assolutamente idoneo per la formazione della figura in esame Dopo il Presidente ANDI, prende la parola il Presidente della Commissione Albo Odontoiatri di Chieti. Anche lui, dall'alto della sua trentennale esperienza di sindacalista e presidente della commissione odontoiatrica dell'ordine dei medici di Chieti, sottolinea la bontà del progetto e la congruità del programma di studi proposto e ritiene che l'istituzione di un secondo cds in Logopedia a Chieti porterà alla Regione gli stessi benefici portati in passato con l'istituzione del secondo cds in Igiene dentale.
Per ultima, la parola, passa alla Prof.ssa Trubiani che sottolinea l'importanza di avere un programma di studi differenziante rispetto a quello del cds dell'Università di L'Aquila e che la Presidentessa della Scuola di sanità si è attivata per avere le convenzioni necessarie all'attivazione del cds.
Il Prof. D'Attilio dichiara chiusa la seduta alle ore 11,00 e da appuntamento ai presenti il 07.01.19 alle ore 9,30 prendendosi l'impegno a spedire a presenti e assenti il resoconto della riunione odierna.
Consultazione con le organizzazioni rappresentative - a livello nazionale e internazionale - della produzione di beni e servizi, delle professioni (Consultazioni successive)
Il giorno 07.01.19, presso la sala Consiliare 'Pietro De Fazio' del Dipartimento di Scienze Mediche, Orali e Biotecnologiche dell'Università 'G. d'Annunzio' di Chieti, si è tenuta la seconda delle due riunioni con le parti sociali per definire il piano di studi del cds in logopedia.
Anche questa riunione è stata indetta dal Prof. Michele D'Attilio Docente di Ortodonzia e Gnatologia presso la medesima Università.
Erano presenti, oltre al Prof. Michele D'Attilio, la Prof.ssa Oriana Trubiani (Delegata dal Rettore all'Orientamento), Il presidente Regionale dell'Associazione Nazionale Dentisti Italiani, la Presidente Regionale della Federazione Logopedisti Italiani accompagnata da una componente del Direttivo Regionale.
Entrambe erano portavoci di consigli e critiche costruttive da parte della Presidente nazionale FLI e delle responsabili della formazione della stessa Federazione, riguardo la composizione del piano di studi.
Nel corso dell'incontro il Prof. D'Attilio ha presentato, nuovamente, la proposta del piano di studi, descrivendo i termini dell'Ordinamento e del percorso formativo che si intende attuare, gli obiettivi formativi specifici, i descrittori di Dublino, la modalità della prova finale.
La presidente Regionale Abruzzo-Molise del FLI ha illustrato il parere della sua associazione dopo essersi consultata con le colleghe che all'interno della federazione nazionale si occupano di formazione e gestione dei cds di logopedia e in seguito ad una conversazione avuta con la Presidente Nazionale riferisce che può andar bene l'impronta che vorremmo dare al corso di studi ma che è necessario porre attenzione ad alcuni criteri per rispettare il core curriculum.
La Presidente regional FLI,relaziona a riguardo e specifica che secondo lei e la FLi si debba orientare il piano di studi in modo da caratterizzare, per quanto possibile, il secondo anno con materie orientate alla diagnosi e il terzo alla riabilitazione.
Dopo ampia discussione dei presenti si concorda che il piano di studi sia modifcato per renderlo aderente al core curruculum del Logopedista ma orientandolo, verso la riabilitazione in campo odontoiatrico e relativo alle problematiche delle apnee ostruttive in sonno, sia perchè ciò permetterebbe di differenziare il curriculum del cds di Chieti da quello di L'Aquila, sia perchè insistendo sul territorio abruzzese e molisano più di 2000 dentisti la richiesta da parte loro di avere la collaborazione di un logopedista è sempre più sentita e sempre più richiesta.
Il Prof. D'Attilio ha elencato altresì le strutture sanitarie della sede formativa presso le quali sarà possibile lo svolgimento della attività professionalizzante (tirocinio) e con le quali sono già in atto convenzioni con l'Università di Chieti Pescara: Istituto Santa Caterina di Francavilla al Mare convenzionata con ASL Lanciano Vasto Chieti.
Le riflessioni emerse dalle consultazioni sono state prese in considerazione della progettazione dei CdS soprattutto con riferimento alle potenzialità occupazionali dei laureati e all'eventuale proseguimento di studi in cicli successivi?

Sulla base di quanto affermato precedentemente circa la presenza di numerosi dentisti sul territorio sia la carenza di logopedisti sul territorio, come riferito dalla Presidente Regione Abruzzo e Molise della FLI, il Prof. D'Attilo sottolinea che quanto deciso dai Rettori degli Atenei Abruzzesi, ovvero di far coesistere due cds sullo stesso territorio non comporterà un saturamento della figura del logopedista sul territorio in funzione di come storicamente afferiscono gli studenti nei due atenei.
Infatti L'Aquila attrae studenti più dall'entroterra Abruzzese e parte del Lazio, Chieti e Pescara sono invece più attrattive verso le altre regioni costiere confinanti, nonchè la Basilicata, parte della Campania e il Molise.
Al termine della presentazione da parte del Prof. D'Attilio e degli unterventi che si sono succeduti la Presidente della FLI, nell'esprimere apprezzamento e compiacimento nei confronti della proposta di istituire il CL Logopedia presso l'Università dell'Aquila, si dichiara favorevole al progetto formativo presentato che rispecchia l'Ordinamento ed il percorso di studi già attivo in altre sedi universitarie.
A seguito di tale incontro, concorde con il Prof. D'Attilio, La Presidentessa della Federazione Logopedisti Italiani Sezione Abruzzo/Molise, ha espresso parere pienamente favorevole alla proposta di istituzione del CL in Logopedia presso l'Università di Chieti-Pescara, allo scopo di soddisfare la domanda di offerta formativa Universitaria nella regione Abruzzo considerando, sia l'elevata potenzialità occupazionale del laureato in logopedia che la capacità dell'Ateneo d'Annunziano di porsi attrattivo verso altre regioni Italiane sia, infine, perché il piano di studi si propone verso una categoria che avrà sempre più bisogno, nel suo team, della figura del logopedista, così come lo è diventata oggi quella dell'igienista.
Infine, Viene anche sottolineata la possibilità, per il futuro laureato in Logopedia di accedere, previo superamento del concorso di ammissione, al Corso di Laurea Magistrale LM-SNT/2 – Scienze riabilitative delle Professioni Sanitarie Prima di dichiarare chiusi i lavori della riunione si definisce che il COMITATO DI INDIRIZZO sarà composto da:
Prof. Michele D'Attilio, Prof.ssa Oriana Trubiani, Prof.ssa Adele Giamberardino, Dr.ssa Alessandra Perluzzo (FLI), Dr.ssa Angela Colagiovanni (FLI)

01.04.22
E' in fase di programmazione una riunione con la Direttrice della didattica professionalizzante, Dr.ssa Maria Beatrice Perilli, Il Presidente della Sezione Abruzzo-Molise della Federazione Logopedisti Italiani, con il Presidente del CDS di Logopedia e le docenti del SSD Med50 del medesimo cds di questa università.
Nel corso dell'anno Accademico 2023 e in particolare a Maggio 2023 è stata Nominata una nuova Direttrice didattica, la Dr.ssa Arcangela Carli incardinata presso la ASL di Pescara ed in particolare presso l'ospedale civile.
Il giorno 8 giugno 2023 è sta tenuta una riunione con la Direttrice della didattica professionalizzante, Dr.ssa Arcangela Carli, Il Presidente della Sezione Abruzzo-Molise della Federazione Logopedisti Italiani, il Presidente del CDS di Logopedia, Prof. Michele D'Attilio, con lo scopo di monitorare l'andamento del corso di studi sulla base dei giudizi degli studenti e dei professori del SSD Med/50. Il Prof. D'Attilio mostra gli esiti dei giudizi sia degli studenti che dei docenti. Dopo un'attenta valutazione e un'adeguata discussione, il commento finale è stato di unanime soddisfazione, individuando anche delle aree di miglioramento.
Dati di ingresso, di percorso e di uscita L'analisi dei dati forniti dal PQA si evince che dei 14 studenti immatricolati, sette di essi sono immatricolati puri ovvero iscritti per la prima volta ad un corso universitario.
Il numero di studenti complessivo del CdS in Logopedia è di 55, tutti regolarmente in corso.
Quest'anno il 71.4% degli studenti proviene dall'Abruzzo I dati relativi al titolo di studio della scuola superiore di provenienza degli studenti immatricolati al cds in Logopedia, evidenzia che il 71,4% proviene dai licei.
Ciò depone per un'inversione di rapporto rispetto all'anno precedente Il 71,4% degli studenti immatricolati al cds di Logopedia ha un voto di diploma compreso tra 80 e 100
Per quanto riguarda i laureati, su 189 laureati 7 si sono laureati prima della durata del percorso formativo, 74 entro la durata del corso, 38 dopo un anno dalla fine del corso e 37 dopo due anni dalla fine dello stesso Caratteristiche della prova finale La prova finale, con valore di Esame di Stato abilitante alla professione di Logopedista (D.Lgs 502/1992, art. 6, comma 3), si compone di: a) una prova pratica nel corso della quale lo studente deve dimostrare di aver acquisito le conoscenze e abilità teorico-pratiche e tecnico-operative proprie dello specifico profilo professionale;
b) redazione di un elaborato di una tesi e sua dissertazione. Cfr DM 19 febbraio 2009, art.7.
Il punteggio finale è espresso in centodecimi.
Se viene raggiunta la votazione complessiva di 110/110, il Presidente della Commissione per l'esame finale mette in votazione l'attribuzione della lode, che potrà essere assegnata solo all'unanimità dei presenti.
La prova finale dà adito all'attribuzione di 5 CFU.
Modalità di svolgimento della prova finale La prova finale (5 CFU) è valutata dalla Commissione di Laurea, composta da almeno 7 fino ad un massimo di undici membri e comprendente due membri designati dall'Associazione professionale di categoria. Nel corso della prova finale, lo studente deve dimostrare di aver acquisito una preparazione scientifica e teorico-pratica, una metodologia e cultura tali da garantire un'autonomia professionale, decisionale e operativa per l'esercizio della professione.
Requisiti della tesi di laurea
. La tesi, di natura sperimentale o compilativa, deve essere elaborata in modo originale dallo studente sotto la guida di un relatore, membro della Commissione. Il suo contenuto deve essere attinente a temi strettamente correlati al profilo professionale. Attraverso la sua dissertazione, il candidato deve dimostrare capacità autonoma di apprendimento e di giudizio, di essere in grado di elaborare, interpretare e discutere i risultati ottenuti e di comunicarli in modo chiaro, anche con l'uso di mezzi informatici. La tesi è redatta in lingua italiana sotto la guida di un relatore.
Il voto di laurea sarà il risultato della media dei voti espressa dal curriculum degli studi del candidato sommato al punteggio che verrà assegnato dalla commissione al lavoro di tesi del laureando.
Gli argomenti che potrebbero essere trattati al termine del percorso di studi e divenire tesi di laurea, possono interessare qualunque ambito della riabilitazione logopedica.
Alcuni esempi possono essere: il ruolo della logopedia nella riabilitazione del paziente autistico; la pedagogia vocale e la terapia riabilitativa anche in ambito attorale; il trattamento logopedico nel paziente affetto da afasia motoria; l'approccio e la terapia nel piccolo paziente con difficoltà nell'apprendimento delle abilità logico-matematiche;
Come la logopedista può essere di aiuto nella risoluzione del deficit comunicativo e linguistico; L'approccio terapeutico alle disprassie in età evolutiva; Come insegnare ad un bambino sordo ad apprendere le lingue Sintesi della relazione tecnica del nucleo di valutazione - Scheda SUA Viste le diverse criticità riscontrate nell'analisi di cui sopra, il parere positivo alla proposta di nuova attivazione del presente CdS è CONDIZIONATO al loro superamento e invio al Nucleo di Valutazione della proposta corretta ed integrata entro una data utile per la presentazione alla seduta di Senato Accademico prevista per il 15 gennaio 2019.
In particolare, si raccomanda di:
- effettuare delle consultazioni dirette con le parti interessate raccogliendo indicazioni utili per la progettazione del CdS;
- perfezionare la convenzione con una struttura assistenziale;
- valutare in maniera puntuale le opportunità di impiego della specifica figura professionale nel bacino di riferimento dell'Ateneo;
- completare la sezione D della SUA CdS, Organizzazione e Gestione della Qualità;
- indicare esplicitamente i docenti di riferimento;
- indicare esplicitamente le strutture e le risorse (aule, laboratori, biblioteche, attrezzature) messe a disposizione del CdS.
Nella seduta del 10.01.2019 il Nucleo di Valutazione ha rilevato che:
- sono state effettuate le consultazioni richieste;
- sono state valutate le opportunità di impego della figura professionale nel bacino di riferimento dell'Ateneo;
- è stata compilata la Sezione D della SUA CdS;
- sono stati indicati i docenti di riferimento;
- sono state indicate le strutture (aule, spazi e biblioteche) disponibili nell'area sanitaria, seppure in maniera generica.
Alla luce delle modifiche, il Nucloe di Valutazione esprime parere favorevole alla proposta.

SECTION: Admission Procedures
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/62

Admission Procedures Provided that admission to the course is not contingent upon passing any examination, in the initial phase of teaching activities (typically after enrollment is complete, no later than February), basic knowledge verification tests (in the linguistic-literary and historical-geographical fields) are scheduled in the form of multiple-choice questionnaires for students who scored below 80/100 in their secondary school diploma. Students transferring from other universities or other study programs at 'G. d'Annunzio' University, as well as those already holding a degree, are exempt from these tests. The test, conducted online, consists of two sections: the first covering the linguistic-literary field with questions on Italian grammar, linguistics, and text comprehension and contextualization; the second covering the historical-geographical field. For illustrative purposes, a sample test is attached. In case of a negative result, students will be assigned additional educational obligations (OFA) to be fulfilled in the first year of study; individual recovery paths will be defined with faculty members in the disciplinary areas where insufficient preparation was identified (these students may also utilize faculty tutoring, which will also function as a teaching office). A verification test for the recovery of initial deficiencies will be held before the summer exam session (passing which will extinguish the OFA). For preparation for the initial test, studying current secondary school textbooks is sufficient; specific guidelines are published on the course website. Regarding classical languages (Greek and Latin), relevant faculty may conduct initial preparation verification tests. However, failing these tests does not result in an OFA, as students may opt for a path that does not include classical disciplines. In any case, the study program offers 0-credit courses in 'Basic Latin Language' (beginner and advanced levels) and 'Basic Greek Language' (beginner and advanced levels) for all students. The fulfillment of OFA may also be achieved by passing a minimum of 18 CFU in foundational and characteristic courses specified in the first-year study plan (or in the first and second year for part-time students). Failure to fulfill OFA by the deadline means students remain obligated to satisfy this requirement and cannot take second-year exams until it is completed (Article 28, paragraph 5 of the University Academic Regulations).

Communication Skills (communication skills)
Graduates in Letters must possess solid linguistic and argumentative skills enabling them to communicate information, ideas, problems and solutions to specialist and non-specialist audiences.
They also acquire communication and presentation skills (in written and oral form) applicable through the use of information and multimedia communication tools, both in Italian and in at least one European language (at B1 level).
The acquisition and verification of written and oral communication skills occur through training activities, including laboratory-based ones specifically dedicated to linguistic-communicative competence, as provided in the course's teaching plan, through seminars and through the production and presentation of papers, and especially through the final exam.

UNIVERSITY: GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO UNIVERSITY – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L270] LETTERS
SECTION: AUTONOMY OF JUDGMENT
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/62

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgments)
Graduates in Letters must be able to independently set up and carry out, even using new technologies, bibliographic and/or field research necessary to establish the required databases for their studies, and then be able to process and interpret such data with a critical spirit attentive to scientific, social, and ethical implications. In particular, they must know, be able to evaluate, and use methods for linguistic, philological, literary, rhetorical, aesthetic, and historical analysis of written documents in order to derive judgments that are both consistent and original.

The student's autonomy of judgment is developed primarily through exercises aimed at personal and conscious analysis of documents, sources, critical literature, etc., to be conducted within individual courses, laboratory experiences, seminars, and internships. It is verified during oral and/or written exams; it also serves as a verification point regarding the student's autonomous judgment abilities developed through the preparation of the final thesis.

Orientation in Entry The 'Gabriele d'Annunzio' University, through its Orientation, Tutoring, Placement, Student Rights, and Disability Office, offers a series of interventions on orientation and placement, structured into Orientation in Entry (targeted at students in the final years of Secondary School), Orientation in Progress, Tutoring, Student Rights, for university students, and Exit Orientation and Placement for students, graduates, and doctoral candidates, as well as the Disability and Specific Learning Disorders (DSA) Service for university students.
However, particularly regarding Orientation in Entry, the Course of Study in Letters, in synergy with the Department of Letters, Arts, and Social Sciences, annually carries out a series of initiatives aimed at enabling students to make a fruitful choice in university selection. These activities are coordinated by the designated orientation officer, Professor Maria Luigia Di Marzio, who collaborates with a specific committee composed of Professors Fabio Andreazza, Luciana Pasquini, Silvia Scorrano, and a student representative. During the 2023/24 academic year, coordination was transferred to Professor Mario Cimini.
The main orientation actions are:
- Orientation meetings at Secondary Schools, particularly in the region, from January to May;
- Participation in orientation fairs and orientation days inside and outside the region for Secondary School students;
- Open Day programming: welcome days organized from January to May each year, allowing students to meet university faculty members of individual courses, senior students, for general information on services and enrollment procedures, or to attend orientation-specific lectures;
- Targeted teaching projects for high school students in collaboration with local schools;
- Specific projects involving current students (such as theatrical activities with mobile performances aimed at engaging local schools);
- Disability and DSA service: welcome and support for students with disabilities and/or learning disorders through targeted interventions to ensure the right to education and facilitate integration into the university community; this support is particularly carried out in synergy with the University's Psychological Listening and Orientation Counseling Service (SAPCO) (see https://www.unich.it/campus/servizi/servizi-di-contesto-agli-studenti);
- Tutoring and assistance service provided by specially trained senior students.
In addition to in-person activities, the Course of Study - in coordination with DiLASS - uses a specific online platform (see https://www.dilass.unich.it/orientamento-0), where the following are uploaded:
- Illustrative materials for the course in video and/or text format;
- Webinars on specific aspects of the Course of Study's educational project (or short lecture-type sessions);
- Calendar of 'remote' meetings with faculty and tutors available to provide information;
- Links to the University's orientation initiatives.
The assessment of admission requirements for the Course of Study also provides an opportunity to initiate tutorial activities that allow for a better understanding of the student, who can then be guided in choosing the study plan most suitable to their aptitudes. All faculty members of the Course of Study dedicate several weekly hours in September and October to meeting with incoming students to guide them, through personalized interviews, both in gaining a mature awareness of their choice and in building their study path. The Course of Study also organizes, at the beginning of the academic year, collective meetings with interested students, with the presence of the Course President and orientation delegates, to provide general information on the annual teaching organization, training opportunities (including partnerships with foreign universities), and the employment prospects offered by the course (see also https://www.dilass.unich.it/orientamento-0).
In the 2023-24 academic year, in addition to re-proposing tested initiatives from previous years (at the Night of Researchers and the University's Open Day), new events were held in the territory, many of which involved direct intervention in Abruzzo schools, also funded through participation in PCTO/PNRR projects. The following activities are highlighted:
- 23 September 2023. Ndr 2023, Chieti Campus "One World, one Health, one thousand Cultures".
- 13 and 14 December 2023. Student Fair. Dromedian Live Campus, via Piaggio 35, Chieti Scalo.
- 14 December 2023 (15:00-18:00): presentation of the Italian university system and the University D'Annunzio's university reality at Aula Giuntella for students from various schools in the province (Marialuigia Di Marzio).
- 1 February 2024. Lanciano, Benito Lanci Theater Fenaroli Fair. M. Di Marzio: "Towards and Metaverse: Professional Horizons", within the event "Choose Your Path. University and Workforce Orientation Days", 13th edition.
- 'Orienta UDA' program, with course presentations once a week.
- 'A Day as a New Student' initiative (guest students from 2 high schools attending DiLASS lectures).
For further details on all implemented initiatives, see the attached PDF.

Ongoing orientation and tutoring All teachers of the Study Course carry out ongoing tutoring activities; each tutor, assigned at the time of admission to the Study Course, follows the student constantly throughout the entire three-year study path, remaining available with a weekly reception schedule easily accessible for information, clarifications, and advice. Additionally, in various courses, dedicated time is allocated for assisted study, which includes targeted training activities to improve the learning of content presented within the course itself.
A specific internal commission within the Study Course, composed of Prof. Fabio Andreazza, Luciana Pasquini, Maria Luigia Di Marzio (chair), Pierluigi Ortolano, coordinates orientation and tutoring initiatives. During the 2023/24 academic year, coordination was transferred to Prof. Mario Cimini.
The Study Course, as easily evident from the Annual Monitoring Sheet of the Course and the Cyclical Review Report, implements periodic checks on the overall progress of student cohorts in acquiring training credits, and identifies strategies to improve study effectiveness, also aiming to reduce student dropout and abandonment. In particular, it activates to rationalize study plans and teaching calendars, evaluates the homogenization of CFU/exam programs and the consistency of programs with the Study Course's educational objectives, and monitors student careers through a specific application (INGRID). Results are verified through the increase of certain key indicators (acquisition of a sufficient number of CFU by students, percentage of students graduating on time, dropout percentage, student satisfaction index). In particular, in the INGRID system, the number of students with a percentage of acquired CFU below 30% compared to the annual course workload remains consistently below 15% (12.5% in 2021, 14.7% in 2022, 13% in 2023).
Tutors and course representatives, taking into account the career monitoring that statistically predominantly leads (or continues) to paths leading to teaching in secondary schools, constantly assist students in calibrating their study plans towards this professional goal, guiding them in meeting the requirements set by current legislation.
To enable students to make informed professional choices, the Study Course promotes a series of internship activities at appropriately selected and contracted institutions and productive structures. Delegates managing this service periodically monitor the effectiveness of internships and propose improvement strategies or enhancements to the service itself.
Ongoing orientation activities are also implemented by the University's Orientation, Tutoring, Placement, Right to Study, and Disability Office, in collaboration with the Study Course and the Department. In particular, this service:
- provides information and administrative support to disabled students and/or their families regarding opportunities reserved by the University;
- in collaboration with Schools and Departments, offers support to students interested in reorganizing or revising their study path;
- makes available assistance services reserved for disabled students or students with Specific Learning Disorders; in this regard, the Study Course, through its President and the delegate for support activities, Prof. Ilaria Filograsso;
- provides support and assistance to students regarding the Right to Study;
- coordinates tutoring calls reserved for students;
- coordinates calls for part-time collaboration activities reserved for students;
- makes available online a series of information reserved for students interested in undertaking internships not for credit.

Internship periods The Course has for years maintained an internal structure that activates and manages internship agreements with cultural institutions, companies, organizations from the world of work and social assistance, newsrooms, libraries, etc. The coordinator of this structure is Prof. Antonella Di Nallo, who also benefits from the support of an administrative unit, Dr. Maria Cristina Ricciardi. International Mobility International student mobility primarily occurs within the Erasmus+ Programme (for both study and internship purposes), with minor activity under extra-European conventions. In this context, the Course's activities are integrated into those of the Department of origin (DILASS) and the University as a whole. The International Relations Office of the University is therefore primarily responsible for coordinating and managing student mobility (see www.unich.it/didattica/studiare-allestero). However, many faculty members affiliated with the Course hold specific conventions with foreign universities, established based on common scientific and research interests, which include Erasmus grants for student mobility. These faculty members also provide information on the modalities and characteristics of study and training periods at the partner universities. Overall, the Course places particular emphasis on internationalizing the education of its students.

Currently, 35 conventions are active (for details, see attached PDF or link, as technical issues prevent listing all conventions in the following screen). For internal coordination of Erasmus mobility, the Course relies on Professors Maria Grazia Del Fuoco and Antonella Di Nallo; the International Relations Delegate is Professor Francesco Caccamo. During the Erasmus mobility call period (February-March), the Course organizes meetings with students, in coordination with the University's International Mobility Delegate (Professor Enrichetta Soccio), to encourage participation and provide all possible information. Faculty members responsible for individual conventions provide information and support upon student request, maintaining contact with foreign university counterparts. To further promote and support international mobility, since 2019 the Course has decided to supplement the Erasmus grant with funds from its own resources (for the 2019/2020 academic year, this contribution equaled the grant amount; for the 2021/2022 academic year, it will be based on the Department's financial availability). The results of students' activities abroad (which inherently involve the internationalization of their education) are discussed in the Annual Monitoring Sheet of the Course and the Cyclical Review Report. Students take exams at partner universities for at least 12 CFU; these exams are recognized in their study plan, and the experience is also valued during graduation with a specific score.

In the 2023/24 academic year, 4 students enrolled in the Letters Course benefited from an Erasmus grant.

The Course, in coordination with the Department, has committed to improving the data on incoming Erasmus students, which was zero in 2019/20, reached 8 in 2022/23, and 12 in 2023/24.

Career Guidance The Program in Letters, for the purpose of facilitating the employment of its graduates, relies on the 'Orientation and Placement' service managed directly by the University through the 'Start' program. The University, therefore, promotes the employment of its graduates and alumni through the activation of a network of relationships between the University, Enterprises, and Research Systems aimed at developing and consolidating a virtuous cycle of relationships and services, facilitating the 'communication' between the needs of enterprises, the processes of labor market integration, and the implications for educational plans, while providing substance and continuity to the transition phase into the workforce. In this context, graduates in Letters can perform tasks and activities related to consulting and cultural promotion in production sectors that require specific disciplinary competencies combined with critical thinking: publishing, management of social services, libraries and museums, training and counseling activities, human resource management, and advertising. The Delegate of the Program for the management of the career guidance service is Prof. Pierluigi Ortolano, who works in coordination with the Departmental Delegate for Placement, Prof. Francesco Berardi.

The Program, together with the Department and the Master's program in Philology, Linguistics, and Literary Traditions, also promotes initiatives that offer graduates a concrete connection with the world of work. Additionally, considering that a significant portion of them pursue teaching careers by continuing their studies in a Master's program, the Program promotes seminar and conference activities featuring experts in the literary, historical, philological, and linguistic fields; these activities aim to deepen methodological and didactic aspects, also in preparation for teaching careers (the activity calendar is available on the website: https://www.dilass.unich.it/dipartimento/tutti-gli-eventi).

The Program evaluates the results of the activities promoted in the area of Placement through the analysis and discussion of data provided by AlmaLaurea and the student office for the corresponding Master's programs LM-14 and LM-15 during one of the meetings held during the year by the Steering Committee, which includes the Placement Delegate.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA

SECTION: Student Opinions
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/62

Student Opinions The survey of student opinions on teaching activities conducted electronically in the 2022-2023 academic year produced a relatively high overall score for the Study Course in Letters, equal to 3.62/4 for attending students, with a constant and significant increase compared to previous years (it was 3.44/4 in 2017-2018 and 3.46/4 in 2018-2019, 3.52/4 in 2019-2020, 3.56/4 in 2020-2021, 3.59/4 in 2021-2022). The data appears particularly positive as it is higher not only than the university average (3.44/4) but also than that of humanities study courses (3.54/4). It should also be noted that the number of students who expressed their evaluation is quite high and increasing since the mandatory connection between exam enrollment and teaching evaluations became operational: for the 2022-2023 academic year, 2,636 evaluations were recorded. Moreover, it is certainly a positive circumstance that the scores achieved by individual courses offered by the Study Course are quite homogeneous, without downward peaks (from the survey of attending students, it emerges that no course has a score below 3.23/4). In line with the trends in the humanities area, the highest ratings concern teaching effectiveness (3.69/4), followed by logistical-organizational aspects (3.66/4), and finally overall satisfaction (3.50/4). Regarding the individual questions, the highest results are those related to professors' availability to provide clarifications on topics covered in class (3.77/4), adherence to class and exercise schedules (3.73/4), and the consistency of programs with what is stated in the Syllabus (3.70/4). Excellent results are also obtained regarding the interest in the disciplines (3.67/4), the teacher's ability to present topics appropriately according to the complexity of the disciplines, and their ability to stimulate interest in the discipline (both at 3.65/4), as well as teaching materials (3.60/4). Slightly lower, but still satisfactory, are the results regarding the study load required in relation to the assigned CFUs (3.46/4), explainable by the fact that part of the students are engaged in work activities in addition to studies, and those regarding the preliminary knowledge possessed (3.38/4), which is explained by the heterogeneity of the students' previous schools. The CPDS, while not reporting significant issues, still suggests carefully monitoring the relationship between the required teaching effort and the number of CFUs delivered by individual disciplines, without compromising the quality of the educational standards. In this regard, the AQ Group annually monitors the syllabi of the disciplines and intervenes in cases of clear discrepancies in the relationship between the required teaching effort and CFUs, requesting the appropriate corrections from the relevant professors. The results of the student opinion survey are presented and discussed in the degree course council meeting in September 2023. Regarding the management of potential student complaints, the Study Course has identified a specific role of 'Student Guarantor' who handles them: the name and procedure are advertised on the course website (https://www.dilass.unich.it/node/8700). A listening service is also managed by the PQA (see the external link).

Opinions of graduates The number of graduates of the degree course for the calendar year 2021 was 93. According to the AlmaLaurea 2022 data, 90.6% of graduates considered the study load of the courses appropriate for the duration of the degree program (42.4% rated it "very appropriate," 48.2% "appropriate"), a percentage that has increased compared to the previous year (in 2021 it was 85.7%). 44.7% of respondents considered the organization of exams (calls, schedules, information, reservations) satisfactory for more than half of the exams, while 32.9% considered it always satisfactory (only 4.7% never or almost never). Similarly, regarding the assessment of the relationship with teachers, the data show an improvement trend: 37.6% rated it "very satisfactory" (it was 34.5% in 2021 and 30.6% in 2020), while 54.1% rated it positively. All data are in line with or slightly above the university averages.
Regarding the evaluation of the classrooms used during the study years, 33.3% found them almost always appropriate, 54.8% often appropriate. Positive evaluation of the number of computer workstations, rated as sufficient by 60.0%, while data on equipment for other teaching activities such as laboratories are slightly lower, rated as sufficient by 79.2% (compared to 83.4% in 2021), and library services rated as sufficient by 81.8% (compared to 88.9% in 2021).
The overall satisfaction rate of graduates is increasing: 76.5% of respondents would enroll in the degree program again (73.8% in 2021). The percentage of students who declare being very satisfied with the course followed remains nearly stable: 50.6% (compared to 51.2% in 2021); however, this figure is about 9 percentage points higher than the university average.
The degree course will continue to work to consolidate and increase student productivity in order to optimize career development and facilitate the completion of the program; in particular, it will pay attention to the organization of teaching activities, seeking to address problems arising from the flexibility and breadth of the educational offer.
The data on AlmaLaurea graduate opinions are presented and discussed in the degree course council meeting in September 2023.
Applying knowledge and understanding
At the end of the program, the student possesses significant flexibility in applying acquired knowledge, based on the development of learning abilities necessary to independently address both work context situations and subsequent studies.
Specifically, the student can conduct comprehensive and up-to-date bibliographic research, both through digital tools and traditional methods, correctly navigating an archive and successfully retrieving and examining sources; can present literary, linguistic, historical, and artistic topics in oral and written form at various levels of depth, from popular to school and specialist; can draft, expand, reduce, or correct a written text for professional use, particularly in journalism, advertising, scientific, institutional, and cultural dissemination contexts; is able to work in the management of archives, libraries, theaters, museums, phonoteques, cinematheques, videoteques for the preservation and dissemination of memory and historical heritage; can address, from a management and organizational perspective, a cultural event, such as an exhibition, theatrical performance, screening, or musical event; can formulate an original critical discourse on a text, engaging with previous readings and interpretations and applying the most up-to-date methodologies, also in a comparative perspective; can appropriately set up the critical edition of a text, even in the face of unpublished material; can linguistically analyze a text, hypothesizing its geographical area and historical period of origin, identifying its characteristics and specificities from a textual perspective and evaluating its communicative adequacy in relation to context and purpose.
The achievement of the above-mentioned applying knowledge and understanding abilities occurs through critical reflection on texts proposed for individual study, stimulated by classroom activities, exercises, and laboratory activities.
The verification of achieving the applying knowledge and understanding abilities occurs primarily through exam tests and/or intermediate and final oral and/or written assessments.
Learning skills
Graduates in Letters must demonstrate the ability to extend and deepen their studies with a high degree of autonomy and methodological awareness (an ability that can be developed through seminar-style lectures within individual disciplines and during the preparation of the final exam).
They also acquire the ability to continuously update their knowledge and expand their training through an effective scientific methodology, using appropriate tools, including digital and telecommunication tools, in a conscious manner.
Learning skills develop through active participation in the teaching activities provided by the degree course, but also and especially through personal study, progressively reinforcing one's study method with the guidance of teachers.
They are verified throughout the study program, especially in individual study activities required to pass each exam, in the preparation of individual and/or group projects, and in activities carried out in preparation for the final exam.
University communications to the CUN The structure of the Letters degree course is based on the idea of a broad educational offer that, starting from a core of foundational disciplines, allows for in-depth study in specific areas aimed at characterizing paths in line with the aptitudes of future graduates and the professional profiles provided for. In light of the presence of four curricula in the framework, the range of basic, characterizing, and related activities has a certain extension, which has been significantly reduced due to the CUN's observations. In line with CUN guidelines (with some limited exceptions), the maximum of a credit range (in an area or educational activity) does not exceed double the minimum, even with specific paths. This approach allows for achieving both the general educational objectives indicated and those more specific to the individual course variations.
Knowledge and understanding
Through attendance and study of basic and characterizing disciplines, the student develops knowledge that is articulated and implemented through related courses, seminars, laboratory activities, internships, and the final written exam. Specifically, at the end of the course, the student acquires solid foundational knowledge regarding the historical phases of literary disciplines offered in the curriculum, being able to navigate between fundamental themes and stylistic traits related to specific eras or specific to individual authors, also in relation to the broader cultural context in which they are inserted; acquires solid foundational knowledge regarding the methods and techniques of philology, starting from the ability to read a critical edition correctly interpreting its apparatus; knows the history and its periodizations and can read and interpret historical sources (narrative, documentary, material, iconographic); knows the historical evolution of Italian artistic, musical, theatrical, and cinematic disciplines, also in their technical aspects; knows the foundations of modern linguistic theories and their main application possibilities and possesses awareness of linguistic variation dynamics, according to the diatopic, diastratic, diafasic, and diamesic axes; knows the main lines of evolution of Romance languages and in more detail those of Italian and Italo-Romance dialects, and can place linguistic traits in their diachronic dimension; knows at a good level the characteristics, both written and oral, of at least one modern language of the European Union.
The above knowledge and understanding abilities are achieved by the student through participation in frontal lectures and seminars, as well as through individual study hours, as provided by the educational activities.
The verification of achieving learning outcomes occurs primarily through oral and/or written exams.

Brief course description The Letters degree course, characterized by a strong interdisciplinarity and complementarity of its courses, aims primarily to train intellectual personnel with a strong humanistic character. It offers four study paths: Classical Letters, Modern Letters, Languages of Music, Theater, and Media, History. The comprehensive set of basic, common courses for all paths allows for orienting the humanistic training, pursued through the progressive consolidation of theoretical knowledge and methodological tools, towards a rigorous in-depth study of the dynamics of languages, texts, and literary traditions (from ancient and medieval to modern and contemporary times), historical phenomena, and contemporary communication. The specific characterization of each path, on the one hand, lays the foundation for a broad training in the respective areas, and on the other, serves as a guide for subsequent educational and professional choices.
Teaching activities include frontal lectures, exercises, seminars, assisted study, as well as spaces dedicated to technical-operational training of students, such as language laboratories, computer laboratories, writing laboratories (also in specific areas such as journalism and the multimedia galaxy), training internships at public and private structures, and stages. The interaction between courses and technical-applicative training activities is aimed at building professional profiles already after the three-year cycle, requiring the implementation of traditional humanistic resources with new knowledge. This broad and flexible multidisciplinary training – always anchored to historical, linguistic, literary, artistic, and philological foundations – can be further tailored to diverse areas through specific specializations more typical of master's courses. In particular, the course allows students to acquire most of the credits required to access, after obtaining a master's degree, the teaching of linguistic-literary and historical disciplines in secondary schools.
External effectiveness Regarding professional opportunities, the primary goal of Letters degree course students is access to the teaching career in schools through the acquisition of a master's degree. The data provided by the AlmaLaurea report for the 2022 survey year confirms this and suggests that the degree course effectively fulfills its role: one year after obtaining the degree, 90.9% of the selected group is enrolled in a master's degree program.
To this end, the degree course ensures, within its competence, that graduates acquire most of the CFU in specific scientific-disciplinary sectors required as current prerequisites for various teaching categories open to graduates with humanistic training. The revision of the course framework has enabled the implementation of study plans with psycho-antropo-pedagogical disciplines necessary to meet the CFU requirements set by current regulations as an additional prerequisite for access to the teaching career.
Regarding other possible occupational areas that the flexibility of humanistic training allows Letters graduates (in particular, access to public administration competitions, publishing, institutional and corporate archiving, business communication, advertising communication, editorial writing, valorization of bibliographic and cultural heritage, activities in theater and performance), they are affected by the ongoing critical situation in youth employment at the national level. In particular, the percentage of graduates who declare working one year after obtaining their degree is low: 20%, a figure that, however, shows a significant increase compared to the previous year (6.9% in 2021).
The degree course, in collaboration with other degree courses under DiLass (in particular with the master's course in Philology, Linguistics, and Literary Traditions, which is the natural continuation of the three-year Letters course), aims to increase and promote student participation in all exit orientation meetings, also promoting their organization.
The data on external effectiveness are presented and discussed in the degree course council meeting in September 2023.
Specific educational objectives and description of the educational path The Letters bachelor's degree aims to provide students with a solid foundational education primarily in literary, linguistic, historical, and historical-artistic disciplines.
Studies are conducted through the acquisition of both theoretical and methodological and applied skills, enabling the three-year graduate to:
- acquire solid, up-to-date bibliographic foundational knowledge regarding the historical phases of Italian literature and literary criticism, also in relation to the broader cultural context in which they are inserted;
- analyze literary texts, ancient and modern, recognizing their constitutive elements and correctly placing them in their era and cultural context;
- interpret documents of various types (written and visual) across very broad chronological spans, from the ancient world to the contemporary age;
- acquire solid foundational knowledge regarding the methods and techniques of classical and/or modern philology, starting from the ability to read a critical edition;
- know the main lines of evolution of Romance languages and in more detail of Italian;
- know history and its periodizations, from the ancient world to the contemporary age, being aware of the main historiographical problems and methodologies of historical sciences;
- examine an artistic, theatrical, musical, and cinematic product, recognizing its constitutive elements and, through appropriate tools, correctly placing it in its era and cultural context.
Starting from a solid common base of knowledge related to Italian literature, history, and the structure of the Italian language, general linguistics, and glottology, classical, Romance, and modern philology, methodological disciplines related to literary text analysis, European literatures, and history, students can then orient their educational path according to different directions: a) a classical orientation aiming to deepen the ancient world, both linguistically-literary and philological, and historically-artistic-archaeological; b) a modern orientation that prioritizes, leveraging always linguistic-literary, philological, and historical-artistic disciplines, study areas from the Middle Ages to the contemporary age; c) an artistic orientation, while maintaining the centrality of linguistic-literary, philological, and historical disciplines, offers the possibility of developing specific knowledge and skills related to musical, theatrical, cinematic, and new communication languages; d) a historical orientation, where the linguistic-literary and philological aspects are complemented by disciplinary deepening in history from antiquity to the contemporary age.
Students can add elective courses to the basic and characterizing activities in each of the indicated areas to build a more defined profile both professionally and in terms of choosing a potential master's study path. The achievement of these objectives is also supported by a wide range of choices among additional educational activities, such as laboratories (linguistic, computer, various forms of writing, or specific to the theater and new media sector) and internships at duly contracted institutions.
The course is also oriented to acquiring good written and oral command of at least one European Union language, in addition to Italian, as well as providing the indispensable knowledge for using the main computer tools and telecommunication in specific areas of competence.
The educational path in the first and second year involves attending basic and characterizing courses, particularly in Italian literature, history of the Italian language, general linguistics, ancient and medieval history, classical or Romance and Italian philology, geography; in the third year, courses in modern and contemporary history, contemporary and comparative Italian literature, archaeological and historical-artistic disciplines that better characterize the individual paths are generally provided.
The graduate's formation is adequate and directed towards continuing studies in a master's degree course. The knowledge and applied abilities acquired are, however, useful - in line with the expected professional profile - for entry into professional sectors requiring full command, both oral and written, of the Italian language in its syntactic and grammatical aspects; good command of linguistic and stylistic forms; a solid foundational humanistic and aesthetic education, necessary to competently frame cultural products and services.
Opinions of organizations and companies with internship/curricular or extra-curricular agreements The Letters degree course has long established a system for monitoring and evaluating the internship experience from the perspective of hosting organizations/companies and interns. The goal is to encourage reflection by interns on the experience, highlight how acquired skills have been utilized, how integration into the work context occurred, which abilities were acquired, and, more generally, to comprehensively monitor internships promoted by the degree course. In particular, students who complete an internship present a report on the experience, which is reviewed by the internship service managers.
In recent years, the degree course has held several consultations with representatives of territorial organizations and stakeholders to better calibrate educational objectives in the perspective of the employability of the degree on the job market. The latest consultation took place on March 28, 2023 (see Table A1.b). Overall, the judgment of these operators regarding the structure of the degree course, the offered training, the teaching objectives, and their alignment with the expected occupational outcomes for graduates is very positive; useful indications emerge for making the professional characteristics of Letters graduates better aligned with the needs of the job market, also through specific laboratory activities and an expansion of the space dedicated to internships and stages, aspects particularly valuable in the communication and human resources management sectors; in particular, the need to strengthen students' training in writing and professional writing uses is emphasized, without neglecting information technology skills and knowledge of at least one foreign language at a good level, to make the degree more employable in the local, national, and international job markets. These suggestions have been received by the degree course, which has adjusted the educational offer in response to the needs of the job market. In particular, new courses have been introduced (Italian Grammar and Linguistics, English Linguistics, Fundamentals of Humanistic Informatics) that not only respond to the need to enrich the profile of graduates but also contribute specifically to a better employability of the university degree, enhancing both disciplinary and transversal skills.
The internship assistance service delegate, Professor Antonella Di Nallo, has recently developed new evaluation questionnaires based on the indications provided by the University Quality Office for monitoring internship activities and their alignment with the expected professional profiles. As illustrated in the meeting of March 28, 2023 (see Table A1.b), the results of the questionnaires have highlighted, from students, a strong interest and positive evaluation of the experience, while some questionnaires returned by the conventioned subjects, such as the one from the State Archives of Pescara, indicate a lack of professional writing skills and knowledge of primary sources (specialized directories) among the student interns. It is also noteworthy that the course in Italian Grammar and Linguistics, established on the request of the Steering Committee and stakeholders, received positive feedback. In the same meeting, stakeholders emphasized the need to develop students' information technology skills for the digitization of archival heritage and strengthen basic skills in cataloging and document management.
Considering that approximately 95% of Letters graduates continue their educational path by enrolling in a master's course to acquire the requirements for entering the teaching career, the degree course has considered as stakeholders students, teachers, and the directing structures of the master's course in Philology, Linguistics, and Literary Traditions, as well as representatives of the school world (specifically, directors). For this reason, these actors were invited to meetings and provided useful contributions to refining some educational strategies of the course.
The degree course established a Steering Committee in 2021 with the aim of ensuring systematic and continuous dialogue with the job market and socioeconomic context, at least at regional and national levels, as well as strengthening and promoting an educational offer consistent with societal needs. It currently includes:
Professor Emiliano (Chair of the Letters degree course); Professor Anna Enrichetta Soccio (Chair of the Philology, Linguistics, and Literary Traditions degree course); Professor Antonella Di Nallo (DILASS delegate for relations with stakeholders); Professor Francesco Berardi (DILASS delegate for placement); Professor Pierluigi Ortolano (Letters degree course delegate for relations with the job market); Professor Mario Cimini; Doctor Nina Celli, head of the online platform ProVersi; Doctor Marilena Staniscia, representative of the Carabba Publishing House of Lanciano; Doctor Pietro Lambertini (newspaper "Il Centro"). The Committee meets on average twice a year (for meeting minutes, see https://www.dilass.unich.it/node/9595).
The data on opinions of organizations and companies are discussed in the September 2023 Council.

Entry, progression, and exit data The total number of enrollments for the 2022-2023 academic year (221), including transfers and movements, has confirmed a positive growth trend that has characterized recent years: in 2021-22 there were 214 enrollments, in 2020-21 there were 220. The distribution among paths remains stable, with a prevalence of Modern Letters (150) and the remaining enrollments distributed between Languages of Theater (31), Classical Letters (28, increasing from 16 in 2021-22) and History (22, increasing from 17 in 2021-22). The number of pure enrollments remains stable at 171 (170 in 2021-22), indicating good attractiveness of the course not only in the provincial and regional Abruzzo territory but also in neighboring regions (Molise and Puglia, in particular): the percentage of enrollments from outside the region has shown a positive recovery already initiated last year, moving from 12.83% in 2020-2021 to 16.96% in 2021-2022 to 17.78% in 2022-23. The majority of new students come from classical, scientific, and human sciences high schools (80.5%). The number of students who choose the course with a high school diploma grade above 80/100 remains stable (45 enrollments, including 45 who achieved a final grade of 100 or 100 cum laude); this is undoubtedly an index of the trust that the student population and families place in the course's educational offer.
Regarding the trend of the latest cohort observable (2020), data show a slight decrease compared to previous cohorts. The percentage of students who confirmed enrollment in the second year is 76.6% (compared to 87.7% the previous year); no transfers out for the 2020 cohort. It should be noted that often, rather than dropouts, it is about non-re-enrollments that are later recovered after some years.
The percentage of students who continue to the second year in the same degree course having acquired at least 40 CFU is 36.9% (2020 cohort), in line with the previous cohort. Good is the percentage of acquired CFU / required CFU, which is 51.4% (for 2020) and 58.5% (for 2021), figures substantially stable compared to the previous cohort.
Regarding exit data, the number of graduates has decreased to 94 (110 in 2021, while in 2020 there were 127, but this figure should be viewed in relation to the number of enrollments in previous years); the percentage of students graduating within the normal duration of the course (four years) remains nearly stable at 43 out of 94 (61 out of 127 in 2020, 54 out of 110 in 2021). This is undoubtedly an effect of the long-term impact of the pandemic, as students who graduated in 2021 fully experienced the health emergency period during their studies.
The degree course, however, sets as a priority objective to continue on the path already taken in recent years, particularly by intensifying orientation activities at entry, during the course, and at exit, promoting the internationalization of the offered training, and carefully monitoring student productivity to intervene promptly in situations of greater criticality.
The data on student careers are constantly monitored by the Quality Assurance Group of the degree course and then transmitted to the Council, which discusses them in assembly (starting from the September 2023 council).
Characteristics of the final exam The final exam requires the preparation and presentation of a written exposition, whose topic falls within the scope of a discipline included by the student in their study plan and belonging to one of the scientific-disciplinary sectors present in the Letters degree course framework; connected to the final exam is also the verification of knowledge of a modern foreign language.
To access the final exam, the student must have acquired the number of university credits specified by the teaching regulations, minus those reserved for the final exam. The judging commission uses as reference criteria for evaluation the ability to synthesize, scientific accuracy, coherence of argumentation, and expressive clarity demonstrated by the graduate. It expresses the overall grade out of 110, taking into account the curriculum and the final exam.
Mode of conducting the final exam The final exam for the degree is public and consists of the discussion of a written work, in Italian (other languages are not permitted), on a topic related to a discipline included by the student in their study plan and agreed with the supervisor (a teacher belonging to the scientific-disciplinary sector of the discipline requested by the graduate) at least four months before the graduation session. The student may request to take the final exam in a discipline for which they have taken or validated the exam. The text of the written work should be approximately forty pages (the editorial criteria are indicated by the supervisor as needed). To access the discussion, the student must have acquired the number of university credits specified by the Teaching Regulations, minus those reserved for the final exam. In the graduation session, after a brief introduction by the supervisor, the student will present their work before a dedicated judging commission appointed by the Department Director and typically composed of five members chosen among professors and researchers. The commission awards up to a maximum of 4 points for the final exam, with reference criteria being the ability to synthesize, scientific accuracy, coherence of argumentation, and expressive clarity demonstrated by the graduate in the written work and oral presentation. Students who have carried out study experiences within ERASMUS programs or international agreements activated by the reference department are awarded an additional point. The judging commission expresses the overall grade out of 110, taking into account the curriculum and the final exam, and, unanimously, may award the highest grade with honors. The minimum passing grade for the exam is 66 out of 110. Before accessing the graduation session, the candidate must have passed the verification of knowledge of a modern foreign language.

The course covers a central area in the humanities sector, scientifically and professionally relevant, and consistently positioned at optimal levels, in reference to its class, in terms of enrollments, students, and graduates. The Faculty can rely on a specific teaching staff for basic and characterizing disciplines that is widely adequate. The proposed framework can contribute to the objectives of rationalization and qualification of the university's educational offer.

Access requirements Required knowledge for admission To be admitted to the L23 Bachelor's Degree in Construction Engineering, it is required to hold a secondary school diploma obtained in Italy or another foreign degree recognized as equivalent.
Additionally, a good logical reasoning ability and adequate basic knowledge in scientific disciplines, particularly in mathematics, physics, and materials science, are required.
Students' initial preparation will be verified through an entrance test following the procedures outlined in the Course's Didactic Regulations.
If the verification of the required access knowledge is not successful, additional mandatory coursework will be assigned to be completed in the first year of the course according to the procedures specified in the aforementioned Regulations.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [801T] ENGINEERING OF CONSTRUCTIONS
SECTION: Admission Requirements
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/5

Admission Requirements The STUDY PROGRAM has OPEN ACCESS, therefore no selective verification is required that could prevent enrollment in the program.
A MANDATORY VERIFICATION OF MINIMUM KNOWLEDGE is however required, consisting of the TOLC-I (Test OnLine Cisia for Engineering) test provided by CISIA (Consorzio Interuniversitario Sistemi Integrati per l'Accesso).
The TOLC-I consists of 50 questions, including 20 on mathematics, 10 on logic, 10 on sciences, and 10 on verbal comprehension. An English section is also included, which does not contribute to the final score.
The total time available is 125 minutes.
The TOLC-I can be taken in person (TOLC at the university) or remotely (TOLC@CASA), at any university campus that adheres to CISIA.
For future students of the academic year 2024-25, our University will offer the TOLC-I in person.
Based on the result obtained, an indication of the student's initial preparation level is provided, as specified in the CISIA Guide for Engineering TOLC-I Test.
During registration on the CISIA portal's TOLC area, students can declare to be holders of disabilities or affected by specific learning disorders (DSA) to correctly define the test administration method.
Attribution of Additional Training Requirements (OFA)
For the purpose of the Bachelor's degree program in Engineering of Constructions, the TOLC-I is considered fully passed if a score of at least 8/20 is achieved in the Mathematics Section and at least 4/10 in the Sciences Section.
If the threshold scores are not achieved, Additional Training Requirements (OFA) are assigned in the insufficient areas.
OFA may consist of individually assigned training activities or other recovery training activities organized by the Study Program on basic notions of the relevant fields.
OFA will be considered fulfilled upon successful completion of the corresponding assessment.
OFA will also be considered fulfilled once at least 18 ECTS credits are acquired in the first-year exams of Mathematical Analysis, Physics, or Materials Science.
Until OFA are fulfilled, it will not be possible to take exams from subsequent years.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI/PESCARA GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO
COURSE: [801T] CONSTRUCTION ENGINEERING
SECTION: Program, texts and objectives
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/5

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The ability to communicate information, ideas, problems and solutions to interlocutors who are not specialists is essential for the effective integration of graduates into the building construction world. It is therefore important for graduates to possess appropriate tools for communicating the results of their work. The degree course will therefore provide all the tools to develop students' communication skills, both written and oral, also in a foreign language, and communication through graphic representation, as well as through the use of computer and telecommunication tools.
These objectives will be pursued in lectures and practical exercises by requiring students to present both oral and written, computerized versions of their work and contributions, also using audiovisual means, particularly in preparing the documents for the construction site.
Assessments of communication abilities will take place in final exams and in specific intermediate assessments, also of a seminar nature.

TYPE:
CURRICULUM:
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/5

Judgment Autonomy (making judgements)
The graduate must possess, at the end of the study course, their own autonomous capacity for judgment regarding decisions to be made in the management of operations transforming the built environment; they will therefore have the ability to collect and interpret data considered useful for determining autonomous judgments, including reflection on social, scientific or ethical issues related to them. To achieve this judgment autonomy, the degree course will provide both technical-scientific tools and socio-cultural knowledge to stimulate the capacity for critical processing at an individual level.
The objective of fostering the formation and growth of judgment autonomy, and stimulating the capacity for individual critical processing, will be pursued in both theoretical and application-design courses. Judgment autonomy will also be encouraged through the study of projects in which the student will be stimulated to develop critical spirit and make reasoned decisions, both individually and in work groups.
The assessment of the achieved capacity and judgment autonomy will be carried out progressively in the examinations, also through the figure of the Tutor, who will follow the evolution of the individual formation process.
