Final Exam Characteristics According to Article 7 of the Interministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, the final exam, with the value of a qualifying State exam - ex Article 6 of Legislative Decree No. 502/1992 and subsequent amendments - consists of:
a) a practical exam during which the student must demonstrate acquisition of theoretical-practical knowledge, technical, and operational skills specific to the professional profile;
b) preparation and defense of a thesis.
The exam is organized nationally in two defined sessions, established by MIUR decree and in the presence of MIUR, Ministry of Health, and IPASVI representatives.
Final Exam Execution Modalities FINAL EXAM MODALITIES The student has 6 CFU available for preparing the final exam and thesis, distributed between the 2nd (2 CFU)* and 3rd year (4 CFU) of the course. Exam sessions are established, as per MUR, in October/November (autumn session) and March/April (extraordinary session), according to a calendar determined within the teaching programming. In the 2nd semester of the 2nd year, the student contacts the thesis supervisor to complete a graduation internship, presents to a commission (composed of three teachers and pre-appointed for approval) the thesis title and topic and the name of the thesis supervisor. The thesis title deposit form must be submitted to the student office within 12 months for experimental theses and 6 months for compiled theses. The certification of credit achievement is issued by the Course President and Teaching Director. The role of a Correlator may be provided.
The Correlator role is provided, a Teacher or Tutor with recognized academic competence, who may, on the proposal of the Supervisor, be listed in the work and participate in the Commission's proceedings, but cannot contribute to the graduation grade.
To be admitted to the graduation exam, the student must:
a. have passed all exams specified in the study plan, at least 30 days before the graduation session date, and in particular for the extraordinary session, by February 28;
b. have completed and passed the annual clinical internship exams;
c. have submitted the graduation application to the Rector through the student office within the deadlines indicated by the student office;
d. have submitted a copy of the thesis on paper/informational support.
The final exam commission is composed of not less than 7 and not more than 11 members appointed by the Rector on proposal of the Course Council and includes at least two members designated by professional colleges. A representative of the Ministry of Health is present, with the role of external supervisor.
The exam structure includes:
1. a practical qualifying exam to evaluate technical skills in performing nursing procedures, holistic approach in patient care, and global ethical-behavioral aspects in prevention, care, and assistance areas, through the extraction of a clinical case. The verification is based on the evaluation of knowledge and applied understanding, autonomy of judgment, and communication skills (Dublin Descriptors 2, 3, 4: Knowledge and Applied Understanding; Autonomy of Judgment; Communication Skills);
2. preparation and discussion of a theoretical-applicative (compiled) or experimental thesis. To discuss the thesis, the student must have passed the final practical exam in the same session.
The final graduation grade, expressed in 110/110, is determined by:
- the average in 110/110 of the exam grades, integrated with the following evaluations:
  the score given by the Commission on the methodology, presentation, and discussion of the thesis, with a maximum of 4 points for both compiled and experimental theses.
  a maximum bonus of 4 points from the practical exam, distributed through the following score ranges:
  score between 18 and 20, 0 points
  score between 21 and 25, 1 point
  score between 26 and 28, 2 points
  score between 29 and 30, 3 points
  Honors, 4 points.
  a bonus of 2 (two) points for participation in the Erasmus Project, with a stay of at least three months.
* The final exam of the Nursing Course, pursuant to Article 7 of the Interministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, has the value of a qualifying exam for the nursing profession and consists of a practical exam and the preparation and defense of a thesis.
The purpose of the thesis is to engage the student in a design and research or in-depth work on specific nursing areas through the analysis and synthesis of relevant bibliographic sources.
Since the study plan provides 2 CFU in the second semester of the second year for presenting the final project, all students are dedicated two hours, embedded in the second-year second-semester teaching calendar, during which all indications and information for preparing a thesis meeting criteria of originality and scientific rigor are provided. During the meeting, guidelines (appropriately published on the Course website, on the page dedicated to the final exam) elaborated by the Course Quality Group for thesis preparation are proposed and deepened, with explanations and examples; all formal steps, also in terms of timing and prerequisites, that the student must respect until the day of the defense are explicitly shared; relevant international bibliographic databases for searching and identifying nursing-related sources are again shared.
Students are met again approximately two months before the thesis defense to, while sharing their work with the supervisor, present the state of the art of their work and receive clear indications on how to revise it, especially regarding source citation in the text body and construction of the final bibliography. Additionally, suggestions are provided on how to design presentation slides to fully highlight the effort put into the final thesis and meet the Commission's expectations. Finally, since the defense day inevitably brings anxiety and concern, simple advice is given on how to face and manage them in the best way.
FNOPI DOCUMENT - FEBRUARY 3, 2020
The Course Council President received the document, dated February 3, 2020, proposed by FNOPI to ensure uniformity in conducting the final exam and the role of representation by the Ordinal Body. FNOPI (National Federation of Nursing Professional Orders) has drafted the GUIDELINES FOR CONDUCTING THE FINAL EXAM OF NURSING AND PEDIATRIC NURSING DEGREE COURSES, with the contribution of referents of the Central Committee, members of the FNOPI Observatory on Training and Research, and external experts from the academic world, to highlight the contribution that OPI representatives act as Commissioners in conducting the State Exam. The document is based on national guidelines for the final exam of Nursing and Pediatric Nursing Degree Courses and on current regulations.
Below is the text of the document:
'FINAL EXAM COMMISSION The final exam commission is composed of not less than 7 and not more than 11 voting members, appointed by the Rector on proposal of the Course Council.
Two members of the commission with voting rights are designated by the provincial OPIs of the territorial reference, taking into account possible different territorial locations of the Course, communicating the names to the University according to the times and methods provided by their respective regulations.
Professional Representatives of the Orders who are part of the Commission must be of the same professional profile (i.e., Nurses for the Nursing Course, Pediatric Nurses for the Pediatric Nursing Course), preferably in active service.
The Ministries of Education, University, and Research and Health may send their experts as representatives to individual sessions.
They oversee the regularity of the exam, signing the minutes. In case of failure to designate the aforementioned members, the Rector may exercise the substitutive power.
Normally, the Commission includes Directors of Professional Teaching Activities/Professional Teaching Coordinators and University Teachers of SSD MED/45 as per the Permanent Conference guidelines.
These guidelines require that the Commission be dedicated, stable, and ensure continuity for the entire final exam.
PRACTICAL EXAM The Permanent Conference document provides that in the practical exam, competencies resulting from Dublin Descriptors 2, 3, and 4 are evaluated:
2. knowledge and applied understanding - applying knowledge and understanding,
3. autonomy of judgment - making judgments,
4. communication skills - communication skills,
and, in particular, the ability to identify problems, make decisions on professional issues, identify priorities for individual patients, groups, or work processes, plan and decide interventions based on available evidence and organizational conditions, act safely, consider ethical, deontological, and legal dimensions in one's actions; demonstrate orientation towards interprofessional practice, evaluate effects on patients.
The document also provides that the modalities of conducting the practical exam may include one or more modalities from the following:
- structured, semi-structured, or open-ended written test on paradigmatic cases/situations of professional practice.
- oral interview with discussion of cases or an elaborated project.
- observation of professional skills (e.g., technical, relational, diagnostic, planning) in real clinical contexts, simulated laboratory contexts, or with video support - structured clinical skills examination (OSCE).
According to the indications provided jointly by MIUR and the Ministry of Health (Circular of September 30, 2016), the exam may be conducted in two alternative modalities:
a) practical simulation, structured to allow the graduate to demonstrate acquisition of knowledge and practical, technical, and relational skills;
b) exam with closed and open-ended questions on clinical cases or paradigmatic situations of professional practice.
The above modalities may be integrated with an interview if the Commission deems it appropriate.
Written exams with quiz evaluations of only theoretical knowledge are not considered valid.
The minimum performance level expected in the practical exam to be considered passed is 60%.
The modalities of practical exams are normally indicated in the Course Academic Regulations and in the SUA Sheet to ensure wide and widespread communication to students, Orders, and stakeholders to reinforce the sharing of exam modalities and content.
The exam must:
a) Be based on the selection of 'core' competencies expected from a graduate. Such competencies are normally identified with professional representatives (L.3/2018 art. 3 comma f) and services;
In particular, it is necessary to select nursing competencies ensuring:
? a balanced sampling of competencies to be evaluated so that they are exemplary of the expected practice, avoiding emphasis on details;
? high relevance to priority health issues selected based on the following criteria: relevance, prevalence, severity, treatability, pedagogical exemplarity, interdisciplinary contribution;
? adequate contextualization in different general practice settings, with particular attention also to territorial, community, and residential services.
b) Be standardized, exposing each student:
? to the same level of complexity;
? to an exam where the outcome measurement is predefined and shared by the Commission to reduce variability in evaluators' judgment.
c) Refer to scientific sources, evidence-based guidelines, and updated texts.
d) Be anonymous, when possible.
THESIS The thesis allows verification of the achievement of competencies indicated in Dublin Descriptor 5, i.e., the student's ability to conduct an autonomous and methodologically rigorous learning process. The purpose of the thesis is to engage the student in a design and research or in-depth work on specific nursing areas through the analysis and synthesis of relevant bibliographic sources. The thesis content must be related to nursing and disciplines covered in the study plan. Normally, the student will have the supervision of at least one supervisor chosen according to the University regulations.
Evaluation System The final graduation score is expressed in 110/110 with possible honors and is formed by the arithmetic or weighted average (according to the University regulations) of the grades obtained in the profit exams, including the three internship exams, scaled to 110, and the sum of the evaluations obtained in the final exam (practical exam + thesis), which contribute to determining the final grade.
The practical exam with applicative value is a barrier: in case of insufficient evaluation, the candidate cannot proceed with the thesis discussion. Therefore, the exam must be repeated in the next graduation session.
Both parts of the single final exam contribute to determining the final grade. The Permanent Conference guidelines recommend valuing the exam with a maximum of 10 points (5 for the practical exam and 5 for the thesis defense).
The Commission may award additional points up to a maximum of 2 in total to candidates who have received honors in teaching profit exams and/or have participated positively in Erasmus/Socrates Programs and are in regular course.
Generally, it is suggested to consider the minimum average of 110/110 of the student's career as the basis for awarding honors.
Recommendations to Nursing Professional Orders It is recommended to:
a) Identify a group of professionals possible Representatives of the Commission,
nurses with an adequate curriculum (preferably holding a Master's Degree in Nursing and Midwifery or a Master's):
not involved as Teachers or Teaching Tutors in the training of students at the location where the qualification exam will be held;
who share the vision expressed by FNOPI regarding Nursing and Pediatric Nursing. For this purpose, specific initiatives for training on the role of OPI representative, the objectives and characteristics of the final exam are recommended.
b) Communicate to the Course the professionals identified to create collaboration and participation in training or design initiatives;
c) Promote initiatives of collaboration with Directors of Professional Teaching Activities/Professional Teaching Coordinators of the reference universities to share the vision of Nursing and Pediatric Nursing, and the competencies expected from the new graduate;
d) Activate strategies for comparison between Nursing Orders within regional coordinations on competencies, methodologies, and tools adopted at the local level in final exams;
e) Participate actively and contribute to the evaluation during the exam session;
f) Elaborate constructive feedback to be analyzed and discussed with Course Council responsible regarding the modality, level required, congruence with core competencies, and outcomes of the practical exam to activate improvement strategies;
g) Ensure transmission to FNOPI of the number of graduates/number of candidates, type of exam, areas of competence verified.
To Directors of Professional Teaching Activities/Professional Teaching Coordinators of Courses Referring to what elaborated by the Permanent Conference of Health Degree Courses, it is necessary to:
a) Emphasize the importance of the final exam, its purpose, and specificity compared to internship exams, recalling its relevance throughout the entire training path.
b) Offer a preparation path for the final exam, making the expected standards transparent and providing guidelines/documents of direction.
c) Promote an adequate distance between the practical exam and the thesis discussion to ensure appropriate information on the outcome, which is a prerequisite for continuing the final exam.
d) Ensure timely feedback on areas of competence not achieved in the qualification exam and accompany preparation for the next exam.
e) Promote initiatives of collaboration with the Nursing Professional Orders of reference to share the vision of Nursing and Pediatric Nursing, the competencies expected from the new graduate, and discuss periodically the outcomes of the exam to activate improvement strategies.
f) Activate strategies for comparison with neighboring Course Councils at provincial and regional level to harmonize the final competencies expected from the new graduate.
g) Activate systematic comparisons with Directors of Nursing Services to develop integration policies, acquire data useful for monitoring the final exam and evaluated competencies, and their effectiveness in job placement.
h) Systematically evaluate the success and failure ratio in the final exam, also in relation to the performance achieved by students in clinical internships.'

Access Requirements Required knowledge for admission Candidates who hold a five-year secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as suitable, and who have achieved a qualifying position in the admission ranking, may be admitted to the Dental Hygiene Bachelor's Degree program, in accordance with current national regulations for admission to programs with limited enrollment. The number of students admitted to the first year is determined annually by the competent authorities based on national programming, available facilities, and teaching staff. Admission to the Bachelor's Degree program takes place according to modalities defined by the Ministry of Education, University and Research (MIUR) and consists of multiple-choice quizzes on Logic and General Culture, Biology, Chemistry, Mathematics, and Physics.
For admission to the Bachelor's Degree program, students must possess adequate prior preparation from previous studies, particularly in Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, Physics, Logic, and General Culture.
The required knowledge for admission will be verified through the national entrance examination for programs with limited enrollment.
The Bachelor's Degree program will also include a verification of the student's adequate preparation according to modalities defined in the Study Program Didactic Regulations. In case of verified deficiencies, students will be assigned additional educational obligations to be fulfilled within the first year.
Admission Modalities The number of students admitted to the Bachelor's Degree program is programmed annually based on the actual availability of human resources, teaching and support staff, suitable facilities and equipment (classrooms, laboratories for practical exercises and biomedical research simulations), services, and operational units in hospital structures and territories affiliated with the National Health Service, as determined annually by the Ministry through a specific decree. Admission modalities for the Bachelor's Degree program will be specified in the University's competitive call.
Students admitted to the program who score below 25% of the maximum score in Biology, Chemistry, Mathematics, and Physics in the entrance test will be assigned additional educational obligations (OFA). They will be informed via email and direct meetings about the deficiencies in their preparation and the activities provided to support their recovery.
Completion of OFA involves the assignment of individual seminar-style training activities for each discipline in which the student showed deficiency, to be carried out during the first semester of the first year.
Verification of results achieved in the preparatory training activities will occur within the evaluation of integrated courses that include the SSDs where OFA were assigned. Additionally, pursuant to Article 49, paragraph 3, point b of the University Didactic Regulations, students who have not fulfilled the additional educational obligations as specified in Article 28 of the Study Program Didactic Regulations cannot enroll in second-year courses. Therefore, while enrollment in the second year is permitted, it will not be possible to take second-year exams before fulfilling the assigned OFA.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI/PESCARA GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate must establish and maintain a relationship with the user, starting from prevention, taking into account the various levels of complexity related to it. This constitutes the foundation of professional practice, which must be centered on the individual, respecting individual differences and considering their influence on dietary habits related to oral health, lifestyle, and the individual's own habits.
The dental hygiene graduate:
- will interview patients for needs assessment;
- will carry out their activity in accordance with the principles of patient/user-centered professional practice;
- will build a relationship/partnership as the foundation of oral hygiene intervention;
- will employ a variety of personalized strategies based on the patient's needs;
- will develop education programs and educational materials to meet the learning needs of individuals and groups.
Graduates must be particularly skilled in interpersonal communication, including oral and written communication with professionals and service users, in group work, and within interdisciplinary work groups with health and social professionals.
To achieve this, the dental hygiene graduate must:
- select appropriate communication methods;
- identify and recognize communication barriers (problems reading or writing, misunderstanding, cultural issues, fear, etc.);
- adapt to a communication style suitable to meet the needs and learning capabilities of individual persons and/or groups;
- employ effective verbal communication skills;
- write clearly, concisely, and professionally, technically and grammatically accurately;
- build educational material taking into account the comprehension ability of the target group and/or individuals;
- facilitate communication in both directions;
- employ active listening techniques;
- interpret and respond to non-verbal communication;
- apply principles of collaboration and negotiation in group work;
- incorporate the knowledge, experiences, and skills of other group members during their activities;
- collaborate with other group members to define objectives;
- adapt their personal approach to group members and situations involving the work group;
- work with other group members to identify and resolve conflicts;
- contribute to decisions made within the work group;
- assume responsibility for completing the assigned task.
Communication skills will be acquired through the teachings of human sciences, psychopedagogical, and sociological disciplines to ensure the learning of necessary behavioral and relational competencies to operate in a complex work environment. Additionally, the internship involves close contact between the student and patients under the supervision of tutors, whose task will be to modulate the approach methodology from the initial phase to the completion of professional training.
Communication skills will be verified by tutors during the related teaching activities, during the internship, and through evaluations of teaching activities, up to the final exam.
Graduates must be able to communicate information, ideas, problems, and solutions to both specialist and non-specialist interlocutors.

Judgment autonomy (making judgements)
Graduates must have the ability to collect and interpret data (typically within their field of study) deemed useful for determining autonomous judgments, including reflection on related social, scientific or ethical issues.
The Dental Hygiene graduate:
-Must be able to independently manage non-surgical periodontal disease treatment and caries prevention, always under the direction of a Dentist or other qualified professionals.
-Must be able to evaluate the effectiveness of the treatment plan, implemented interventions, and achieved results.
-Must be able to recognize their own limitations in patient care and recognize the need to refer the patient to other competencies for dental-rehabilitative or medical therapies.
Graduates' judgment autonomy will be expressed through the recognition and ability to autonomously assess issues related to the patient's condition, in relation to oral hygiene aspects and prevention of dental pathologies, and in developing practical and/or experimental prevention schemes, and in choosing optimal methodologies, strategies, and possible use of equipment to achieve expected results, also through critical review of information obtained via bibliographic and/or computer research.
The development of these abilities will occur and be verified during internships, where encounters with people, professionals, structures and different methodologies will facilitate the development of independent critical thinking. Equally important will be active participation in lectures, preparation for exams and the final exam, further moments of development and verification.
Knowledge of relevant regulations, professional, legal, and health regulations and their subsequent application will be aimed at achieving specific professional competencies, i.e., the ability to master and manage independently and/or in teams procedures, technologies and acts.
Acquiring a behavior consistent with ethical foundations will be one of the objectives that will complete the educational path.
Judgment autonomy will be verified through evaluations by assigned tutors, through internship exams, and through verification related to the final exam.

ALMALAUREA Data Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
Dental Hygiene graduates must be able to independently organize the knowledge and operational techniques acquired for the practice of the profession of Dental Hygienist.
In particular, graduates must:
- recognize, at the level of the oral cavity, clinical signs of local and systemic pathologies, as well as typical morphological-functional aspects of oral and dental health;
- be able to recognize vital signs and perform first aid maneuvers in the workplace;
- be able to perform the full range of operational procedures specific to the professional profile;
- be able to control cross-infection in the practice of the profession;
- know and apply anti-smoking counseling techniques (brief intervention), patient motivation techniques for home hygiene, periodic professional check-ups, and rational dietary habits aimed at protecting oral health;
- know how to interact with other members of the dental team: dentist, dental office assistant, administrative staff.
Teaching tools aimed at achieving the ability to apply knowledge within the core activities include, in addition to the overall teaching activities directed at students (lectures, self-learning, etc.), individual bench pre-clinical activities and clinical internships with patients.
Other fundamental tools will be the use of information technology, consultation and/or construction and updating of databases, bibliographic research, use of textbooks, and preparation of the final thesis.
These skills will be assessed through exams, periodic practical evaluations within internship activities aimed at verifying the acquisition of manual and technical-operative skills in various clinical activities specific to the professional profile, and through the final exam itself.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
Dental Hygiene graduates must possess the ability to update theoretical knowledge through consultation and analysis of scientific publications in Dental Hygiene Sciences, also using online databases.
Graduates must achieve sufficient methodological knowledge and skills to continue their academic and cultural development independently (Specialist Degree, University Advanced Courses, University Master's Degrees).
Graduates must be able to correctly interpret the legislation concerning the practice of the Dental Hygienist profession in the European Union country where they practice and carry out professional activities in compliance with the applicable medical-legal and ethical standards in the country of practice.
The ability to learn is assessed through continuous verification during training activities, integrating knowledge acquired during specific activities with those gained through personal study, evaluating the critical contribution demonstrated during seminar and clinical internship activities, as well as through the assessment of the ability to self-learn developed during the final thesis (final exam).
Graduates must have developed the learning skills necessary to pursue further studies with a high degree of autonomy.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
Dental Hygiene graduates must acquire post-secondary level knowledge in the fields of basic biomedical disciplines and clinical disciplines, manual skills, and operational techniques, necessary for the practice of the Dental Hygienist profession.
In particular, a Dental Hygiene graduate must:
- possess knowledge of the fundamentals of human morphology, physiology, and pathology;
- know the main disease patterns and complementary medical and surgical therapeutic procedures relevant to the Dental Hygienist profession;
- understand the effects of pharmacological therapy for systemic diseases on oral health and any implications for therapeutic procedures specified in the professional profile;
- know the demographic aspects, prevention, and treatment of oral and dental diseases in pediatric, adult, and geriatric age groups, including in medically compromised or physically/mentally disabled patients.
The aforementioned knowledge is acquired through basic and core activities. The teaching method includes lectures, laboratories, exercises, and clinical internships.
Verification methods are based on oral interviews, written assignments, and, where required, practical tests on simulators and patients.
Graduates must know how to use the specific language of Dental Hygiene Sciences.

Brief Course Description The Dental Hygiene Course (enabling the healthcare profession of Dental Hygienist, Degree Class L/SNT 3 for Healthcare Technical Professions) aims to train healthcare professionals in the technical-diagnostic and technical-assistive areas who, in accordance with Article 3 of Law 10 August 2000, No. 251, independently perform technical procedures necessary for diagnostic methods on biological materials or on individuals, or technical-assistive activities, in line with regulations defining professional figures and their profiles established by the Minister of Health's decree.
The Course was activated in the academic year 2008-2009 (Regulation 509) by Rectoral Decree No. 116 of November 26, 2008, in accordance with Article 6 of Ministerial Decree No. 509 of November 3, 1999. In the academic year 2011-2012, the first year of the Course was activated in accordance with Ministerial Decree 270/2004 and subsequent implementing decrees. The Course lasts three years and is divided into six semesters; the first year is dedicated to basic training activities, while the following two years are characterized by core and integrative training activities. The acquisition of scientific and technical competencies and specific professional skills is measured in University Credit Units (CFU), totaling 180 CFU over three years, including 60 CFU of Professional Practical Internship (1,500 hours total, supervised by a Tutor, where students work directly with patients to acquire necessary manual and technical skills) and 6 CFU of Optional Teaching Activities. To achieve these educational goals, the three-year Course with programmed access (multiple-choice test) includes both basic disciplines (biology, anatomy, chemistry, physics, human physiology) and professional disciplines (periodontology, pediatric dentistry, oral surgery, oral medicine).
To be eligible for the final exam, which requires 3 CFU for English language knowledge and 6 CFU for thesis preparation and discussion, students must pass all exams specified in their Didactic Program.
The final exam is equivalent to a state exam, enabling the practice of the profession.
The degree qualifies graduates for enrollment in Master's Degree programs in the Class of Healthcare Technical Professions (LM/SNT 3), without academic debts, as well as Level I Master's Degrees and Advanced Courses.
The Dental Hygienist is a healthcare professional trained to work within the dental team. They play a crucial role in maintaining oral health and general population health. Their primary task is to prevent and treat gum diseases through therapies that remove bacterial plaque and subgingival calculus, providing instructions for maintaining good oral hygiene. Additionally, they reduce childhood cavities by applying special sealants on teeth and decrease dental sensitivity through appropriate procedures involving fluoride-based products. They also contribute to overall health by providing dietary advice aimed at reducing sugar consumption to prevent cavities, as well as addressing issues like obesity or metabolic diseases such as diabetes. An important aspect is their anti-smoking activities, as smoking is responsible for dental discoloration, oral mucosal diseases, and is a leading cause of cardiovascular disorders and many cancers.
External Effectiveness The Interuniversity Consortium ALMALAUREA conducted a survey on the employment status of Dental Hygiene graduates; the data provided, updated to 2022, is based on 13 out of 15 graduates who obtained their academic degree in the calendar year 2022. The responses revealed the following situation:
76.9% found employment within one year of obtaining their degree, with 100% of these individuals utilizing their acquired skills extensively. The average net monthly salary is 1,764.
The data confirms that university education is highly effective for entering the workforce, with graduates typically entering the job market within the first six months after obtaining their degree.
ALMALAUREA Data Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description Within the Dental Hygienist healthcare profession, graduates are healthcare professionals entitled to the duties specified in Ministerial Decree No. 137 of March 15, 1999, and subsequent amendments, performing preventive activities for oral diseases under the direction of Dentists and Medical Surgeons authorized to practice dentistry. Dental Hygiene graduates perform dental health education activities and participate in primary prevention projects within the public healthcare system; they collaborate in compiling dental and oral clinical records and collect technical-statistical data; they perform tartar removal, root planing, and application of topical preventive measures; they provide instruction on various oral hygiene methods and the use of diagnostic tools to detect bacterial plaque and dental film, motivating the need for periodic clinical check-ups; they recommend dietary guidelines for protecting dental health.
Dental Hygiene graduates possess adequate foundational knowledge to understand the most relevant elements underlying pathological processes developing in pediatric, adult, and geriatric age groups, which form the focus of their clinical interventions. They must also be able to use at least one European Union language, in addition to Italian, within their specific field and for general information exchange.
The teaching structures identify specific training paths for this profession through the appropriate selection of disciplinary areas within core training activities, with particular attention to professionalizing scientific-disciplinary sectors.
Professional competencies are achieved through a structured theoretical and practical training program that, in the first three semesters, acquires the necessary basic knowledge, followed by the acquisition of specific professional competencies in the subsequent three semesters.
It is specified that specific professional competencies will be acquired through both traditional lectures and specific activities conducted within the professional internship, which thus assumes equal importance to theoretical training.
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Practical Training Agreements The Review Group aims to establish contacts with local public bodies, professional associations, and school districts to integrate these figures into public dental hygiene prevention.
Additionally, the Course will propose to the Department of Medical, Oral, and Biotechnological Sciences, where it is based, the activation of post-graduate courses, particularly update and specialization courses aimed at deepening knowledge and innovative technologies for both new graduates and those who graduated in previous years, especially for holders of the previous regulation diploma enabling the practice of the profession.

Following negotiations with social partners on February 16, 2018, within the National Commission for Dental Hygiene Courses, the following decisions were reached and approved as follows:
- On February 16, 2018, following email agreements (February 9, 2018) between Dr. Michela Rossini, Vice-President of the National Commission for Dental Hygiene Courses, and the Presidents of AIDI and UNID, the National Commission for Dental Hygiene Courses executive board and Dr. Antonia Abbinante, President of AIDI, and Dr. Maurizio Luperini, President of UNID, met in Rome during the Listerine Award Congress to evaluate proposals for improving professional teaching activities. Specifically:
1. Whether the functions and competencies characterizing the Dental Hygienist professional profile are adequately described, thus providing a clear basis for defining expected learning outcomes;
2. Whether the specific expected learning outcomes are consistent with the general ones prescribed by the regulation, ensuring that graduates' preparation meets the broader needs of society and the labor market (training demand). Both association representatives confirmed, as in the June 2017 meeting, that the functions and competencies characterizing the Dental Hygienist professional profile are adequately described, providing a clear basis for defining expected learning outcomes; the specific and general expected learning outcomes are consistent with professional needs, and graduates' preparation meets society's and the labor market's broader needs.
It is reiterated that teaching qualifications for Healthcare Professions courses must be respected, and the inclusion of Dental Hygienists in territorial healthcare structures must be supported. The Presidents of AIDI and UNID agree that MED/50 subjects and internships must be managed by Dental Hygienists, not by Dentists or other medical figures not belonging to the professional profile. Regarding the June 2017 meeting, where the proposal for category association representatives to participate in annual internship exams was discussed, it is agreed that the second-year internship exam is ideal and functional, as the first year is too early for proper evaluation and the third year is less useful due to subsequent professional licensing exams. The proposal remains to be further defined and will be the subject of future consultations.

Characteristics of the Final Exam The final exam consists of two sequential phases:
- The first phase involves performing specific professional techniques typical of the Dental Hygienist profession.
- The second phase consists of presenting a written summary of the three-year academic journey.
The purpose of both phases is to verify the acquisition of specific theoretical-practical professional skills necessary for practicing the profession.
Final Exam Execution Method The final exam, equivalent to a state exam enabling professional practice, is conducted in two sessions, as prescribed by Ministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, further clarified by the Ministry of Health/MIUR circular (0046319-P-30/09/2016). Specifically, the latter note reiterates that the final exam, a single exam, consists of two distinct moments: the thesis presentation and a practical test.
The final exam is conducted in two sessions: the first, typically in October/November, is the Regular session; the second, in March/April, is the Extraordinary session. The final exam will cover:
a. A practical test where the student must demonstrate acquisition of theoretical, practical, and technical-operative knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile. This test may involve performing specific professional techniques on a selected patient, or, in the absence of suitable patients or at the committee's discretion, a practical test on a mannequin, communicated to candidates in advance;
b. The preparation and presentation of a thesis, under the supervision of a Course professor (Supervisor), and possibly external co-supervisors.
The thesis aims to engage the student in formalization, planning, and research, substantially contributing to the completion of their professional and scientific training. The thesis content must relate to themes or disciplines closely connected to the Dental Hygienist professional profile. Thesis evaluation will be based on the following criteria: level of depth and scientific relevance of the work, critical contribution of the graduate, accuracy of the methodology used, and presentation/discussion of the thesis.
The final exam grade, expressed in hundredths, is determined by summing the following parameters:
a) The weighted average in thirtieths of the grades obtained in curricular exams (Integrated Courses, Professional Internships, A.D.O., and other activities specified in the study plan);
b) Points assigned by the Committee for the Laboratory Test: 18/30 to 21/30 = 0.50 points; 22/30 to 24/30 = 1 point; 25/30 to 27/30 = 1.50 points; 28/30 to 30/30 = 2 points;
c) Points assigned by the Committee for the thesis discussion (from 0 to a maximum of 5 points, for both experimental and compilation theses).
The highest honor (summa cum laude) may be awarded, with the Committee's unanimous decision, to graduates achieving a final score of at least 110.
Students may submit the thesis in English. The deadline for submitting the graduation application and related documentation will be indicated in the notices on the Course's website.
The Final Exam Committee consists of at least 7 and no more than 11 members, appointed by the Rector on the Course Council's proposal, including 2 members designated by the professional association, selected from their members.
The dates of sessions are communicated in advance to the Ministries of University, Scientific Research, and Health, which may send experts as representatives to individual sessions. In case of failure to designate the aforementioned members, the Rector exercises the substitute power. The President of the Committee is the Course Director, who may appoint a substitute from among the Course's permanent professors in case of absence. The Committee composition cannot change during the two evaluation phases, except in cases of serious impediments requiring substitution by a pre-appointed alternate.

The Course covers a clearly relevant professional area. The proposed regulation appears significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, contributing to the University's goals of rationalizing and qualifying its educational offerings.

Program, texts and objectives Communication Skills
The graduate at the end of the study path must be able to manage communication effectively, understood as the ability to establish a meaningful therapeutic relationship with the person and to establish an effective relationship with all other professionals from the same or other disciplines; they must also be capable of using communication tools in the healthcare context, demonstrating the ability to complete the physiotherapy chart, draft a therapeutic report, design a physiotherapy intervention, etc., communicating clearly, concisely, and professionally in both spoken and written form, technically and grammatically accurate, and able to translate technical language into understandable terms for non-specialists; they must be able to communicate appropriately in international scientific contexts to convey ideas, problems, and related solutions.
Teaching tools: classroom activities, simulation laboratories, internship.
Assessment methods: written reports on the communication aspects of the rehabilitation setting; briefings with tutors and the coordinator; oral and written presentation of projects; internship.

CURRICULUM: CURRICULUM
SECTION: JUDGMENT AUTONOMY
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/611

Judgment autonomy (making judgments)
The graduate at the end of the study path will be able to:
- use communication and therapeutic relationship skills, also non-verbal, with people of all ages and their families, and establish an effective relationship with other health professionals;
- adapt communication according to context and respect cultural, ethnic and value differences of the people assisted; communicate appropriately in national and international scientific contexts to convey ideas, problems and related solutions;
- communicate clearly, concisely and professionally in verbal and written form, technically and grammatically accurate, also knowing how to translate technical language in a comprehensible way for patients and the team;
- listen, inform, dialogue effectively and understandably with patients and families, communicate, argue and justify one's actions and decisions with colleagues and different professional figures.
The graduate's judgment autonomy will be fully realized through the habitual and judicious use of communication, knowledge, technical skills, clinical reasoning (diagnostic and evaluative process), emotions, values, and reflection in daily practice for the benefit of the individual or the community.
Teaching tools: frontal lectures in classroom, teaching laboratories, practical lectures in laboratory and/or equipped classrooms, internship, reading and interpretation of international literature.
Assessment methods: written and oral reports on technical/professional aspects, discussion of clinical cases, definition of rehabilitation project/program and completion of physiotherapy and/or rehabilitation file on real clinical cases; practical demonstration of planning and execution of specific maneuvers and techniques.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA

SECTION: Graduate Opinions
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/611

Graduate Opinions According to data available on the Alma Laurea website, it is evident that in 2022, 29 students obtained the Bachelor's Degree in Physiotherapy at our University, and 86.2% of them responded to the Alma Laurea questions.
Graduates in 2022 are predominantly male (60%) with an average age at graduation of 25.6 years. Over 50% of graduates (52%) reside outside the region, highlighting the constant high attractiveness of the Physiotherapy Degree Course. The high school diploma continues to be the most represented pre-university education among graduates (64%), although it shows a decline compared to 2012 (64% vs 87.8%), while the percentage of technical diplomas increases (36% vs 12.2%). The choice of the Degree Course is primarily driven by cultural and professional factors (60%). The average exam score (27.6) improves compared to the previous academic year (28.1 vs 26.7); similarly, there is an increase in the average graduation score, which rises from 111.1 in 2021 to 112.3 in 2022. 88% of graduates completed curricular training internships, but only 36% had work experience during their university studies, making this cohort predominantly focused on studies, as highlighted by their excellent performance.
84% of the considered cohort attended more than 75% of the required courses, with the majority (68%) considering the study load appropriate for the duration of the Study Course, thus confirming the overall good organization of the Physiotherapy Study Course (CdS), although this figure is lower than that observed for the University (89.4%). 16% of the cohort considered the exam organization (appeals, schedules, information, reservations, etc.) always or almost always satisfactory; this figure shows a decline compared to the previous academic year. 8% considered the exam organization never or almost never satisfactory, thus registering an improvement in this parameter.
During the 2021-2022 academic year, the CdS, following a proposal from the GAQ, implemented initiatives to improve the organization of exam sessions to avoid overlapping appeals and to increase the number of available exam sessions for students. Over 90% of the appeals for the first year of the course were scheduled without overlapping dates and times, with slightly lower percentages recorded for the second and third years.
Although the majority of interviewed graduates (84%) are satisfied with their relationships with professors in general, unfortunately, there is a lower appreciation for the University's Study Courses (CdS). This data, which contradicts the high attractiveness of the CdS and the high employment rate one year after graduation, merits discussion in a future CdS Council to identify improvement strategies. Most students (62.5%) highlighted the inadequacy of computer workstations. Regarding this, the Presidency Office reiterated the request to the Medical School for the creation of computer classrooms and equipped study rooms for individual study at the CUMS branch campus and obtained the allocation of an 80-seat classroom to accommodate the increased number of first- and second-year students. The current cohort is also quite critical of the job placement office/services, remaining largely dissatisfied with the support services for job searching.
24.1% of the interviewed cohort would enroll again in the same Degree Course, compared to 68% who would enroll in the same course at another University, showing a negative trend compared to the previous year.
In conclusion, the Degree Course confirms its attractiveness for students motivated by cultural and professional factors. Moreover, the regularity of studies (demonstrated by the high percentage of students enrolled: 80%), the high average exam and graduation scores confirm the quality of the Degree Course. The main criticisms concern the availability of classrooms, teaching equipment, and computer workstations. These points will be further discussed in upcoming Degree Course Councils and Quality Group meetings to collaboratively identify improvement solutions, which will necessarily involve the University Governance.
Learning Skills
Graduates in Physiotherapy will be able to:
- conduct a self-assessment of their educational level to maintain their knowledge at the highest level required for professional practice;
- design self-training paths to enhance their skills, particularly focusing on Evidence-Based Practice in rehabilitation and physiotherapy;
- develop competent and independent problem-solving abilities, demonstrating the capacity to continuously seek opportunities for self-learning;
- take responsibility for their professional development and respond to the continuous changes in knowledge and healthcare and social needs.
Over the three years of the course, they will acquire learning skills and competencies that will allow, at the end of the program, the continuation of studies through a Master's Degree in Class LM/SNT/02, scientific specialization courses, and permanent and recurring advanced training (1st and 2nd level Master's, specialization courses), update and in-depth courses (Continuing Medical Education) with a high degree of autonomy. This skill will be developed and verified through exam preparation, attendance and evaluation of the internship, where theory is combined with practice, through the critical use of scientific literature and bibliography for final exam preparation.
Teaching tools: classroom activities, seminars, simulation laboratories, internship.
Assessment of learning skills will be carried out through the following verification methods: theoretical-practical exams, written and oral reports on technical/professional aspects, discussion of clinical cases, definition of rehabilitation project/program and compilation of physiotherapy and/or rehabilitation records for simulated and real clinical cases; research and production of teaching materials.

Short Course Description The Physiotherapy Study Course is a three-year, limited-enrollment degree course aimed at training healthcare professionals who, in accordance with the Ministry of Health Decree of September 14, 1994, No. 741, perform prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation interventions in the areas of motor skills, cortical functions, and visceral functions resulting from pathological events of various etiology, congenital or acquired. Physiotherapy graduates are adequately prepared in basic disciplines, enabling them to best understand the key elements underlying pathological processes on which their rehabilitation and/or therapeutic interventions focus, in pediatric, adult, and geriatric age groups, as well as to collaborate maximally with doctors, physiatrists, and other graduates of the class or other classes in the technical-health area. They must also be able to use at least English, in addition to Italian, within their specific area of competence and for general information exchange. Physiotherapy graduates, in reference to the doctor's diagnosis and prescriptions, within their scope of competence, develop, also in multidisciplinary teams, a rehabilitation protocol aimed at identifying and overcoming the health needs of patients with disabilities; provide functional rehabilitation for motor, psychomotor, and cognitive disabilities using physical, manual, and occupational therapies; propose the use of prostheses and aids, train patients in their use, and verify their effectiveness; verify the alignment of the implemented rehabilitation methodology with functional recovery goals; conduct research, teaching, and professional consulting activities in healthcare services and those requiring their professional skills. The achievement of professional competencies is achieved through theoretical and practical training that also includes the acquisition of specific behavioral skills of the profile, thus ensuring, at the end of the training course, full mastery of all necessary competencies and their immediate application in the workplace. The physiotherapist performs their professional activity in healthcare facilities, public or private, in a dependent or self-employed capacity.
External Effectiveness Regarding those employed one year after graduation, data from the Alma Laurea website shows that only 15 of the 30 graduates from 2021 were interviewed. The one-year employment rate is 84.6%, a figure that, although high, shows a decline compared to the previous cohort (96.6%) and the same course at other universities (91%). The 15.4% who have never worked after graduation include 7.7% of graduates who are not working or seeking work, being engaged in another course or internship/practicum. Notably, 90.9% (vs 75% of the previous cohort) of graduates who continued the work started before graduation have noted an improvement in their work due to the degree, attesting to the educational effectiveness of the Physiotherapy CdS. Consistent with this data, 100% (vs 97.1% of the previous cohort) of graduates consider the degree very effective in their work, with an average satisfaction score of 7.8 (scale 1-10). The net monthly salary of a physiotherapist one year after graduation is 1251 €. No gender differences are evident in the Alma Laurea sheet. Overall, it is noted that the improvement strategies implemented by the CdS GAQ have led graduates to a higher level of satisfaction with the CdS. Only a small percentage prefers to continue post-graduation education rather than entering the workforce.
Reasons for Establishing More Courses in Class L The establishment of more courses in the class was requested by the regional administration.
Specific Educational Objectives of the Course and Course Description In line with Article 6, paragraph 3, of Legislative Decree December 30, 1992, No. 502, and subsequent amendments, in accordance with Law February 26, 1999, No. 42, and Law August 10, 2000, No. 251, the specific educational objective of the course is to train graduates suitable for the healthcare profession. The Physiotherapy graduate, at the end of the training course, having acquired knowledge, skills, and communication abilities, has the following abilities:
a) define and plan the physiotherapy intervention. The area that translates the professional's assumption of responsibility in all professional actions.
The graduate at the end of the three-year course is able to:
- involve the patient by requesting active participation and informing them of the sequence of the physiotherapy course;
- identify problems and the related physiotherapy goals to be achieved, progressively setting them in therapeutic steps;
- identify possible preventive, educational, and therapeutic interventions;
- formulate physiotherapy proposals to the team for defining the rehabilitation project goals for the patient;
- participate in planning educational-informative interventions by suggesting activities focused on managing the person and self-care for patients and families.
b) manage one's work considering goals and priorities. The area that translates the physiotherapist's skills and knowledge.
The graduate at the end of the three-year course is able to:
- correctly perform functional assessment;
- formulate the functional diagnosis;
- define goals and evaluate their achievement by measuring the outcomes of the physiotherapy intervention;
- perform physiotherapy treatment;
- choose physiotherapy proposals in relation to the presence of any comorbidities;
- prepare the setting to implement the physiotherapy intervention;
- use aids/orthoses to facilitate functional abilities;
- maintain a growing and continuous process of collaboration, in the care process, with the patient and/or family and/or caregivers;
- verify and evaluate the results obtained;
- verify interim results of the physiotherapy proposal in collaboration with other professionals;
- document professional acts and activities performed.
c) management. The area that translates the physiotherapist's knowledge regarding resources, information, and economic aspects.
The graduate at the end of the three-year course is able to:
- understand the essential management tools for correctly implementing daily actions in the physiotherapy field, using appropriate tools such as acting according to quality criteria, managing privacy and clinical risk, making decisions after implementing a correct problem-solving process;
- ensure a rehabilitation path based on efficacy evidence, aiming to provide an effective, useful, and economically sustainable service.
TRAINING PATH: The courses (Integrated Courses) are structured into modules and are conducted through frontal lectures, classroom or laboratory exercises, and elective and student-choice activities. Learning outcomes are assessed through in-course self-evaluation tests for the student and a final oral or written exam, an opportunity to verify the achievement of the intended goals, unique and simultaneous for each integrated course, necessary for acquiring educational credits. Learning outcomes of laboratory courses, English, and the first-year internship result in a pass. The total knowledge acquired by the graduate is 180 CFU, consisting of 96 frontal teaching, 60 clinical professional internship, and 24 teaching activities (other, optional: language, thesis preparation). These are essential to form the necessary cultural, scientific, and relational background to acquire full professional competence and to understand, address, and manage pathological events requiring rehabilitation and/or therapeutic intervention in all age groups. Specifically, the training path includes disciplines represented by the Basic Scientific Disciplinary Sectors such as:
- BIO/10, BIO/12, BIO/13, MED/03, BIO/09, BIO/16, BIO/17, MDEA/01, MPED/01, MPSI/01, SPS/07, SPS/08, INF/01, MED/01, FIS/07, ING-INF/06, aimed at acquiring a solid foundation of knowledge of the integrated biological aspects and functions of human organs and systems, statistical methodology for detecting phenomena regulating individual and social human life, and concepts of emergency and first aid preparation for the characteristic disciplines of the CdL. Specific professional training is realized through the Characteristic Scientific Disciplinary Sectors such as:
- MED/48, MED/34, MED/33, MED/09, MEDF/01, MED/10, MED/36, MED/38, MED/39, MED/50, MED/12, MED/26, IUS/10, IUS/07, MED/44, which allow for specific professional training and the learning of fundamental concepts of human sciences and behavior, ethics and professional deontology, pathophysiology of physical activity and locomotor system diseases, physiotherapy methodologies and techniques, disease etiology and pathogenesis, pathology and clinical practice, person treatment, neurological diseases and sensory organs, and reproductive and maternal-infant medicine, as well as management and operational elements useful for professional development in work contexts.
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Training Agreements The CdS has established agreements with numerous rehabilitation structures to optimize the professional training of Physiotherapy CdS students across the Abruzzo region and nationally. The currently active agreements have been established with the following structures: Pescara and Chieti ASL, Don Orione Institute Pescara, Paolo VI Foundation Pescara, Villa Serena Clinic Pescara, Sant'Agnese Rehabilitation Center Pineto, Santa Camilla Clinic Chieti. To support and assist students during the training path, the CdS has a Professional Teaching Coordinator, Clinical Tutors, and Teaching Tutors distributed nationwide based on the students' regions of origin. The number of professional tutors and agreements with structures outside the region has recently been increased. To collect the opinions of entities and/or companies that have hosted students for internships, the CdS has established a dedicated Committee (Tutor Committee, CdS Council of October 14, 2021) to prepare a student evaluation form from all partner structures. The form is currently in the distribution phase. Overall, despite not yet having objective data, based on positive verbal feedback from Tutors, the continuous renewal of agreements, and the constant increase in requests for agreements from new structures, we believe the CdS has a good impact on the territory and the quality of student training.
Consultation with Representative Organizations - at National and International Levels - of Goods and Services Production, Professions (Course Establishment) The Physiotherapy Study Course consults with: the representative organizations of professionals AIFI (category organization: Italian Physiotherapists Association) and FIF (Italian Physiotherapists Federation). This consultation has been codified since 2007 and includes:
1. the convocation and presence of a category representative at graduation sessions;
2. the presence of a category representative within the tutor training group;
3. the presence of AIFI and FIF clinical tutors.
AIFI and FIF professional representatives have expressed full agreement with the identified educational objectives for the Physiotherapy Study Course planning, as they are relevant to the professional profile; satisfaction with the emphasis on professional internship and professional teaching, and appreciation for the involvement of faculty from the SSN.
Consultation with Representative Organizations - at National and International Levels - of Goods and Services Production, Professions (Subsequent Consultations) The Physiotherapy Study Course, already modified based on the reform of the regulations under Ministerial Decree No. 270 of October 22, 2004, and submitted to consultation, which was positive during the accreditation phase with national professional representative organizations, as provided for in Article 11, paragraph 4 of the aforementioned Decree, enables graduates to perform professional activities in the sector specified by law. This consultation led to the drafting of a plan that defines the course's educational objectives in relation to their relevance to the legal professional profile. Consultation with representative organizations is normally conducted annually before the start of the new Academic Year and/or during Tutor Committee meetings and/or graduation sessions. The Physiotherapy Study Course has long-term consultations with the representative organizations of professionals AIFI (category organization: Italian Physiotherapists Association) and FIF (Italian Physiotherapists Federation), and more recently with the newly established Order of Physiotherapists (FNOFI). These consultations include:
1. the convocation and presence of a category representative at graduation sessions;
2. the presence of a category representative within the tutor training group;
3. the presence of AIFI and FIF clinical tutors.
During these occasions, the representative organizations expressed full agreement with the identified educational objectives in the Physiotherapy Study Course design, as they are relevant to the professional profile; satisfaction with the emphasis on professional internship and professional teaching; appreciation for the involvement of faculty from the SSN. In recent years, due to the hiring of faculty belonging to SSD MED/48, teaching assignments to specialized figures and physiotherapists have gradually decreased, a criticality that often emerges during meetings and more or less formal discussions with social partners. Considering the outcomes of ongoing interactions with interested parties in a systematic manner, also for the periodic updating of educational profiles, the CdS has implemented improvement actions by modifying the didactic regulations and planned educational offerings for the academic years 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25, reducing the number of modules, increasing the number of CFU for basic and characteristic disciplines fundamental to the professional profile (Human Anatomy, etc.), and organizing external seminars, professional workshops, ADE, and Physiotherapy area courses. To make meetings with representative organizations more formal and periodic, the CdS has recently established the Steering Committee, including CdS faculty, professional figures, student representatives, and social partners. Faculty, students, and technical-administrative staff can easily submit their observations and improvement proposals by interfacing directly with the CdS President and/or during CdS Council meetings. The CdS systematically analyzes and considers the results of opinion surveys from students, graduates, and alumni, and gives credit and visibility to the overall considerations of the CPDS and other AQ bodies. The CdS President and Secretary have excellent relationships with students, allowing for easy and direct management of student complaints. Through the periodic GAQ meetings (composed of the President, Vice President, two clinical area faculty, and the student representative), the CdS systematically analyzes the identified problems, their causes, and defines improvement actions where necessary. In recent years, the GAQ has promoted initiatives to rationalize teaching schedules, internships, and exams to alternate lecture periods with training internship periods and to avoid overlapping exam sessions. The CdS also:
- systematically analyzes the results of learning assessments and the final exam to improve student career management;
- systematically analyzes and monitors the employment outcomes (short, medium, and long term) of CdS graduates, also in relation to those of the same class at national, macroregional, or regional levels;
- defines and implements improvement actions based on the developed analyses and proposals from various actors in the AQ system, monitors their implementation, and evaluates their effectiveness.
All CdS activities are reported in the minutes of the CdS Councils, GAQ meeting minutes, SMA, and SUA-CdS.
Entry, Progression, and Exit Data In the 2022/23 academic year, the Physiotherapy CdS had an increase in enrolled students compared to the previous academic year (76 vs 67 students), reaching a total of 221 students, of which 206 are enrolled, representing 93.2% of students, a figure in line with the previous year (94%). Over 85% of enrolled students come from outside the region, confirming the ongoing attractiveness of the CdS, significantly improving the percentage from previous years (52% and 65.2%). The majority of enrolled students (76%) have obtained a high school diploma, while 12% come from technical institutes, 5% from magistral institutes, and the remaining 7% from other types of schools. The diploma grade was 100 with honors for 3 enrolled students and 100 for 16 enrolled students, between 80 and 99 for 60 students, and up to 80 for the remaining 35 students, testifying to a good cultural starting level. In the calendar year 2022, 29 students obtained the degree with a grade equal to or above 105/110. In particular, 21 students (67.7% of graduates) achieved a grade of 110/110 with honors (a significant increase compared to the previous two years: 54.4% and 39.3%), 3 students achieved a grade of 110/110, while the remaining 7 students, 22.6%, achieved a grade of 105/110, indicating an excellent cultural and educational level achieved at the end of the study path. 71% (slightly decreased compared to the previous cohort) obtained the degree within the 3-year course, while 16.1% took one additional year, and 12.9% took more than two years, slightly increased compared to the previous cohort. Overall, there is a slight decrease in the percentage of enrolled graduates (81% vs 71%): this data will be discussed by the GAQ and CdS to identify solutions with the support of CdS faculty, particularly teaching tutors. A significant increase in enrollments, particularly from students outside the region, demonstrates the ongoing attractiveness of the CdS, especially for students from high schools.
Final Exam Characteristics The final exam, with the value of a State Exam enabling the profession of Physiotherapist (D.Lgs 502/1992, Article 6, Paragraph 3), consists of:
a) a practical test during which the student must demonstrate having acquired the theoretical-practical and technical-operative knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile;
b) preparation of a research thesis and its dissertation.
The final score is expressed in hundredths. If a total score of 110/110 is achieved, the President of the Final Exam Commission puts the awarding of honors to a vote, which can only be assigned unanimously by those present in the Commission. The final exam results in the attribution of 5 CFU.
Final Exam Procedure To be admitted to take the Final Exam, the student must:
a) have attended all Integrated Courses and passed the respective exams;
b) have obtained, in total, 180 CFU structured over the years of the Study Course;
c) have passed (minimum grade 18/30) the mandatory professional training internship;
d) have submitted the thesis request to the Student Secretariat and uploaded an online copy of the Thesis by the indicated deadlines.
The student, to be able to discuss the Thesis, must have passed (minimum grade 18/30) the practical exam enabling the profession, scheduled in the same session that also includes the Thesis dissertation. The Thesis assigned by the Supervisor and approved by the CdS President must be related to the topics covered in the Supervisor's course. The role of the Co-Supervisor is provided for.
The following parameters contribute to determining the graduation grade, expressed in hundredths:
1) the average in thirtieths (then converted to hundredths) obtained from the thirtieth grades achieved in the Integrated Courses' exams and the evaluation of the mandatory internship;
2) points assigned by the Commission to the Practical Exam (from 18/30 to 24/30 = 0 points = pass; from 25/30 to 27/30 = 0.5 points; from 28/30 to 30/30 = 1 point; 30/30 with honors = 1.5 points);
3) points assigned by the Graduation Commission during the Thesis discussion, corresponding to the average of individual scores assigned by the Commissioners up to a maximum of 7 points:
- research type (experimental study; compilation study): maximum score 4 points;
- quality of presentation: maximum score 1 point;
- mastery of the topic: maximum score 1 point;
- ability in discussion: maximum score 1 point.
4) years of graduation: 1 point for graduates in course;
5) number of honors obtained in exams: 0.1 points per honor;
6) involvement in international programs of minimum duration of three months: yes = 0.5 points; no = 0 points.
Honors can be awarded with the unanimous opinion of the Commission to candidates who achieve a final score > 111. The use of any teaching aids (slides, projections, PowerPoint presentations, etc.) should be considered as support for the graduate to better understand the presentation, therefore should not contain purely discursive parts but graphs, figures, and tables, and may be prepared in English. The Thesis dissertation takes place in the presence of the Thesis Supervisor and the Co-Supervisor, while the Graduation Commission President acts as the Counter-Supervisor. The Graduation Commission is composed of 2 external category representatives, a minimum of 5 to a maximum of 9 Faculty members of the Degree Course, and the Delegate of the Ministry of University and Research. The Final Exam is only conducted in Italian.
Summary of the Technical Report of the Evaluation Committee The study course has teaching and structural resources commensurate with the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The course covers an area of certain professional relevance. The proposed organization appears significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, contributing to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the University's educational offer.

Admission requirements Required knowledge for admission For admission to the Bachelor's degree course - Education track - students must possess adequate general culture and basic knowledge required by the secondary school curriculum of any secondary school or other foreign degree recognized as suitable. The Bachelor's degree includes specific training activities for acquiring basic knowledge related to education and training sciences, particularly aimed at students who did not complete such activities in secondary school. The verification of the required knowledge for admission will be carried out through a multiple-choice test (and/or other type of assessment) for students enrolled in the Education track, non-selective, on general culture content, on basic disciplinary content required by any secondary school curriculum, and on basic knowledge of the disciplines characterizing the Bachelor's degree course. Negative verification results do not prejudice the possibility of enrolling in the course. Specific additional activities are provided for the recovery of any educational deficits in the disciplines characterizing the Bachelor's degree course, to be followed in the first year of the course to support regular training activities. For admission to the Bachelor's degree course - Philosophy track - students must possess adequate general culture and basic knowledge required by the secondary school curriculum and certified by the corresponding Italian degree, or by another foreign degree recognized as equivalent. At the beginning of the study course, the possession and extent of basic philosophical knowledge within the required general culture will be verified, particularly through an interview and/or written test. An unfavorable verification result does not prejudice enrollment in the course. In case of total absence or insufficiency of even minimal basic philosophical culture, specific additional teaching activities on the disciplines characterizing the Bachelor's degree course will be offered, which the student must follow to support regular training activities.
