Reasons for establishing multiple courses in the class
The course, compared to others activated in the same class, is able to provide a diversified and flexible training, ensuring mastery of fundamental analysis tools, as well as well-characterized professional skills, especially oriented towards understanding and governing the main issues of growth and development models. Particular attention is paid to the role of markets, regulations, and Agencies and Entities for development promotion, as well as to financial services markets for the functions supporting the real economy; diversification is evidenced by the presence of numerous disciplines not found in other Bachelor's Degree courses related to the same class L-33, exceeding the required differentiation requirement of at least 40 CFU.
Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description
The Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets Bachelor's Degree aims to provide training for understanding the functioning of modern economic systems through the acquisition of methodologies and tools used by decision-makers in different business contexts, as well as to provide the necessary knowledge for understanding the functioning of markets with specific (but not exclusive) reference to financial markets, through the study of methods and processes used by intermediaries, particularly banks and insurance companies.
Training activities aim primarily at students learning the logic and tools necessary for implementing decisions by different actors operating in the real and financial sectors. In particular, the Course of Study provides a training offer aimed at acquiring fundamental knowledge to operate in public and private companies, banks, and other financial intermediaries.
The course offers students a broad training, covering around a core of economic-quantitative disciplines, the essential methodological aspects of business, legal, historical, and political-institutional subjects. This training is aimed at ensuring students acquire all necessary analytical tools for understanding the basic mechanisms regulating the operations of public and private companies, financial intermediaries, and markets on which different economic agents interact.
The Course of Study provides adequate training for those aiming to work in business management and financial management, as well as at financial market intermediaries.
More specifically, the Course of Study:
- Provides tools to understand business operations, focusing on interactions between decisions made at the company level and the functioning of markets on which companies operate;
- Allows acquisition of necessary skills to make rational decisions in different economic contexts, such as production sectors, financial markets, and institutional systems, providing appropriate tools to identify and handle data supporting decisions and measure their impacts;
- Develops the ability to analyze economic problems from an interdisciplinary perspective, based on economic-financial, managerial, legal, statistical-mathematical, historical, and political-institutional competencies.
The Course of Study was designed to train junior professionals capable of addressing typical issues of business realities operating in both the real and financial sectors of the economy, thanks to the use of main explanatory and interpretive models of market functioning and their growth dynamics. The broad training ensures the ability to analyze both macro and micro and sectoral aspects, as well as to understand the role of public and private entities guiding growth and development processes and the role of financial institutions supporting these processes within the rules established by national and international regulators. At the same time, the training path provides the foundation for accessing a master's academic path, not only in the same fields as the three-year course but also in socioeconomic development programming and its management.
The interdisciplinary approach of the Course of Study will also allow addressing the complexity of territorial governance combined with socioeconomic development sustainability. Indeed, to ensure the adequacy of decision-making processes, the Course of Study allows acquisition of indispensable knowledge of organizational structures and legal institutions influencing economic choices and behaviors in general and financial markets in particular.
Opinions of organizations and companies with internship agreements
The data still refers mainly to students enrolled in the Economics, Markets and Development Course who can carry out internships at entities contracted with the University for training purposes consistent with the CdS training path, and with entities and companies directly contracted with the CdS.
Based on the single agreement between the CdS and the Host Entity, the internship is based on a training project defining the location, duration, objectives, methods, and obligations of the intern. Each intern is assigned an internal tutor (a CdS professor) and a company tutor. The duration of the curricular internship is set at 125 hours (5 CFU) for students in the 2020.21 cohort and 150 hours (6 CFU) for students in the 2021.22 cohort.
At the end of the internship period, the company has always submitted a final report. To allow a more comprehensive assessment of the student's activities, the CdS approved on November 27, 2019, an analytical form that the company tutor must return at the end of the internship; on January 28, 2020, the same form was approved for interns.
In the 2022/23 academic year, 30 agreements were activated, 33 training projects with 28 interns.

Consultation with representative organizations of goods and services production, professions (Course establishment)
The new structure of the CdS Didactic Ordinance is the result of a consultation process initiated with stakeholders represented in the Steering Committee, established on October 11, 2018, and was presented and discussed in the same Committee at the meeting on January 14, 2021.
In previous meetings (October 11, 2018, February 11, 2019, and November 6, 2019), stakeholders emphasized the opportunity to include in the training path content directly usable in the workplace, to provide acquisition of IT and/or language skills, to increase laboratory and seminar activities conducted by representatives of the business world and professions, and to increase the CFU allocated to training internships. Among the rationalization interventions suggested during the meetings, the possibility of modifying the course name to make it fully consistent with the training offer content was also proposed.
At the Steering Committee meeting on January 14, 2021, proposals for modifying the Didactic Ordinance to improve the CdS training offer were presented, discussed, and shared. In particular, the modifications concerned, besides expanding some ranges of basic activities, a detailed intervention on related activities and a corrective intervention on other activities.
Regarding the name change, the Committee proposed to submit a name containing, besides the term Economics (which distinguishes class L33), the expression Enterprises from which it can easily be inferred that the business phenomenon is studied from an economic, financial, and managerial perspective, and the term Markets, denoting the objective of providing students with knowledge and tools to analyze and understand different market structures, their functioning, and evolutionary dynamics, and their placement within an institutional framework.
At the Economics, Markets and Development Bachelor's Degree Course Council meeting on January 21, 2021, all proposals for modifying the Ordinance were approved. Regarding the new name, the Council decided to complete it by adding the term Financial to Markets. In this way, emphasis is given, also in the course name, to one of the most relevant profiles in the study of different markets and which in the training offer is the subject of in-depth study, without neglecting other specific production sectors (particularly related to tourism and cultural and creative activities, in line with the Steering Committee's suggestions).
The name Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets replaces the previous name Economics, Markets and Development for which the Consultation Committee on Didactic Ordinances met on March 1, 2013, in the presence of: Prof. Carmine DI ILIO (Rector), Prof. Anna MORGANTE (Dean of Economics Faculty), Prof. Riccardo PALUMBO (Deputy Dean of Management Sciences Faculty), Prof. Ezio SCIARRA (Chair of Social Services Bachelor's Degree, Faculty of Social Sciences), Dott. Ermando BOZZA (Chair of Commercialists' Order LANCIANO), Massimo D'ONOFRIO (Vice Chair of Commercialists' Order), Dott. Silvano PAGLIUCA (Delegate of Industrial Union PE), Dott. Marina DI IORIO (Chair of Social Assistants' Order Reg.), Dott. Paolo PRIMAVERA (Chair of Industrial Union CH), Dott. Domenico DI MICHELE (Chair of Commercialists' Order PE), Dott. Below are summarized the results of the Steering Committee meetings over time.
On October 11, 2018, the Steering Committee for the Bachelor's Degree Course in 'Economics, Markets and Development', L33, was established, in the presence of the following participants: for the CdS: Prof. Paola Nardone, Chair of the Bachelor's Degree Course, Prof. Gianfranco Giulioni, Chair of the Master's Degree Course, Prof. Rita Martella, Head of the Quality Assurance Group, Prof. Natascia Ridolfi (CdS Teacher); for territory representatives: Dott. Alessandro Felizzi (President of FIRA, Chartered Accountant), Dott.ssa Liliana Marcella (Administrative Manager of BLUSERENA Spa, Chartered Accountant), Dott. Dino Salese (Administrator of DOA Consult), Dott. Enzo Stellabotte (Federmanager Abruzzo and Molise); for student representatives Valentina Pirovano (CdS representative).
Prof. Paola Nardone presented the essential characteristics of the Bachelor's Degree Course and emphasized that the CdL in Economics, Markets and Development, established in the 2013/14 academic year, has a stable number of enrollments, if not slightly increasing (303 enrollments in 2017-2018, of which 271 in course and 32 out of course), compared to the average for CdLs of the same L-33 class in the South of Italy and Italy, which is slightly lower. Therefore, the Economics, Markets and Development CdL does not have an attractiveness problem but must perhaps consider how to differentiate itself from other first-level CdLs of the Economic Sciences class (L33) and how to meet the training needs of a labor market in continuous evolution at global and national levels, tending to stagnate at the local level.
All stakeholders unanimously agreed that it would be appropriate to include in the training offer, possibly as optional courses, courses focused on certain specializations, such as the tourism-hotel sector and the agri-food sector. In any case, it was emphasized that courses, besides offering content, should aim to train students, preparing them for entry into the workforce. For this purpose, it could be useful to organize meetings with operators where students learn to create a CV and face a job interview. Mr. Felizzi, President of FIRA (S.p.A. a public capital company of the Abruzzo Region), hopes for an increase in laboratory and seminar activities conducted by representatives of the business world and professions (ALL. Unico,1/a).
Subsequently, on February 11, 2019, a meeting was held at the initiative of the Chairs of the Bachelor's and Master's Degree Courses to monitor the reference context of the Economics, Markets and Development Course and identify potential sectors of expansion where the professional figure the CdS aims to train could find opportunities, with the following participants: Prof. Paola Nardone, Chair L-33, Prof. Gianfranco Giulioni, Chair LM-56, Prof. Nicola Mattoscio, General Director of Fondazione Pescarabruzzo, Prof. Rita Martella, CdS Teacher, Dott. Dino Salese (Administrator of DOA Consult), Dott. Enzo Stellabotte (Federmanager Abruzzo and Molise).
Mr. Salese proposed conducting a survey on training needs for the tourism-hotel and agri-food sectors of Abruzzo, involving individual companies, consortia, and sector associations, to verify the current state of organizational development of companies in these sectors, the professional figures present, their training methods, and the training needs perceived by the companies themselves to better manage their business strategies. The University can use the collected information to better design and direct its training offer, making it more aligned with specific sector/filiera needs, as well as to play a facilitating role in the development of entire sectors (ALL. UNICO 1/b).
On November 6, 2019, the Committee met again. The Chair spoke to illustrate events since the last meeting and the current state of the CdS, and the intention to propose to the Council for the 2020.21 academic year some modifications to the Didactic Regulation to correct some issues that emerged over the years. In particular, it is considered appropriate to include an English language course, to adjust the placement of some disciplines in the years, and to increase the number of CFU dedicated to internships, following the indications from the previous Steering Committee meeting. During the discussion, the opportunity to create more opportunities to bring students closer to the world of work was highlighted, and the invitation to observe the markets of more developed geographical areas, which can provide guidance for anticipating, in the design of training activities, the changes in the labor market of the reference context (all. 1.c.).
On January 14, 2021, the Steering Committee met to discuss modifications to the Didactic Ordinance and the change of the Course name.
At the Economics, Markets and Development Bachelor's Degree Course Council meeting on January 21, 2021, the Steering Committee was integrated with the following stakeholders:
Dott. Felice Simonelli, Senior Research Fellow and Head of Policy Evaluation and Project Development at CEPS (Centre for European Policy Studies)

Subsequently, the Steering Committee met on December 22, 2021, jointly for the Bachelor's and Master's Degree Courses to discuss proposals for revising the Master's Degree Ordinance through a comprehensive evaluation of both paths.
On March 28, 2023, the Committee met jointly again; the CdS Chair presented some modifications to the training offer following the arrival of some business area teachers in the department. Numerous reflections emerged during the discussion regarding a comprehensive evaluation of both paths. Among these, Mr. Massolo emphasized the need for practice to support the good theoretical training offer and to give more publicity to our CdS; Mr. Scamuffa highlighted that the path is well projected towards the future as it opens to digital transition and even if we want green/ecological, which are priorities in Bank of Italy policies and international monetary policies; Mr. Salese emphasized the importance of intercepting the demand from the change in organization of public institutions (municipalities, etc.) that face huge difficulties in finding graduates capable of handling and managing public accounting; and Mr. Stellabotte invited to develop the necessary skills to manage EU PNRR funds, as many funds return because Italy lacks the skills to organize their use.

The Course Chair, after illustrating the characteristics of the study course, highlighting content, educational objectives, and purposes, focused on the positive enrollment trend over the three years of the Course's existence, which was established starting from 2013/14. In particular, it was noted that the number of enrollments for the 2013/14 academic year was 46, for 2014/15 was 110, and for 2015/16 (partial data) was 112. The evident success of the enrollment performance demonstrates the significant appreciation the didactic project has received so far. It was also added that the evaluation of the Course of Study expressed by students themselves is very high. The Chair then proceeded to illustrate the proposal to modify the Ordinance, consisting of including History of Economics (SECS-P/12) among the related courses. This is deemed appropriate to enrich the training path with basic knowledge of economic models in their historical experimentation, as prototypes for normative and prescriptive study. All consulted parties emphasized appreciation for the results achieved by the CdS three years after its establishment, sharing the choice to enrich the Ordinance with the inclusion of History of Economics among the related courses. The consultation concluded at 11:00.

- Of the 53 enrolled in 2020, 32 students renewed their enrollment in 2021 (6 explicit withdrawals, 14 non-renewals, and 1 transfer out) and 25 in 2022 (with a transfer, 2 withdrawals, and 4 non-renewals).
- The average number of exams passed per student is 2.92 in 2020, 5.28 in 2021, and 6 in 2022 (this data is partial as the academic year is not yet closed).
- The percentage of CFU acquired compared to required CFU is increasing annually: 41.7% in 2020, 64.8% in 2021; in 2022 (academic year not yet closed), it currently stands at 74.9%.
From data provided by the Quality Office regarding 'Co-hort Analysis 2021/2022 - First-year enrollments and progression to second year', it results that 64.29% (previous year 62.75%) of students continue to the second year having acquired, for 36.90% (previous year 35.21%), more than 40 CFU, for 38.10% (previous year 37.25%), less than 20 CFU, and for 26.19% (previous year 23.53%), are completely inactive.
Finally, it results that students have acquired 45.95% (previous year 44.41%) of CFU, compared to required CFU.

Final Exam Characteristics
The final exam, considering its role in training, consists of verifying knowledge and skills within one or more disciplinary fields provided in the Course of Study Ordinance. The Didactic Regulation will specify its modalities.
Final Exam Execution
To obtain the three-year Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets Bachelor's Degree, the student, after passing all exams provided in the study plan, including those related to autonomously chosen training activities, and after acquiring credits for other training activities (laboratories and/or training internships), must also cover the credits assigned to the final exam, whose objective is to evaluate the ability to correctly apply economic reasoning and methodological and professional tools acquired during the study path.
The final exam, which provides for the attribution of 3 CFU, consists of the approval by the supervisor of a written work on a specific topic related to one of the course's teachings. The topic of the work must be agreed upon by the student with the professor designated as supervisor.
The evaluation of the work, which can, upon favorable opinion of the Course Council, be written in a foreign language, is carried out by a Commission appointed by the Head of the Competent Department, whose composition is regulated in the University's Didactic Regulation (Article 37).
The Graduation Commission is normally composed of seven members, but at least five, appointed by the Department Head. The Graduation Commission, after acquiring the documentation related to the candidates' curricula and assigning the graduation grade in hundredths, proceeds to the proclamation.
The details regarding the form and consistency of the work, the modalities of the final exam, the scores assigned and related criteria, the Commission composition, and the admissibility of languages other than Italian are described in the Course's Didactic Regulation.

Admission requirements Required knowledge for admission To be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree course, one must hold a five-year secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent, or a four-year secondary school diploma plus the corresponding supplementary year.
Additionally, for admission to the Economics and Management Bachelor's Degree:
- Verbal and linguistic skills for understanding, processing, and presenting texts in Italian;
- Basic knowledge of English;
- General culture enabling understanding of socio-economic phenomena;
- Logical and deductive skills;
- Basic mathematical and computer science knowledge.
As provided in Article 6 of Ministerial Decree 270/2004, verification of these knowledge and skills is conducted through an entrance test, carried out according to criteria established annually by the University and indicated on the Course website. The test aims to assess students' initial preparation in the following areas: ability to understand written texts; mathematics; logic.
In case of failure or non-attendance at the test, the student is assigned an Additional Mandatory Training (OFA), to be completed within the first year of the course, according to the procedures set forth in the Course's Academic Regulations.

Admission Procedures All students who pass the entrance test, written, typically held by September 30 according to the criteria defined by the University, are admitted to the first year of the Economics and Management degree course. The test requires achieving a minimum score of 10 to pass. Students can practice the test in the "Practice" section of the website www.cisiaonline.it.
In case of failure to pass or not taking the test, students may enroll but will be assigned an Additional Educational Obligation (OFA), in accordance with Article 28 of the current Academic Regulations. The verification of OFA fulfillment occurs through the acquisition, by September 30 of the following calendar year, of at least 18 CFU related to exams for basic or characterizing courses of the first year of the study plan. Failure to fulfill the OFA by the deadline will prevent students from taking exams in the second and third years unless they have earned the required 18 CFU. Therefore, for students assigned an OFA, it constitutes a prerequisite for all exams in the second and third years.
Transfers, course changes, and single exam admissions are subject to approval by the Course Council. The Council may grant full or partial recognition of the student's previous academic record, including validation of completed exams and acquired credits, and specify the year of study at which the student is enrolled and any OFA to be fulfilled.

Communication Skills
The activities contributing to the educational path are designed to encourage active student participation and the development of appropriate communication skills. Graduates in Economy and Management acquire the following general and specific skills in the business context, as well as interdisciplinary skills in the economic, legal, and quantitative fields:
- ability to express concepts and argue both generally and in reference to business situations;
- ability to communicate effectively and comprehensively, particularly in business situations and problems, using appropriate communication and representation technologies;
- ability to express main concepts in a second language (English) acquired through specific training activities and verified through the relevant exam.
To this end, in addition to the internship report and final exam, discussions, seminars, and presentations of business cases, empirical investigations, and documents produced by domestic and international economic and financial institutions are scheduled within some courses, either individually or in groups. The Study Course also promotes and encourages student participation in mobility programs to foster the development of appropriate communication skills in an international context. Communication skills are assessed through various methods:
- exams are organized using different modalities, requiring students to develop a wide range of communication skills;
- students are invited to participate actively by asking questions and engaging in class discussions.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L018] ECONOMY AND MANAGEMENT
SECTION: Autonomy of judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/573

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
Mastery of appropriate technical skills and the genuinely interdisciplinary nature of the training path enable the graduate in Economy and Management to develop the ability to identify and solve decision-making problems of an economic management nature, applying an appropriate combination of qualitative and quantitative approaches while fully aware of the ethical and social responsibilities underlying their actions and the ethical-professional principles forming the basis of economic and business activities. The training offer aims to provide theoretical education supported by empirical analysis, enabling the Economy and Management graduate to evaluate economic-financial data acquired from the market or internally processed within business contexts, necessary to support strategic and operational decisions of companies. The development of an autonomous judgment capacity is contributed to by both participation in internship and/or placement activities and frequent meetings with external experts, organized in a way that allows active student participation, with students called upon to express their viewpoint on the topics discussed. This outcome will also be achieved through:
- classroom discussion in working groups with teachers and students;
- personal contribution provided in assessment of learning;
- critical contribution demonstrated in the preparation of the final work.

Student associations have organized additional seminars to promote student psychological well-being, debates against gender violence, sustainability seminars in collaboration with startup RE-CIG, activated a study rights office to support students in completing scholarship applications, and organized a welcome day for new students (October 2023), as well as promoted and secured the allocation of bunker spaces for associative meetings and study for students.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO - CHIETI/PESCARA

Graduate opinions The Almalaurea surveys (updated as of April 2023) and the PQA data (extracted as of August 2023) involve a collective of 221 graduates from 2022, of whom 215 responded, representing 97.3%.
66.5% of respondents state they graduated on time, a figure increasing compared to the 2021 surveys (61%).
Overall, 90.3% of respondents are satisfied with the CDS (94% last year; 89.8% university average); in particular, 90% rate the relationship with professors as satisfactory (95% last year; 90% university average), 95.3% consider the teaching load generally satisfactory (97% last year; 88.7% university average), and 79.5% find the exam organization adequate for most exams (86% last year; 79.8% university average).
Less appreciation is expressed for equipment, especially IT equipment, and library services, rated generally adequate. The evaluation of classroom suitability remains critical, with 76% of graduates considering classrooms adequate overall (university average 84.3%).
Regarding support services for entering the workforce, 74% are generally satisfied with post-graduation orientation activities, and 55.7% consider job search support services generally adequate.
In summary, 69.8% of graduates would enroll again in the same CDS (76% last year; 67.4% university average), and of the 85% intending to pursue a master's degree, 45% wish to remain at the same university, 19.6% want to continue at a northern university, and 15.7% at a central university.
The satisfaction data expressed by graduates, together with employment data, is presented and discussed in the CDS minutes of September 13, 2023, and the Steering Committee meeting of May 17, 2023, receiving general consensus and appreciation from the social partners involved, as demonstrated by the attached minutes for SUA Section A1.b. for the previous academic year data.
Additionally, the CDS has an account for reporting complaints and suggestions from students and graduates, visible on the CDS institutional pages and communicated through student representatives.

Ability to apply knowledge and understanding
The graduate in Economics and Management must be able to apply the basic theoretical knowledge and technical skills acquired, adapting them to different contexts they may be called to operate in. Graduates will be able to logically and coherently apply the body of knowledge in economic, legal, business, and quantitative fields offered by the course to various business scenarios of all types and sizes, public and private, as well as regarding the multiple functions they may perform, especially if graduates intend to enter the workforce directly after the three-year program. If graduates plan to pursue a master's degree, the acquired knowledge forms the foundation upon which to build new knowledge, with the advantage of a thorough internalization of the course's content and the ability to use them critically. The opportunity offered to all students of the Course to include an internship at companies or institutions affiliated with the Department, before the final exam, supervised and verified by a professor acting as tutor (in addition to the company tutor), aims to enhance the graduate's understanding of business issues as they arise in specific work situations and to experience the application of skills developed during the study path.
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is achieved through attendance at the planned training activities and laboratory activities.
Verification of these abilities is conducted through oral discussions and written in-course assessments. During exams and the final thesis defense, the abilities to present, communicate, and critically argue thesis topics are also evaluated.

Learning skills
The training process is designed to provide the basic cognitive tools for developing and updating acquired skills and for developing the ability to autonomously select the most appropriate theoretical frameworks and analytical tools to support continuous learning, introducing students to a higher-level study approach that allows decomposing problems in their complexity and managing their solutions in specific applications. The acquisition and consolidation of fundamental general and specific knowledge in economic-business disciplines and interdisciplinary knowledge in economic-political, legal, and quantitative fields provide the structured competencies necessary to address second-level university studies with the required scientific solidity. The Course allows students to enter the productive world, easily assimilating on-the-job specific training and being able to learn autonomously, also through e-learning tools.
The ability to learn is pursued through a path moving from intuitive concepts to formal theorizations, from general to specific concepts, to concrete applications. These forms of deepening are acquired both through participation in classroom activities, in traditional and/or interactive form, and through individual study, particularly through the research work required for the final project, which also requires active participation from the tutor professor who will support individual students in acquiring learning abilities and overcoming theoretical (research and acquisition of appropriate models) and practical barriers (ability to access and process material coherently with set objectives). Verification of the acquisition of learning ability is conducted by evaluating the quality of individual or group assignments and the quality of the final exam.

Knowledge and understanding
The graduate in Economics and Management must possess adequate knowledge of business disciplines, both by functional areas and by classes of companies in different sectors, and be able to understand main economic phenomena and identify critical contextual variables. Graduates must reach the knowledge and demonstrate the understanding expressed in the general and specific training objectives declaration, with particular regard to the principles and foundations of business economics, with broad reference to problems and perspectives of companies in contemporary realities. Additionally, they must develop basic conceptual and analytical knowledge, both theoretical and applied, of economic disciplines, regarding both the instrumentation and modeling of economics, and applied analysis; basic knowledge in the legal discipline area, complementary to economic sciences, particularly in relation to business management (in its social, commercial, tax, and human resources aspects); and a good level of English, acquired possibly through a study period abroad. Such knowledge and understanding provide the basis for operating in companies, where they can perform administrative, managerial, or entrepreneurial functions, in public administrations, and in free professions.
This knowledge and understanding are achieved through attendance at the planned course activities and the mandatory internship. Verification is conducted through in-course learning assessments, exam tests, and the graduation exam.

Organizational structure and responsibilities at university level The Quality Assurance Office plays a central role in promoting the culture of Quality and Quality Assurance (QA), ensuring compliance with the Quality Assurance Requirements set forth in Annex C of Ministerial Decree 30 January 2013, No. 47.
For the QA of study courses, it specifically organizes and verifies the continuous updating of information contained in the SUA-CdS of each study course at the university; oversees the regular conduct of QA procedures for teaching activities in accordance with planned and declared procedures; regulates and verifies periodic review activities of study courses; evaluates the effectiveness of improvement interventions and their actual consequences; ensures the correct information flow to and from the Evaluation Unit and the Joint Teacher-Student Committees.
For the QA of departmental research, it specifically verifies the continuous updating of information contained in the SUA-RD of each Department; oversees the regular conduct of QA procedures for research activities in accordance with planned and declared procedures; ensures the correct information flow to and from the Evaluation Unit.
The Quality Assurance Office is composed of the Rector's delegate for 'Quality', a full-time professor of the first rank who has opted for full-time work, responsible for overseeing the Office's activities, as well as three professors of the first rank belonging to the following ERC (European Research Council) fields: Physical Sciences & Engineering; Social Sciences & Humanities; Life Sciences.

Organization and responsibilities of QA at course level Responsible for ReAQD-D: Prof. Daniela Di Berardino The Department of Business Economics has established within itself a system of bodies and committees involved in the Quality Assurance process for study courses and the management of primary processes for CDS affiliated with the Department. This system is structured into bodies with specific competencies and responsibilities for QA, being involved in monitoring primary processes related to teaching. These bodies are listed below:

Course Director – Prof. Lorenzo Lucianetti
Responsibility: Coordinates the CDS QA system and oversees compliance with requirements set by regulations, with the collaboration of the QA Committee, the Joint Teacher-Student Committee (CPDS), in accordance with guidelines from the university's central bodies on QA and ANVUR directions. The Director, with the collaboration of the QA Group, leads the cyclical and annual review of the CDS, drafting the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA) and the Cyclical Review Report (RRC), and proceeds with the insertion of the SUA-CdS, with the collaboration of the QA Group. According to annual deadlines, it handles teaching coverage and redefines the study path and training objectives, based on periodic consultations with social partners. Finally, it is responsible for promoting a quality-oriented culture within the Course Council.

QA Committee and Review Group
Composition: Course Director (Prof. Lorenzo Lucianetti), Coordinator and QA Representative at the Department of Business Economics (Prof. Daniela Di Berardino), Department professors (Prof. Prof. Helen Chiappini and Prof. Christian Morbidoni until February 2024), a student representative, a technical-administrative staff representative (Fabiano Di Muzio).
Responsibility: The QA and Review Group oversees the CDS quality management policy; specifically, the coordinator manages all quality activities and the specific committees established within the Department for monitoring primary CDS processes. The coordinator also maintains direct relationships with the PQA, the Evaluation Unit, and the Joint Teacher-Student Committee. The Course Director is constantly updated on the activities of the Department committees. The QA Group as a whole oversees compliance with the quality policy, regulations, and requirements, in line with PQA guidelines and ANVUR directions, conducting periodic monitoring of indicators, analysis of criticalities, and evaluation of possible improvement actions. The QA Group collaborates in drafting the SUA-CdS, SMA, and RRC.

Joint Teacher-Student Committee
Composition: Committee Coordinator and CDS professor (Prof. Antonio D'Andreamatteo) and a student representative.
Responsibility: The committee monitors the training offer, teaching quality, and contextual services provided to students by teachers and structures, with particular emphasis on criticalities, which are periodically communicated to the Course Director, the Course Council, and the Department's Teaching QA Representative.

Course Council
Composition: Professors responsible for courses and student representatives enrolled in the Course, elected according to the procedures set by the General University Regulation.
Responsibility: The Council deliberates on the content of the SUA, the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA), and evaluates and deliberates on the related improvement proposals identified by the Course Director and the QA Committee; periodically, it deliberates on the content of the Cyclical Review Report (RRC); collaborates in implementing the CDS quality improvement policies.

The quality policy in the CDS is also exercised through decentralized activities within the committees activated in the Department as follows:
- Teaching Committee: Members are professors responsible for scientific areas represented in the study path; it harmonizes teaching programs and evaluates the quality of the training offer, as well as verifying the completeness of syllabi inserted by professors;
- Orientation Committee (structured in entry, in-course, exit, and placement): Evaluates student opinions on tutoring initiatives, monitors careers, welcomes and guides new students, monitors the effectiveness of curricular internships and placement, plans and evaluates the effectiveness of support services for entering the workforce;
- International Relations Committee: Coordinates mobility services for students, provides support and orientation for Erasmus students;
- Relations with Territory Committee, Steering Committee, and CDS Director: Monitors employment effectiveness, social partner consultations, redefines training offer, activates agreements;
- Communication Committee: Coordinates contextual support services for students, updates CDS information documentation (student guide, CDS functioning, e-learning platform, social networks, department website), manages media relations;
- Credit Recognition Committee: Verifies access and admission requirements. The teaching office and the Department internship office also collaborate in acquiring information.

- Within the appropriate timeframes for inserting information into the SUA-CdS (February-April; July-September), for the SMA (October-December), and the RRC (at least 3 months before internal deadlines), analyze and evaluate interventions aimed at continuous improvement of the CDS in various organizational aspects, monitor teaching indicators, with particular reference to student, graduate, and candidate opinions, contextual services, external effectiveness of the study course, Erasmus path, effectiveness of curricular internships, and results of actions taken. Reference indicators are drawn from the Department Strategic Plan (% students out of course contacted; % recovered out of course, enrolled, internationalization), internal surveys from the Internship Office and Orientation Committee (student opinions; opinions from companies and organizations; career monitoring, quality forum results), and analyses provided by the University's Applied and Teaching Department (enrolments, career monitoring, student opinions, employment).

- Within the appropriate timeframes for inserting information into the SUA-CdS (February-April; July-September), final collegial meetings for discussing frameworks and drafting the SUA;

Based on indications from the Evaluation Unit and the Teaching Delegate, the Department QA Representative will interact with the Course Director before approving the training offer to allow timely verification of CDS sustainability and alignment of training objectives with the planned offer, also verifying the effectiveness of elective courses in the CDS, with biennial checks;
- By the annual deadline set by the PQA (October-December), at least two meetings to analyze SMA indicators and evaluate causes and improvement proposals;
- Periodically, verify the correctness and proper insertion of syllabi, in coordination with the Teaching Committee;
- Periodically, through the Coordinator of the QA Committee and Review Group and the Course Director, promote a quality culture within the CDS, both within Councils and through periodic communications to Department committees.

Improvement initiatives emerging from periodic meetings are highlighted cyclically in the Course Council to plan improvement actions, as evidenced by the minutes of the Course Council meetings.

Brief course description The Study Course in Economics and Management provides students with a solid foundational preparation in economic-business disciplines necessary to understand and address the challenges of the contemporary economic system. Through theoretical lessons, case studies, business games, internships, and field training internships, students will acquire fundamental competencies in business economics, accounting and financial statements, corporate finance, marketing, strategy, and communication, leadership, and human resource management. The CDS is therefore aimed at training professional figures capable of understanding and interpreting changes within the economic system and translating them into strategic competitiveness and sustainability factors for the company.

The courses of the first three semesters aim to provide students with a common set of concepts, methodologies, and essential notions covering business, economic, mathematical-statistical, and legal areas. In the last three semesters, students first attend courses aimed at deepening management topics (from strategy to production and marketing), business organization (also from an accounting perspective), and topics related to financial markets and financial management. The study plan also includes English language courses, quantitative discipline deepening activities using spreadsheets, and training internships.

The organization of courses and content is aimed at ensuring effective entry into local business realities with an adequate level of knowledge and skills to interpret the main needs of business management. At the end of the training path, the graduate in Economics and Management will possess adequate knowledge of the main investigation methods of economic and business management sciences, be able to acquire fundamental information to interpret economic phenomena and analyze business phenomena, and possess advanced professional skills to perform specific business functions or carry out activities within specific sectors (manufacturing, commerce, services, financial intermediation, public administration).

The study plan also includes an English language course, quantitative discipline deepening activities using spreadsheets and open source R software, a career orientation laboratory (3 ECTS), and training internship activity (6 ECTS) for 150 hours.

At the end of the training path, the graduate in Economics and Management:
- Possesses adequate knowledge of business economics, basic mathematics and statistics, political economy, accounting, and management control, public and private management, private and commercial law;
- Knows the main investigation methods of economic and business management sciences;
- Is able to acquire fundamental information to interpret economic phenomena and analyze business phenomena;
- Is able to apply the main tools for business management and possesses advanced professional skills to perform specific business functions or carry out activities within specific sectors (manufacturing, commerce, services, financial intermediation, public administration);
- Possesses the basic cognitive tools for developing and updating acquired knowledge.

External effectiveness C2 EXTERNAL EFFECTIVENESS The Almalaurea surveys (updated as of April 2023) involve a collective of 215 graduates from 2022, of whom 161 responded, representing 75.9%.
75.8% are enrolled in a master's course one year after obtaining the degree, of whom 51.6% remain at the university where they obtained their three-year degree.
29.2% of graduates have undertaken post-graduation training activities, such as first-level master's programs, internships, or company training courses, professional training courses, or specialization schools.
29.8% of graduates (25% in the previous survey) are employed one year after obtaining the degree: of these, 13% are also enrolled in a second-level CDS.
Of the employed, 50% found work after the three-year degree, in line with the previous survey. Similarly to the previous survey, fixed-term contracts and training contracts exceed 50% of total contractual forms, while 35% of employed individuals report holding a stable position (permanent contracts and self-employment), compared to 30% in the previous survey.
91.7% of the employed work in the private sector, and the sector absorbing 70.8% of the employed is services, where commerce (16.7%) and consulting (12.5%) prevail, followed by financial and insurance services (12.5%).
50% of graduates who continue the work started before graduation have noticed an improvement in their work due to the degree itself, in line with the previous survey. Among these, 50% have noticed an economic improvement, 16.7% in professional skills, 16.7% in job duties, and another 16.7% in job position, although the position held allows using acquired skills to a high degree only for 35.4% of graduates who continue the work started before graduation.
Observing the overall employed sample, 43.5% (27% in the previous survey) considers the degree very effective, and 39.1% (40% in the previous survey) fairly effective for the work performed, compared to 17.4% (33% in the previous survey) who consider it little effective.
The CDS will evaluate in the next council the possibility of implementing sustainable improvement actions to enhance external effectiveness.
Employment data are presented and discussed annually in the Steering Committee, as evidenced by the attached minutes in QUADRO A1.b., and in the Course Councils.

Reasons for establishing multiple courses in the class I The following three-year courses are activated by the Gabriele d'Annunzio University in class L-18:
- Business Economics
- Economics and Management
The motivations for establishing these courses within the same class can be attributed to the following aspects:
a) They belong to two different Schools/Departments (the Business Economics degree belongs to the School of Economic, Business, Legal, and Sociological Sciences; the Economics and Management degree belongs to the Department of Business Economics);
b) The number of enrolled students for each of these courses in the triennium 2012/2015 has always been in line with the reference number for the same class; merging the two courses would exceed the maximum number allowed for courses in the class;
c) The courses pursue substantially different training objectives:
- The Business Economics degree is oriented towards studying the institutional aspects of companies of all types and sizes; additionally, the course pays particular attention to aspects related to the environmental sustainability of economic production and consumption activities;
- The Economics and Management degree is oriented towards studying the economy and management of public and private companies, with particular reference to human capital aspects and socio-psychological profiles of company management.

Specific training objectives and description of the study path
The Study Course in Economics and Management aims to provide a solid foundational preparation in business, economic, quantitative, and legal disciplines to ensure mastery of all topics related to business functions (organization, strategic planning, programming and control, administration, marketing, production, financial markets, and corporate finance) for all company types (commercial, service, public administration). The Course is therefore aimed at training professional figures capable of understanding and interpreting changes within the national and international economic system and translating them into strategic competitiveness factors, as required by the increasingly accentuated process of globalization. The acquired competencies characterize a professional figure suitable for performing operational functions in business contexts at managerial and operational levels and for external consulting.

The course develops over the planned time for obtaining the degree, during which basic and characteristic courses are delivered, enabling students to acquire knowledge and skills in business (accounting, management control, marketing, finance, business organization, strategic management), legal (both in private and commercial law), economic, and political economic areas, quantitative (mathematical-statistical), as well as courses in the psycho-sociological area that contribute to providing students with a systemic and motivational vision of the context in which companies operate.

The study plan also includes an English language course and the internship activity.

At the end of the training path, the graduate in Economics and Management:
- Possesses adequate basic knowledge of mathematics and statistics, political economy, accounting, and business economics, law;
- Knows the main investigation methods of economic and business management sciences;
- Is able to acquire fundamental information to interpret economic phenomena and analyze business phenomena;
- Is able to apply the main tools for business management and possesses advanced professional skills to perform specific business functions or carry out activities within specific sectors (manufacturing, commerce, services, financial intermediation, public administration);
- Possesses the basic cognitive tools for developing and updating acquired knowledge.

Opinions of companies and organizations with internship agreements / curricular or extra-curricular internships
The following data will be reported and discussed in the CDS meeting of September 13, 2023.
Since academic year 2014/15, the CDS has administered questionnaires to host organizations and companies for students undertaking internships, to collect their opinions regarding the adequacy of students' competencies and skills relative to the work context. The questionnaire uses a rating scale from 1 (insufficient) to 5 (excellent). In the current academic year 2022/23, the teaching office collected and provided to the Course Director and the QA Committee the evaluations expressed by company tutors on the 148 students who completed curricular internships within the affiliated structures. The affiliated companies have public and private legal nature and represent almost all major service and manufacturing sectors.

The first evaluation concerns the achievement of student objectives. According to host companies, 66% of students achieved excellent objectives, while 30% achieved good objectives.
Regarding the Ability to integrate into the business context, 52% of respondents gave an excellent rating and 34% a good rating, while regarding the variable Adequacy of academic training to business needs, 64% gave an excellent rating (5) and 28% a good rating (4).
Regarding the Level of technical knowledge acquired, 78% of respondents gave a value of 5, 21% a value of 4.
The variable regarding the Degree of autonomy in performing assigned tasks recorded 76% at 5 and 21% of evaluations at 4.
Regarding the evaluation of behavioral and relational aspects of students, 28% of respondents gave a rating of 4 and 65% an excellent rating for the aspect of Ability to work in a group.
Regarding Work ethic/responsibility, 65% of students received a rating of 5, 28% received a rating of 4, and the remainder received a rating of 3.
The synthetic judgment of tutors on the satisfaction level regarding the overall internship experience conducted in agreement with the CDS shows that 71% of respondents rated the experience excellent, 28% gave a rating of 4, and the remaining gave a rating of 3.

The CDS has continued to intensify, also remotely, in the current academic year the involvement of companies within individual courses through company testimonials, fostering continuous moments of encounter and discussion, training seminars, and in some cases, student support in company problem-solving. It is also noted that following the Career Day organized by the Department of Business Economics on May 17, 2023, a questionnaire was administered to participating companies. Responding companies (29 out of 33 participants) expressed a high degree of appreciation for the initiative (average rating 5.8 on a scale from 1 to 7). On average, companies rated the likelihood of hiring students after the Career Day as very probable (score 4.9 on a scale from 1 to 7).

Consultation with representative organizations - at national and international level - of goods and service production, professions (Course establishment)
On January 26, 2015, the Department of Business Economics, to which the three-year Economics and Management Study Course belongs, organized a meeting to consult representative organizations of professions and goods and service production on changes to the course curriculum.
The following attended the meeting:
Prof. Giuseppe Mauro as President of the Department's Territory Relations Committee;
Dr. Teodoro Ivano Calabrese as representative of the Inoltra Pole;
Dr. Donatantonio De Falcis as representative of the Agire Agroalimentare Pole;
Dr. Massimo D'Onofrio as representative of the Chieti Chamber of Commerce;
Dr. Enrico Giaquinto as representative of the Capitank Chemical Pharmaceutical Pole;
Dr. Claudia Pelagatti as representative of Confindustria Pescara;
Dr. Maurizio Tambascia as representative of the Pescara Chamber of Commerce;
Dr. Alessandro Rasetta as business consultant;
Prof. Francesco De Luca as member of the Department's Territory Committee;
Prof. Gianluca Antonucci as member of the Department's Territory Committee;
Prof. Antonio Gitto as member of the Department's Territory Committee;
Prof. Armando Della Porta as representative of the Master's Course in Economics and Management Steering Committee;
Prof. Massimo Sargiacomo as Director of the three-year Economics and Management Study Course;
Prof. Michelina Venditti as Director of the Master's Course in Economics and Management.

The Director of the three-year Economics and Management Study Course presented the changes to the course curriculum.
Prof. Sargiacomo also illustrated the training objectives, structure, and professional outcomes of the course. Regarding the latter, the Course Director presented a modification that increases the CFU for the training internship from 6 to 9, aiming for a more professionalizing path and closer to the workforce. However, students can still limit the training internship to 6 CFU, earning the remaining 3 CFU through "Additional Activities for Workforce Entry," as specified below:
Additional knowledge for workforce entry: min. 0 CFU - max. 3 CFU;
For internships and traineeships at companies, public or private bodies, professional orders: min. 6 CFU - max. 9 CFU.

An extensive debate followed with the participants. Dr. Tambascia emphasized the importance of strengthening the already established relationships between the Study Course and the professional world, which could be further developed for drafting the Course's Didactic Regulation.
At the conclusion of the interventions, Prof. Sargiacomo invited the Steering Committee to express an opinion on the proposed changes. The Committee, after thorough examination, unanimously expressed a positive opinion.

Consultation with representative organizations - at national and international level - of goods and service production, professions (Subsequent consultations)
Reflections from consultations and impact on CDS design regarding graduates' employment potential and possible continuation of studies
The CDS has activated since 2013 a Steering Committee and a Territory Relations Committee to establish various and continuous relationships with companies, the professional world, and innovation poles, aiming to stimulate discussion with the labor market, identify professional and training needs and their evolution, and verify the attractiveness of the offered training in terms of recruitment. Annually, during the CDS teaching programming, the Steering Committee initiates consultations with stakeholders, addressing the delicate issue of the effectiveness of the CDS training offer to guide the construction of an appropriate training path, responsive also to the professional needs expressed by the labor market. Each year, the main stakeholders in cultural/professional profiles have been identified and consulted, such as the Chamber of Commerce, Confindustria, and the Agire innovation pole. From these consultations, useful guidelines have emerged for redefining the training offer with social partners who have generally appreciated the three-year Economics and Management Study Course's teachings, which focus on highlighting 'know-how' and specific competencies.

On January 26, 2015, the Department of Business Economics, to which the three-year Economics and Management Study Course belongs, organized a meeting to consult representative organizations of professions and goods and service production on changes to the study course curriculum. The following attended: the Department's Territory Relations Committee, the Inoltra Pole, the Agire Agroalimentare Pole; the Chieti Chamber of Commerce; the Capitank Chemical Pharmaceutical Pole; Confindustria Pescara; the Pescara Chamber of Commerce. The Director of the three-year Study Course presented the training objectives, structure, professional outcomes, and a modification to the curriculum that increases the CFU for the training internship from 6 to 9, aiming for a more professionalizing path and closer to the workforce. Students could still limit the training internship to 6 CFU, earning the remaining 3 CFU through "Additional knowledge for workforce entry," as specified below:
Additional knowledge for workforce entry: min. 0 CFU - max. 3 CFU;
For internships and traineeships at companies, public or private bodies, professional orders: min. 6 CFU - max. 9 CFU.
The subsequent debate highlighted the importance of strengthening the already established relationships between the Study Course and the professional world. At the conclusion of the interventions, the Course Director invited the Steering Committee to express an opinion on the proposed changes. The Committee, after thorough examination, unanimously expressed a positive opinion.

In a subsequent meeting with social partners (March 12, 2015), the Director of CDS L18 presented the main changes intended to be proposed in light of new training needs arising primarily from managing a high number of enrollments. The Economics and Management degree, being the most numerous course in economic-business disciplines and exceeding the legal threshold for maintaining single courses, had to necessarily split some fundamental courses. Therefore, while maintaining the approach that ensured its recent success, the splitting aimed to safeguard and strengthen the quality of the three-year teaching. The Director explained to the participants the complete course structure, focusing particularly on the courses to be split, emphasizing both the strengthening of the three-year teaching quality and the opening towards the labor market due to the increased CFU dedicated to professional internships, which is also preparatory for the substantial innovations planned for the master's path. The Pescara Chamber of Commerce, applauding the training path and agreeing with the Director, particularly emphasized the need to refine specific accounting knowledge and skills due to the current economic-financial situation of the country. The Artisanry and High-Quality Art Innovation Pole, fully agreeing with the Director, requested to view the complete documentation of the new study paths. Similarly, Confindustria Pescara found the proposed changes interesting and stimulating.

In a subsequent meeting (March 18, 2016) between the Steering Committee and social partners, the CDS Director presented the new features characterizing the three-year degree, highlighting a significant attraction of the course from students outside the region. Indeed, 30% of the course students came from regions other than Abruzzo, particularly from Lazio, Puglia, Campania, Marche, Tuscany, Basilicata, and Molise. This is a good result that, confirming the quality of the Study Course, makes the teaching staff even more responsible for improving the courses and services offered to students. The Director explained to the participants the complete course structure, indicating the general lines followed in preparing the new training path, highlighting the introduction of the course Strategic Communication, emphasizing the relevance given to sociology and basic statistics, as well as macroeconomics. The Confindustria Chieti-Pescara delegate welcomed the three-year training offer, noting the importance of addressing e-commerce and web marketing topics. Therefore, incorporating these observations, the training offer was enriched in the third year with the introduction of the course Web and Marketing, which occupies a prominent position in the changed commercial exchange scenario where the web role is increasingly prevailing. Among optional courses, the introduction of two English language courses: English for Communication at Intermediate and Advanced levels, the introduction of Start-up and Organizational Models, the course Economics and Management of Transport Companies, the course Private Law of the European Union, and the course Economics of the Financial Market were noted.

Subsequently, on July 21, 2016, another consultation meeting was held with social partners (Chieti Chamber of Commerce; Pescara Chamber of Commerce; Confindustria Pescara; Agire Pole, Pilkington NSG; Tecnomatic spa; Unipmi; PriceWaterhouscoopers). At this meeting, the CDS Director deemed it appropriate to initiate a detailed discussion on how the CDS could respond to the new needs expressed by social partners and the territory, and if necessary, how to modify the training offer accordingly. After extensive discussion, the Director suggested a modification to the didactic curriculum. Specifically, he proposed increasing the CFU of the business discipline area for characteristic activities (currently 54) up to 63, while simultaneously decreasing the CFU of the economic discipline area for characteristic activities (currently 18) down to 9. This curriculum modification was necessary to propose a subsequent modification to the Didactic Regulation to align the training offer with emerging training needs from the market and companies and professions, as emerged from the Steering Committee meeting with social partners. Specifically, it was proposed to make the courses Marketing (SECS-P/08) for 9 CFU and Advanced Accounting and Financial Statements (SECS-P/07) for 9 CFU mandatory starting from the 2017-2018 training offer, until then mutually exclusive at the third year of the course, eliminating the course Political Economy (SECS-P/02) for 9 CFU at the third year of the course.

On July 14, 2017, the Director reconvened the Steering Committee to discuss the programming of the training path (2017-18). Confirming the growing success of the CDS in terms of enrollments, the Director recalled the successful participation in the seminar series (https://www.dea.unich.it/news/seminari-formativi-il-career-day-2017) culminating in the Career Day 2017, which enabled hundreds of students enrolled in the Economics and Management degree to have individual interviews with numerous local and national companies (Aptargroup, Ciodue Italia S.p.A., DeCecco, FederManager, Fira S.p.A., Hertz Corporation, Humangest, Klindex S.r.l., Pangea Consorzio Stabile S.c.a.r.l., Pilkington Italia S.p.A., PwC Italy, Valagro S.p.A., Walter Tosto S.p.A.) (https://www.dea.unich.it/news/dea-career-day-22-giugno-2017).

The main changes made, also thanks to observations from social partners, concerned the consolidation of the course Macroeconomics with Political Economy into a single course Macroeconomics and Political Economy placed in the 4th semester of the 2nd year, as requested by stakeholders in the previous consultation; the elimination of the option between Marketing and Accounting and Financial Statements at the 5th semester of the third year, also requested by stakeholders; a more pronounced characterization of the course Mathematics for Economics in financial terms (Mathematics for Economics and Finance instead of Mathematics for Economics), and at the same time the mandatory introduction of the course Business Statistics placed in the 5th semester of the third year. In this way, the option to choose between two highly valuable courses was definitively eliminated, now both mandatory, and the mathematics course was made more functional to the needs of managers. The transformation of the course Web and Marketing into Business Informatics. A rationalization of optional courses. In particular, the course Economics of Companies and Public Administration was added, the course English for Communication was strengthened (from Intermediate to Upper Intermediate), the course English for Communication (Advanced) was refocused as English for Management and Global Business, the linguistic offer was enriched with the introduction of Spanish and German courses, the course Negotiation and Persuasion was refocused as Team Performance Management, and finally, the courses Economics of Transport Companies, Private Law of the European Union, Economics of the Financial Market, and Start-Up and Organizational Models were confirmed. The CDS Director, on behalf of the Steering Committee, will continue to organize periodic meetings.

On June 29, 2018 at 4:00 PM, the Director reconvened the Steering Committee to discuss the programming of the training path (2018-19). At this meeting, Prof. Della Porta, coordinator of the Steering Committee, presented the results of the analysis conducted on Almalaurea data for L18 for the triennium 2015-2017 regarding the employment situation of L18 graduates from DEA (attached minutes). In summary, the vast majority of graduates in economic-statistical sciences in Italy have chosen a business-oriented training. L18 DEA graduates, in particular, have high expectations regarding this training. They consider it a more useful than necessary investment. Indeed, although they consider it only 'fairly effective' in the work they perform, they tend to pursue further studies and report increasing satisfaction with enrollment in the master's degree. Two main indications seem to emerge from the analysis of Almalaurea data related to the three-year Economics and Management degree. The first is to make the overall training project increasingly aligned with the needs of the labor market, paying more attention to professional aspects rather than just academic ones. The second concerns companies and employers, who are requested to better utilize the acquired skills. In this sense, the reduction in satisfaction regarding the work performed is significant. It is also obvious that companies and the professional world are invited to dialogue more with the university to build a shared training path capable of effectively facing the challenges posed by a continuously transforming environment.

Regarding the 2018-2019 training offer for L18 Degree, the Director of the Economics and Management Degree confirmed the growing success of the degree in terms of enrollments, thanking the participants for accepting the discussion and communicating that no substantial changes were made to the training offer for the new academic year. He also emphasized the importance of building the training offer in a shared manner to verify the consistency of courses with the cultural and professional profiles identified by the course and to improve its professionalizing content, as emerged from the analysis of graduate data. He also highlighted the success of the 'Career Day' initiative for 2018, which saw the participation of the most important regional production realities that were not only willing to conduct job interviews but also, in some cases, to transform such interviews into actual employment contracts, as in the case of Hertz SPA.

Entry, path, and exit data
The data below will be presented and discussed in the CDS meeting of September 13, 2023.

C1 ENTRY, PATH, EXIT SECTION C1 Entry, path, and exit data

ENTRY
The data provided by the University Quality Office Statistics, extracted as of August 28, 2023, have been integrated with Sicas system indicators updated as of June 2023.

The trend of enrollments in recent academic years shows a nearly constant trend in the last two years: 356 in 2020/21; 372 in 2021/22; 371 in 2022/23. The total number of enrolled students corresponds to 1164, of which 78% are in course compared to 80.4% in 2021/22.

Sicas records, for the 2022/23 cohort, 22 internal transfers from other CDSs at the university and 6 external transfers from other universities, as well as 8 internal transfers out and 7 withdrawals. Part-time enrolled students number 8.

In the 2022/23 academic year, strong attractiveness of students from the region (81%) is confirmed, while the number of students from outside the region slightly decreases (18.86%). The percentage of students with technical institute diplomas (42%) and high school diplomas (41.7%) remains similar, but a strong incidence of students entering with a high school grade below 80 (51%) persists, followed by the 80-99 range (38%), while the share of students in the 100 and 100 cum laude range remains low, albeit slightly increasing (11%). This aspect constitutes a criticality for the knowledge possessed at entry and necessary for a fruitful approach to the first-year courses. To address this, for years the CDS has adopted tools for guidance and selection that encourage the elevation of basic knowledge of enrolled students and motivate them to greater commitment. In addition to adherence to the national test organized by CISIA, the obligation to earn 18 CFU in basic and characteristic disciplines of the first year, the activation of OFA recovery tutors, and tutors for conducting integrated teaching activities on critical courses are noted.

PATH
The data acquired for this analysis come from PQA statistics and describe the enrollment trend of the 2021/22 cohort. These data have been compared with Sicas indicators and the Profit Exam Monitoring data elaborated by the Applied and Teaching Department, which include a longer observation period.

From the first, excluding part-time students, it is noted that 74% of enrolled students continue to the second year, a figure increasing compared to the previous cohort (70.4%), however, the percentage of those who complete more than 40 CFU in the first year decreases to 32% (43% in 2020/21), and consequently, the percentage of CFU acquired relative to the planned CFU decreases to 47.4% (53% in 2020/21). The number of inactive students increases to 25.6% (21% in 2020/21), while the share of those who do not earn even one CFU remains at 19.47% (19% in 2020/21).

Integrating these data with Sicas updates as of June 2023, for the 2020/22 cohort, the average number of exams taken is 3.5 with an average grade of 22.3. For the last valid cohort, 1 transfer out and 8 withdrawals are noted.

Sustainable improvement action: preparation of new tutors for in-course orientation on specific courses for the upcoming academic year.

EXIT
Internal PQA statistics do not allow for cohort-specific analysis, but for the year of degree completion. Graduates in 2022 number 222, of whom 65% are in course, a figure increasing compared to 2021 (58%). 79% of 2022 graduates (79% in 2021) achieved a grade of 105 or lower, while the figure for those who achieved a grade between 110 and the declaration of honors remains at 10.3% (10% in 2021).

Characteristics of the final exam
The final exam consists of a thesis prepared by the student under the supervision of a supervisor, according to the modalities specified in the Course Didactic Regulation.

Final exam implementation modalities
After passing all exams required by the study plan, including those related to autonomously chosen training activities, and after earning credits for other training activities (laboratories and/or training internships), the student can take the final exam according to the annual schedule set by the Department Council.

The final exam consists of a thesis on: i) in-depth study of a topic covered in one of the course courses, ii) case study, iii) collection and analysis of data for research projects, iv) in-depth study of the activity carried out during the internship.

The topic of the report must be agreed upon by the student with the professor designated as supervisor. The final exam will be evaluated by a 'Final Exam Committee' appointed by the Department Director and composed of at least three professors, including the supervisor.

The final exam aims to verify the ability to deepen the knowledge acquired during the training path on a specific topic and the argumentative and presentation abilities of concepts of economic-business, quantitative, and legal matrix.

The 'Final Exam Committee' will assign a score out of 110 according to the Final Exam Regulation approved by the Course Council. The President of the Course Council may authorize the final exam to be taken in English.

Teaching method Conventional Knowledge verification required for admission Yes Course instructors View list Admission requirements Required knowledge To be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Commerce, it is necessary to have obtained a high school diploma or another foreign degree recognized as equivalent.
To be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Commerce, it is also necessary to take an initial knowledge verification test.
The Academic Regulations for the Study Program regulate the methods for verifying the required knowledge and the additional training obligations to be fulfilled in case of negative verification results. In particular:
1. The test for verifying the required knowledge for admission to the Bachelor's Degree, as per Article 6 of Ministerial Decree 270/2004, is considered passed if the student achieves a score equal to or higher than a minimum set by the Board of the School of Economic, Business, Judicial and Sociological Sciences. In the absence of an explicit resolution, the minimum set in the previous year is considered adopted.
2. A negative result in the knowledge verification test results in the assignment of an additional training obligation (OFA), consisting of attending a recovery course on the required knowledge for admission, offered in the first semester.
3. Verification of the fulfillment of the OFA is achieved by passing a minimum of 18 CFU, related to courses specified in the first year of the study plan, within the basic, characterizing and related subjects, by the end of the extraordinary exam session of the first academic year.
4. In case of failure to fulfill the OFA within the deadline specified in the previous paragraph 3, students remain required to fulfill the OFA and to re-enroll in the first year of the course.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [613L] ECONOMIA E COMMERCIO
SECTION: Admission Requirements
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/566

Admission Requirements Required knowledge for entry:
To be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Commerce, it is necessary to have obtained a secondary school diploma (five-year or four-year with the corresponding supplementary year) or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent.
No specific knowledge is required for entry into the Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Commerce, except for knowledge related to the common parts of the basic curriculum of secondary schools. Such knowledge must be accompanied by the possession of linguistic and logical-mathematical skills normally required by secondary school programs.
Entry to the Bachelor's Degree also requires an initial verification test of knowledge, in accordance with Article 6 of Ministerial Decree 270/2004, conducted through the TOLC-E test managed by CISIA. The verification test aims to assess students' initial preparation in the following areas: ability to understand written text; mathematics; logic. The required or recommended entry knowledge are clearly identified and described on the website www.cisiaonline.it, where it is also possible to access the 'practice' area with TOLC simulations and the 'test guide' area with examples of tests featuring commented and solved questions.
Failure to take or fail the initial verification test allows admission to the Bachelor's Degree with the assignment of an Additional Educational Obligation (OFA).
