UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [613L] ECONOMIA E COMMERCIO
SECTION: Admission Procedures
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/566

Admission Procedures:
The Teaching Regulations of the Study Program regulate the procedures for verifying the required knowledge and the Additional Training Requirements to be fulfilled in case of negative verification results.
1. The examination for verifying the required knowledge for access to the degree program, as per Article 6 of Ministerial Decree 270/2004, is considered passed if the student achieves a score equal to or higher than a threshold set by the School Board of the School of Economic, Business, Legal and Social Sciences, currently set at 10. A negative result or failure to take the knowledge verification examination results in the assignment of an Additional Training Requirement (OFA).
2. Students assigned an Additional Training Requirement may take exams from the second and third years only when they meet at least one of the following conditions:
a) having passed the OFA suitability examination by October 31 of the calendar year following the year of enrollment (for full-time students) or by October 31 of the second year following enrollment (for part-time students).
b) having passed the General Mathematics examination by October 31 of the calendar year following the year of enrollment (for full-time students) or by October 31 of the second year following enrollment (for part-time students).
c) having acquired at least 18 cfu related to courses specified in the first year of the study plan, within the basic and characteristic subjects.
Conditions a) and b) are provided for by the Teaching Regulations of the Economics and Commerce Study Program (pursuant to Article 28, paragraph 4 of the University Teaching Regulations), while condition c) is stipulated by the University Teaching Regulations (Article 28, paragraph 5).
3. During the academic year, and until September, at least six examination sessions for the OFA suitability examination will be offered. In the first semester, a Recovery Course on the required knowledge for access is offered.
4. The degree program council may decide not to assign additional training requirements to students transferring or changing degree programs, provided that at least one exam is recognized.
5. The TOLC-E entrance test taken in previous years is considered valid if the score is equal to or higher than the threshold set in paragraph 1.
6. The TOLC-I entrance test is considered equivalent and valid for passing the knowledge verification examination if the score is equal to or higher than the threshold set in paragraph 1.
The responsible for the knowledge verification examination is Prof. Fausto Di Biase.
The Recovery Course offered by the Study Program (8 cfu, 64 hours of frontal teaching) focuses on mathematics, the subject in which students most frequently require recovery, as evidenced by previous entrance test results. Additionally, student meetings are held by the Recovery Course instructor to identify recommended entry-level knowledge and as supplementary support activities for the course.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [613L] ECONOMICS AND COMMERCE
SECTION: Program, texts and objectives
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/566

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate in Economics and Commerce must be able to communicate autonomously and effectively on issues related to economic affairs. In particular, the graduate must:
- possess appropriate competencies to represent the issues of economic institutions, businesses and labor;
- possess lexical and terminological knowledge to operate efficiently and effectively within their field of study;
- be able to dialogue and express economic-business knowledge clearly even to non-specialist personnel;
- be able to express ideas and formulate solutions for specific economic and business projects in order to identify appropriate organizational and management choices.
Seminars, group work and laboratory activities are tools through which students can develop exchanges and fruitful idea sharing. In this context, particular attention is given to the final exam where the graduate has the opportunity to demonstrate the communication skills acquired during their studies.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [613L] ECONOMICS AND COMMERCE
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/566

Judgment Autonomy (making judgements)
The graduate in Economics and Commerce must be able to manage the economic data they become aware of in order to trace back from the indicator to an autonomous evaluation of the analyzed phenomena. In particular, the graduate must possess:
- the ability to collect and select data and information relevant to economic analysis in its various applied aspects;
- the ability to conduct quantitative investigations;
- the ability to analyze business cases and documents and to express autonomous judgments on the examined issues, with specific considerations of an economic, quantitative, and legal nature.
Interdisciplinary learning and the knowledge and application in the statistical field allow for the implementation of those skills deemed necessary to arrive at an individual judgment.

SECTION: Orientation in entry

Orientation in entry The orientation in entry is coordinated by the orientation coordinator of the SEAGS School (School of Economic, Business, Legal and Sociological Sciences) and the orientation coordinator of the CdS. The orientation in entry activity provides students from the final years of High Schools with information about the educational offerings of the SEAGS School through presentations by the School's delegate and the delegates of the individual CdS, as well as through seminars or lectures given by CdS professors. The CdS delegate works with a group of professors. The orientation activity is carried out both at the School's premises and at High Schools and other suitable locations (e.g., Student Fairs).
Orientation in entry is also conducted through information desks during the summer months at the V.le Pindaro location and through the preparation and dissemination of printed informational material. In line with the SEAGS orientation in entry guidelines, the CLEC continued to promote the CdS on its dedicated webpage (https://scuolaeconomia.unich.it/pagina-futuri-studenti-2021-967) and a dedicated page on the University website (https://clec.unich.it/pagina-studiare-941). Additionally, it continued to manage the Facebook and Instagram social media pages and the YouTube channel. On the latter, there are mini-lectures by professors and testimonials from former students who obtained the degree.
In addition to the activities organized by the SEAGS School through direct contact with High Schools, the University organizes events for this purpose, interacting with regional and non-regional Upper Secondary Schools, including guided tours of the Pescara Campus for Schools, meetings of its professors directly at various school locations, and participation in University Orientation events such as Open Days and Student Fairs. Starting from the 2023-24 academic year, the centralized coordination carried out by the University has become the predominant mode of organizing orientation activities.

Ass. training periods The Economics and Commerce Degree Programme allows students in the Economics and Commerce track to complete a 3-credit curricular internship. It is a training experience that students can undertake at a cooperating institution, organization, or company, to gain direct contact and knowledge of the working world, and may be aimed at developing the graduation thesis under the supervision of the professor responsible for the student's training path.
To make this action more effective, a dedicated webpage (https://scuolaeconomia.unich.it/visualizza.php?type=pagina&id=245) has been created on the website of the School of Economic, Business, Legal and Sociological Sciences (SEAGS), which hosts the Degree Programme. The webpage collects information about internship offers, access procedures, and the list of cooperating companies. All information is also accessible from the CLEC website: https://clec.unich.it/visualizza.php?type=pagina&id=218
To promote and offer students opportunities for internships at public and private organizations operating in their reference territory, the SEAGS School has established specific agreements and memoranda of understanding with over 500 companies, professional organizations, and public administrations aimed at carrying out field training activities, writing graduation theses, and developing integrated university/work training paths. To facilitate contact between students/graduates and local companies, the 'Stage & Placement' office is active at the School's presidency office, managed by Ms. Erika Malandra, Email: erika.malandra@unich.it. Students from CLEC who completed curricular internships during the 2023 academic year totalled 5. The following is the list of involved organizations:

and on the University website:
https://www.unich.it/didattica/erasmus
International mobility assistance and agreements for students through Lifelong Learning/Erasmus services for the SEAGS School are managed by Professor Diego Valentinetti, Email: diego.valentinetti@unich.it.
From the 2020/2021 academic year, the Erasmus coordinator for the Degree Programme is Professor Luca Zarrilli (Email: luca.zarrilli@unich.it), who is also Coordinator of the Department of Economics and International Relations. The International Agreements coordinator for the Degree Programme is Professor Gianfranco Piras (Email: gianfranco.piras@unich.it).
The Erasmus coordinator's activities mainly include:
- supporting the preparation of the study plan;
- examining and evaluating the activities carried out by the student for the recognition of credits earned at the foreign university;
- tutoring students during their study period abroad.
At the University level, two specific coordination roles are established: the Rector's Delegate for Erasmus, Professor Marcello Costantini, and the Rector's Delegate for Mobility and International Relations, Professor Pierluigi Sacco.
To encourage participation, for the 2018/19 and 2019/20 academic years, the Degree Programme allocated a funding of 6,000 euros to be equally distributed (with a minimum of 500 euros and a maximum of 1,000 euros) among the most deserving enrolled students who were selected winners and actually participated with success in the project (i.e., earning at least 12 curricular credits abroad) for a period of no less than three months. Starting from the 2020/21 academic year, the Degree Programme could no longer rely on dedicated resources (i.e., teaching funds previously allocated by the University) but, for the Erasmus calls 2021/22, 2022/23, and 2023/24, the Department of Economics has nonetheless allocated its own funds to incentivize Erasmus activities for students enrolled in its Degree Programmes. For the 2024/25 academic year, the Department Council has not provided economic incentives for Erasmus activities for students enrolled in its Degree Programmes.
Participation in the Erasmus project is still considered significant for enhancing the study path and results in the assignment of 2 points towards the academic curriculum points available for the student's academic record.
The list of foreign universities with which the DEC currently has an active Erasmus agreement now includes the following as partners of the INGENIUM European Campus Project: Rouen Normandie (France), Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (Germany), Munster Technological Institute (Ireland), University of Skövde (Sweden), South-Eastern Finland University of Applied Sciences (Finland), Gheorghe Asachi Technical University of Iasi (Romania), University of Crete (Greece).
Also noteworthy is the Erasmus for Traineeships programme, whose latest call for the 2023/24 academic year was published on March 30, 2023. This initiative allows Ud'A students to complete an internship at one of the participating countries in the Erasmus Programme. The internship activity is recognized by the University of 'G. d'Annunzio' Chieti-Pescara as part of the student's study programme. Winners receive a monthly allowance of up to 700 euros.
Erasmus Student Network Chieti-Pescara organizes annual AskErasmus Meeting - Mov'in Europe events to help future Erasmus University students explore all opportunities within Erasmus+. Specifically, meetings are organized to promote the Erasmus+ call and to provide information to scholarship winners regarding the organization of departure and stay.
The following information sessions were held within the 2024 AskErasmus Meeting:

- March 8, 2024 at 2:00 PM at the Pescara campus - Room 31.

The effectiveness of the initiatives implemented by the Degree Programme to encourage student international mobility is evidenced by the latest data provided by the Department of Economics Erasmus coordinator: half of the students from the Department of Economics who went on Erasmus in 2022 were enrolled in the Economics and Commerce Degree Programme (8 out of 16).
These results are monitored annually by the Degree Programme following the submission of data in the annual monitoring sheet (SMA).

Student Opinions STUDENT OPINIONS A.Y. 2022/23
Starting in 2023, the PQA has implemented a new dynamic portal dedicated to visualizing the results of the Student Opinion Survey. For the academic year 2022/23, 1,042 questionnaires were processed, covering 86.11% of the CLEC's teaching activities (31 out of 36). The questions considered regarding the courses are as follows:
D0 Are the topics of this course interesting to you?
D1 Were the prior knowledge you possessed sufficient for understanding the topics covered in the exam program?
D3 Is the study load required by the course proportional to the assigned credits?
D9 Is the teaching material (indicated and available) adequate for studying the subject?
D13 Was the course delivered consistently with what was stated on the Study Program's website?
D14 Are the schedules for lectures, exercises, and other teaching activities respected?
D16 Were the examination methods clearly defined?
D20 Does the instructor stimulate/motivate interest in the subject?
D21 Does the instructor present the topics appropriately considering the complexity of the subject?
D22 Is the instructor available during lectures and/or office hours to clarify the topics covered?
For the CLEC, the average rating of opinions, expressed on a scale ranging from 1 to 4, is 3.5. This value is higher than the average of previous academic years and confirms the growth trend that seemed to have paused last year (3.30 in 2016/17, 3.33 in 2017/18, 3.36 in 2018/19, 3.40 in 2019/20, 3.44 in 2020/21, 3.4 in 2021/22). The value is also higher than the average of Social Science Study Programs (3.49) and the University average (3.44).
More than positive ratings concern the instructor's punctuality in delivering lectures and exercises (D14: 3.67), instructor availability and accessibility (D22: 3.66), consistency of courses with what was stated on the Study Program's website (D13: 3.57), and clarity in defining examination methods (D16: 3.54). The lowest average score continues to be related to the adequacy of prior knowledge (D1), which is the only one below the University average, although still satisfactory (3.27) and significantly increasing compared to previous years (3.07 in 2019/20 and 3.09 in 2020/21 and 3.14 in 2021/22).
Within the portal prepared by the PQA, in the area accessible only to the Study Program Director, the data for the academic year 2022/23 regarding the evaluation of individual courses are available. It emerges that 54.84% of the courses in the Economics and Commerce Study Program received a rating between 3.5 and 4, while the remaining 45.16% received a rating between 3 and 3.5. Therefore, no courses received an average score below 3. Regarding the distribution of ratings across different courses, the average scores range from 3.17 to 3.87.
Student opinions are continuously monitored by the Study Program, also benefiting from the work of the Parity Commission (Teachers-Students), whose latest report from December 2022 was discussed together with the report by CLEC representatives at the Study Program Council meeting on February 23, 2023. Furthermore, the Study Program, particularly through the work of the GAQ, periodically analyzes the data provided by the PQA and those collected through the Ingrid platform to identify potential areas for improvement. For example, following the monitoring conducted over the past year, the Study Program Council meeting on July 17, 2023, decided on the following improvement actions:
- establishment, starting from the academic year 2023/24, of the role of tutor professor to be assigned to each first-year student;
- activation of an 8-hour Economics preparatory course, to be held in the week preceding the start of the first semester's teaching activities, aimed at facilitating students i) in approaching the first-year courses with a sufficiently clear understanding of how each contributes to their knowledge and skills formation, and ii) in understanding the reasoning used by economic disciplines to analyze market functioning and the behavior of agents operating within them.
The data on student opinions for the academic year 2022/23 were released by the PQA in August 2023 and will be discussed by the Economics and Commerce Study Program Council in the September meeting.

GRADUATE OPINIONS The data presented in this section comes from the XXV Survey conducted by AlmaLaurea (2023) titled “Profile of Graduates 2022”, referring to graduates in the calendar year 2022.
The average age of CLEC graduates is 24.1 years, and 75.7% are aged 24 or younger.
Men represent 48.6% of graduates while women represent 51.4%.
Regarding the graduates' family backgrounds, 37.5% of CLEC graduates have at least one parent with a degree, another 37.5% have parents with a secondary school diploma, and the remaining 25% have parents with professional qualifications, lower qualifications, or no qualifications.
The educational background of our graduates is 52.7% from high school (liceo), 43.2% hold a technical diploma (economic or technological), and 1.4% hold a professional diploma. The average diploma grade is 83 out of 100.
60.8% of graduates are currently enrolled, and less than 19% graduate beyond the second year outside the regular schedule. The average graduation grade is 98.5 out of 110.
90.6% of CLEC graduates report overall satisfaction with the degree program, and 87.5% state they intend to pursue a two-year master's degree or a university master's program.
In the calendar year 2022, the response rate to the AlmaLaurea questionnaire on the graduate profile was 43.2% (32 out of 74), a very satisfactory result that highlights the effectiveness of the intervention actions introduced starting from the autumn 2022 graduation session (reminder emails sent to graduates near the deadlines for submitting required documentation to the student office for the final exam) to curb the phenomenon of non-completion of questionnaires, which had been recorded in the previous two years when response rates were around 6%.
Further information is provided in the AlmaLaurea document containing data on the CLEC 2022 graduate profile, attached to the present SUA-CdS sheet.
The 2022 survey on graduate opinions will be discussed at the next meeting of the Economics and Commerce Degree Course Council.

Learning Skills
The Economics and Commerce graduate must be able to tackle subsequent and specialized study paths with significant analytical ability. The knowledge acquired in various fields of knowledge must constitute the indispensable premise to ensure transitions to more complex study fields. The graduate must be able to:
- apply the methodology and tools acquired for their use in various professional contexts;
- deepen and update the content of the studied disciplines to adapt them to various professional contexts.
In this case as well, the profit exams and the final thesis constitute a relevant test to verify this learning rate.

Brief Course Description The Economics and Commerce Degree Course (CLEC) is part of the educational offer of the School of Economic, Business, Legal, and Social Sciences (SEAGS) of the 'G. d'Annunzio' University, consisting of the Department of Economics and the Department of Legal and Social Sciences.
The CLEC Director is Prof. Edilio Valentini. The location is viale Pindaro 42, 65127 Pescara.
The Economics and Commerce Degree Course (CLEC) aims to provide solid cultural foundations for all areas of economics: from microeconomic and macroeconomic models to economic policy, finance, and business economics. To this end, students, in addition to learning economic and business disciplines, acquire a good preparation in legal and mathematical-statistical fields. The CLEC offers immediate professional opportunities in private companies, cooperatives, non-profit sectors, banks, insurance companies, financial sectors, public administration, and professional offices.
The natural continuation is the Master's Degree Course in Economics and Commerce (CLECM), but it should be noted that the CLEC provides excellent preparation to continue studies in all areas of economics.
The CLEC is structured into two distinct educational paths:
-Economics and Commerce
-Economics and Finance.
The first path, Economics and Commerce, more attentive to general and regulatory aspects, is primarily intended for those interested in professional opportunities, business management, and administrative offices of public entities.
The second path, Economics and Finance, is characterized by providing mathematical tools currently highly sought after in both economic and financial contexts, for example in the assessment of financial risks. Its more substantial quantitative content makes it unique in the educational offer of the 'G. d'Annunzio' University.

External Effectiveness EMPLOYMENT STATUS OF CLEC GRADUATES IN THE CALENDAR YEAR 2021, ONE YEAR AFTER GRADUATION (AlmaLaurea Data Updated to April 2023. Number of Respondents: 59)
Graduates currently enrolled in a second-level degree course: 72.9% (73.5% is the national average for the same degree class).
Employment rate for graduates not enrolled in another degree course: 73.3% (70.7% is the national average for the same degree class).
Employed individuals who significantly use the skills acquired through their degree: 36.4% (33.5% is the national average for the same degree class).
Net monthly salary: €1,132 (€1,284 is the national average for the same degree class).
For more details on the employed graduates (not enrolled in another degree course): see the attached file.
Comments:
The percentage of our graduates choosing to enroll in a second-level degree continues to remain at high levels (although slightly lower than the 75.4% recorded last year), confirming the primary vocation of the Economics and Commerce Degree Course to provide a solid foundational preparation enabling graduates to successfully continue their university studies in various fields of economic, business, legal, and mathematical-statistical disciplines.
The percentage of respondents working has increased to 25.42% compared to 23.1% in 2021, 15.1% in 2020, and 12.6% in 2019. Graduates who significantly use the skills acquired through their degree have increased compared to last year (36.4% versus 33.3%).
The net monthly salary of those working has improved to €1,132 (not far from the national average for the same degree class) and has grown significantly compared to previous years' averages (€997 in 2021, €742 in 2020, €876 in 2019, €629 in 2018, €657 in 2017).
Updated data on the employment status of graduates will be discussed at the next Course Council meeting scheduled for September, also to evaluate the opportunity to undertake potential improvement actions.

Reasons for Establishing Multiple Courses in the Same Degree Class The Economics and Commerce Degree Course focuses on economic, financial, and legal disciplines. The Economics and Business Informatics Degree Course, thanks to the contribution of the Faculty of Mathematical, Physical, and Natural Sciences, integrates economic disciplines with some knowledge of mathematics and informatics, to train graduates capable of responding with scientific and technological skills to societal changes in the economic field. Both Degree Courses provide solid foundations for continuing studies and at the same time adequate knowledge for entering the workforce.

Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description In accordance with the previously indicated educational objectives qualifying the Degree Class, the Economics and Commerce Degree Course aims to:
- provide economic, technical, mathematical-statistical, and legal competencies for a proper understanding of the economic system, markets, and public and private entities;
- develop knowledge and analytical methods to interpret business, economic, and institutional dynamics;
- provide a multidisciplinary framework under the economic-business and legal aspects for the exercise of the profession as a chartered accountant;
- possess adequate knowledge of organizational culture in work contexts;
- address and deepen issues related to the evaluation and control of complex systems such as management, marketing, quality control, and human resource management.
In addition to the specific objectives mentioned above, the Course ensures a valid interdisciplinary preparation in computer science, legal-administrative, and linguistic fields to enable adequate professional entry, even at the European level.
The Course, in fact, issues an English language certification according to the Council of Europe Language Portfolio.
The Economics and Commerce Degree Course is structured into various educational paths to provide interdisciplinary preparation in economic-business-legal fields, with reference to statistical-mathematical methodologies, to allow appropriate basic knowledge and various immediate professional opportunities, with managerial skills in the business, banking, financial, public administration, non-profit, and social economy sectors; and to foster knowledge in disciplines most oriented towards professional activities.
Students, in addition to being assisted by a tutor, are encouraged to spend periods of internship and traineeship in public and private companies. The educational objectives achieved during the three years can be further deepened through a master's degree, specialized courses, or doctoral programs.

Opinions of Companies and Organizations with Internship/Traineeship Agreements The internship activity for the 2022/2023 academic year involved ten CLEC students. It is recalled that internships are not part of the curriculum in the Economics and Finance path of the Course, while in the Economics and Commerce path, internships are included among the "other useful knowledge for entering the workforce" (3 CFU of letter F), but they are not mandatory as the educational requirement can also be met through attendance at seminars, participation in company visits, or obtaining the French Language proficiency certificate. However, it is noted that the number of students benefiting from internship experiences has increased by 150% compared to last year, which was a transitional year between the pandemic phase and its resolution. Additionally, it is reported that 50% of the internships were characterized by a number of hours significantly exceeding the required 3 CFU, resulting in seven hours.
Below is the analysis of opinions from companies and organizations with curriculum or extracurricular internship/traineeship agreements involving the aforementioned students.
The data were collected by the School of Economic, Business, Legal, and Social Sciences (SEAGS) and relate to end-of-internship evaluations completed by company supervisors. The analyzed forms include specific evaluations with scores on a scale from 1 to 5. Evaluations specifically regarding the intern were conducted on two main aspects:
-Q1: Educational and professional aspects (divided into dimensions: Q1.1: Motivation and commitment; Q1.2: Achievement of educational goals; Q1.3: Appropriateness of university preparation for company needs; Q1.4: Analytical/synthetic ability and critical thinking; Q1.5: Problem-solving ability)
-Q2: Relational and managerial aspects (divided into dimensions: Q2.1: Ability to work in a group; Q2.2: Willingness to collaborate; Q2.3: Autonomy in task execution; Q2.4: Punctuality and reliability; Q2.5: Ability to assume responsibility).
All forms were completed in full regarding the above aspects.
Regarding educational and professional aspects, the excellent evaluations (5 out of 5) obtained were:
-Q1.1. Motivation and commitment: 90% (9 forms)
-Q1.2. Achievement of educational goals: 60% (6 forms)
-Q1.3. Appropriateness of university preparation for company needs: 60% (6 forms)
-Q1.4. Analytical/synthetic ability and critical thinking: 70% (7 forms)
-Q1.5: Problem-solving ability: 70% (7 forms).
Regarding relational and managerial aspects, the excellent evaluations (5 out of 5) achieved were:
-Q2.1. Ability to work in a group: 90% (9 forms)
-Q2.2. Willingness to collaborate: 89% (8 forms)
-Q2.3. Autonomy in task execution: 60% (6 forms)
-Q2.4: Punctuality and reliability: 90% (9 forms)
-Q2.5: Ability to assume responsibility: 80% (8 forms).
For both educational and relational aspects, it is noted that no student received insufficient evaluations (scores of 2 or lower). This confirms the high satisfaction of host companies with CLEC students, as evidenced in previous years.
The forms also include a comprehensive evaluation of the internship/traineeship activities by companies and organizations, indicated in point Q5.1: satisfaction level regarding the activation and management of internships, expressed on a scale from 1 to 5.
90% of the involved companies rated the internship activation and management as excellent (score 5).
However, it is noted that in none of the cases analyzed did the company propose a job offer at the end of the internship, while only one was extended beyond the initially agreed period.
In conclusion, companies did not report any issues regarding the interns or the internship service offered by the Economics School; regarding the latter, no improvement suggestions were provided either.
The opinions of companies and organizations regarding the internship and traineeship activities carried out by CLEC students in the 2022/2023 academic year will be discussed at the Course Council meeting in September 2023, also to evaluate the opportunity to undertake potential improvement actions.

Final Exam Characteristics
1. The final exam consists of a written thesis prepared by the student on a theoretical or practical topic within the course's educational activities. The topic is agreed upon with a faculty member who serves as the thesis advisor.
2. In the final exam, the student must demonstrate adequate knowledge and understanding of the topic under analysis and independent ability to synthesize and re-elaborate.
3. Once approved by the advisor, the thesis will be evaluated by a judging committee composed of at least five faculty members. The committee includes the advisor and at least four other faculty members primarily belonging to the same scientific-disciplinary group as the advisor or related disciplines. The School Director appoints the committee, after consulting the Department to which the course belongs.
4. The committee evaluates the thesis in a public session; subsequently, it assigns a score not exceeding six points. The committee also evaluates the student's entire academic path, awarding an additional merit score not exceeding four points for enrolled students and two points for students outside the regular schedule. The graduation grade is calculated as the sum of the points assigned to the thesis and academic record, plus the weighted average (on a scale of 110) of the exam grades, rounded up to the nearest integer. If the final grade is 110 or higher, the committee, upon confirming the excellence of the results, may award the honors unanimously.
5. The announcement of the graduation grade and the delivery of the diploma are public and take place at the end of each graduation session.

Final Exam Procedure
The final exam consists of preparing a written thesis, in Italian or English, aimed at deepening a topic related to a specific course, under the guidance of the relevant faculty member as the advisor. The analysis allows evaluating the depth of the graduate's specific competencies in the chosen discipline, as well as the solidity of broader preparation, which contributes to highlighting logical and expressive abilities.
Once approved by the advisor, the thesis will be evaluated by a judging committee composed of at least five faculty members. The committee includes the advisor and at least four other faculty members primarily belonging to the same scientific-disciplinary group as the advisor or related disciplines. The SEAGS School Director, after consulting the Department of Economics to which CLEC belongs, appoints the committee.
The committee evaluates the candidate's thesis; subsequently, it assigns a score not exceeding six points. The committee also evaluates the candidate's entire academic path, awarding an additional merit score not exceeding four points for enrolled students and two points for students outside the regular schedule. Participation in the Erasmus project is considered significant for qualifying the academic path and results in the assignment of two points toward the academic record's total points.
The graduation grade is calculated as the sum of the points assigned to the thesis and academic record, plus the weighted average (on a scale of 110) of the exam grades, rounded up to the nearest integer. If the final grade is 110 or higher, the committee, upon confirming the excellence of the results, may award the honors unanimously.
The announcement of the graduation grade and the delivery of the diploma are public and take place at the end of each graduation session.
To support students in choosing the discipline for their thesis, CLEC has opened a web page titled 'Thesis Proposals', where each faculty member proposes possible topics to be deepened for their course.

Department DEPARTMENT OF ECONOMICS Website https://clea.unich.it Teaching Method Conventional Verification of Required Knowledge for Admission Yes Course Instructors View List Admission Requirements Required Knowledge for Admission To be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree, it is generally necessary to hold a five-year secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent, or a four-year secondary school diploma plus the corresponding supplementary year.
For admission to the Bachelor's Degree in Business Economics, the following are specifically required:
- Knowledge of the Italian language and linguistic skills as contained in the curricula of any type of secondary school;
- General culture enabling understanding and contextualization of fundamental phenomena of society in which economic entities operate;
- Aptitude towards economic-business disciplines;
- Basic knowledge of English;
- Basic logical-mathematical and computer skills.
The Bachelor's Degree includes an admission test as specified in Article 6 of Ministerial Decree 270/2004.
The verification of required knowledge for admission is considered passed if the student achieves a score equal to or higher than the minimum set by the Board of the School of Economic, Business, Legal and Sociological Sciences. In the absence of an explicit resolution, the minimum from the previous year is applied.
Failure in the knowledge verification test results in an Additional Educational Requirement (OFA), consisting of attendance at a recovery course offered on the required knowledge, held in the first semester.
The fulfillment of the OFA is verified by passing at least 18 CFU, related to courses specified in the first year of the study plan, within the basic, characterizing and related subjects, by the end of the extraordinary exam session of the first academic year.
Failure to fulfill the OFA by the deadline requires students to complete the OFA and repeat enrollment in the first year of the course.
Transfers, course changes, and admission to single exams are subject to approval by the Course Council. The Council may grant full or partial recognition of the student's academic record to date, including validation of completed exams and acquired credits, and specify the year of study at which the student is enrolled and any OFA to be fulfilled.

Admission Procedures The Study Regulations for the Degree Programme regulate the procedures for verifying the required knowledge and the additional training requirements to be fulfilled in case of negative verification results.
1. The examination to verify the required knowledge for entry into the degree programme, as per Article 6 of Ministerial Decree 270/2004, is considered passed if the student achieves a score equal to or higher than a threshold set by the School Board of the School of Economic, Business, Legal and Social Sciences, currently set at 10. A negative result in the knowledge verification examination results in the assignment of an Additional Training Requirement (OFA).
2. Students assigned an Additional Training Requirement may take exams from the second and third years only when they meet at least one of the following conditions:
a) having passed the OFA suitability examination by October 31 of the calendar year following the year of enrollment (for full-time students) or by October 31 of the second year following enrollment (for part-time students);
b) having passed the General Mathematics examination by October 31 of the calendar year following the year of enrollment (for full-time students) or by October 31 of the second year following enrollment (for part-time students);
c) having earned at least 18 cfu related to courses specified in the first year of the study plan, within the basic and characteristic subjects.
3. During the academic year, and until September, at least six examination sessions for the OFA suitability examination will be offered. In the first semester, a recovery course on the required knowledge for entry will be offered.
4. The Degree Programme Council may decide not to assign additional training requirements to students transferring or changing degree programmes, provided at least one exam is recognized.
5. The CISIA entrance test taken in previous years is considered valid if the score is equal to or higher than the threshold set in paragraph 1.
6. The TOLC-I and TOLC-E entrance tests are considered valid for passing the knowledge verification examination if the score is equal to or higher than the threshold set in paragraph 1.
7. The OFA requirements specified in this Regulation (pursuant to Article 28, paragraph 4 of the University Study Regulations) are indicated in points 2.a and 2.b (and consist of meeting at least one of them within the specified deadlines), while the condition described in point 2.c is established by the University Study Regulations (Article 28, paragraph 5).
The Degree Programme recognizes the "TOLC@casa" method, allowing students to take tests remotely. International students intending to enroll in the Degree Programme may take the CISIA Italian language test.

COURSE: [610L] ECONOMY
SECTION: Judgment autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/564

Judgment autonomy (making judgments)
The graduate:
- is able to study the relationships between the company and financial markets, viewed as a place from which the company obtains the resources necessary for investment and where, at the same time, it is judged and evaluated based on achieved performance;
- possesses basic skills for processing economic data;
- has the necessary knowledge to frame and solve some of the main problems of business management through the use of appropriate statistical-economic methodologies;
- is able to understand the specifics of the entrepreneur's role and the constraints and opportunities imposed by public regulation.
Judgment autonomy is developed in particular through exercises, seminars, preparation of reports, during internship and training activities, and through the activities carried out for the preparation of the final exam.
The verification of the acquisition of judgment autonomy occurs through the evaluation of the degree of autonomy and ability to work, also in groups, during the internship and the activities assigned for the preparation of the final exam.

During March-May 2023, a series of meetings were held between the President, the Orientation Coordinator, and the Presidents and Representatives of the CdS under the School. In line with University-level communications, the following orientation channels have been established:

In addition to and complementing activities carried out at the University and SEAGS School levels, the CdS has enhanced existing activities and introduced new orientation initiatives, described below:
1. Online Meetings with Schools (in addition to SEAGS)
Based on a review of Provincial Offices lists, selected high schools with study programs potentially aligned with business economics were identified. - Display of the 'walk-in' meeting calendar (showing dates and times when CdS representatives are available for open orientation activities; these activities, starting from summer months, will replace traditional fixed stations near the academic building entrance) and links to online meetings;
- One-to-one appointments - a form in the 'Orientation' section to request an appointment with a CdS representative (88 contact requests via form).
3. OTHER SOCIAL CHANNELS
The CdS's social channels (Facebook with 709 followers, Instagram with 926 followers, LinkedIn group with 598 followers, YouTube, and a new LinkedIn account with 164 followers) already play a significant role in promoting and disseminating the educational and non-educational activities of the CdS, particularly benefiting enrolled students.
The shift of many orientation initiatives to online formats has further increased the relevance of these channels for reaching and retaining potential students. To this end, a preliminary contact procedure has been established for each school involved in the training meetings, inviting them to follow the CdS's social media pages. The knowledge, experience, and tools developed to support these activities have led to many initiatives (including those during the pandemic period) becoming a stable part of the CdS's orientation toolset.

Student opinions The University analyzes data from the "Student Opinion Survey" for the Academic Year 2022-2023 (new portal https://opinionistudenti.unich.it/), comparing it with previous surveys, namely Academic Years (AYs.) 2015-2016, 2016-2017, 2017-2018, 2018-2019, 2019-2020, 2020-2021, 2021-2022. Disaggregated data is made available by the University starting in August of each year. It is noted that the new portal does not provide data for non-attending students.
University data comes from questionnaires administered until August 1st for all courses of the CLEA for the current Academic Year (2022-2023). See Attachment B6.1.
It is specified that the student opinion data for the Academic Year 2022-2023 is provisional (until the final extraordinary exam session of AY 22-23) and that the current procedure does not allow viewing opinions for non-attending students.
It is recalled that:
• Students are required to accept completing the questionnaire; it is optional to answer a specific question (or all). Therefore, a questionnaire may be filled without answers: effectively, the only mandatory response is whether classes were attended or not, which determines the type of questionnaire completed (attending/non-attending);
• Calculations are performed only with questions considered for the average and that allow responses ranging from 1 to 4 (1 strongly disagree, 2 more disagree than agree, 3 more agree than disagree, 4 strongly agree);
• The overall picture collecting all registered responses is considered here, divided into statistically relevant responses and more narrative responses, respectively "Analytical Summary" and "Suggestions";
• Additionally, the picture relative to individual "Courses" is considered. In this picture, only information (question) for which the course received at least 6 evaluations is reported; therefore, totals and averages may differ from those of other sections "CUN Area", "SSD".
In the "Analytical Summary" section, it is possible to observe that the average score recorded in the Academic Year 2022-2023 from questionnaires administered to attending students is 3.47, which is substantially in line with the previous year's average rating (3.49). The figure is positive when compared to the average ratings recorded by the University in the latest available report (AY 2020-2021 - data as of 28/02/2022) for all Social Area Courses of Study (3.49) and for all University Courses of Study (3.46).
Regarding attending students, the questions receiving particularly positive evaluations are:
• The course was delivered consistently with what was declared on the Course of Study website? (3.57)
• Are the schedules for lectures, exercises, and other teaching activities respected? (3.65)
• Were the exam modalities clearly defined? (3.52)
• Does the professor present the topics appropriately according to the complexity of the subject? (3.47)
• Is the professor available during lectures and/or office hours to clarify the topics covered? (3.67)
Conversely, responses with a score equal to or below the Course of Study average concerned, in particular:
• Are the topics of this course interesting to you? (3.38)
• Were the prior knowledge sufficient for understanding the topics in the exam program? (3.27)
• Is the study load required by the course proportional to the assigned credits? (3.31)
• Is the teaching material (indicated and available) adequate for studying the subject? (3.41)
• Does the professor stimulate/motivate interest in the discipline? (3.41)
To better understand this Academic Year's results, with exams still ongoing at the time of data collection, some contextual data for attending students should be considered:
• Number of students contacted: 1143;
• Number of courses considered: 29;
• Number of involved professors: 23.
Analyzing aggregated data on individual courses allows identifying 4 response levels and evaluating how attending students' evaluations are distributed in percentage terms:
• Level A (from 3.5 to 4 inclusive), 41% of courses;
• Level B (from 3 to 3.5 not inclusive), 59% of courses;
• Level C (from 2.5 to 3 not inclusive), 0% of courses;
• Level D (from 1 to 2.5 not inclusive), 0% of courses.
Generally, considering all analyses performed (Attachment B6.1), the points requiring action to improve students' perception of the CLEA are:
• Periodically update teaching programs to account for, where not already done, students' prior knowledge;
• Periodically update teaching programs to ensure study load is proportional to assigned credits;
• Improve teaching material (indicated and available) to make it adequate for studying various disciplines;
• Enhance professors' ability to stimulate and motivate interest in disciplines.
It is necessary to consider the suggestions from attending students and seek to reduce the number of non-attending students. To this end, the CLEA submits information questionnaires to monitor student requests regarding the effectiveness of the educational offer. In particular, in August 2022, a questionnaire was sent via email to CLEA students to collect feedback for revising the educational offer. The response rate was not very high (approximately 10% of enrolled students), but it provided indications that will certainly be considered to avoid overlaps in teaching programs and to make the Course content more up-to-date.
The results of various surveys are shared during Course of Study Council meetings with all CLEA professors, who commit to adapting their courses and behavior to improve the overall teaching quality provided by the Course of Study.

• Attachment B6.1 - Student opinions of the Bachelor's Degree in Business Economics - A.Y. 2022-2023;
• Attachment B6.2 - Student opinions of the Bachelor's Degree in Business Economics - A.Y. 2021-2022.

Graduate Opinions The AlmaLaurea data on the student's university experience (updated September 2023, data on 2022 Graduates at CLEA, Bachelor's Degree L18 – Business Economics, 49 graduates, 11 graduates who completed the questionnaire, completion rate 22.44%) shows an increase compared to the previous year (2021 CLEA Graduates 91) and a convergence, sometimes exceeding, the national average evaluations for courses of the same class (VMN L-18, 17).
In particular (see Attachment B7.1):
• 100% of 2022 graduates are satisfied with the Course (100% of 2021 graduates), National Average Value (VMN) 90.9%;
• 100% are satisfied with the relationship with professors (100% of 2021 graduates), VMN 89%;
• 90.9% are satisfied with the relationship with other students (84.6% of 2021 graduates), VMN 92%;
• 85.7% are satisfied with the teaching quality (77.8% of 2021 graduates), VMN 83.3%;
• 87.5% are satisfied with the support services (77.8% of 2021 graduates), VMN 80.6%;
• 85.7% are satisfied with the career guidance (77.8% of 2021 graduates), VMN 80.6%.
The data on classroom quality shows a significant improvement compared to previous years, positioning above the national average. The average evaluation of libraries shows a significant increase compared to previous years, even compared to the national average:
• 90% of 2022 graduates consider the classrooms where teaching activities take place adequate (61.5% of 2021 graduates), VMN 83.8%;
• 100% of 2022 graduates consider the libraries adequate (83.4% of 2021 graduates), VMN 93.4%.
The average age of graduates also improves (24.4) compared to last year (24.6) but not compared to the national average VMN (23.9). A strength of CLEA continues to be the data on the number of graduates who completed an internship or recognized work activities by the Course during the training path (81.8%), although decreasing compared to 2021 graduates (100%) but significantly higher than the national VM (55.9%). It is specified that the internship activity (curricular internship) is an obligatory activity of the Course; however, sometimes a student who has carried out, or previously carried out, consistent work activity may request recognition of said activity instead of the internship hours. In fact, disaggregating the data reveals that 54.5% (39.9% VMN) completed an internship organized by the Course at public or private structures contracted with the School of Economics. 27.3% (VMN 11.3%) completed a recognized work activity by the Course.
Analysis of the characteristics of 2022 graduates shows that:
• the percentage of graduates residing in Abruzzo has decreased (75.6% of 2022 graduates, 80% of 2021 graduates) while the percentage of graduates from other regions has increased (24.5% of 2022 graduates, 20% of 2021 graduates);
• the average high school diploma grade improves (81.7 for 2022 graduates, 79.8 for 2021 graduates), exceeding the VMN (80.6);
• the study duration (4 years for 2022 graduates, 4.3 years for 2021 graduates), the graduation delay (1 year for 2022 graduates, 1.3 years for 2021 graduates), and the delay index, calculated as the ratio between delay and the legal course duration, (0.35 for 2022 graduates, 0.44 for 2021 graduates) are substantially aligned with the national average values;
• the percentage of graduates who completed an internship or recognized work activity during the training path is 81.8% (100% for 2021 graduates), significantly higher than the national VM (55.9%).

Short Course Description The Bachelor's Degree in Business Economics (CLEA) was activated (as a Four-Year Degree) in the academic year 1995-1996 following the revision of the Faculty of Economics and Commerce, where the Business Economics path was already active. The renewed faculty took the name of Faculty of Economics. With the application of Ministerial Decree No. 509 of 1999, the three-year Bachelor's Degree in Business Economics was established. With the application of Ministerial Decree No. 270 of 2004, CLEA was merged with the Bachelor's Degree in Environmental Economics and structured into two curricular paths: the Business Management path and the Environmental Management path. In the academic year 2012-2013, to rationalize and make the Faculty of Economics' training offer more transparent, CLEA was merged with the Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Business Administration. From this second merger, the Professional curricular path was born. With the application of Ministerial Decree No. 240 of 2010, CLEA (assigned to the Department of Economics) belongs to the School of Economic, Business, Legal, and Sociological Sciences (SEAGS). CLEA is currently structured into three training paths:
1. Business Management path – focused on studying, according to the traditional institutional approach, the information and operational systems of companies;
2. Environmental Management path – focused on studying eco-compatible management of production and consumption activities;
3. Professional path – focused on studying the most qualifying aspects of accounting and business consulting professions.
Specific Educational Objectives of the Course and Description of the Training Path The Bachelor's Degree in Business Economics is oriented towards bringing students closer to a broader knowledge of business activities with the specific purpose of enabling the study of companies from a dual perspective "internal/external," i.e., integrating within the strictly economic-management approach (also attentive to the environmental sustainability of economic activities), a perspective of studying companies attentive to the training needs of professional and consulting activities. To respond to these general purposes, the Course is structured into the following curricular paths:
a) Business Management;
b) Environmental Management;
c) Professional.
Consistent with the objectives described above, the study curriculum allows the acquisition of the following competencies:
in the first year: knowledge of quantitative analysis methods and critical interpretation of economic-business phenomena; economic and legal aspects characterizing productive organizations and environmental dynamics in which they operate;
in the second and third years: more in-depth knowledge of disciplines related to company management, outlined according to the traditional institutional approach (focused on studying the information and operational systems of companies); according to an approach more directly related to the themes of environmental sustainability of production and consumption activities; or the exercise of accounting professions and business consulting.
For each of the three paths, the training activities fall into the following four learning areas, identified based on criteria of scientific-disciplinary homogeneity:
• Business Area;
• Economic Area;
• Legal Area;
• Mathematical-Statistical Area.
Opinions of Organizations and Companies with Curricular or Extracurricular Internship Agreements The CLEA curriculum provides for an obligatory internship (or training) activity for all enrolled students, recognized with 6 CFU corresponding to 150 hours. The date of the last data collection is August 2023. The general information derived from the data collection is as follows:
• RECRUITMENT CHANNEL – Direct (0), School (0), NS (61);
• HOSTING ENTITY – Public Company (3), Company (23), Professional Office (31), Non-Profit Organization (2), Other (2);
• ACTIVITY SECTOR – General Management (1), Administration and Control (18), Tax Assistance (2), Commercial (purchases/sales) (4), Production/Research and Development (0), Logistics/Warehouse (1), Human Resources (0), Consulting (20), Other (9);
• COMPANY AREA/SECTOR OF REFERENCE – General Management (1), Administration and Control (18), Tax Assistance (2), Commercial (purchases/sales) (4), Production/Research and Development (0), Logistics/Warehouse (1), Human Resources (0), Consulting (20), Other (9).

Consultation with Representative Organizations – at National and International Levels – of Goods and Service Production, and Professions (Course Establishment) To ensure continuous dialogue with all its main external stakeholders, CLEA primarily uses two tools:
1 – the Steering Committee (CI), in common with the Master's Degree CLEAM;
2 – a questionnaire administered to companies at the conclusion of their students' curricular internships.
This Committee first met in 2017 (Minutes of March 13, 2017). During this meeting, the main novelties regarding the didactic programming of the 2019–2020 cohort of the two Courses in Business Economics were presented, and suggestions and collaboration proposals from attendees were collected for improving the teaching, which was then delivered by the Course during the following academic year. Among the proposals from stakeholders, the importance of professional figures capable of providing consultancy to companies facing increasingly complex and competitive markets and environments; the need to encourage students to develop linguistic skills (at least a good knowledge of English) to better face international competition in the job market; the importance of acquiring skills regarding the functioning and structure of European funds to develop projects supporting territorial development.
With the aim of effectively bringing students closer to the economic and business reality of their direct interest, CLEA and CLEAM have promoted the creation of a virtual group on LinkedIn (CLEA Alumni) of graduates from the Business Economics Courses at d'Annunzio, with whom to promote initiatives benefiting current students of the same courses. A significant and substantial initiative in this regard is the professionalizing seminar series “CLEA Alumni – Welcome Back!” aimed at sharing graduates' work and professional experiences with current students of the two Courses.

Final Exam Characteristics The final exam, assigned 3 CFU, consists of writing a written paper on a theoretical or practical topic within the training activities of the degree course. The topic is agreed upon with a teacher who assumes the role of supervisor. In the final exam, the student must demonstrate adequate knowledge and understanding of the topic under analysis, ability to apply knowledge and understanding, and synthesis and re-elaboration capabilities. Participation in the Erasmus+ project is considered significant for qualifying the study path and results in the assignment of 2 points to the student at the graduation exam, counting towards the total points for the academic curriculum.
Summary of the Technical Report of the Evaluation Committee The resources provided to the study course are appropriate, effective, and fully commensurate with the new programming and prospects for its complete implementation. The course covers part of the class of economic and business management sciences in the University's training offer, positioning at optimal levels (in reference to the class of belonging) in terms of enrollments. The proposed structure, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the University's training offer.

SECTION: Admission procedures
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/567

Admission procedures The Degree Program follows the provisions of Article 6 of Ministerial Decree 270/2004 regarding admission verification.
An entrance test TOLC-E organized in collaboration with the 'Interuniversity Consortium for Integrated Systems for Access' (CISIA) is required. The test is administered according to a schedule established in agreement with CISIA, available on the CISIA portal website www.cisiaonline.it, and can be taken at any CISIA member institution, including other universities. The test is divided into three sections: Logic, Verbal Comprehension, and Mathematics. The optional English language section, provided by the CISIA test, will not be considered for admission to the Degree Program.
1. The entrance test is considered passed if the student achieves a score equal to or higher than the minimum set by the School of Economic, Business, Legal and Social Sciences Board. In the absence of an explicit resolution, the minimum from the previous year is applied. A failed test results in the assignment of an Additional Educational Obligation (OFA).
2. Students assigned an OFA may take exams from the second and third years only if they meet at least one of the following conditions:
a) having passed the General Mathematics exam by October 31, 2025 for full-time students, or by October 31, 2026 for part-time students;
b) having passed the Mathematics Reinforcement Course exam by October 31, 2025 for full-time students, or by October 31, 2026 for part-time students;
c) having earned at least 18 CFU related to courses in the first year of the study plan, within basic and characteristic subjects.
3. In the first semester, a Mathematics Reinforcement Course related to the required knowledge for admission is offered. During the academic year, and until September, at least six examination sessions for the Mathematics Reinforcement Course will be available.
4. The Degree Program Council may decide not to assign additional educational obligations to students transferring or changing Degree Programs with the recognition of at least one exam.
5. The CISIA entrance test taken in previous years is valid if the score is equal to or higher than the minimum set in paragraph 1.
6. The TOLC-I and TOLC-S entrance tests are valid for passing the knowledge verification test if the score is equal to or higher than the minimum set in paragraph 1.
7. When registering on the CISIA portal, students may declare to be holders of disabilities or specific learning disorders (DSA), submitting the necessary certifications to arrange specific test accommodations in accordance with current regulations.
8. Transfers, course changes, and single exam admissions are subject to Council approval. University credits earned through passing exams are recognized through the validation of equivalent courses within the Degree Program's training path, possibly through an individual study plan. The Council also specifies the year of enrollment and any additional educational obligation. The Degree Program Council may tolerate minor discrepancies in the number of university credits.
The Degree Program ensures, in case of emergency due to health situations, in line with University guidelines, the possibility to take the admission test remotely. International students intending to enroll in the Degree Program may take the CISIA test for Italian language proficiency.
Students enrolling or registering for years beyond the first, or those transferring from other universities, who cannot meet study commitments within the standard timeframe and mode due to justified work, family, health reasons, or other valid causes, may opt for part-time enrollment, agreeing on a training path with a credit load between 24 and 36 instead of the standard 60 credits/year.
Starting from the 2021/2022 academic year, the Degree Program has adhered to the Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry for Public Administration and D'Annunzio University of Chieti-Pescara to strengthen the knowledge and skills of public administration staff and allow their enrollment in the Degree Program in Economics and Informatics for Business, also through reduced costs and the development of specific training paths.

Syllabus, Texts, and Objectives Communication Skills (communication skills)
The graduate in Economics and Information Technology for Business must possess good communication skills. They will be able to leverage their multidisciplinary training to interact with clients and users of information systems and with specialists who may need to be consulted, and to effectively operate individually and as a team member. They will also have the ability to effectively manage communication regarding projects and work groups, leveraging information technologies to enhance their communication skills, with particular reference to tools offered on the Web. This skill is acquired through the presentation and discussion of projects and, if applicable, through an internship or placement, and verified with the final exam.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [614L] ECONOMICS AND INFORMATICS FOR BUSINESS
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/567

Judgment Autonomy (making judgements)
The multidisciplinary training path will enable the graduate in Economics and Informatics for Business to independently and critically collect and interpret data and information (both inside and outside the company) and use them to form judgments and make decisions on specific problems. In particular, they will be able to critically evaluate information management and processing systems and identify appropriate solutions using new technologies, as well as judge, in relation to the type of company or public administration, the effectiveness of the presence and services offered on the Internet.
The graduate in Economics and Informatics for Business will also be able to reflect on the social, economic, and legal issues connected to the development of the information society.
This judgment autonomy is achieved through the implementation of the aforementioned projects and critical discussion with professors, and verified through passing exams and, especially, through the final exam.

Ongoing Orientation and Tutoring Ongoing orientation is expressed through various delivery methods involving the CdS teachers, the academic tutor, and selected student tutors through calls for applications.
Ongoing tutoring is carried out by all CdS teachers, typically during office hours, and is aimed at assisting students in resolving their issues (e.g., suggesting a correct study method, providing assistance and guidance in completing exercises).
Dr. Mauro Cianci, the academic tutor, is responsible for supporting students in preparing their study plans and resolving any administrative issues, in line with the University's Academic Regulations.
Additionally, designated reference teachers (Gianluca Amato, Fabio Fioravanti, Luigi Ippoliti, Marialisa Mazzocchitti, Maria Chiara Meo, Gianpiero Monaco, Luca Moscardelli, Maurizio Parton, and Francesca Scozzari) are available for students to request personalized tutoring services and agree on the corresponding delivery methods.
Support tutoring and assisted study are formative activities aimed at improving study and understanding of specific courses, generally those identified by students themselves through surveys organized by their representatives as the most challenging. The study program annually selects tutors to provide study assistance through calls for applications targeting doctoral and master's students. Furthermore, a Mathematics Reinforcement Course is offered in the first semester for students facing difficulties with the General Mathematics course.
In 2023, the Department of Economics activated 5 Orientation Tutoring calls.
In March 2024, the Study Program also activated 4 assignments for tutoring, didactic-integrative, preparatory, and recovery activities (Decree Law 105/2003 – Ministerial Decree MUR 289/2021 art. 7) for the preparation of exams in General Mathematics, Informatics, and Statistics for CLEII. The tutors were selected from students enrolled in Master's and Doctoral programs at the University.
Finally, the instructor of the Microeconomics course activated tutoring for the preparation of the Microeconomics exam, conducted by students enrolled in the Degree Course who have already passed the exam for the said course.
Tutoring meetings in the last year were held both online using the University's Teams platform and in person.
MEETINGS Meeting with first-year students: At the start of lectures, a meeting is organized between teachers and first-year students of the CdS to provide information on the organization of the CdS and the teaching methods of the courses.
Meeting with third-year students: At the beginning of the third year, a meeting is organized between teachers and third-year students to illustrate optional training activities, including disciplinary deepening and internships at companies, public or private bodies, or professional orders.
Meeting with students of the Study Program on December 21, 2023, to monitor possible student issues.
Meeting with first and third-year students at the start of the second semester courses for the presentation of Academic Tutors.
The study program also utilizes the following services activated at the University level (https://www.unich.it/campus/servizi/servizi-di-contesto-agli-studenti):
Psychological Listening Service (SAPCO)
The service is available to all UdA students and identifies their needs and any psychological obstacles encountered during their university journey, providing appropriate support/clarification in crisis/distress situations (e.g., difficulties in study methodology, interpersonal relationships, social integration issues, etc.).
Specific Learning Disorders Service (DSA)
The service is available to all UdA students with DSA (dyslexia, dysgraphia, dysorthography, and dyscalculia). Specialized operators provide free consultations and interventions to facilitate student integration and improve their quality of life.
Disability Orientation and Welcome Service (SOASD)
The service is available to all UdA students with disabilities and their families.
The service provides physical accompaniment/assistance in classrooms, secretariats, libraries, and dining halls; personalized assistance during lectures (note-taking) and exams; collaborative support for study, research, and cultural activities (retrieving texts, photocopying, compiling notes).
The CdS website and the University website provide information on:
- how to contact ongoing tutors to schedule individual or group meetings for preparing study plans and resolving issues related to lecture attendance, including the coordinators of tutoring contracts;
- the activities and services offered to students by the University and the body responsible for the right to study (ADSU), such as scholarships, IT resources, libraries, dining halls, accommodation, medical services, and sports and cultural activities;
- opportunities to study abroad through participation in the Erasmus+ program.

Training periods The study plan for CLEII includes an optional internship. Students wishing to complete a curricular internship may use their elective credits (letter D) from their study plan. Internships and traineeships at companies, public or private entities, or professional orders are permitted up to a maximum of 9 CFU. Training internships and orientation internships (also within the university) are permitted up to a maximum of 9 CFU. Each CFU must correspond to at least 25 hours of internship/traineeship.
Internships may be carried out at local companies that have signed an agreement with the School of Economic, Business, Legal and Sociological Sciences. The School's internship office has established 350 agreements with companies, public entities, and professional offices over time.
The administrative contact for internships and traineeships is Ms. Erika Malandra (member of the School's Secretariat staff), tel: 085 4537613, E-mail: erika.malandra@unich.it.
Some local companies (e.g. Digimetrica, Aptar Italia, Konvergence, Do It Yourself, Assiunion, New job, etc.) with which the CLEII course frequently interacts have offered internships and thesis opportunities at companies to CLEII students.
The forms for signing agreements with companies, for completing the training project, and for the evaluation questionnaire from companies are available at:
https://cleii.unich.it/visualizza.php?type=pagina&id=132
Further information is available on the CLEII website, on the page dedicated to 'Internships and Traineeships' (https://cleii.unich.it/pagina-stage-e-tirocini-132). Information about internship or traineeship opportunities is also promptly communicated to students through the CLEII communication channels: notices on the website and on the CLEII Facebook and Instagram pages.
Although CLEII does not require an obligatory internship, the number of students who completed internships at private companies or public entities was eight in 2017, thirteen in 2018, eight in 2019 and 2020, five in 2021, eleven in 2022, and ten in 2023.
Regarding educational, professional, and relational aspects, the following results are particularly noteworthy, calculated on internships completed in the last year (2023):
- motivation and commitment: average 4.9 out of 5;
- achievement of educational objectives: average 4.8 out of 5;
- ability to work in a team and sense of collaboration: average 4.9 out of 5.
Regarding future prospects, 33% of companies offered a job position at the end of the activity. Finally, 71% of host organizations expressed willingness to collaborate again.
These values are substantially similar to those of 2022, as follows:
- motivation and commitment: average 4.7 out of 5;
- achievement of educational objectives: average 4.5 out of 5;
- ability to work in a team and sense of collaboration: average 4.7 out of 5.
Regarding future prospects, 9% of companies offered a job position at the end of the activity. Finally, 73% of host organizations expressed willingness to collaborate again.
The most evident difference in percentage terms is the increase in the number of companies offering a job position at the end of the activity, rising from 9% to 33%.
To provide students with additional knowledge about the world of work, CLEII frequently organizes seminars and other professionalizing activities, particularly in the field of information technology, with company managers, professionals, and sector experts.
The head of the Internship Evaluation Committee is Prof. Fabio Fioravanti, email fabio.fioravanti@unich.it. Training periods
International mobility
Compatible with the requirements set by individual bilateral agreements, students enrolled in the CLEII course may participate in the Erasmus+ program, which allows a stay of 3 to 12 months at EU universities or non-EU countries admitted to the program, for equivalent study activities to those carried out at the CLEII course.
The Erasmus+ coordinator for the CLEII course is Prof. Vincenzo Acciaro (email: vincenzo.acciaro@unich.it) with administrative support from Dr. Mauro Cianci (email: mauro.cianci@unich.it), a member of the School SEAGS Academic Secretariat staff.
The coordinator's activities primarily include:
- supporting the preparation of the study plan;
- examining and evaluating the activities carried out by the student for the recognition of CFU acquired at the foreign university;
- tutoring students during the overseas study period.
With the release of calls each year, events are organized to raise student awareness, promote initiatives, and provide all necessary information.
In the 2024/2025 academic year, eight CLEII students were awarded Erasmus grants, representing an increase compared to previous years (four in 2023/2024, two in 2022/2023, five in 2021/202, zero students in 2019/2020 and 2020/2021).
Regarding the Erasmus+ 2022/2023 call, the Department of Economics allocated a funding of 1,000 Euros (2 incentives of 500 Euros each) for students who were successful in the selection process and who actually participated with success in the project (i.e., earning at least 12 curricular CFU abroad for a period of no less than three months).
The Department has also prepared an Erasmus+ Handbook for students to provide participants with useful information on what to do before, during, and after the study experience.
Participation in the Erasmus project will be considered significant for qualifying the study path and will result in the assignment of 2 points towards the total points available for the study path at the time of the graduation exam.
International mobility activities for students are carried out in collaboration with the Department of Economics' international relations officers:
- Prof. Diego Valentinetti - Department Erasmus Delegate, email: diego.valentinetti@unich.it;
- Prof. Luca Zarrilli - Coordinator of the Department of Economics for International Relations, email: luca.zarrilli@unich.it.
At the university level, specific coordination and administrative roles are provided:
- the Delegate for Mobility and International Relations, Prof. Pierluigi Sacco;
- the University Erasmus Coordinator, Prof. Marcello Costantini;
- the Head of the INTERNATIONALIZATION AND ERASMUS SECTION, PTA, Dr. Glauco Antonio Conte.
CLEII students may also participate in the Overseas Mobility Call, aimed at Ud'A students wishing to spend a semester of study at one of the foreign universities with which the university has agreements in non-European countries. Students will benefit from a monthly grant that varies depending on the destination country.
Other study opportunities abroad are communicated on the University website: https://www.unich.it/didattica/international/mobilita/studenti/erasmus

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
