Graduate Opinions In this section, data from the AlmaLaurea survey, updated as of April 2023, is presented regarding satisfaction with the completed study course. The data specifically concerns graduates from the calendar year 2022: 74 (interviewed 64).
The overall judgment on the study course is favorable: 87.5% of graduates consider it very positive or at least positive, slightly below the university average of 89.8% and the total class average of 88.4%, but significantly higher for satisfaction with teacher relationships (93.8%), compared to the university average (90.3%) and the national average (86.7%). The positive judgment is confirmed by the 2023 data showing graduates would enroll in the same Design course at the university (76.6%), a strong increase from 2022 (63.4%) and 2021 (59.8%), exceeding the university average of 67.4% and the total class average of 65.8%.
Regular course attendance was achieved by over 75% of courses, with 90.6%, significantly higher than the university average of 67.5% and the total class average of 84.9%. The evaluation of classrooms is improving: 87.1% of graduates, compared to 70.5% in 2022 and 65.3% in 2021, consider classrooms always or often adequate, exceeding the university value (84.3%) and the Italian universities average (82.0%). More problematic is the evaluation of computer workstations, deemed sufficient in number by only 52.6% of graduates compared to 56.3% at the university and 50.1% at Italian universities. The data on equipment for other teaching activities (69.5%) is also below the university average (73.2%) and Italian universities (69.9%). Conversely, the data on library services is encouraging and improving (94.5%). Similarly, 90.6% of respondents consider the teaching load appropriate for the duration of the study course, exceeding the university average (88.7%) and the average of other universities (89.5%). The 93.7% of graduates who found the exam organization satisfactory is noteworthy, exceeding the university average (79.8%) and the total class average (85.6%). As with library services, the evaluation of 94.5% is higher than the university (89.3%) and national data (91.8%).
The survey results indicate that improvement actions should primarily focus on enhancing support structures for the study course (classrooms, laboratories, computer workstations, considered by students not always adequate for teaching activities). In this regard, the study course consistently requests the Department and the university to implement rapid interventions in the Pindaro Campus facilities to close the gap with other national sites.
The results of the AlmaLaurea 2022 survey on graduate opinions were discussed in the Course Council meeting on September 14, 2023.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The graduate is able to apply the knowledge acquired during the training path and in relation to the different fields of product design, interior design, and communication design. Specifically, they are capable of using theoretical-critical tools, methodological approaches, and technical-economic evaluation methods learned to perform the various professional activities required by the production system. They are prepared to apply the acquired knowledge through problem setting (structuring knowledge), problem solving (concretizing solutions), and continuous orientation of the company towards innovation.
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is achieved through attendance at the planned training activities, particularly through the activities programmed by the design courses and the Final Synthesis Laboratory. Verification of these abilities is carried out through interviews and the presentation of written/graphic, multimedia, and physical/virtual product models. During exams and the final degree thesis, the abilities in exposition, communication, and critical argumentation of the chosen design solutions are also evaluated.

Learning Skills
The graduate is capable, autonomously, of using the learning tools acquired to deepen the studied content in technical, economic, and humanistic fields, to pursue further studies after the three-year degree, and for continuous professional updating, especially in the field of material, technology, and new production process innovation.
The acquisition of learning skills is realized through the use of computer tools for drafting research reports, developing project syntheses, and formalizing graphic interpretations of critical data. Verification of the acquisition of learning skills is achieved through evaluation, during exams, the Final Synthesis Laboratory, and Internship, of the student's elaborations in constructing information that also involves the use of online databases, graphic and communicative representation of identified issues, and specific project applications oriented towards innovation.

Course Description in Brief The three-year Design degree course aims to train a professional profile of designer with technical skills in the fields of product design, interior design, and communication design. The activities provided by the study course are directed towards acquiring knowledge, abilities, methods, and tools to operate in all phases of the industrial product and communication artifact design process, from pre-competitive analysis to the brief, from idea generation and evaluation to concept design, from concept development to pre-engineering, production, and distribution phases.
The guiding thread of the study course is the concept of innovation related to value creation processes in the different application fields of the project. The training model is interdisciplinary and expressed through theoretical-critical lectures, multidisciplinary laboratories, workshops, an internship in companies and professional studios, and the thesis. Students, after a common two-year theoretical, methodological, and instrumental training in various disciplines of the humanities, economics, scientific-technological, and design areas, as well as project areas, are offered the possibility to characterize their path in the third year by choosing the Final Synthesis Laboratory in product design, interior design, or communication design. This results in a learning method capable of fostering students' creative processes through direct interactions, both with teachers and with nationally and internationally renowned designers, and with important manufacturing companies and research networks operating internationally on design themes.

The training path of the Design degree course defines the competencies associated with different professional profiles in the fields of product design, interior design, and communication design. Design graduates have a wide range of professional opportunities to enter the workforce within companies, studios, and design firms, cultural institutions, public bodies, editorial offices, and service agencies. The course trains the following professional profiles: product designer, interior designer, communication designer, graphic designer, web designer, product ergonomist. The obtained degree allows access to master's degree and first-level master's courses.

External Effectiveness In this section, the summary of employment data for Design graduates is presented, referring only to graduates who did not enroll in another degree course. The data is extracted from the AlmaLaurea 2022 survey one year after graduation (data updated as of April 2023). Among 98 graduates, 69 interviewed, and 29 examined (58.6% women and 41.4% men), the survey reveals an average age at graduation of 24 years, an average graduation mark of 105.6, an average study duration of 4.1 years with a delay index of 0.37.

Currently enrolled in a second-level degree course are 52.2% of graduates (51.9% total universities - 68% university), mostly to improve their cultural education (35.1%) or to improve job prospects (37.8%). 39.1% of respondents participated in at least one post-graduation training. Main reasons for not enrolling in another degree course are work-related (31%) and economic (6.9%). Graduates not interested because planning to pursue post-graduation training are 20.7%.

The employment rate, considering data only for graduates who did not enroll in another degree course, is 55.2%, below the university value (69.4%) and the total class average (64.4%). Only 24.1% are not working, not enrolled in a second-level degree, and not seeking. 20.7% of the examined group are seeking work. On average, graduates take 4.5 months from graduation to find their first job.

Regarding current job characteristics, the predominant profession is technical (21.7% of the examined group), followed by intellectual, scientific, and highly specialized professions (17.4%) and other professions (21.7%), while the percentage of executive professions in office work is reduced (13.0%). Part-time work is widespread in 34.8% of cases with an average of 33.1 hours per week. 87.0% work in the private sector. Predominantly in industry (26.1%), including manufacturing industry (4.3%) and construction (21.7%). 73.9% in commerce, consulting, and other business services. Predominantly in the South (73.9%). Only 4.3% in the Center. The average monthly net salary (1 year) is 954, below the national average (1,121) and the university (1,333).

37.5% of employed graduates use the competencies acquired with the degree extensively in their work, below the total class average (49.7%) and the university (56.8%). Even more encouraging is the 50.0% of graduates who consider the degree very effective and effective in their work, with 37.5% considering it fairly effective. Only 12.5% consider it little effective. Job satisfaction is rated 8.2 out of 10, exceeding the total class average (7.8) and the university (8.0).

To encourage graduates to enroll in a second-level degree course, starting from academic year 2021-2022, the Master's degree in Eco Inclusive Design has been activated at our campus.

The results of the AlmaLaurea survey on the employment status of graduates were discussed in the Course Council meeting on September 14, 2023.

Specific Educational Objectives and Course Path Description The three-year Design degree course aims to train a professional profile of a project technician with operational skills in the fields of product design, interior design, and communication design.
The specific objective is the acquisition of knowledge, abilities, methods, and tools to operate in all phases of the project of material and digital industrial artifacts, from pre-competitive analysis activities to the project brief, from idea generation and evaluation to concept design development, from product development to pre-engineering phases.

The training path aims to prepare a designer who possesses both knowledge of methods and tools to guide and manage incremental and radical product innovation processes, and cultural sensitivities and critical abilities to act consciously within the socio-cultural, technological, productive, and economic contexts where companies in the visual, multimedia, and interactive communication sectors, and industrial products sectors operate.

The training model is interdisciplinary and involves the fields of product design, interior design, and communication design. The guiding thread of the study course is the concept of innovation related to value creation processes in the different project application fields, as a result of the intersection between the technical potential field and the social potential field. Indeed, the encounter between the possible and the desired requires a particular ability to move between different disciplinary universes, from technical and economic knowledge to artistic and socio-cultural sensitivities, from environmental awareness to linguistic and communicative analysis.

Alongside individual theoretical study and applied investigations of methods and tools related to industrial design, students, also through group work, are prompted to reflect closely related to the project's different dimensions and degrees of complexity. In particular, the project activity follows an inductive form that produces knowledge through continuous ideative and logical-interpretative processes of hypothesis formulation, solution experimentation, and result evaluation.

Training is expressed through theoretical-critical lectures, multidisciplinary laboratories, workshops, an obligatory internship in the third year at companies and professional studios, and the thesis. Specifically, students, after a common two-year theoretical-methodological and instrumental training (humanities, economics, scientific-technological areas, design), and applied training (product design, interior design, and communication design fields), are offered the possibility in the third year to characterize their path by emphasizing preparation in one of the three project areas through the choice of the Final Synthesis Laboratory in Product design, Interior design, or Communication design.

This results in a learning method capable of fostering creative processes of mutual enrichment between project, cultural, productive, and economic fields, through direct interactions with teachers and nationally and internationally renowned designers, relationships with important manufacturing companies at the internship level, and research networks operating internationally on Innovation Design driven themes.

The training project is structured around four spheres of knowledge:
- Basic humanities and scientific knowledge. These are information technology, logical-mathematical, economic, historical-critical, artistic, and aesthetic-communicative knowledge, capable of supporting the various application fields of product design, interior design, and communication design. They do not directly concern professional activity but are fundamental to combining technical knowledge with the humanistic dimension and the designer's ability to imagine.
- Specific technical-professional knowledge in the field of production of a technical, project, and engineering nature specific to the exercise of professional activity. Specifically, these are competencies aimed at technological innovation, structural verification, and economic evaluation of projects and products, methods and tools of production, ergonomic approach and eco-design, chemical, physical, and mechanical properties of materials, execution design, and product realization techniques, prototype development, and use of modeling and rapid prototyping techniques.
- Characterizing knowledge of the communication field of a theoretical and technical nature in the fields of visual communication, graphic, and motion design. Specifically, these are knowledge of linguistic and communicative analysis, methodologies, strategies, and techniques of design and realization of interactive interfaces for material products and digital communication artifacts.
- Transversal knowledge related to the development of communicative (written and oral in at least one European Union language, besides Italian), relational, and decision-making abilities of designers with the professional and business world, and the growth of abilities in problem setting and problem solving to structure and concretize the solution to the design problem in a way consistent with given and identified constraints, essential for improving the efficiency and value of professional activity.

Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Traineeship Agreements The survey to collect opinions from accredited companies and professional studios for the study course's internship activities, as well as opinions from interns, was conducted from September 1, 2022, to July 31, 2023. The sites are mostly present in Abruzzo and southern regions, from which most enrolled students originate. The list, available on the Department website, is divided by each of the three thesis areas (Product, Interior, Communication) to ensure coherence with the specific training profiles.

The survey involved 90 interns and over 80 host sites, as each hosted more than one intern.

The survey method was based on questionnaires: Form 1 to be completed by the host organization's Tutor for evaluating the intern's activity and overall judgment on the internship's progress and results; Form 2 to be completed by the Intern on the internship experience.

The survey results show that almost all host organization tutors (83.5%) gave an excellent evaluation of the intern's activity, 15.5% a good evaluation, and only 1.0% a sufficient evaluation. None were insufficient.

The overall judgments provided by tutors on the internship's progress and results particularly highlight: the intern's design ability and learning capacity; the ability to perform assigned work with attention and precision; abilities in problem solving and teamwork; knowledge of graphic programs and main 2D and 3D software; creative attitude, responsibility, and decision-making autonomy; determination and reliability in achieving set goals; good methodological, theoretical, and technical preparation.

Regarding internship satisfaction, 91.0% of interns gave a positive evaluation. Among the positive aspects reported by interns, the reception received and the quality of the work environment, the good relationship with the tutor and work staff, appreciation for the practical and concrete nature of the work experience, successful integration into the company organization, the opportunity to learn new design software, and the professional and relational opportunity, and the acquisition of new technical and professional skills were mentioned.

Among negative aspects, some interns reported difficulty balancing internship activities with class and exam schedules, the limited duration of the internship (125 hours) not allowing a complete and satisfying experience, and distance or difficulty reaching the host site. Some interns suggested increasing the number of design practice hours in the study course, streamlining the activation and conclusion of internships through an online procedure. In response to these suggestions, the study course has: increased internship hours to 150 hours; repeatedly requested the university offices to activate a digital system for managing the entire internship procedure, which would also make monitoring and evaluation of final results and internship experience more accurate.

The results of the internal survey on opinions from companies and design studios that hosted the study course's interns were discussed in the Course Council meeting on September 14, 2023.

Summary of the Regional Coordination Committee Opinion THE REGIONAL COORDINATION COMMITTEE OF ABRUZZO UNIVERSITIES, on December 10, 2015, expressed a favorable opinion on the proposal to establish the Design for Innovation Study Course (L-4).

During the meeting, the following participated:
- The Rector of the Chieti-Pescara University, who noted that there is no L-4 Industrial Design study course in the three Abruzzo universities and thus it is a strategic choice to recover design training demand in Abruzzo;
- The Rector of the University of Teramo, who, expressing a favorable opinion on the course activation, emphasized that design is among the five priority domains of the Abruzzo Region;
- The Rector of the University of L'Aquila communicated the university's willingness to collaborate, involving teachers with supplementary contracts, and expressed the intention, in the future, to collaborate on an inter-university master's course.

After extensive discussion, the activation of the Design for Innovation study course at the University of Chieti-Pescara was unanimously approved.

- absence of a study course in class L-4 on the regional territory;
- demand from the regional socio-economic and business context for project technicians capable of operating in the design field;
- data on the level of industrialization, presented at a recent meeting held at the Abruzzo Region, shows the need to combine instrumental training with reflective research aspects.

Taking inspiration from the above motivations, Prof. Marano noted that in Abruzzo there is a significant demand for professional profiles capable of performing a technical-design role for innovation in the fields of:
Product design: Innovation poles require project operators to facilitate design innovation processes from the perspective of typological, technological, functional, and aesthetic innovation, with particular attention to the development of new materials and the ergonomic and environmental characteristics of products.
Interior design: The sector of temporary installations in cultural, museum, and commercial spaces and the furnishing of private and public internal spaces such as residences, offices, shops, restaurants, and entertainment venues is a field of professional practice requiring a specific interior design technician profile.
Communication design: Communication design is a continuously expanding professional sector. Its presence is transversal and active in companies for brand, product, and service communication, as well as in large retail where the consumer encounters merchandise. In publishing, advertising, tourism, transportation, sports events, entertainment, and wherever content and information dissemination in analog and/or digital form is fundamental.

Subsequently, the following professional profiles were analyzed:
Product design technician: Capable of conceiving and articulating all characteristics determining the quality aspects of an industrial product in relation to use and technological and production possibilities.
Interior design technician: Able to define the systems of installation and furnishing, and the range of components that allow internal spaces to be inhabited from a cultural and functional point of view.
Communication design technician: Expert in designing analog and digital communication artifacts in the fields of electronic publishing, advertising graphics, digital interfaces, multimedia, and web design.

Entry, Path, and Exit Data In this section, the annual survey summary data elaborated by the University Quality Office is presented, referring to entry, path, and exit data of the three-year Design L-4 study course.

Entry Data The enrollment flow is stable. After the 2020/2021 cohort with free access and 204 enrollments, the number of enrollments for the 2021/2022 and 2022/2023 cohorts has remained constant due to the introduction of a maximum of 80 students through programmed access. For academic year 2023-24, the study course has programmed access for 80 students. In academic year 2022/23, total enrollments were 325, of which 284 in course and 41 out of course. Geographic origin analysis of enrollments for academic year 2022/23 indicates that 55.7% of enrolled students come from Abruzzo and 44.3% from other regions. Regarding origin by type of secondary school, 70% of enrolled students in academic year 2022/22 come from High Schools, 17.2% from technical and professional institutes, 10% from magistrali, and other (2.8%). Regarding the diploma grade, it is important to note that 54.3% of students achieved a diploma grade between 80 and 100. 24.3% of students enrolled with a grade of 100 or 100 and Lode. 21.4% with a grade up to 80.

Path Data Compared to the 2020 cohort (data extraction: June 30, 2023), enrolled students: in academic year 2020, 193 with an 80.5% ratio of acquired CFU to required CFU and an average of 5.28 exams passed per student; in academic year 2021, 160 with a 68.4% ratio of acquired CFU to required CFU and an average of 6.14 exams passed per student; in academic year 2022, 149 with a 58.1% ratio of acquired CFU to required CFU and an average of 6.26 exams passed per student (2022 data is partial as academic year 2022/23 is not yet didactically concluded). Withdrawals and non-renewals of enrollments are contained.

Path data demonstrates good efficiency of the study course. Indeed, in the analysis of the 2021/22 cohort with 77 enrolled students, 77.92% of students continued to the second year and 64.94% of students acquired more than 40 CFU, while inactive enrolled students were 6.49%. Only 5.19% of the cohort had zero CFU acquired.

Exit Data Exit data also expresses good study efficiency. Indeed, in the calendar year 2022, 72.97% of students graduated on time, 12.16% after one year, 13.51% after two years or more. Early graduates were 1 out of 74. In the same year, among 74 graduates, 33 obtained a graduation mark of 110 and Lode, 2 obtained a mark of 110, 16 obtained a mark between 105 and 109, and 23 graduated with a mark below 105.

Improvement actions can be directed mainly towards exit orientation to strengthen opportunities for dialogue and networking between graduates and the business world. The study course plans to organize specific JOB DAY events to support Design study course graduates and alumni in the transition from university studies to work activities in close collaboration with companies, bodies, and design studios.

The annual survey summary data elaborated by the University Quality Office, referring to entry, path, and exit data of the Design study course, was discussed in the Course Council meeting on September 14, 2023.

Final Exam Characteristics The final exam consists of a critical reflection and in-depth study of the project developed in one of the Final Synthesis Laboratories (LSF in Product design, LSF in Interior design, LSF in Communication design). The thesis is carried out under the guidance of a supervisor and evaluated by a degree committee.

Final Exam Execution Method - Operational Guidelines In the Design degree course, the preparation of the thesis is structured in two successive phases:
- The first is carried out by the student within one of the three Final Synthesis Laboratories (LSF) of choice (third year, second semester) in Product design, Interior design, or Communication design. The LSFs are composed of a characteristic design discipline and two didactic modules that complete the thematic framework. Activities of each LSF are coordinated by the teacher of the characteristic project discipline. The LSF concludes with a pass exam by the committee composed of the LSF teachers;
- The second, following the pass exam, is carried out by the student under the guidance of one of the teachers responsible for the LSFs, who assumes the role of supervisor, and consists of a critical reflection and in-depth study of the project developed in one of the three LSFs. External personalities may also serve as co-supervisors.

Committee Structure The graduation session is organized with a committee composed of a minimum of 5 to a maximum of 7 teachers of the study course, including teachers who assume the roles of President and Secretary. Normally, all thesis supervisors are present in each committee.

Final Exam Grade Attribution Method The grades are expressed in 110s. The graduation mark is composed of the weighted average of the exam marks reported by the student in their study plan, to which is added the score attributed by the degree committee for the final thesis according to the following criteria:
- max 6 points, by majority of the committee
- max additional 2 points by unanimous committee, for theses considered of exceptional merit.
By unanimous decision, the committee can award the grade of 110/110 with Lode only if the weighted average of exam marks is equal to or above 102/110. The committee, at the public proclamation of each graduation session, confers the title of Doctor/Doctora in Design.

Summary of the Technical Report of the Evaluation Committee Summary Report of the Evaluation Committee The educational objectives of the proposed study course are clearly and effectively outlined and aim to capture a training demand certainly present in the reference territory, confirmed by consultations with social parties and the student population, ensuring a correct prognostic evaluation of possible employment opportunities. The range of consulted organizations appears sufficiently representative at the regional level (and, although to a lesser extent, also at the national level). The expected learning outcomes are adequately delineated, as well as the methods for verifying entry knowledge, the organization of teaching and courses. The commitment of the teaching body to align the study course's teaching activities exclusively to the specific educational objectives of the course and to carry out constant coordination and interdisciplinary cooperation activities is appreciated.

The available infrastructure for the study course's activities appears adequate, and the accreditation requirements requested by current regulations for activating new study courses are also met.

The proposed study course appears consistent with the University's three-year programming plan, positioning itself in a segment of the training offer currently not present in the regional territory.

UNIVERSITY: GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L648] HEALTH ASSISTANCE
SECTION: Admission Procedures
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/608

Admission Procedures Admission to the Degree Program is granted following successful completion of a specific entrance examination based on ministerial decrees regarding the procedures and content of entrance examinations for university courses with national quota-based access.
Additional Educational Obligations Additional Educational Obligations (OFA) are required for candidates scoring below a specified threshold. Beyond serving a selective function for entry into the first year of the program, the entrance test also fulfills the obligation (pursuant to DM 270/04) to verify the foundational preparation of all students enrolling for the first time in the Health Assistance Degree Program at 'G. d'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara. This verification aims to identify any educational gaps among new enrollees and organize necessary recovery activities (in addition to the regular teaching activities of the Degree Program), thereby providing academic support to students assigned Additional Educational Obligations (OFA) based on gaps identified through the entrance test/initial knowledge assessment.
For the purpose of initial knowledge verification, only responses to questions in the entrance test related to the following subjects are considered:
- Biology
- Chemistry
- Physics and Mathematics Questions related to general culture and logical reasoning are not taken into account.
How Additional Educational Obligations are Determined For the disciplinary areas listed above where recovery activities are provided, students who answer correctly less than 25% of the questions in individual subjects will be assigned OFA to be completed obligatorily within the first year, following the procedures established by the Course Director and the instructors of the relevant disciplines after enrollment.
Completing OFA within the first year is mandatory to be eligible to take the official examinations specified in the Study Plan.
Recovery Procedures If necessary, the Degree Program will activate recovery courses—additional to regular course lectures—in each disciplinary area where students have educational deficits. In this regard, instructors of the disciplines subject to OFA will establish 1 or 2 weekly hours dedicated to recovery. Attendance at the recovery course is mandatory. Students attending recovery courses are not exempt from the obligation to attend regular courses. The educational deficit is considered fulfilled upon passing a verification test, which can be taken on dates published on the Degree Program website: http://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-laurea/assistenza-sanitaria If the deficit is not fulfilled within the first year, enrollment in the second year will be permitted, but students cannot take the corresponding examinations specified in the Study Plan until the OFA are completed.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate in Health Assistance must have acquired the ability to:
- communicate with users and colleagues using appropriate language;
- structure the reception of individuals, families and groups in services;
- transmit information and communications of a health, psychological and social nature appropriate to the target audience;
- establish correct and effective relationships aimed at obtaining useful elements for the collection of anamnesis and the implementation of epidemiological and health-social research;
- report and document;
- identify appropriate communication methods for each specific operational situation;
- structure effective relationships with educational, supportive or promotional purposes for the individual in different life stages, for the family and for the community;
- establish correct communication within the institutional context for hierarchical and functional aspects;
- structure an interview setting for analyzing the demand and evaluating health needs, considering both manifest and latent aspects;
- speak publicly using effective bidirectional engagement methods;
- develop effective communication within monoprofessional and interdisciplinary work groups, facilitating information circulation and task/project work;
- promote network work by demonstrating ability to build community networks;
- motivate citizens to engage in prevention and health promotion practices within the community;
- apply individual interview and group device communication skills for the promotion of sexual, reproductive, socio-affective health and family planning;
- apply specific relational skills for participation in family therapy programs;
- express relational skills within problematic settings related to family difficulties, relational issues, infectious or genetic risks, work risks, etc.
- express relational skills for structuring effective pedagogical and promotional settings specific to childhood, adulthood, problematic population groups, immigrants, etc.
- express relational skills for managing and conducting preventive interventions, including health emergency situations;
- express relational skills in the use of tools for verifying processes regarding the quality of health service performance;
- use communication and marketing techniques related to prevention, promotion and health education;
- be competent in listening to safeguard citizens' rights.
Communication skills will be acquired through theoretical teachings in psychology, pedagogy, sociology, and professional methodology, as well as through professional workshops and internship.
The acquisition of behavioral competencies will be verified by tutors through teaching activities, during the internship and in workshops, and through final assessment.

Autonomy of judgment (making judgments)
The graduate in Health Assistance must have the ability to collect and interpret data for the areas of health promotion, prevention, and health education, and to reflect on the main social, scientific, and ethical issues related to them in order to formulate autonomous judgments that take into account the complexity and variability of contexts. In particular, the graduate must demonstrate autonomy of judgment in identifying health needs, in identifying biological and social risk factors, in designing, implementing, and evaluating educational projects, and in identifying priorities for preventive, educational, and recovery interventions.
The graduate must possess analytical, critical, and responsible skills in performing the functions specified by the professional profile.
They must demonstrate the ability to apply ethical principles in professional practice.
They must be able to recognize their own limitations in professional practice, activate network resources, and participate in multidisciplinary team work useful for implementing prevention strategies.
Autonomy of judgment will be verified through evaluations by assigned tutors, through exams, internship assessments, and through verification related to the final exam.

Learning Skills
The graduate must have developed learning skills enabling them to continue studying independently in their specific fields of interest.
Since prevention and health promotion interventions, which constitute one of the main areas of interest for the Health Assistant, require not only already acquired knowledge but also the ability to analyze individual problems and develop an applicable intervention model in specific situations, the Health Assistant graduate must be able to:
- seek the necessary information to resolve professional practice problems or uncertainties, critically selecting sources;
- structure circular learning environments;
- study independently;
- learn within the work group;
- update theoretical knowledge through consultation and analysis of scientific publications, also using databases and retrieving information available on the internet, while critically examining them;
- achieve sufficient knowledge and methodological skills to continue their academic and cultural development independently (Master's Degree, University Specialization Courses, University Master's Degrees).
Learning skills are assessed through continuous verification during training activities, integrating knowledge acquired through specific activities with those gained through personal study, evaluating the critical contribution demonstrated during seminar and internship activities, as well as the ability to self-learn developed during the final project activity.

Brief Course Description The Health Care Course of Study was established by Ministerial Decree of April 2, 2001.
The Course requires a total of 180 CFU, divided into three academic years, with at least 60 CFU to be acquired through training activities aimed at developing specific professional skills (internship).
Each CFU corresponds to 25 hours of student work, including lecture hours, tutorial activity hours, seminar hours, hours spent by the student in other training activities specified in the Academic Curriculum, and hours of independent study necessary to complete their education.
The Health Care Course concludes with a licensing examination and the award of the Health Assistant degree, a professional profile identified as the prevention, promotion, and health education specialist. Their activity is directed toward the individual, family, and community, identifying health needs and priority preventive, educational, and recovery interventions. They primarily operate at the territorial level within social medicine, public hygiene and environmental health, epidemiological research, health care, prevention, and health education. They also intervene in situations requiring constant health monitoring and the development of targeted, comprehensive, and continuous prevention and health education programs.
The Health Assistant carries out their activities in public and private structures, in dependent or freelance practice.
External Effectiveness The employment data relate to 11 of the 14 2021 graduates interviewed one year after graduation. 90.9% of respondents reported working. 80% found employment in the "Health" economic sector and work in the public sector. Regarding time to enter the workforce, an average of 3.6 months passed after graduation. 60% have an indefinite-term contract, and the average working hours are 38. 90% of working graduates reported using their degree-acquired skills extensively, and 90% rated their university professional training as very appropriate. 90% evaluated the degree as very effective/effective in their work, and the satisfaction score (on a scale from 1 to 10) was 9.
External effectiveness data will be presented and discussed within the Course Council.
Specific Course Objectives and Training Path Description The Health Care Course aims to train operators with scientific and technical knowledge necessary to responsibly perform the functions of Health Assistant according to the principles and methods of prevention, promotion, and health education as per Ministerial Decree 17.01.1997, n. 69.
The Course aims to provide students with an integrated health-social culture, a fundamental prerequisite for learning the content and methods of preventive, educational, recovery, and support interventions for individual and community health.
In particular, graduates must possess competencies to:
- carry out prevention, promotion, and health education activities using specific methods, techniques, and tools;
- identify health needs and priority preventive, educational, and recovery interventions for the individual, family, and community;
- identify health needs based on epidemiological and socio-cultural data;
- identify biological and social risk factors;
- design, plan, implement, and evaluate health education interventions in all life stages;
- collaborate in defining communication methodologies, programs, and campaigns for health promotion and education;
- contribute to the training and updating of health and school operators regarding health education methodology;
- intervene in family planning and health, sexual, and socio-emotional education programs;
- implement specific support interventions for families;
- activate network resources in collaboration with general practitioners and other territorial operators;
- participate in family therapy programs;
- monitor, within their competence, hygienic-sanitary conditions in families, schools, and assisted communities;
- control environmental hygiene and infectious risk;
- report and document to competent authorities and propose operational solutions;
- operate within centers jointly or alternatively with health education services, in public relations offices;
- collaborate, within their competence, in health promotion and education initiatives in schools;
- participate in initiatives for evaluating and improving the quality of health services, particularly focusing on user satisfaction levels;
- contribute to initiatives aimed at protecting citizens' rights, with particular reference to health promotion;
- participate in activities organized at the departmental level, both district and hospital, with interprofessional coordination functions, especially in departments implementing national, regional, and local health programming objectives;
- perform their functions with professional autonomy using specific techniques and tools;
- carry out teaching and consulting activities in services where their professional competence is required;
- act individually or in collaboration with other health, social, and school operators, utilizing support staff when necessary;
- contribute to the training of support staff and directly participate in updating related to their professional profile;
- work in teams and integrate with health and social professions.
TRAINING PATH The first year aims to provide knowledge related to the somatic-psychic development of the individual and the study of the community to understand factors influencing individual and community health production. The training path, oriented toward health study, places the knowledge of the bio-psychosocial development of the individual in relation to historical, cultural, and social context. The development of methodological and instrumental competencies relates to research and observation in health, social, and psychological fields to guide the identification of health needs and the methodology for identifying biological and social risk factors, essential and preliminary steps for planning preventive, promotional, educational, and support interventions.
In the second year, the etiopathogenesis of infectious and mental diseases of greater health-social relevance is addressed, along with some clinical-assistive and environmental aspects of considerable importance for management and preventive purposes. The concept of individual and community psycho-physical risk in relation to the environmental context is deepened, and knowledge and skills regarding individual and collective operational methods and tools for implementing prevention, promotion, and health education interventions are acquired. Additionally, knowledge regarding the areas of preventive, educational, promotional, and recovery interventions, such as family, school, work, and daily life, is deepened, where the methodological approach becomes specific to each context.
In the third year, the etiopathogenesis of chronic-degenerative diseases with greater health and social impact is addressed, and knowledge of emergency medicine is deepened. Additionally, competencies for safeguarding citizens' rights, public relations, and the quality process of health services are acquired. Finally, the study of managerial and health economics aspects aims to understand how resources can be best managed in the socio-health field, particularly in prevention and health promotion areas.

Final Exam Characteristics To be admitted to the final exam, the student must have passed all exams specified in the Course Academic Curriculum, including those related to professional training and internship, and acquired the relevant credits.
The final exam has the value of a state licensing examination for the exercise of the profession.
The final exam consists of:
a) a practical test during which the student must demonstrate acquisition of theoretical-practical and technical-operative knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile;
b) preparation and defense of a thesis.
The final exam is organized, by Ministerial Decree of the Minister of Education, University, and Research in conjunction with the Minister of Labor, Health, and Social Policies, into two national sessions.
Final Exam Execution The final exam aims to assess the achievement of expected competencies as expressed by the Dublin Descriptors and the Course-specific Learning Outcomes (RAD). In accordance with the Bologna Process and subsequent harmonization documents for European training paths, the following areas are evaluated in the final exam:
- Applied knowledge and understanding – Applying knowledge and understanding,
- Judgment autonomy – Making judgments,
- Communication skills – Communication skills,
- Learning skills – Learning skills,
corresponding respectively to the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th Dublin Descriptor.
Therefore, final licensing is granted to students capable of:
- applying their knowledge with a professional approach and adequate skills to solve problems in their field of study;
- making decisions to effectively resolve complex problems/situations in their field of study;
- collecting and interpreting data to formulate autonomous professional judgments, even on social, scientific, or ethical issues;
- activating effective communication on clinical, social, scientific, or ethical topics related to their profile;
- learning independently.
In accordance with current regulations, the final exam consists of:
1. a practical test (applied value) where the candidate must demonstrate acquisition of competencies specific to the professional profile;
2. preparation and defense of a written thesis.
The tests are normally conducted on two separate days.
The final exam is held, as per Article 7 of Ministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, in two sessions defined: the first, typically in October/November, and the second in March/April. Session dates are communicated to the Ministries of University and Research and Health, which may send experts as representatives to individual sessions. In case of failure to designate the aforementioned members, the Rector exercises the substitutive power.
The practical test consists of a written document with open-ended questions on cases, with a 90-minute time limit.
It aims to assess the achievement of the professional profile competencies. In this test, competencies corresponding to Dublin Descriptors 2, 3, and 4 are evaluated:
2. Applied knowledge and understanding,
3. Judgment autonomy,
4. Communication skills.
In particular, the ability to identify problems, make decisions, prioritize for individual patients, patient groups, or work processes; design and decide interventions based on available evidence and given organizational conditions; act safely, considering ethical, deontological, and legal dimensions in their actions; demonstrate orientation toward interprofessional practice and risk and patient effect evaluation.
Written document evaluations are conducted anonymously, with grades expressed in thirtieths, which are then converted to scores according to the following parameters:
- 18/30 to 21/30: 1 point
- 22/30 to 24/30: 2 points
- 25/30 to 27/30: 3 points
- 28/30 to 30/30: 4 points
- 30/30 and honors: 5 points.
After this procedure, the candidate's identity is assigned to the respective task.
The thesis allows verification of the achievement of the competencies indicated in the 5th Dublin Descriptor, i.e., the student's ability to conduct an independent and methodologically rigorous learning process. The purpose of the thesis is to engage the student in a design and research work contributing to the completion of their professional and scientific training. The thesis content must relate to themes closely connected to the professional profile.
Typically, the student will be supervised by a Course teacher, called the Supervisor, and possibly by Co-Supervisors, also external to the Course.
The graduation grade is expressed in hundredths and is determined by the following parameters:
a. the average of grades obtained in curricular exams, elective activities, and internship, expressed in hundredths;
b. the score achieved in the practical test, maximum 5 points based on collegial evaluation;
c. the points assigned by the Graduation Committee during the thesis defense, obtained by summing individual points assigned by committee members up to a maximum of 7 (related to the thesis value, clarity and effectiveness of the candidate's presentation, and quality of the slides presented).
The total grade, determined by combining the scores from the above points, is rounded to the nearest whole number. The honors proposed by the Graduation Committee Chair may be awarded with unanimous committee agreement to candidates achieving a final score > 110.
The Final Exam Committee consists of at least 7 and no more than 11 members, appointed by the Rector on proposal from the Course Council, including at least 2 members designated by the Order of Medical Radiology and Health Technical Professions, Rehabilitation, and Prevention (TSRM-PSTRP). The professional representatives on the Committee must be of the same profile, in active service, and must not hold the role of University Teacher or Teaching Tutor in the same Course to ensure an external and independent quality and relevance control of students' professional preparation. The Committee composition cannot change during the two evaluation sessions, unless the aforementioned Rectorial decree is amended.

The Course covers a clearly relevant professional area. The proposed curriculum appears significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, contributing to the University's goals of rationalizing and qualifying its training offer.

TYPE:

SECTION: ADMISSION PROCEDURES
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/63

Admission Procedures Eligible to enroll are graduates of Italian and foreign secondary schools (subject to verification of equivalence of the academic qualification), with knowledge of at least one European Union language in addition to Italian.
Regarding the assessment of adequate personal preparation, the Course Council appoints a Committee that verifies through a test the possession of the required knowledge.
Exempt from the test are graduates who have achieved a final high school grade of at least a minimum threshold to ensure the possession of the required qualifications and preparation. This minimum threshold is set at 80/100.
The test consists of questions on basic knowledge in the field of cultural heritage with multiple-choice answers, only one of which is correct. To pass the test, at least 60% of the questions must be answered correctly. The test is conducted in the first semester and may be repeated in the second semester if necessary.
Students who have not passed or have not taken the test in either of the two opportunities may be assigned Additional Educational Obligations (OFA) within the framework of basic and characteristic courses. For this purpose, individual recovery paths will be defined with the instructors of the disciplinary areas where insufficient preparation was identified, or specific credit 0 learning activities organized within the Department. OFA are considered fulfilled if students have earned a minimum of 18 CFU related to basic and characteristic courses prescribed in the first year of the study plan (or in the first and second year for part-time students).
In case of failure to fulfill OFA by the specified deadline, students remain obligated to meet this requirement and cannot take second-year exams until they have done so (Article 28, paragraph 5 of the University Academic Regulations).
For all matters not covered by this article, refer to current regulations and the University Academic Regulations.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills (communication skills)

Training Periods Assignment All students in the Course of Study in Cultural Heritage carry out an Internship activity to respond to requests from the job market, as highlighted by the steering committee, and by the University. This activity has been expanded from 3 to 6 CFU starting from the 2023 cohort. This activity can be counted towards the experience required by the Ministry of Culture to be included in the lists of professionals (Archaeologists and Art Historians).
Students can choose between:
Internal Internships, i.e., within the same University (e.g., at the DILASS Photo Archive, DISPUTER Photo Archive, University Museum)
External Internships at numerous public and private entities with which the Department has agreements, such as Superintendencies, Archives, Libraries, Museums, both regionally and outside the region, carrying out study, cataloging, valorization, and protection activities for archaeological and historical-artistic cultural heritage (see attached list).
Students also participate in numerous excavation campaigns promoted by the Course of Study professors in Italy (Corfinio, Cencelle/Tarquinia, Capestrano, Palombaro, Iuvanum) and abroad (Egypt, Cyprus, France, Albania, India, Libya). During the health emergency, substitute activities for excavations were organized.
For the procedures and forms, refer to the link to the Department's Internship page. Internship Coordinators: Prof. Maria Giulia Aurigemma and Dr. Maria Cristina Ricciardi. Coordinator for procedures: Dr. Maria Cristina Ricciardi, 0871/3556508 cristina.ricciardi@unich.it During the health emergency, students could also complete remote internships or substitute them with in-person or remote laboratory activities.
To facilitate these activities, an ad hoc Team has been set up for meetings with students and with the internship entities.

The Study Course has also implemented the following initiatives over time to develop student international mobility:
- To encourage student participation in international mobility, the Study Course has provided (Article 9 of the Didactic Regulations) from the 2019 cohort that for the final exam: 'Students who have completed a study experience within the Erasmus project or international agreements activated by the reference Department (DILASS) and the involved Department (DISPUTER) are awarded an additional point.'
- To support mobility in 2021, Study Course students received an additional grant funded by DILASS

Additionally, extensive communication was provided to students about Erasmus Day on October 16, 2020, through the Erasmus Coffee initiative and all initiatives promoted by the specific university department https://www.unich.it/didattica/international/mobilita/studenti/erasmus).
Following these initiatives, there has been a growing student interest in international mobility projects, which in the initial years of the Study Course had recorded very low participation.
In the academic year 2022-23, the outgoing Erasmus agreements for 5 students have already been approved. In the academic year 2019-20 (first semester), 2 students utilized the Erasmus program. In the academic year 2018-19, 5 students utilized the Erasmus program. For the academic year 2022-2023, the Study Course has set a quota of 15 incoming foreign students.
- From the academic year 2018-2019, the EuroTeCH project (European Technologies and strategies for Cultural Heritage at risk) has been activated (European Technologies and strategies for Cultural Heritage at risk. Project line: ERASMUS PLUS. Coordinator: Prof. Oliva Menozzi).
The EuroTeCH project (see attached PDF) secured fifth place among 800 projects submitted in the 2018 KA203 Erasmus Plus-Strategic Partnerships for Higher Education call and is part of the European Year of Cultural Heritage 2018. The project targets students of Bachelor's, Master's, and PhD programs in Letters, Cultural Heritage, and Archaeological and Art History Heritage, as well as professionals in public sectors (museums, superintendencies, archaeological parks) and private sectors.
The formation of a consortium involving academic and private partners enables the provision of a continuous training path aimed at developing an academic curriculum for a professional course. Specifically, a new competitive professional figure for the current job market is being defined, thanks to the application of ICT, to allow professional growth through training modules that integrate practical training with theoretical paths, laboratory activities, applied technology, and advanced diagnostic protocols. In addition to ECTS credit recognition, the training path will acquire EQF characteristics, respecting transparency and quality criteria to facilitate access to the European job market.
The teaching modules, also translated into English, will be made available as open course OER on an e-learning platform, enabling professionals to continuously update on specific techniques and application systems. The integration of teaching modules with innovative applications, such as GIS systems, augmented reality, virtual reality, and video lessons, goes beyond traditional learning methodologies, promoting the inclusion of ICT in academic training.
- For student international mobility, the Study Course also relies on the support of the University's structures, whose activities are described in the dedicated section of the website (https://www.unich.it/percorsi/international). The University also hosts the Europe Direct Chieti Community Information Centre, a free information and mediation service between citizens and the European Union.

Work Placement
- The Placement Service is managed by the University's Orientation, Tutoring, Placement, Student Rights and Disability Sector (see link). For outgoing orientation, understood as training and professional orientation specifically aimed at integrating graduates and graduates into the workforce, the University has activated a true placement structure aimed at increasing the employment and employability of its students through the experimentation of assisted work placement pathways. To this end, the University has implemented the online platform S.T.A.R.T. (Stages, Internships, Advanced Training, Research, Territory and Placement) with the aim of consolidating an active network of relationships between the University, businesses and research systems, to develop a virtuous process of relationships and services oriented both to facilitating the 'communication' between business needs, employment integration processes and impacts on educational plans, and to providing substance and continuity to the transition phase to work for qualified knowledge resources that allow the economic/productive system to sustain the comparison with the continuous challenges of the market. In particular, for work placement, the computer platform JOB is active, which is linked to the aforementioned post-graduation orientation program S.T.A.R.T. and is the tool used by the University's Placement Service to carry out mediation activities.
The calendar of work placement and business start-up orientation events organized by the University's Placement Service is published at the indicated link.
- The Study Course also works to foster contacts with public and private entities active in Cultural Heritage professions. Frequent meetings are organized with representatives of the working world, both on the University Campus and at the sites of interested bodies and companies. In particular, during site visits that integrate the teaching of each course, meetings are facilitated with managers and officials responsible for the protection and valorization of Cultural Heritage, such as Superintendents, museum directors, but also professionals working in companies, publishing houses, etc., fostering personal contacts that can consolidate during internships and traineeships.

UNIVERSITY: University of Studies Gabriele d'Annunzio - Chieti-Pescara

SECTION: Student Opinions
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/63

Student Opinions: From the survey of student opinions as of July 31, 2023, provided by the new dynamic portal prepared by the university (see link and attached PDF), a fully positive evaluation of the Course of Study emerges (see the specific PQA page for the survey methodology: https://pqa.unich.it/rilevazione-opinioni/rilevazione-opinioni-studenti-e-docenti-2023).
The evaluation indeed records an average score of 3.53, in line with the previous year (3.55%) and 2021 (3.50).
Specifically, 67.44% of teaching activities fall under Level A; 30.23% of teaching activities fall under Level B, and only one teaching activity (2.33%) falls under Level C, with a score of 2.98, thus very close to the threshold of Level B. No teaching activity falls under Level D.
All indicators also record a high degree of satisfaction, confirming and in some cases exceeding the already positive data from previous years.
In all responses to the questionnaire provided by students, the average score of the Course of Study is higher than or equal to the area and university averages, with only a slight decline (Course 3.27; area 3.33; university 3.31) regarding question D1: "Were the preliminary knowledge possessed sufficient for understanding the topics covered in the exam program?". This data is likely due to the presence of many technical courses addressing disciplines absent from standard school curricula.
Generally, student suggestions indicate that they consider the basic knowledge and teaching load adequate.
The request for intermediate exams is numerically very limited and restricted to teaching activities with a high number of CFU.
These data suggest that some critical issues previously reported on these points have been resolved through corrective measures applied to the study path and the delivery methods of basic courses, particularly in the first year.
The Course of Study continues to monitor student opinions closely, which were discussed in a GAQ meeting on July 5, 2023, and will be further debated in the Course Council meeting scheduled for September 21, 2023.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [OBC7] CULTURAL HERITAGE
SECTION: GRADUATE OPINIONS
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/63

GRADUATE OPINIONS The information presented in this section has been extracted from the AlmaLaurea data updated as of April 2023 (see link and attached PDF).
Graduate evaluations are favorable and exceed the university's average, particularly the positive responses (definitely yes / more yes than no) to the question of whether they are overall satisfied with the degree course and to the question about their relationship with professors reach 100% of respondents, and to the question of whether they considered the study load of the courses appropriate for the duration of the degree program, exceeding 93% compared to 90% from last year.
Also the attendance rate, in my opinion extremely indicative after the pandemic, records positive responses from over 96%, exceeding the university's average.
All these satisfaction indicators are also higher than the average of the degree class across other universities (https://pqa.unich.it/sites/st16/files/allegatiparagrafo/09-05-2023/l-1_beni_culturali.pdf).
Other indicators on the organization of teaching and the use of classrooms, libraries, and laboratories also show a generally higher level of satisfaction than the university's and national averages, while strong dissatisfaction is reported among users of computer workstations. This issue is shared by professors and has been reported multiple times. However, some restructuring and modernization interventions have been carried out on the facilities and their equipment, which should improve this aspect of the student experience.
Regarding the organization of exams, schedules, and reservations, 86.7% of students are satisfied, a figure in line with 2022 and significantly higher than previous years, exceeding both the university's and national averages.
81.8% of graduates are currently enrolled in a second-level degree course. This is an increase compared to 2022 (80%) and higher than the university's average (68.6%) and the class average across all universities (74.7%).
79.3% would enroll again in the same course at the same university, an increase from 2022 (73.3%) and higher than the university's (67.3%) and class average (71.3%).
Graduates are 69.7% women and 30.3% men, thus confirming a certain balance in this historical imbalance that characterizes this study direction.
The average age of graduates is 26.2 years, decreasing from 2022 (27.4), thanks to ongoing efforts to improve study paths and regularize student careers; the overall figure, in my opinion, is also affected by the presence of some 'senior' students, i.e., students who enroll at an advanced age, even after retirement, in this study program to pursue an interest they could not follow in their youth.
Compared to the previous year, there is an improvement in the regularity of the study path, likely due to overcoming the pandemic, which hindered access to archives and libraries necessary for completing a thesis in these disciplines.
The origin of new students remains highly diversified, practically from all high school tracks, with a predominance of Artistic High School (30.3%).
The social origin of graduates is also highly diversified, with 75.9% having no parent with a degree, while 48% come from the middle class, 31% from the executive labor class, and the remainder from the upper class (see attached PDF).
The insights from the surveys of students, graduates, and alumni were discussed in the meeting of the GAQ Review Group of the Course of Study on May 5-7, 2023, and will be thoroughly examined in the Course of Study Council meeting scheduled for September.
Learning Skills
Graduates will have developed a solid foundational education in the field of Cultural Heritage, covering both archaeological and historical-artistic areas, enabling them to subsequently choose a deeper focus in either methodological or chronological aspects.
This diversified training will allow graduates in the three pathways to acquire specific skills applicable in various occupational sectors related to the management, historical interpretation, and conservation of Cultural Heritage.

Brief Course Description
The purpose of the study course is to train professionals in the knowledge, valorization, management, and protection of Cultural Heritage from Antiquity to the Contemporary Era. The Course is structured into two pathways: archaeological and historical-artistic.
The training includes theoretical and technical courses, along with field internships, laboratory work, and activities in institutions responsible for protection. There are also agreements with private and mixed-management entities for training activities related to the valorization and use of Cultural Heritage.
During the three-year program, students receive a foundational humanistic education through the study of historical, literary, linguistic, anthropological, geographical, and philosophical subjects. These are complemented by solid knowledge of archaeology and art history from prehistory to the Contemporary Era, with a geographical scope ranging from Italy to Europe to the East. Foreign language skills, applied informatics, and Cultural Heritage legislation are also acquired.
Graduates may find employment at various levels in public and private entities active in the fields of Archaeological and Historical-Artistic Heritage. They may also manage and organize events related to the valorization and protection of Cultural Heritage and work in Tourism or specialized Publishing.
External Effectiveness
The most recent data on this topic are those published by AlmaLaurea (see link and attached PDF) and relate to 2022.
Of these, 55.2% of students have had work experience during their studies; in 24.1% of cases, this was occasional, seasonal, or part-time work, and in 12.5% of cases, it was work related to their studies, a figure that has significantly increased from the previous year (4%).
The employment rate is 18.2%, slightly higher than 17.7% in 2022, but none of these individuals extensively use the skills acquired through their degree. However, as this is a first-level degree, to improve job prospects and complete their training, almost 82% of students are enrolled in a two-year master's degree, a percentage that has increased from the previous year. 100% have enrolled in a master's degree, which is the natural continuation of the three-year program, with about half doing so at the same university.
Only 3% intend to enroll in another first-level degree course, a figure that could be interpreted as a high level of satisfaction with the study path.
It should be noted that, although the three-year degree provides skills and professionalism that can be applied in the job market, to operate effectively in the Cultural Heritage sector, further study is advisable. This 'necessity', as highlighted by the data mentioned above, has been recognized by graduates, who were informed during orientation sessions about the opportunity for a 3+2 study path. Only 10.3% (down from 11.6% the previous year) of these students do not intend to continue their studies.
Specific Course Learning Objectives and Course Path Description
The study course aims to train qualified personnel to work in the study, research, protection, and valorization of Cultural Heritage, including archaeological, historical, and historical-artistic heritage, covering the chronological range from prehistory to the Contemporary Era in the two specified pathways. Students must acquire, within the three-year program, specific skills in historical-methodological and technical-operational areas, with particular attention to restoring the contexts in which Cultural Heritage is located. The purpose of the study course is to provide the basic knowledge and interpretative tools in the fields of archaeological, historical, and historical-artistic Cultural Heritage. Key and fundamental themes will be addressed, adapting to the sector's cutting-edge methodologies. The course aims to provide the technical and scientific tools required by the two pathways for data collection, interpretation, contextualization, and communication. Additionally, the course aims to enable students to collaborate and work within institutions dealing with Cultural Heritage (Superintendencies, Departments, Museums, Foundations, Galleries, Archives, Libraries, Research Centers, etc.), with a basic level of technical preparation that may include cataloging and educational assistance tasks, as well as specific administrative duties. The course, in its two pathways, aims to train Cultural Heritage operators with basic knowledge in archaeological and historical-artistic fields, complementing theoretical knowledge with specific skills in conservation and valorization of Cultural Heritage. Archaeological, historical-artistic, and historical subjects will naturally be prioritized to meet the requirements of each descriptor. A complement of philosophical, geographical, and literary subjects is also necessary to prepare for subsequent teaching activities or employment in public and private sectors. Theoretical lectures will be complemented by direct field investigations, particularly in archaeology (through excavation internships) and art history, sharing common research areas (through guided visits to museums, restoration studies, deposits and archives, churches and historic palaces, public and private collections, etc.).
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Curricular or Extra-Curricular Internship Agreements
The curricular internship activities, as per the teaching regulations, involve all students enrolled in the Course of Study and include internal internships (University Museum; DILASS and DISPUTER photographic archives; Co.Media, the university's media and social network working group) and especially external internships, carried out at public, private, and ecclesiastical cultural entities with a wide variety of training types and geographical areas (see the attached list in SUA Course of Study 2023 Table B5).
Particularly noteworthy is the internal internship at the DILASS photographic archive, an online archive (see link) managed by students, which has been recognized as part of the national-level photography network, a nationally significant information structure.
Since the 2018-2019 academic year, to make the collection of opinions from host entities and companies more effective, a final internship evaluation form has been prepared, to be completed by the host organization's tutor, consisting of seven items plus a final comment.
All forms received since then have been extremely positive in evaluating individual aspects of the experience, particularly the competencies and relational skills of the interns; the final comments, where present, are also positive, with no significant criticisms.
It is also noted that entities and companies that have previously hosted graduates and alumni of the Course of Study have consistently renewed their availability.
Entities, particularly those in the local area, periodically attend meetings with internship coordinators, and to facilitate this contact, the TEAMS platform has been configured with the 'Internships of Course of Study in Cultural Heritage and BASA' team, aimed at meetings between teachers, tutors, students, and internship entities.
However, for all of 2021 and the first part of 2022, due to the prolonged pandemic, the possibility introduced in 2020 during the full Covid emergency to replace the internship with a laboratory activity (in-person and/or remote) was renewed to avoid hindering the completion of the study path, considering the difficulty for entities and institutions in accommodating external personnel.
This activity has been progressively resumed.
In 2022, from January to July, five students participated in external internships, all receiving positive evaluation forms from the host entities.
In the 2022/23 academic year, 16 students have already completed external internships, receiving positive feedback.
A detailed report on student participation in external internships, including the distribution by Course of Study and host entities for the years 2019-2023, is attached (see attached PDF), prepared by Dr. Ricciardi, the DILASS internship coordinator.
Consultation with Representative Organizations of Goods and Service Production and Professions (Course Establishment)
The President invites Prof. Stefano Trinchese, Dean of the Faculty of Letters and Philosophy, to present the modified Cultural Heritage Bachelor's Degree in line with the new teaching regulations (D.M. n. 270 of October 22, 2004).
Prof. Stefano Trinchese then presents the course's objectives and purposes, also highlighting the related professional opportunities.
In particular, he notes that graduates of the Cultural Heritage Bachelor's Degree can collaborate or work with bodies responsible for the protection, management, and valorization of the territory, including Archaeological Superintendencies and Superintendencies for Architectural, Artistic, Environmental, and Historical Heritage, public and private research or protection entities in the Cultural Heritage sector, both local, national, and international. They can also work with Libraries and Archives, both national and local. Graduates will be able to actively collaborate with these institutions in creating archaeological maps, territorial surveys, exhibitions, and cultural routes.
Having taken note of what was reported by Prof. Trinchese, the consultation provided for in Article 11, Paragraph 4 of D.M. n. 270 of October 22, 2004, is carried out. Following a thorough examination, this consultation is positive.

The Museum Pole analyzes the territorial context (demographic data, education, tourist flows, infrastructure availability, and so on) to identify strategic objectives and initiate a cultural development program starting from a territorial area around Chieti up to including Sulmona. A collaboration has thus been initiated, aimed at creating agreements that can expand the cultural offering. The Courses participate with interest and have shared contacts within the field of cultural economy for the analysis of the territorial context and strategic programming.
