Wednesday, March 9, 2016, in room A of the Department of Letters, Arts, and Social Sciences at the Università G. d'Annunzio of Chieti, the round table 'Abruzzo Cultural Heritage. Development, Perspectives, Critical Issues' was held, coordinated by the director of DiLASS Stefano Trinchese, as a consultation meeting between representatives of the Study Courses and representatives of heritage protection on the territory. The following were present at the meeting:
For social partners:
The Superintendent of Archaeological Heritage of Abruzzo
The Superintendent of Fine Arts and Landscape of Abruzzo
The Director of the National Museum of Abruzzo
For the three-year and master's Study Courses in Cultural Heritage and Archaeological and Historical-Artistic Heritage, the Presidents of the Study Courses:
Sara Santoro, President of the Master's Study Course BASA
Gaetano Curzi, organizer of the meeting, delegate of Alessandro Tomei, President of the Three-year Study Course in Cultural Heritage.
Maria Giulia Aurigemma, Full Professor of Modern Art History.
It was an important and open opportunity for discussion with stakeholders active on the territory, animated by the presence of the main responsible persons and representatives of the regional cultural context, involved in a constructive debate aimed at comparing different realities within the cultural heritage landscape, both with the Study Courses and among social partners.
The meeting demonstrated the need for constant and periodic dialogue on current issues, such as involving the university world in territorial valorization programs through broader cooperation axes, and especially to resolve the issue of transitioning from university training to the workplace in the field of cultural heritage, which in the Abruzzo regional context is linked to the dramatic consequences of earthquakes on the historical-artistic and architectural heritage. The discussion also examined the training objectives of the Study Courses and expected outcomes, the different professional figures within the broad training activities, from ancient to contemporary, of the Study Courses, and potential employment opportunities in light of current legislation. Representatives of the Region and the three territorial Superintendencies discussed with the numerous present teachers who over the years have trained a large number of archaeologists and art historians, some of whom have been independently active on the territory for some time, in a frank and constructive debate that, at a time of ongoing reforms, assessed what the Study Courses can mean for protection and valorization in Abruzzo.
At the end of the meeting, Prof. Aurigemma presented the volume 'The Collegiate of Saints Cesidio and Rufino in Trasacco. A Sanctuary in Marsica' edited by Gaetano Curzi and with the collaboration of PhD students M. D'Attanasio and S. Manzoli: a project, an editorial initiative of great scope entirely focused on the study of a monument in all its aspects, confirming the role and commitment of the BASA and BC Study Courses, DiLASS, and the PhD program for the territory, reconnecting to the recently concluded debate.
Entry, Path, and Exit Data From the data provided by the University, it emerges that:
In the academic year 2021/2022, the enrolled students in the Study Course amount to 76, showing a decline compared to 89 in 2021/2022; to reverse this trend, the Study Course is implementing enhanced orientation activities.
The total enrolled students are 301, of which 204 are currently enrolled, 184 regular, and 97 out of course.
The majority of students come from the Abruzzo region (90.9%), while the number of students from other regions is slightly decreasing (9.1%), probably as a residual effect of the pandemic that has hindered student mobility in and out, although this non-negligible figure confirms the attractiveness of the Study Course.
84.9% of the enrolled students come from high schools, and the others from all types of higher education programs.
The data suggest that students' careers have also recovered in the ratio of acquired CFU/required CFU (31.3%), after the pandemic years caused a decline due to lack of in-person attendance, which particularly affected new students.
In particular, over 40% of students have achieved between 75% and 100% of the required credits, with over a third having obtained between 30% and 75% of the required CFU, reducing the percentage of students who have not acquired CFU to approximately 5% (source INGRID), data consistent with last year. Finally, the latest available data indicate the absence of outgoing transfers and explicit withdrawals or suspensions for the 2022 cohort.
The number of graduates in the calendar year 2022 was 33, with an average grade of 103.6/110, of which approximately 20% with honors. Of these, about 39.4% completed within the regular period and equally many in the first year of extension (I year f.c.), a figure improving compared to the previous year (26%), 9.1% in the second year f.c., and about 12% between the second and fifth year and beyond f.c.
Characteristics of the Final Exam The final exam consists of two parts. The first involves the oral discussion of a written paper drafted by the candidate, from which the candidate's ability to analyze and illustrate issues related to the Study Course followed should emerge, taking into account the most up-to-date research tools. The second part involves a verification of knowledge of a foreign language in oral form. The final exam substantially contributes to achieving and verifying the learning outcomes.
Procedure for Conducting the Final Exam The topic of the final paper is assigned by a supervising professor (the supervisor), who will follow its drafting. The topic must be assigned within the scope of a course belonging to one of the disciplinary scientific sectors characteristic of the curriculum followed (see, for example, the attached file with a list of recently assigned topics). With prior authorization from the Study Course Council, topics may also be assigned within courses belonging to basic or related and integrative disciplinary scientific sectors.
The paper must be accompanied by bibliographic references and have an approximate length of fifty pages.
The training path will culminate in the discussion of the paper during the graduation session.
The examination board (composed of a minimum of five professors) will assign the final grade on a scale of 110, and may, unanimously, award the highest grade with honors. The minimum grade is 66/110. The examination board awards up to a maximum of 4 points for the final exam based on the following criteria:
- The scientific quality and originality of the paper
- The candidate's scientific and critical maturity
- The ability to synthesize and clarity of exposition demonstrated during the exam itself.
Students who have completed a study experience within the ERASMUS project or international agreements activated by the referring Department (DILASS) and the involved Department (DISPUTER) will be awarded an additional point.
Summary of the Technical Report by the Evaluation Unit The course covers a scientifically and professionally relevant area and has consistently maintained optimal levels, in reference to its class, in terms of enrolled and registered students. The Faculty has adequately equipped, appropriate, and effective spaces, and following a program in an advanced phase of deep restructuring of the Chieti Campus, new teaching and scientific spaces will be acquired in the short term, fully commensurate with the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The situation regarding Faculty teaching presents some critical aspects, although it should be noted that the basic and characteristic disciplines of the course are also represented within the University outside the Faculty: with a targeted use of the University's specific teaching, the course could therefore adjust its teaching. The proposed organization, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the University's educational offer.

Single Cycle Master's Degree in PRIMARY EDUCATION SCIENCES
Specific Educational Objectives.
The five-year single-cycle Master's Degree Course in Primary Education Sciences (CdLM-SFP) of class LM-85 bis is subject to programmed admission. The number of places, date, content, and mode of the selection test are determined annually by a decree of the MIUR.
The Master's Degree Course (CdL) is organized according to the provisions of the Master's Degree Class in Primary Education Sciences as per DM 249 of September 10, 2010 (G.U. January 31, 2011) and is the transformation of the previous four-year Bachelor's Degree in Primary Education Sciences. It provides training and professional qualification for:
- kindergarten teachers;
- primary school teachers.
The CdL is managed by the Didactic Area Council (CAD) for Primary Education and belongs to the Department of Human Sciences of the University of L'Aquila.
The academic organization of the Course presents specific educational objectives and a general framework of training activities in line with the ministerial scheme, while the study plan details the training path and the courses offered, indicating also the scientific-disciplinary sector to which each course belongs, the possible division into modules, and the number of CFU attributed to each teaching activity.
The acquisition of CFU related to the training activities carried out during the curriculum leads to the Single Cycle Master's Degree in Primary Education Sciences, after which graduates of the class obtain the qualification to teach in kindergarten and primary school.
The attainment of the degree is the result of a comprehensive evaluation of the study curriculum, the thesis, and the internship report by a committee composed of university professors, tutors, and a representative appointed by the Regional School Office for Abruzzo (MIUR).
To obtain the Single Cycle Master's Degree, it is necessary to have acquired 300 CFU in the areas and scientific-disciplinary sectors specified in the Academic Regulations.
Graduates must acquire solid knowledge and skills in the various disciplinary areas taught and be able to propose, translate, and apply them in the specific contexts of kindergarten and primary school. Such knowledge and skills are closely connected from the beginning of the course with the ability to manage the class and design the educational and teaching path for all students, as well as to facilitate school integration and support the learning process of students with special needs. In particular, graduates must possess knowledge and skills:
1) pedagogical and methodological-didactic to manage the class group and the progression of individual student learning through appropriate forms and tools of planning, programming, and scheduling, also using personalized and individualized intervention strategies;
2) disciplinary related to the teaching areas (linguistic-literary area, historical-geographical area, scientific-technological area, artistic area, motor area, foreign language area: English);
3) transversal to be able to articulate objectives and content of different disciplines according to different school levels and contexts: kindergarten and primary school;
4) relational and managerial to make classroom work beneficial for each student on cognitive, affective-relational/social, and psychomotor levels, fostering a favorable attitude toward learning and facilitating the coexistence of different cultures and religions;
5) social to actively participate in school and teaching management, collaborating with colleagues in both the design of teaching and internal and external collegial activities, also in relation to the needs of the territory where the school operates.
The teaching activities are structured in the following forms:
a. courses;
b. laboratories;
c. direct and indirect internship.
The CdL, in line with the stated objectives, provides alongside basic and characteristic disciplines one or more pedagogical-didactic laboratories aimed at simulating, transposing practical examples, etc., of what is learned in courses, and mandatory internship activities:
a. indirect, carried out at the Department's structures or other locations, with the aim of preparing, reflecting, and discussing observation and documentation methods to be used in direct internship phases and in writing the final internship report;
b. direct, carried out in accredited and contracted kindergarten and primary schools, with the aim of applying knowledge and skills acquired through courses, laboratories, and indirect internship.
The CdL also organizes seminar activities and other coordination and curricular connection initiatives.
The internship activities include 600 hours equal to 24 CFU, which, from the second year to the fifth year, conclude with a mandatory final report and are followed and coordinated by teachers, tutors, coordinators, and organizers, partially or fully detached from the CdL, and by welcoming tutors identified at the schools. The internship constitutes a professional training path aimed at enabling students to use disciplinary knowledge in specific school situations, combining skills, theoretical and practical knowledge, and applying them in real contexts, including activities (observation, guided work, etc.) designed to make the student autonomous in constructing their learning path.
The study plan aims to provide internal coherence and consistency to the various training activities and to harmonize the relationship between families of knowledge and skills belonging to different disciplinary areas, linking them to laboratory and internship activities. The skills have been grouped into mastery domains to make the curriculum professionally impactful, responsive to student needs, and aligned with the goals to be achieved and the exit skills. The plan is structured as follows:
- in the first year, knowledge and skills related mainly to the pedagogical and methodological-didactic, legal, and school history areas have been grouped;
- in the second year, knowledge and skills related to the linguistic and literary area, historical and geographical areas have been grouped;
- in the third year, knowledge and skills of didactic intersection and scientific-mathematical and musical areas have been grouped;
- in the fourth year, knowledge and skills of psychological, social, motor, and disability areas have been grouped;
- in the fifth year, knowledge and skills of scientific and technological areas have been grouped.
An English Language Laboratory (2 CFU) is provided for each year of the Course (for a total of 10 CFU) and a final B2 level test (2 CFU).
The curriculum structure, cohesive and coherent in terms of progression, continuity, and adjacency between activities, experiences, and the didactic load supported by the student per semester, allows for adequate organization of work, fulfillment of didactic obligations, and development of a professional habitus enabling the student to:
- integrate elements such as creativity, flexibility, and motivation for knowledge, typical of kindergarten, with disciplinary security, characteristic of primary school;
- effectively address learning difficulties and disorders with targeted interventions based on the latest psycho-pedagogical research, and facilitate the welcome of children with disabilities to better integrate diversity, value personalization elements, and establish better collaboration between class teacher and support teacher;
- positively value and integrate differences determined by the intercultural composition of the class;
- promote continuity between the two school levels thanks to the presence of professionals competent in both levels.

The course provides:
- "Basic training activities" for acquiring psycho-pedagogical, methodological-didactic, socio-anthropological, and digital skills; training includes in-depth disciplinary study and strategies to effectively foster authentic learning and develop students' motivation;
- "Characteristic training activities" dedicated to in-depth study (first area) of content to be taught in the two school levels considered ("school knowledge") and (second area) of content related to the welcome and full integration of students with disabilities;
- "Other activities" that complete the profile.
Content Areas and Domains.
A) Specific objectives and description of the basic training path: psycho-pedagogical and methodological-didactic.
The student must:
- possess a critical knowledge of the main pedagogical-didactic models integrated with elements of developmental and educational psychology to better understand students;
- acquire knowledge of child development regarding the following processes: sensory, attentional, linguistic, memory, thinking, reasoning, and problem-solving;
- acquire knowledge of the volitional-motivational and emotional-affective sphere and socialization processes;
- consolidate skills in systematic observation of child behavior;
- possess didactic skills (ability to organize the class as a learning environment and community of relationships, mastery of a variety of teaching methodologies that favor the learning process; ability to adopt and use integrated and flexible teaching strategies based on students' needs and actual learning processes; ability to share with the class teacher flexible models of planning-implementation of activities and evaluation models);
- consolidate professional reflexivity in relation to one's own and others' actions in didactic contexts, within a dynamic and evolving vision of the teacher's professional profile;
- recognize the didactic potential of new technologies and integrate them functionally in the preparation of appropriate learning environments;
- know ludic methodologies;
- know the foundations and strategies of educational research useful to verify and innovate educational and teaching practices;
- be able to develop field-based educational research projects based on observation, documentation, innovation, and evaluation of teaching actions and their results;
- have knowledge of the historical-social contexts of professional practice;
- understand one's work in relation to the regulatory processes of the educational system and, from a comparative perspective, to European and international developments in educational policy;
- be able to act in conditions of diversity and heterogeneity in the classroom, as inclusion action for students of different origins and/or with special educational needs, under the principles of equity and equality in school.
Teaching Methods for Achieving Objectives Lectures, also with multimedia technology (software, video recordings, etc.), exercises, guided practices; laboratory activities with analysis and production of projects (individual and group), teaching interventions, and evaluation tools; simulations; debates with experts; collective discussions and focus groups.
B) Specific objectives and description of the characteristic training path.
Area 1: School Knowledge.
1a. Disciplinary Area: Linguistic.
Specific Objectives
- knowledge of the national linguistic heritage in its historical formation on the political-cultural events and structural phonetic, morphosyntactic, and semantic-lexical levels;
- knowledge of the territory on the linguistic level, with reflections on dialects and regional varieties and their usage contexts; brief references to languages of allophone areas;
- knowledge of linguistic codification processes and unification factors of Italian, with particular reference to the role of school;
- knowledge of the main dimensions of variation of written, transmitted, and spoken language, with relevant communication styles and usage registers;
- knowledge of the structures of the Italian language, on phonological, morphosyntactic, lexical, textual, and pragmatic levels, with particular reference to the peculiarities of contemporary Italian;
- knowledge of the grammatical expression of cognitive and communicative categories. Brief reference to typological dimension;
- knowledge of ministerial guidelines regarding the objectives and content of Italian language teaching in a vertical perspective, referring to kindergarten and primary school, and the debate on linguistic education;
- knowledge of criteria for describing different linguistic abilities (speaking, listening, reading, writing) and the cognitive processes underlying them;
- knowledge of different ways of organizing oral interaction with brief references to intercultural pragmatics;
- knowledge of the processes underlying writing (from early learning stages to expert models) aimed at developing complex textual skills (planning, scheduling, information hierarchy, structuring, and revision);
- knowledge of processes related to the development of reading skills and strategies;
- knowledge of models of reflection on language within linguistic education; the concept of error between norm and use;
- knowledge of various models and types of grammar (historical, normative, descriptive, cognitive, and pedagogical) as tools for reflection on language consistent with and functional to the cognitive development of learners and specific guidelines for primary school, and in a vertical continuity perspective for lower secondary school;
- knowledge of procedures, tools, and criteria for analyzing and evaluating linguistic and communicative skills of students and valuing different starting repertoires;
- knowledge of the phases of acquiring Italian L2 in natural and guided contexts, with particular reference to interlanguage and error treatment;
- knowledge of issues related to text comprehensibility in Italian L1 and L2 teaching.
Teaching Methods for Achieving Objectives
The teaching methodologies include:
- integrated frontal lectures;
- exercises and practical laboratories, referring to paper and electronic tools for linguistics and reading and analysis of texts (dictionaries, linguistic corpora, etc.) and specific tools for primary school (educational software, etc.).
1b. Disciplinary Area: Literary.
Specific Objectives
Literary education aims to:
- create a habit of reading as continuous personal formation;
- know the formative potential of literary texts, intended as a true dialogue with the other self, based on hermeneutic respect;
- know the Italian literary tradition;
- learn to interpret, analyze, and comment on literary texts, especially poetic ones;
- understand narrative thought and its structures;
- provide tools to identify aesthetic qualities and values carried by texts, to choose passages or works to propose to children, educating their taste;
- know criteria for analyzing and evaluating literary works for children;
- understand the different characteristics of literary genres for children.
Teaching Methods for Achieving Objectives
The teaching methodologies include:
- frontal lectures;
- participatory lectures;
- exercises and practical laboratories.
2) Disciplinary Area: English Language.
Specific Objectives:
- linguistic knowledge and skills at B2 level, as indicated in the Common European Framework, by the end of the study path;
- linguistic and practical glottodidactic knowledge related to the ability to program and manage an English class;
- ability to retrieve professional update sources in LS and understand documents from the Council of Europe and current affairs related to linguistic policies for young learners and teacher in-service training.
Teaching Methods for Achieving Objectives:
- language laboratories (also conducted with native speakers and in self-learning mode);
- lectures on English language and linguistics content, as well as English language didactics.
3) Disciplinary Area: Historical-Geographical.
Specific Objectives:
The aim is to acquire:
- basic historical and geographical knowledge and skills regarding different historical periods and the characteristics of the landscape, territory, and natural, socio-cultural, economic, and political systems that define their organization, relationships, transformation processes, and identity configuration;
- research methodologies for history and inductive construction of historical knowledge, through the retrieval and analysis of documents; verification of source authenticity; collation of sources for historical reconstruction;
- main models of history didactics;
- methods for constructing geographical knowledge through direct observation, questionnaires, interviews, and data collection methods;
- skills in using geographical tools through the analysis of general and thematic maps, statistical and information sources, subjective, literary, and iconographic sources;
- skills for developing projects and educational interventions related to the environment, landscape, and cultural heritage.
Teaching Methods for Achieving Objectives.
The teaching methodologies include:
- frontal lectures with multimedia technology;
- guided practical exercises;
- disciplinary deepening laboratory activities;
- use of software or video recordings and films;
- field trips.
4) Disciplinary Area: Mathematical-Scientific (botanical-biological, physical-chemical disciplines).
Specific Objectives:
- acquisition of fundamental scientific concepts, selected based on their relevance and accessibility in the context of kindergarten and primary school and their regional territorial specifics;
- awareness of the existence of a complex and eco-systemic nature, highlighted by interdependencies between living beings and the chemical-physical context;
- acquisition of knowledge and didactic skills related to interconnected scientific disciplines (learning to identify structuring scientific concepts and their connections, reflecting on cognitive obstacles, developing possible integrated teaching activities and paths, and developing a systemic vision);
- acquisition of the ability to carry out practical activities and critical didactic reflections.
For the mathematical area, the following specific objectives are highlighted:
- acquisition of fundamental mathematical concepts related to various domains (arithmetic, geometry, logic, probability, and statistics);
- acquisition of knowledge and didactic skills related to the discipline;
- awareness of the role of problem solving as a fundamental and pervasive moment of doing mathematics at every level of schooling;
- acquisition of the ability to carry out practical activities and critical didactic reflections and implement appropriate evaluation strategies.
Teaching Methods for Achieving Objectives.
Frontal lectures, didactic exercises in the laboratory, use of software for interactive whiteboards, guided visits to resources in the territory, comments on videos with observations and experiments in botany, biology, chemistry, and physics; design of teaching units and experiments with natural resources and low-cost materials, realizable in class, aimed at helping students to construct scientific knowledge and laws and verify their coherence with observed phenomena.
5) Musical, Artistic, Motor, and Legal Area.
Specific Objectives:
- ability to design teaching paths according to the National Guidelines for the first cycle of education in the artistic, musical, and motor areas;
- knowledge of the main models of education in the three areas: artistic, musical, and motor-sport;
- learning of fundamental concepts and techniques of artistic, musical, and motor culture;
- acquisition of knowledge regarding motor development (motor control, movement play, sports education);
- learning of elements of constitutional law, school legislation, and safety regulations.
Teaching Methods for Achieving Objectives.
Frontal lectures; video projections; document analysis; use of software for interactive whiteboards; interventions by artists, musicians, and athletes; exercises in gym, auditorium, and artistic laboratories; guided visits to resources in the territory.
Area 2: Courses for Welcoming Students with Disabilities.
The specific educational objectives and planned teaching activities aim to develop knowledge, skills, and competencies related to the profile of a teacher who can combine a solid basic cultural training with an adequate in-depth study of special pedagogical, didactic, psychological, and legal disciplines, tailored to the education of students with special educational needs integrated into the classroom. It is therefore provided to strengthen knowledge in the field of special pedagogical-didactic sciences and integrate them with those related to medical disciplines. The future teacher must:
- be able to recognize the special educational needs of more vulnerable students, interpreting them in terms of educational-didactic planning and cognitive mediation capacity, through a consistent management of interventions, in the perspective of valuing the personality of each student and available resources, using specific monitoring and documentation devices for processes and outcomes;
- develop socio-relational skills necessary for teamwork with class colleagues, families, and other socio-health professionals, and cultivate dispositions and skills useful for building meaningful educational relationships, in the presence of students with difficulties, as well as self-evaluative abilities regarding ethical-value orientations, also in relation to available deontological references, with the aim of making critically founded and socially legitimate professional choices, oriented towards promoting the global development of all students' personalities, especially those with more problems.
Specific Objectives.
Acquire knowledge, skills, and competencies aimed at:
- valuing the framework of possibilities offered by national and international school integration legislation, history, and practice;
- interacting with health specialists and families for knowledge of the diagnosis and functional profile of students with disabilities, and for the elaboration, management, and evaluation of the individualized educational-didactic plan, open to the perspective of the life project;
- actively collaborating with other class teachers and the support teacher for the design, programming, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of the individualized educational-didactic plan, well integrated with class programming, also to conduct continuity and educational orientation actions in relation to teachers of other school levels and grades;
- adopting enhanced and specialized teaching strategies in different disciplines, appropriate to the needs of students with disabilities: integrate verbal and non-verbal languages;
- knowing and using techniques, methodologies, multimedia and information technologies, specific aids, structured materials;
- knowing theoretical models, diagnostic and intervention models in disability, and intervention strategies for integrating students with disabilities;
- being able to recognize the originality factors present in each student, in particular: learning and thinking styles, emotional-relational aspects, presence of specific learning disorders or behavioral disorders, disabilities;
- preparing dispensative and compensatory interventions at the planning-programming and evaluation level;
- managing and valuing the heterogeneous composition of the class, in the presence of students with special educational needs.
Working Methods.
Frontal lectures supported by multimedia products, lectures with exercises, open lectures (integrated by group discussions, sector experts, and family comparisons); thematic seminars; laboratories (case studies, guided teaching actions; simulations; productions, projects, and materials, individual and group, for activating enhanced, specialized, and individualized teaching interventions; critical analysis and evaluation of tools, techniques, etc.); oral or written presentations or reports on the outcomes of experiences or training activities (participation in laboratory and internship activities, experiences, lived experiences, etc.); activities based on simulation and dramatization, aimed at refining the use of non-verbal languages for expressive, communicative, and learning purposes, as well as acquiring systematic knowledge, access, and critical use of information and professional cultural update sources, also within the ICT context. Observational activities, analysis of practices, self-analysis of field experience, and reports during the internship will constitute an integrated training moment with classroom teaching. In-person teaching will be integrated with the use of distance learning platforms for documenting training content and developing individual and small group exercises and re-elaboration activities.
Internship.
With direct internship activities, students will develop the ability to:
- critically analyze teaching experience, their own and others';
- plan their own teaching action and evaluate its results;
- reread their professional experience in relation to a teacher profile articulated in terms of classroom management, meta-level planning/evaluation, and professional role;
- use didactic technologies functionally to the educational-didactic intentions underlying teaching action;
- critically reflect on experience, with particular attention to the integration of students with special educational needs and specific attention to those with learning disorders and disabilities.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding The curriculum of the Single Cycle Master's Degree in class LM-85 is structured to provide adequate knowledge and understanding of educational phenomena, in light of the history of education, pedagogical, didactic, and disciplinary culture, to ensure the acquisition of advanced methodological and disciplinary didactic knowledge and skills.
The graduate from the Master's Degree Course in Primary Education Sciences must therefore possess organic knowledge in diverse areas.
1) Possession of theoretical foundations and disciplinary scientific languages.
2) Critical knowledge of the main knowledge related to teaching disciplines.
3) Applied didactic knowledge in different disciplinary, interdisciplinary, and transdisciplinary areas.
4) Knowledge of the use of multimedia technologies.
5) Knowledge of English at B2 level.
6) Knowledge of research methods related to disciplinary areas and also applied to school contexts.
7) Specific knowledge for welcoming students with disabilities, specific learning disorders, and various school difficulties.
The planned teaching methods will consist of lectures, deepening laboratories, and the realization of direct and indirect internship.
Assessment will take place through written and oral exams related to exams and other training activities.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding The Single Cycle Master's Degree in class LM-85 aims to foster in students the ability to address, manage, and solve complex educational problems, identifying operational solutions to ensure the educational success of kindergarten and primary school students. At the end of the training path, the graduate will have the ability to adapt their basic knowledge to emerging problems in specific school realities, integrating and combining skills, knowledge, and experiences acquired to develop effective interventions in precise real situations and contexts.
In this sense, within a curriculum path that harmonizes courses, laboratories, and internships, guided by professors and tutors, and through comparison with other students, the Master's Degree Course aims to provide the following abilities to apply acquired knowledge in a professional context:
- design educational interventions that respond to even complex needs through integrated support forms that help the individual and involve the class group, in collaboration with colleagues, families, and other professionals in the territory;
- design flexible and appropriate learning paths according to students' educational needs and levels;
- organize and carry out teaching interventions consistent with the skills to be achieved and the specificities of the class group to which the teaching actions are directed;
- promote intrinsic motivation in students;
- choose evaluation models, construct and adopt appropriate tools, evaluate learning processes and products;
- use technologies for teaching to optimize work and be able to apply them in class;
- understand and structure educational research, demonstrating the ability to recognize, evaluate, and use empirical study outcomes to build knowledge and improve interventions;
- work in groups for the design, organization, and verification of educational-didactic interventions.
The planned teaching methods will consist of lectures, laboratories, in which simulations, teaching products, and tools are realized, and the realization of direct and indirect internship.
Assessment will take place through written and oral exams related to exams and other training activities.
III - Independent Judgment The graduates of Primary Education Sciences must, at the end of the training path, be able to address educational problems, situations, and contexts critically, reflectively, and constructively with full independence of judgment. To this end, to be able to read, interpret, and formulate judgments, as well as choose, decide, and develop appropriate interventions for different training recipients and critically evaluate the adequacy of training processes and products, graduates must:
- acquire the ability for autonomous and critical reflection on educational and cultural phenomena foreseen by professional practice;
- be able to problematize educational phenomena, critically analyze, and choose educational programs and interventions;
- be able to self-evaluate their didactic-educative skills.
These abilities are stimulated through various types of training activities: group discussions; internship activities aimed at supervision and re-elaboration of experience; simulation practices; critical presentation of content, activating reflection and problem-solving through case discussion.
The assessment of independent judgment also occurs through discussion in specific meetings of the criteria adopted in evaluation tests (written and/or oral). In the evaluation of internship and final thesis, the ability of the future professional to autonomously and reflectively elaborate must be considered.
IV - Communication Skills Graduates must be able to:
- master different communication codes;
- communicate information related to educational and teaching situations, possible interventions in light of theoretical models and research literature, and control methods for outcomes;
- possess skills in managing relationships and communication processes with students, colleagues, families, and other professionals;
- possess skills in documenting interventions and disseminating good practices.
The training activities that contribute to achieving the above skills include laboratory, seminar activities, linguistic skills, English language skills, and the final exam. To achieve these skills, various verification methods are provided, ranging from the discussion of written works and design tests to the presentation of teaching lessons and simulation activities, also using multimedia tools and computer presentations. The final exam also offers students an additional opportunity for in-depth study and verification of analysis, elaboration, communication, and argumentation skills.
V - Learning Ability The Master's Degree Course aims to provide skills in using study strategies for continuous training, i.e., meaningful learning strategies and the ability to retrieve sources to update and deepen professional knowledge and skills.
It is also expected that graduates possess team learning abilities for the realization of collective projects.
The planned teaching methods will consist of lectures, deepening laboratories, and the realization of direct and indirect internship.
Assessment will take place through written and oral exams related to exams and other training activities.
Professional Role in Work Context.
Professional Role in Work Context:
The specific set of competencies of the kindergarten and primary school teacher profile focuses not only on a solid repertoire of psycho-pedagogical skills in the field of education sciences but also, and especially, on an articulated domain of methodological-didactic, communicative, relational, and disciplinary competencies. Graduates must also have adequate competence in English corresponding to the B2 level.
The graduate of the Master's Degree Course in class LM-85 bis must also be able to translate and apply such knowledge and competencies in the real and specific contexts of kindergarten and primary school. The curriculum is directed to make the graduate in Primary Education Sciences capable of effectively managing a class and teaching-learning processes, designing appropriate teaching proposals for all students. The profile is completed by knowledge and abilities that enable the graduate to facilitate school integration and support the learning process of students with special needs. In particular, the graduate must:
1. possess pedagogical and methodological-didactic knowledge and skills to manage the class group in the progression of individual student learning through appropriate forms and tools of planning, programming, and scheduling, also using personalized and individualized intervention strategies;
2. disciplinary knowledge and skills related to the teaching areas (linguistic-literary area, historical-geographical area, scientific-technological area,
3. artistic area and motor area, foreign language area: English);
4. be able to articulate objectives and content of different disciplines according to different school levels and contexts: kindergarten and primary school;
5. possess relational and managerial skills to make classroom work beneficial for each student on cognitive, affective-relational/social, and psychomotor levels, creating and fostering a favorable attitude toward learning and facilitating the coexistence of different cultures and religions;
6. be able to actively participate in school and teaching management, collaborating with colleagues in both the design of teaching and internal and external collegial activities, also in relation to the needs of the territory where the school operates.
Associated Competencies for the Role.
Associated Competencies for the Role:
The curriculum, not differentiating between the two profiles (kindergarten teacher and primary school teacher), encompasses a body of methodological, instrumental, and technical competencies that ensure the formation of a complete professional habitus capable of enabling the future teacher to act appropriately in both educational contexts (kindergarten and primary school), fully fulfilling their professional functions.
In reference to the two contexts considered, these knowledge and competencies outline an open, creative, and flexible figure capable of:
- effectively managing a class group;
- planning, organizing, and managing teaching-learning processes in terms of objectives, strategies, techniques, methodologies, and tools used;
- designing, planning, and realizing effective teaching proposals responsive to specific learner needs;
- defining, developing, and managing assessment and evaluation processes of learning and teaching;
- developing individualized and personalized interventions to make the learning process effective for all students;
- developing appropriate educational communication corresponding to the adopted teaching action system;
- building educational relationships aimed at motivating and tending to stimulate a favorable attitude toward learning in all students.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Career Opportunities:
The graduate in Primary Education Sciences carries out the activity of teacher in the following professional areas:
– kindergarten;
– primary school.

Program, Texts, and Objectives Official teaching and assessment languages. ITALIAN Degree Awarded. Master's Degree in Single Cycle in DENTISTRY AND DENTAL PROSTHETICS
Specific Educational Objectives. The general objectives and the structure of the study plan described below are based on the content of the Ministerial Decree on New Degree Classes – Regulation of Master's Degree Courses (LM-46, Master's Degree Class in Dentistry and Dental Prosthetics), which defines Master's Degree Courses in compliance with European Union directives and the University of L'Aquila's Academic Regulations.
The Master's Degree program aims to enable students to understand and comprehend fundamental elements of etiology, pathogenesis, symptoms, diagnosis, and therapy for the main congenital and acquired pathologies and anomalies of teeth, oral cavity, jaw bones, temporomandibular joints, and related tissues, as well as dental rehabilitation. Acquiring this knowledge and understanding allows students to plan an appropriate and specific treatment plan for each patient.
The academic plan includes 360 ECTS Credits (CFU) over 6 years, typically around 60 CFU per year. The distribution of the 360 CFU is determined in accordance with the requirements specified in the annexes of the decree, which establishes the credits to be allocated to disciplinary areas including essential training activities for the formation of a dentist.
For the University Credit (CFU), equivalent to an average of 25 hours of student effort, and the ratio of CFU hours for frontal lectures/practical sessions/laboratory and CFU hours for professional internship, refer to the University of L'Aquila's Guidelines and the course's Academic Regulations. The remaining portion of the credit is available for independent study. The instructors of professional courses are responsible for the related internship. For each internship, an evaluation must be conducted, which the instructor will consider for the final exam grade. The physiological and clinical knowledge of general medicine and odontostomatology acquired through the training activities included in the academic plan and clinical practical activities determine and define the professional profile of a dentist operating in European Union countries.
Upon completion of six years, the graduate in Dentistry and Dental Prosthetics has acquired the knowledge and technical skills to enter the dental profession in both private and public sectors. Graduates have also developed the foundational knowledge and learning abilities necessary to pursue specialized studies.
Master's graduates in this class must be able to fluently use at least one European Union language, in both written and oral form, in addition to Italian, with reference to disciplinary terminology. Pursuant to Articles 1 and 3 of Law 8 November 2021, No. 163, the final exam for the Master's Degree in Single Cycle in Dentistry and Dental Prosthetics - Class LM-46 authorizes the exercise of the profession of dentist. For this purpose, the final exam includes the performance of a Practical Assessment Test (PPV) of professional skills acquired through a Practical Assessment Internship (TPV) within the study program, aimed at verifying the candidate's practical preparation level for professional authorization, preceding the thesis defense. The PPV is organized through the student's discussion of three multidisciplinary clinical cases treated as the primary operator during the TPV, involving multidisciplinary treatment plans with services related to the majority of disciplines covered by the TPV, according to the procedures outlined in the protocol drafted by the Permanent Conference of Presidents of Dentistry and Dental Prosthetics Degree Courses, in agreement with the National Dental Register Commission. To pass the PPV, students receive a suitability assessment, after which they proceed to the thesis defense. Graduates must achieve the competencies specified in the professional profile.
The graduate in Dentistry and Dental Prosthetics performs activities related to the prevention, diagnosis, and therapy of congenital and acquired diseases and anomalies of teeth, mouth, jaw bones, temporomandibular joints, and related tissues, as well as dental rehabilitation, prescribing all necessary medications and devices for the exercise of the profession. They possess a level of professional, cultural, decision-making, and operational autonomy enabling continuous updating, having followed a training path characterized by an holistic approach to oral health issues of both healthy and sick individuals, also in relation to the physical and social environment surrounding them.
In general, the first three years focus on foundational training activities aimed at familiarizing students with the structural organization and vital functions of the human body, including courses addressing the doctor-patient relationship and understanding the principles underlying the scientific methodology. Students learn the method for approaching patients with dental issues. The subsequent three years involve the study of medical, surgical, and specialist disciplines related to clinical problems concerning odontostomatology. These training activities occur concurrently with the study of dental disciplines and professional clinical internships. Theoretical courses and clinical internships in oral pathology, restorative dentistry, endodontics, oral surgery, periodontology, orthodontics, pediatric dentistry, and prosthetics, while developing different skills, aim to mature abilities and experiences to address and resolve oral health issues from a preventive, diagnostic, prognostic, therapeutic, and rehabilitative perspective, respecting medical-legal and ethical regulations in Italy and European Union countries. In the fifth year, a course in maxillofacial pathology and therapy and implantology is introduced, with a global approach to patient treatment, similar to previous courses. The sixth year includes professional training activities focused on treating patients with odontostomatology issues, particularly through clinical internships.
Particular emphasis is placed on the preparatory TPV training activity preceding the acquisition of the qualifying academic degree. Within the 90 CFU to be earned throughout the study program for professional training activities, 30 CFU are allocated to the TPV conducted within the study program, involving practical activities as the primary operator in preventive, diagnostic, and therapeutic areas of odontostomatology, covering disciplines such as oral surgery, restorative dentistry, endodontics, implantology, oral pathology and medicine, pediatric dentistry, special dentistry, orthognathics, periodontology, and prosthetics, as specified in the protocol drafted by the Permanent Conference of Presidents of Dentistry and Dental Prosthetics Degree Courses, in agreement with the National Dental Register Commission. For each CFU equivalent to 25 hours dedicated to TPV, at least 20 hours of professional training activities as the primary operator are required; the remaining 5 hours may be dedicated to individual study or other professional training activities.
Clinical sessions in oral pathology and medicine, preventive and community dentistry, conservative dentistry and endodontics, oral surgery, periodontology, orthodontics, gnathology, pediatric dentistry, and prosthetics continue and enhance competencies developed in previous years, emphasizing relationships between systemic pathology and the oral cavity. TPV CFU can only be earned through activities performed as the primary operator under the direct supervision of a faculty mentor at university or National Health Service facilities following a convention. Pursuant to Article 2, Paragraph 9 of Ministerial Decree No. 653 of 5-7 2022, TPV credits are earned in the sixth year of study, with up to 30% of the total possibly earned in the fifth year.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding The Master's graduate in Dentistry and Dental Prosthetics must possess sufficient biomedical, technical, and clinical science knowledge to understand normal and pathological conditions relevant to dentistry and have the ability to comprehend the importance of this information in clinical professional situations. In particular, these abilities manifest in the following domains: - Essential theoretical knowledge derived from basic sciences in the context of its subsequent professional application; - Critical thinking and acquisition of clinical-epidemiological data related to the health and disease status of the stomatognathic system of an individual, interpreted in light of basic scientific knowledge, pathophysiology, and stomatognathic and systemic pathologies; - Self-assessment capabilities combined with skills and experience to responsibly address and resolve priority health issues from a preventive, diagnostic, prognostic, therapeutic, and rehabilitative perspective; - Ability to recognize oral health issues in the community and intervene competently.
ACQUISITION METHOD. Knowledge and understanding are acquired through lectures delivered primarily through traditional methods, audiovisual aids, e-learning, and lesson scheduling consistent with planned CFU. Students attend both frontal and non-frontal, professional, and elective activities of individual courses, aligning the acquisition of knowledge and competencies with specific educational objectives and the study path of the program.
VERIFICATION METHOD. Verification and assessment of acquired knowledge and competencies are conducted through methods independently determined by instructors. These assessments may include written and oral exams, laboratory tests, project evaluations, and aptitude tests, either through comprehensive evaluations or in-course assessments. Attendance certification for mandatory activities is required to take the related course exam.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding The Master's graduate in Dentistry and Dental Prosthetics must have acquired the knowledge of the foundations for understanding qualitative and quantitative biological, physiological, and pathological phenomena for maintaining oral health and apply this knowledge to dental therapies, including the practical internship within professional disciplines. In particular, this application manifests in communication and relational skills, diagnostic and treatment planning capabilities, and health promotion. The graduate is therefore able to: - Perform the full range of general dentistry within the context of global patient treatment without producing additional risks to the patient or environment; - Identify treatment priorities in line with needs, participating with other parties in planning interventions aimed at reducing oral diseases in the community based on knowledge of community dentistry principles and practice; - Control cross-infection to prevent physical, chemical, and microbiological contamination in professional practice; - Apply the full range of anxiety and pain control techniques related to dental treatments (within the limits permitted to dentists); - Communicate clearly and humanely with patients and families, collaborate with various healthcare professionals in group activities, organize team work, understand communication and human resource management issues, and apply principles of healthcare economics; - Organize and lead the dental team using the full range of available auxiliary dental personnel.
The professional profile also includes having performed clinical practical activities with technical-professional autonomy under faculty guidance during the study program, including some diagnostic, therapeutic, and emergency management skills: - Obtain a correct medical history (including medical history), conduct an objective oral cavity examination, recognize conditions different from normal, diagnose dental and oral pathologies, assess the patient's general health, and recognize relationships between systemic pathology and oral cavity; formulate and adjust a global and dental treatment plan in relation to systemic pathology, and perform appropriate therapies or refer the patient to other expertise when necessary; diagnose and manage dental, oro-facial, and craniomandibular pain, or refer the patient to appropriate expertise; perform screening, diagnosis, and management of common oral and dental pathologies, including cancer, mucosal and bone pathologies, or refer the patient to appropriate expertise; perform dental radiographic exams using routine techniques while respecting radiation protection regulations; recognize radiological signs deviating from normal. - Perform basic periodontal treatments, conduct minor oral surgical interventions; perform complete endodontic treatments on single-rooted and multi-rooted teeth; replace missing teeth, when indicated and appropriate, with the most suitable prosthetic rehabilitation solution. Know indications for implant therapy, perform it, or refer the patient to appropriate expertise; correctly use all available materials accepted by the scientific community; perform minor occlusal orthodontic corrections, recognizing the need to refer the patient to other expertise in the presence of more complex pathologies. - Perform basic life support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation maneuvers (BLS: Basic Life Support).
ACQUISITION METHOD. Teaching tools aimed at achieving the ability to apply knowledge within characteristic activities include intensive individual bench laboratory activities and clinical patient internships, reflection, re-elaboration, and presentation of scientific texts analyzed by individuals or student groups, and frontal-seminar teaching primarily focused on interdisciplinary discussion of assigned clinical cases.
VERIFICATION METHOD. Instructors of professional courses are responsible for the related internship. For each internship, an in-course evaluation is conducted, which the instructor considers for the final exam grade. Verification methods may include written and oral exams, laboratory tests, internship evaluations and/or projects, and aptitude tests, either through comprehensive evaluations or in-course assessments. Attendance certification for mandatory activities is required to take the related course exam.
A specific type of internship is the Practical Assessment Internship (TPV), where the student must acquire the ability to independently apply diagnostic and clinical-therapeutic professional skills and reach a practical preparation level sufficient for professional authorization.
The TPV will be evaluated through judgments characterizing the level of maturity and awareness of one's professional identity achieved during the training path.
TPV CFU are earned following certification by identified mentors from the Course Councils and validation by the President, who attests to the authenticity and assumes responsibility for the hours of activity performed, number of procedures executed, and positive evaluation according to specific criteria, including technical knowledge and operational protocols and safety; manual skills; work organization and collaboration abilities; and approach to patients. TPV attendance and related clinical activities are certified through completion of a dedicated logbook.
III - Independent Judgment The graduate: - Possesses the ability to independently design and implement therapeutic programs for the care and rehabilitation of the stomatognathic system; - Is able to recognize personal limitations in patient care and recognize the need to refer the patient to other medical and/or specialized dental expertise; - Is able to independently manage the dental treatment of the patient; - Is able to evaluate the effectiveness of the treatment plan, interventions performed, and results achieved, having followed a training path characterized by an holistic approach to oral health issues.
Independent judgment is cultivated in students through critical reviews of scientific literature, clinical cases treated, and participation in the development of scientific projects, discussed and evaluated by instructors responsible for individual courses. Exercise and laboratory activities also provide opportunities to develop decision-making and judgment abilities, with instructor evaluations aimed at progressively building the essential clinical judgment autonomy for future professional practice. The primary teaching tool remains the significant clinical internship, particularly the Practical Assessment Internship (TPV), where the acquisition of necessary judgment autonomy for dental practice is verified by instructors and mentors during daily patient activities and during the critical analysis and evaluation of student results. The overall level of judgment autonomy is further refined through activities conducted during the thesis period on an original topic.
IV - Communication Skills The graduate: - Possesses intermediate English language knowledge necessary for consulting scientific texts and journals; - Is able to communicate effectively with patients and educate them on appropriate and effective oral hygiene techniques, providing adequate information based on scientifically accepted knowledge to obtain informed consent for therapy; - Is able to develop an interdisciplinary approach to clinical cases, especially in collaboration with other members of the healthcare team, deepening knowledge of the rules and dynamics characterizing the work of healthcare operators.
Communication skills are particularly developed during clinical internships and during the TPV, where they constitute a criterion for evaluation. Additionally, they are refined in the preparation of the final thesis and the final dissertation.
The acquisition of the aforementioned skills is evaluated at various levels within training activities, primarily during assessments consisting of oral exams, written tests, and laboratory reports, as well as during clinical internships, and participation in work groups formed within courses.
V - Learning Ability The graduate: - Possesses the ability to consult databases to acquire scientific documentation and analyze scientific literature, applying research results to therapy reliably; - Is able to correctly interpret legislation concerning the exercise of dentistry in the European Union country where the dentist practices and provide assistance in compliance with medical-legal and ethical regulations in the country of practice.
Learning ability is assessed through verification methods during training activities, integrating knowledge acquired through specific activities with those gained through independent study, evaluating the critical contribution demonstrated during practical, seminar, and clinical internship activities, as well as during the TPV, and through verification of self-learning ability developed during the final exam activity. For this purpose, the final exam includes the performance of a Practical Assessment Test (PPV) of professional skills acquired through the TPV within the study program, aimed at verifying the candidate's practical preparation level for professional authorization, preceding the thesis defense.
Professional Role in Work Context.
Professional Role in Work Context:
The graduate can perform the professional role and related functions in the occupational areas indicated: Dentist.
Skills Associated with the Role.
Skills Associated with the Role:
The graduate can perform the professional role and related functions: - Performs activities related to the prevention, diagnosis, and therapy of congenital and acquired diseases and anomalies of teeth, mouth, jaw bones, temporomandibular joints, and related tissues; - Manages dental rehabilitation, prescribing all necessary medications and devices for the exercise of the profession; - Designs, verifies, and inserts dental medical devices, controlling their appropriateness.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Employment Prospects:
Graduates in Dentistry and Dental Prosthetics have employment prospects in the field of Independent Dental Practice.
They may perform, in accordance with current regulations, Level I and II managerial activities within the National Health System.
