Degree Awarded. Single Cycle Master's Degree in MEDICINE AND SURGERY
Specific Educational Objectives.
The professional profile of the medical doctor to be trained is aimed at developing professional competence and the values of professionalism. It is based on the importance of integrating the biomedical paradigm of treating disease with the psychosocial paradigm of caring for the human being.
The profile, which identifies the specific mission of the Master's degree course, is that of a medical doctor at an initial professional level, who possesses:
- a multidisciplinary, interprofessional and integrated vision of the most common health and disease problems;
- education oriented towards disease prevention, health promotion within the community and territory, timely diagnosis and treatment of acute diseases, management and rehabilitation of chronic diseases, with special attention to the principles of 'precision medicine';
- a deep understanding of new care and health needs, focused not only on disease but especially on the centrality of the sick person, considered in their entirety of physical, psychological and affective health needs, with expressed or implicit needs to be cared for and welcomed, and integrated into a specific social, cultural and economic context.
The teaching method adopted, useful for achieving the expected qualifying characteristics, provides for the horizontal (between different disciplines in the same semester or year) and vertical (for similar or complementary topics over multiple years of study) integration of knowledge, a teaching method based on a solid cultural and methodological foundation acquired through the study of pre-clinical disciplines and subsequently predominantly focused on the ability to solve problems and make decisions, early contact with the patient, and the acquisition of good clinical and interpersonal skills with the patient.
The specific content of courses and educational objectives are derived from the tasks inherent to the medical profession, responding to a health need and coinciding with the indispensable knowledge and skills necessary for professional practice, identified by a 'core curriculum' shared. Professionalizing credits and practical training activities must ensure the acquisition of a series of indispensable skills also identified by the 'core curriculum'.
In the didactic project of the Master's Degree course, the correct balance between vertical and horizontal integration is proposed among:
a) Basic sciences, which must be broad and include knowledge of evolutionary biology, molecular biology, genetics, and biological complexity aimed at understanding the structure and function of the human body in normal conditions, for maintaining health conditions and correctly applying translational scientific research;
b) Knowledge of pathological processes and the mechanisms that cause them, also to establish prevention, diagnosis, therapy, and rehabilitation;
c) Clinical medical practice and its methodological foundations, which must be particularly solid, through extensive use of tutorial teaching, capable of transforming theoretical knowledge into personal experience to acquire professional skills useful for managing the complexity of medicine;
d) Humanities, which must constitute a useful background to achieve awareness of the medical role and the deep values of medical professionalism, in relation to those of the patient and society;
e) Acquisition of scientific, medical, clinical, and professional methodology directed towards health problems of the individual and the community, with due attention to population and gender differences.
The achievement of educational objectives occurs through reproducible assessment procedures, based on objective elements, not influenced by external factors (reliability) and fair (respecting the educational agreement between teacher and student), using valid and appropriate methodologies for the dimension to be verified, both in terms of knowledge and skills and competencies.
The Single Cycle Master's Degree in Medicine and Surgery provides for a total of 360 University Credits (CFU), structured over six years of study, of which 60 must be acquired in practical training activities aimed at developing specific professional skills (professionalizing CFU). In compliance with the regulations concerning the qualifying degree, the practical-evaluative internship is included within the 60 professionalizing CFU. It is intended to verify the student's abilities related to the 'know-how' and 'knowing how to be' as a medical doctor, which consists in applying biomedical and clinical knowledge to medical practice, resolving questions of professional deontology and medical ethics, demonstrating aptitude to solve clinical problems related to the fields of medicine and surgery, laboratory and instrumental diagnostics, and public health, applying the principles of effective communication; it lasts a total of three months (15 CFU), is carried out not before the fifth year of study and only after all exams related to the first four years of study, as per the course's academic structure, are passed; it is conducted for a number of hours corresponding to at least 5 CFU per month (each CFU allocated to the internship must correspond to at least 20 hours of professionalizing teaching activity and no more than 5 hours of individual study) and is structured in the following periods, not necessarily consecutive: one month in surgical area, one month in medical area, one month in the specific field of General Medicine, the latter to be carried out not before the sixth year of study, at the office of a General Practitioner. The certification of attendance and evaluation of the internship periods is carried out under the direct responsibility and care of the university professor or medical director, responsible for the structure visited by the intern, and the General Practitioner, who issue a formal certificate of attendance and, after evaluating the results related to the demonstrated competencies, issue a suitability assessment in a logbook, which consists of a descriptive part of the activities carried out and an evaluative part of the demonstrated competencies; it is considered passed only upon obtaining a suitability assessment for each of the three periods.
The Master's Degree course is organized into 12 semesters and no more than 36 integrated courses; specific CFU are assigned to these by the teaching structure's council. Each CFU corresponds to a student workload of 25 hours. 1 CFU corresponds to 12.5 hours of lecture, or 12.5 hours of laboratory or guided exercise, or 25 hours of professionalizing training (with teacher guidance in small groups) or assisted study (students' autonomous exercises in classroom/laboratory with didactic support), or for student-selected activities and the final exam.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding
Graduates must have knowledge and abilities sufficient to describe and correlate the fundamental aspects of the bio-molecular, macro and microscopic structure, functions, and pathological processes, as well as the main disease patterns of the human being.
To this end, graduates will be able to:
1) correlate the structure and functionality of the organism as a complex of biological systems in continuous adaptation, interpreting morpho-functional anomalies found in various diseases.
2) identify normal and abnormal human behavior, being able to indicate the determinants of health and the main risk factors for disease, considering the 'interaction between the human being and their physical and social environment, with attention to gender/sex and population differences.
3) describe the fundamental molecular, cellular, biochemical, and physiological mechanisms that maintain the organism's homeostasis, knowing how to describe the human life cycle and the effects of growth, development, and aging on the individual, with attention to gender/sex and population differences.
4) illustrate the origin and natural history of acute and chronic diseases, having essential knowledge related to pathology, pathophysiology, epidemiology, health economics, and principles of health management.
5) interpret the global needs of patients and their families in various disease phases, from diagnosis to incurable and terminal stages, through competent communication and an interdisciplinary approach that also considers cultural, psychological, spiritual factors modulating the relationship between patient, family, and disease. Ability to discuss the globality of clinical problems and approach the diagnostic-therapeutic process considering the centrality of the patient and knowledge of pain therapy.
6) correlate the principles of drug action with their indications, paying attention to gender/sex and population differences, and describe the main interventions of instrumental diagnosis, surgical and physical therapy, in acute and chronic disease, rehabilitation, prevention, and end-of-life care.
7) discuss the essential elements of professionalism, including moral and ethical principles and legal responsibilities underlying the profession.
Achieving these objectives will occur through attendance at basic, characteristic, and related training activities, organized in 'specific integrated courses', ensuring a unified and interdisciplinary vision of the educational objectives.
The teaching methods provided include frontal lectures, conferences, seminars, discussion groups. The teaching/learning process also uses tutorial teaching in small groups, with teacher-tutors collaborating in the student's educational process with facilitation functions (area tutors) and personal support (personal tutors). Innovative teaching methods such as flipped classroom, problem-oriented learning, problem solving, decision making, and role-playing are strongly encouraged.
Particular attention is also given to scientific research topics, encouraging: 1) involvement in planning basic research in the first three years of study, 2) participation in research programs during the internship period for the preparation of the thesis.
Particular attention is given to humanities through the presence of integrated courses and optional vertical training activities that accompany students from the second to the last year of study. As a general rule valid for all integrated courses, certification assessments will be based on written and/or oral exams. Student assessment will also occur through formative assessments (self-assessment tests and intermediate interviews). Exam procedures may be structured, beyond traditional oral or written exams, as a sequence of items to verify acquired knowledge, such as multiple-choice tests or short written answers.
Certification assessments, which contribute to forming individual exams, will be chosen based on criteria of objectivity and relevance to learning objectives and will primarily aim at evaluating the cognitive and interpretative competencies acquired by the student.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding
Graduates must be able to apply their knowledge to understand and solve health problems of individuals, with attention to gender specificity, group, and population differences. Clinical skills must be directed towards addressing the complexity of health problems of the population, social groups, and individual patients, complexity characterized by age, multi-morbidity, and the interplay of biological, socio-cultural, and gender-specific determinants.
To this end, graduates will be able to:
1) correctly collect a clinical history, including social aspects, and perform a physical and mental examination of the patient. They will be able to apply clinical reasoning principles, perform basic diagnostic procedures and techniques, analyze and interpret their results, to correctly define the nature of a problem, applying appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, also based on knowledge from gender medicine, and more specifically, precision medicine.
2) recognize any condition that immediately endangers the patient's life, knowing how to correctly and independently manage common medical emergencies.
3) effectively, efficiently, and ethically care for diseases and patients, promoting health and preventing disease, fulfilling the moral obligation to provide medical care in the terminal phases of life, including palliative symptom and pain therapy and existential suffering. Be aware of the limits of care, especially in chronic degenerative incurable diseases or in elderly conditions, so that palliative care programs can be activated earlier than terminality.
4) undertake appropriate preventive and protective actions against diseases, maintaining and promoting the health of the individual, family, and community. They will refer to the basic organization of health systems, including policies, organization, funding, cost-restrictive measures, and principles of efficient management in the correct delivery of healthcare. They will therefore be able to correctly use, in health decisions, local, regional, and national demographic and epidemiological surveillance data.
5) respect professional values including excellence, altruism, responsibility, compassion, empathy, reliability, honesty, and integrity, and commitment to following scientific methods.
6) correctly apply principles of moral reasoning and adopt appropriate decisions regarding possible conflicts in ethical, legal, and professional values, including those emerging from the commercialization of healthcare and new scientific discoveries. They will respect colleagues and other health professionals, demonstrating the ability to establish collaborative relationships with them.
III - Independent Judgment
Graduates must have the ability to integrate knowledge and manage complexity, as well as formulate judgments based on limited or incomplete information.
To this end, graduates will be able to:
1) demonstrate a critical approach, constructive skepticism, and creative attitude towards research in professional activities. They will be able to consider the importance and limitations of scientific thinking based on information from various sources to establish the cause, treatment, and prevention of diseases.
2) formulate personal judgments to solve analytical and complex problems and autonomously seek scientific information without waiting for it to be provided, using the basis of scientific evidence.
3) formulate hypotheses, collect and critically evaluate data to solve problems, being aware of the role of complexity, uncertainty, and probability in medical decision-making. They will be able to effectively plan and efficiently manage their time and activities to face uncertain conditions, and exercise the ability to adapt to changes.
4) exercise personal responsibility in caring for individual patients, respecting the medical profession's code of ethics.
Achieving these objectives will occur through attendance at basic, characteristic, and related training activities, organized in 'specific integrated courses', ensuring a unified and interdisciplinary vision of the educational objectives.
The teaching methods provided include frontal lectures, conferences, seminars, discussion groups, journal club. The teaching/learning process also extensively uses tutorial teaching in small groups, with teacher-tutors collaborating in the student's educational process with facilitation functions (area tutors) and personal support (personal tutors). Innovative teaching methods such as flipped classroom, problem-oriented learning, problem solving, problem setting, decision making, and role-playing are strongly encouraged.
For this level, attendance at hospital wards and university/hospital outpatient clinics (clinical internship - from II to VI year of study) and territorial structures, such as General Practitioners' offices and other territorial structures (from IV to VI year of study), for the completion of clinical internship in the final years of the course and the internship period for thesis preparation, represent the ideal context for testing judgment abilities. Active tutoring is an essential tool in this phase. As a general rule valid for all integrated courses, certification assessments will be based on written and/or oral exams. Student assessment will also occur through formative assessments (self-assessment tests and intermediate interviews), written reports on assigned topics. Exam procedures may be structured, beyond traditional oral or written exams, as a sequence of items to verify acquired knowledge, such as multiple-choice tests or short written answers, organized around interdisciplinary clinical cases, followed by exams to verify acquired clinical competencies. These may occur through the use of simulators, simulated patients, and real patients, as well as discussion of clinical cases.
For this descriptor as well, certification assessments, which contribute to forming individual exams, will be chosen based on criteria of objectivity and relevance to learning objectives and will primarily aim at evaluating the clinical and operational competencies acquired by the student.
IV - Communication Skills
Graduates must be able to communicate their conclusions, knowledge, and rationale clearly and unambiguously to specialist and non-specialist interlocutors, as well as to their patients, using the appropriate methods for the circumstances.
To this end, graduates will be able to:
1) listen attentively to extract and synthesize relevant information on all issues, understanding their content, and exercising communication skills to facilitate understanding with patients and their relatives, making them capable of sharing decisions.
2) demonstrate aptitude and ability to work in teams, including inter-professional teams.
3) demonstrate good sensitivity towards cultural and personal factors that improve interactions with patients and the community.
4) demonstrate in a simulation how to handle critical communication situations, such as communicating serious diagnoses, discussing sensitive topics related to sexual and reproductive life, and end-of-life decisions.
Achieving these objectives will occur through attendance at basic, characteristic, and related training activities, organized in 'specific integrated courses', ensuring a unified and interdisciplinary vision of the educational objectives.
The teaching methods provided include frontal lectures, conferences, seminars, discussion groups, journal club. The teaching/learning process also extensively uses tutorial teaching in small groups, with teacher-tutors collaborating in the student's educational process with facilitation functions (area tutors) and personal support (personal tutors). Innovative teaching methods such as flipped classroom, problem-oriented learning, problem solving, problem setting, decision making, and role-playing are strongly encouraged.
Particular attention is given to acquiring practical skills through didactic laboratories and Information and Communication Technologies for virtual simulation. Attendance at hospital wards and university/hospital outpatient clinics (clinical internship - from II to VI year of study) and territorial structures, such as General Practitioners' offices and other territorial structures (from IV to VI year of study), for the completion of clinical internship in the final years of the course and the internship period for thesis preparation, represent the ideal context for testing communication skills.
The role of humanities in this level is almost predominant, contributing to forming not just technical communication skills, but the indispensable human substrate necessary for an authentic therapeutic relationship.
As a general rule valid for all integrated courses, certification assessments will be based on written and/or oral exams. Student assessment will also occur through formative assessments (self-assessment tests and intermediate interviews), written reports on assigned topics. Exams may occur through the use of simulators, simulated patients, and real patients. Certification assessments, which contribute to forming individual exams, will be chosen based on criteria of objectivity and relevance to learning objectives specific to the Dublin Descriptor and will primarily aim at evaluating the clinical and relational competencies acquired by the student.
V - Learning Ability
Graduates must have developed learning abilities that allow them to continue studying mostly in an autonomous and self-directed manner.
To this end, graduates:
1) will be able to collect, organize, and critically interpret new scientific knowledge and health/biomedical information from various resources and databases.
2) will be able to obtain specific patient information from clinical data management systems, using information and communication technology as a valid support for diagnostic, therapeutic, and preventive practices and for health status surveillance and monitoring, understanding its application and also the limitations of information technology.
3) will be able to identify their own training needs, starting from audits of their student career, and design self-training paths.
Achieving these objectives will occur through attendance at basic, characteristic, and related training activities, organized in 'specific integrated courses', ensuring a unified and interdisciplinary vision of the educational objectives.
The teaching methods provided include frontal lectures, conferences, seminars, discussion groups. The teaching/learning process also extensively uses tutorial teaching in small groups, with teacher-tutors collaborating in the student's educational process with facilitation functions (area tutors) and personal support (personal tutors). Innovative teaching methods such as flipped classroom, problem-oriented learning, problem solving, problem setting, decision making, and role-playing are strongly encouraged.
Particular attention is given to group activities and simulation laboratories, as well as attendance at hospital wards and university/hospital outpatient clinics (clinical internship - from II to VI year of study) and territorial structures, such as General Practitioners' offices and other territorial structures (from IV to VI year of study), for the completion of clinical internship in the final years of the course and the internship period for thesis preparation.
As a general rule valid for all integrated courses, certification assessments will be based on written and/or oral exams. Student assessment will also occur through formative assessments (self-assessment tests and intermediate interviews), written reports on assigned topics.
For this descriptor as well, certification assessments, which contribute to forming individual exams, will be chosen based on criteria of objectivity and relevance to learning objectives and will primarily aim at evaluating the operational and clinical competencies acquired by the student.
Professional Role in the Workplace.
Professional Role in the Workplace:
The medical doctor exercises their profession within the norms established by the European Community, national and regional regulations, both within the National Health Service and in contracted or private structures. They operate with the aim of maintaining or achieving the complete state of health of the individual and society. To carry out their professional activity, they collaborate with other health professionals. The medical doctor, to perform this function, must possess a strong sense of their professional role. This includes clinical competence, i.e., the habitual and correct use of knowledge, communication skills, technical abilities, clinical reasoning, commitment to pursuing accurate professional updating, health promotion, adherence to professional ethical principles, and values such as personal integrity, honesty, altruism, humility, respect for diversity, transparency, and respect for conflicts of interest.
The medical doctor must therefore maintain: a constant commitment to patients, being able to apply the best clinical practices while respecting a high ethical profile; a constant commitment to society, being able to understand and respond to its expectations regarding healthcare; a continuous commitment to professional duties, respecting the rules and codes of professional ethics.
Competencies Associated with the Role.
Competencies Associated with the Role:
Competencies must be those of an expert medical doctor, who places the patient at the center of a high-quality and safe care process, based on their updated knowledge, clinical skills, and professional values. They must therefore be able to collect information from the patient and interpret it, make clinical decisions leading to correct diagnosis and targeted therapeutic interventions, based on scientific evidence from national and international guidelines, while being aware of the need for their correct and non-automatic application to the individual patient, in the context of precision medicine. They must also consider the patient's wishes and the economic availability of the healthcare system in the country where they operate. Their clinical practice must therefore be highly updated, ethical, and capable of ensuring efficient use of available resources. A fundamental task of the Master's Degree course is to provide up-to-date technical competencies and instruct on their constant future updating, as well as verify their acquisition through usual assessment procedures.
Being an Expert Medical Doctor is central to performing the profession and brings with it other intrinsically linked competencies, as specified below:
Effective Communicator. The medical doctor must be able to establish a relationship with the patient and their family that facilitates the collection and shared understanding of essential information for effective care. They will therefore be able to explore symptoms related to pathology, dedicating the appropriate time to listening to the patient. They must be able to explore the patient's perspective on their illness, fears, and health expectations, taking into account gender differences. The medical doctor must be able to integrate their scientific knowledge within the specific context of the patient, their socio-economic status, personal life history, current life and work situation, educational and cultural level, being able to detect particular states related to social and psychological spheres. Very important, to place the patient at the center of the care process, is the ability to share decisions in a way that aligns health needs with the patient's desires, values, and preferences. Teaching communication skills is an integral part of the core curriculum of individual courses and is evaluated in the related exams.
Good Collaborator. The medical doctor must be able to work efficiently and effectively with other members of intra- and inter-professional teams to deliver safe, high-quality, patient-centered care. Correct collaboration requires relationships based on trust, respect, and sharing, capable of ensuring continuity in the care process. This requires sharing knowledge, perspectives, and responsibilities, and a willingness to learn from each other.
Health Defender. In this role, the medical doctor must put their experience at the service of the community to improve its general health and well-being. In this context, improving health must include disease prevention, promotion, and protection. This also implies equity in health promotion, meaning that individuals and communities should not be disadvantaged based on ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, age, social class, economic status, or educational level. Medical doctors will support patients in navigating the national healthcare system and help them receive care in a timely manner. Courses in Professional Ethics and Principles of Introduction to Medical Profession and Clinical Bioethics constitute the privileged venue for acquiring the essential knowledge and competencies for the student to assume their social role.
Scholar. The medical doctor must demonstrate commitment to achieving and maintaining excellence in clinical practice through continuous education, be able to teach other colleagues, make decisions based on evidence-based medicine, and actively contribute to clinical renewal through translational scientific research. Medical doctors will pursue excellence in their daily work through active comparison with colleagues and seeking feedback from patient satisfaction and safety. They will be able to correctly integrate international scientific evidence into applied clinical practice, incorporating the patient's preferences and values into decision-making.
Professional. The concept of professionalism implies that the medical doctor must commit to caring for the health and well-being of individual patients and the community through correct ethical conduct, high professional behavior standards, responsibility towards the profession and society, maintaining a lifestyle that does not discredit the profession. They must be aware that their professional role fully reflects the expectations of modern society, i.e., clinical competence, commitment to professional updating, health promotion, complete adherence to ethical standards, and values such as personal integrity, altruism, humility, respect for others and diversity, transparency, and respect for potential conflicts of interest.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Career Opportunities:
The Medical Doctor, qualified to practice and registered with the Provincial Medical and Dental Association, will have job opportunities in public hospitals, private accredited or private structures. They may also perform their service in other territorial structures of ASL, such as outpatient clinics, Hospices, Residential Care Facilities (RSA), Drug Addiction Services (SerT), Pathological Dependency Services (SerD), Psychiatric Facilities, Disability Centers, and Long-Term Care Facilities. They may perform their service in Scientific Research and Care Institutes (IRCCS), Universities, or practice their profession independently.
Graduates in Medicine may pursue academic careers and research, both in Universities and in Public or Private Organizations.
Entry into National Health Service roles requires the possession of Specialization, obtained through enrollment and attendance at Specialization Schools, while entry into General Practitioner rankings requires attendance at Regional General Medicine Training Schools.
Specialization Schools are accessed through the successful completion of a national competition, while Regional Schools are accessed through the successful completion of a regional competition.

Master's Degree in BUILDING ENGINEERING-ARCHITECTURE Specific educational objectives.
The study course aims to create a professional figure that combines specific architectural and urban design skills with mastery of tools related to the construction feasibility of the conceived work, up to being able to competently follow its correct execution from an aesthetic, functional, and technical-economic perspective.
Therefore, a qualitative integration of historical-critical training with scientific training is implemented, according to a didactic approach that conceives design as a synthesis process, granting such a professional full title to operate, even at a European level, in the field of architectural and urban design.
The Master's degree in Building Engineering-Architecture has an organization specifically oriented to respect the European Parliament and Council Directive 2005/36/EC of 7 September 2005, concerning the recognition of professional qualifications, section 8, Architect, article 46, published in the Official Journal of the European Union L 255 on 30.09.2005.
The degree course is a five-year single cycle, and upon completion of studies, the title of Master's Degree in Building Engineering-Architecture is awarded.
The training path for the figure of Building Engineer-Architect combines engineering and architecture training through a series of mostly mandatory disciplinary courses, and although organized over five years, it is structured into three significant learning phases, appropriately diversified.
The first phase (first and second year) is preparatory in nature and includes basic courses in both engineering (mathematics, geometry, physics, computer science) and architectural culture (drawing and surveying, history of architecture, architectural composition, urban planning).
The second phase (third and fourth year) is characterized by synthesis design activities, with the elaboration of integrated projects concerning technological, formal, figurative, and structural aspects of architecture (Technical Architecture, Composition, Science and Technology of Constructions, Hydraulics), and cultural enrichment through the study of specialized disciplines that integrate learning and training in technical-professional and cultural-critical areas.
The third phase (fifth year) is aimed at completing professional preparation according to specific objectives and cultural choices made primarily autonomously by the student.
Indeed, in line with the general training model, optional courses are provided within appropriately differentiated orientations, allowing the choice of the thematic area in which to develop the thesis (Architectural Project, Restoration Project, Urban Planning Project, Technological Project for Architecture, Recovery Project of Existing Building Heritage).
Since the entire study course is aimed at design training, courses in all three learning phases are conducted by addressing not only theoretical and methodological content but also practical aspects through exercises and especially design and thesis laboratories where students develop skills in understanding, application, and communication.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding The graduate in the five-year Building Engineering-Architecture course must possess fundamental disciplinary knowledge for a full understanding of the complexity of phenomena related to the design of a building, recovery, management, and transformation of the built environment.
To this end, they must know both the technical literature produced in the field of technological and structural, environmental, and plant design, as well as management and urban planning, and the methods of analysis and understanding of building, urban, infrastructural, and territorial phenomena and processes.
These objectives are particularly addressed by courses of SSD that connect analytical content with theoretical-methodological disciplinary content regarding:
a) knowledge of the foundations of mathematical, physical, and geometric disciplines – (MAT/03, MAT/05, MAT/07);
b) knowledge of the foundations of physical-technical-environmental and plant disciplines for architecture, knowledge and understanding of physical problems and technologies, as well as the function of buildings to make them internally comfortable and protect them from climatic factors – (ING-IND/11);
c) knowledge of the history and theories of architecture as well as arts, technologies, and humanities related to it, knowledge of fine arts as factors that can influence architectural design quality – (ICAR/18);
d) knowledge and understanding of the science of representation (projective methods), methods and techniques of architectural surveying, methods and techniques for representing and communicating architecture, cartography, and methods and techniques for representing cities and environments – (ICAR/17, ICAR/06);
e) knowledge of the foundations of valuation disciplines for architecture and urban planning – (ICAR/22);
f) knowledge of the foundations of legal, economic, and social disciplines for architecture and urban planning, with particular reference to urban law, public works and building legislation – (IUS/10);
g) knowledge of the foundations of hydraulics (statics and kinematics of fluids) and hydraulic constructions (water supply and sewers) – (ICAR/01, ICAR/02);
h) knowledge of territory infrastructure, urban planning, planning, and applied techniques in planning processes, knowledge and understanding of landscape-related issues and their protection – (ICAR/20, ICAR/21, ICAR/04);
i) knowledge of structural conception, construction, and civil engineering problems connected with building design – (ICAR/07, ICAR/08, ICAR/09);
l) knowledge and understanding of distributive, typological, and morphological aspects of architectural spaces, the relationship between architectural morphology and construction equipment, methods of investigation and preparation of construction projects, methods of investigation and preparation of projects for the recovery of existing building heritage – (ICAR/10);
m) knowledge of industries, organizations, regulations, and procedures necessary to realize building projects – (ICAR/11);
n) knowledge and understanding of morphological, formal, and figurative values in architectural design, ability to perceive relationships between humans and architectural works and between architectural works and their environment, as well as the ability to perceive the need to adapt architectural works and spaces according to human needs and scale;
o) knowledge of the history of restoration, theories, techniques, and technologies of architectural restoration – (ICAR/19);
n) knowledge and understanding of the foundations of chemistry, materials technology, and applied chemistry – (ING-IND/22, ING-IND/23).
The teaching tools provided for acquiring knowledge and understanding are institutional lectures and exercises within courses, seminar activities, integrative or complementary activities promoted by the Course Council and Faculty, and participation in external conference activities.
II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding The graduate in the five-year Building Engineering-Architecture course must be able to apply different disciplinary knowledge and tools acquired during the training path to the design of complex building systems, not only for technological and structural aspects but also for those related to formal and figurative qualities, and environmental quality, with particular attention to well-being conditions, energy issues, and environmental impact.
The abilities indicated in this descriptor are ensured by courses with explicitly design-oriented objectives for architectural, technological, and urban planning design, and by others with training objectives related to the organization and rationalization of production processes. In particular:
a) Ability to use architectural representation techniques in all their aspects, morphological, figurative, and constructive; ability to apply operational methods and instrumentation, even technologically advanced, for architectural surveying; ability to produce architectural drawings at all required scales, up to the development of detailed execution drawings – (ICAR/17 + ICAR/17 laboratories);
b) Ability to elaborate, based on original ideas, the architectural project as a formal and figurative synthesis of technical-functional, aesthetic, and social values – (ICAR/14 + ICAR/14 laboratories);
c) Technical ability that allows designing sustainable buildings that meet user needs within the constraints imposed by cost factors and construction regulations; ability to identify and apply the most suitable techniques for the recovery, redevelopment, maintenance, and management of existing building heritage, management of technological and production processes related to new construction in the building sector, with attention also to safety issues; ability to address the analysis of problems related to the development of the building process, for operational, economic, and management aspects, for technological innovation and the testing of quality control of materials, components, products, and works – (ICAR/10 + ICAR/10 laboratories, ICAR/11 + ICAR/11 laboratory);
d) Ability to apply disciplinary analytical methods to the study of urban phenomena, territorial systems, and their transformation processes in relation to socio-economic dynamics that determine them; ability to elaborate infrastructure and urban plans and projects, and territorial plans; ability to analyze landscape-environmental values and elaborate plans and projects for protection – (ICAR/20 + ICAR/20 laboratory, ICAR/21 + ICAR/21 laboratory, ICAR/04);
e) Ability to control the sizing and develop technological networks projects (ICAR/01, ICAR/02);
f) Ability to develop restoration projects methodically and disciplinarily based on historical-critical analysis, and analysis of typological, morphological, figurative values, construction equipment, and macroscopic-surface and structural degradation – (ICAR/18 + ICAR/18 laboratory, ICAR/19 + ICAR/19 laboratory).
The teaching tools provided for these training objectives are exercises within courses, particularly design laboratories connected with courses of the ICAR/10, ICAR/11, ICAR/17, ICAR/18, ICAR/19, ICAR/20, ICAR/21 sectors, as well as the final thesis laboratory.
III - Judgment autonomy The Master's graduate in Building Engineering-Architecture is equipped with:
- Sensitivity and critical attention towards social transformation processes in the fields of culture, economy, and technology, including the ability to reflect on social and ethical responsibilities related to the application of their knowledge and judgments;
- Ability to integrate knowledge and manage complexity and interdisciplinarity within architectural, urban, landscape-territorial, and restoration projects, particularly in the role of coordinating various disciplinary and/or specialist inputs to the project;
- Ability to critically read existing building systems at spatial, social, and economic levels regarding quantitative and qualitative aspects;
- Ability to autonomously make motivated choices based on acquired knowledge regarding engineering methodologies;
- Ability to appropriately contextualize, in relation to different design scales, project and recovery interventions, management and organizational activities, anticipating and predicting the repercussions that proposed transformations may induce on urban, economic, social structures, as well as on product quality, energy impact, and environmental impact.
These training objectives are supported by the previously mentioned SSDs, particularly the design laboratories and the final thesis design laboratory. It is in the project experimentation activities, where integrated disciplinary knowledge is applied, that critical sensitivity and the ability to make motivated choices develop, also through discussion with teachers and tutors.
IV - Communication skills The Master's graduate in Building Engineering-Architecture:
- Is able to correctly use at least one European Union language besides Italian, with reference to disciplinary lexicons;
- Is able to communicate using appropriate means, verbal, graphical, and computer-based;
- Is able to communicate clearly and unambiguously the premises, content, and outcomes of their design elaborations and productions to both specialist and non-specialist interlocutors;
- Is able to argue the reasons for their design choices clearly and appropriately, both in technically detailed and in synthetic and illustrative ways;
- Has developed the necessary skills to successfully integrate into a work team in various design activity sectors, potentially serving as coordinator and manager.
These communication skills are primarily acquired during course exercises, especially during the development of design activities in the laboratory, where students are involved in group work with other students, discussing and exchanging views with peers, teachers, and tutors, as well as preparing written reports and appropriate presentations of visual elaborations.
In particular, the thesis work is particularly extensive and articulated, always accompanied by written reports and supported by presentations of complex digital elaborations.
Not least, the contribution to acquiring communication skills comes from the same exam discussions, required for all courses, and the presentation during the thesis defense.
V - Learning ability The Master's graduate must have developed learning abilities that allow:
- Continuing to develop autonomously knowledge and their ability to elaborate design in relation to the evolution of sciences, techniques, technologies, and changing socio-economic scenarios;
- Having the ability to analyze the most diverse design problems, developing autonomous and innovative solutions.
This training objective is achieved through project activities in design laboratories and the thesis, where, starting from a research topic assigned, the student must autonomously implement their preparation on the specificity of the study topic.
The same stimulus for autonomous learning is developed in courses, which are more oriented towards acquiring a correct theoretical-methodological approach for disciplinary knowledge rather than mere factual and informative content.
Professional status conferred by the degree.
The main employment opportunities provided by Master's degree courses in the class are:
- Activities in which Master's graduates of the class are able to design, through the tools proper to architecture and building engineering-architecture, urban planning, and architectural restoration, and having mastery of tools related to the construction and economic feasibility of the conceived work, the operations of construction, transformation, and modification of the physical environment and landscape, with full knowledge of aesthetic, distributive, functional, structural, technical-constructive, management, economic, and environmental aspects, and critical attention to cultural changes and needs expressed by contemporary society.
- Activities in which Master's graduates of the class prepare projects for works and direct their realization in the fields of architecture and building engineering-architecture, urban planning, architectural restoration, and in general the urban and landscape environment, coordinating, where necessary, other Master's graduates and operators.

ITALIANO Degree Awarded.
Master's Degree in REHABILITATION SCIENCES OF HEALTH PROFESSIONS Specific Educational Objectives.
The Master's Degree Course in Rehabilitation Health Professions has the following specific objectives: the in-depth knowledge and application of:
- the essential methodological elements of epidemiology;
- the essential elements of human resource management, with particular reference to issues in the healthcare sector;
- the principles of Law, including the acquisition of the main legislative norms governing healthcare organization, as well as ethical norms and professional responsibility;
- basic notions of public and business economics, essential elements, and main techniques of business organization, with particular reference to the healthcare services sector and processes for optimizing the use of human, information, and technological resources.
Additionally, the specific educational objectives of the course are:
- the appropriate use of effectiveness and efficiency indicators for healthcare services for specific diseases and disease groups;
- verifying the application of research activity results to continuously improve the quality of care;
- identifying the essential components of organizational and management problems of technical healthcare staff in medium or high complexity facilities;
- knowing and applying appropriate techniques for individual and group communication and managing interpersonal relationships with patients and their families; managing work groups and applying appropriate strategies to promote multi-professional and organizational integration processes;
- implementing the method for independent study and continuous education;
- conducting systematic bibliographic research, also through databases, and periodic updates;
- critically reading scientific articles;
- developing research and teaching, as well as deepening personnel management strategies regarding the specific professional role;
- achieving a sufficient level of written and spoken English;
- acquiring computer skills useful for managing information systems of services and self-education processes.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding The final second-level degree is awarded at the end of the educational path to students who:
- have demonstrated knowledge and understanding that extend and strengthen those typically associated with the first cycle of studies, and allow for the development and application of original ideas, even in a research context;
- have acquired a thorough scientific preparation in the disciplines already analyzed and interdisciplinary methodologies that allow for an integrated view of knowledge;
- have learned and/or implemented advanced skills and developed and applied original ideas, both on priority population health issues within rehabilitation, and on service quality issues and specific research areas.
Such knowledge and understanding are achieved through attendance at characteristic and related educational activities organized in specific integrated courses, ensuring a unified and at the same time interdisciplinary view of the educational objectives, with further deepening of knowledge derived from characteristic disciplinary fields, even those more specifically professionalizing, and from related and integrative disciplinary fields.
Pursuant to DM 8 January 2009, each activated course provides a sufficient integer number of credit points to avoid fragmentation of the information transmitted to students.
The teaching methods include frontal lessons, conferences, seminars, discussion groups aimed at achieving the educational path objectives. The teaching process will utilize modern teaching tools.
Traditional teaching is complemented by guided internship and training activities at public healthcare and specialized training services in Italy or abroad, linked by specific agreements. This training allows for progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy, within which students propose targeted simulations and their intervention projects, integrating with potential rehabilitation competencies in the management of public facilities.
Laboratory and internship activities are carried out under the supervision and guidance of professional tutors specifically designated and assigned to each student, coordinated by a faculty member belonging to the highest educational level provided for the specific profile and corresponding to European-level regulations where applicable.
The study plan provides a maximum of 12 exams and/or final assessments, organized as integrated exams for multiple courses or coordinated modules. The assessment of this learning is verified through exams, which, beyond traditional oral or written formats, also include a sequence of in-course assessments (self-assessment tests and intermediate discussions) to verify acquired knowledge. Regarding written exams, the tools used are:
1) multiple-choice or short written answers, organized around interdisciplinary issues, followed by exams to verify acquired competencies;
2) written reports on assigned topics and analysis of activities and reports related to the final exam, as well as comments on field and laboratory exercises, and evaluation of the overall profile based on predefined criteria.
The course's didactic regulations will define, within legal limits, the proportion of the total student study time available for personal study or other individual training activities.
The educational path is structured, monitored, validated, and optimized in a continuum to acquire the skills, technical competencies, and knowledge specified in the curriculum profile established by current regulations and the specific objectives of the Course.
These specific educational objectives are supported by a faculty body aware of the need to use all institutional tools activated by competent bodies (NVF and NVA) for the accreditation of teaching quality. Through these tools, it is possible to measure improvements in teaching performance in all different phases contributing to the attainment of the Master's Degree, in terms of educational path, exams, perceived quality assessment by students, and acquisition of professional competencies falling within the specific objectives of the educational path.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding The final second-level degree is awarded at the end of the educational path to students who:
- have demonstrated knowledge and understanding that extend and strengthen those typically associated with the first cycle of studies, and allow for the development and application of original ideas, even in a research context;
- have acquired a thorough scientific preparation in the disciplines already analyzed and interdisciplinary methodologies that allow for an integrated view of knowledge;
- have learned and/or implemented advanced skills and developed and applied original ideas, both on priority population health issues within rehabilitation, and on service quality issues and specific research areas.
Such knowledge and understanding are achieved through attendance at characteristic and related educational activities organized in specific integrated courses, ensuring a unified and at the same time interdisciplinary view of the educational objectives, with further deepening of knowledge derived from characteristic disciplinary fields, even those more specifically professionalizing.
Knowledge growth and understanding will be achieved through frontal lessons, conferences, seminars, discussion groups, as well as internship and laboratory activities and field-based stages.
The teaching process will utilize modern teaching tools.
The assessment of this learning is verified through exams, which, beyond traditional oral or written formats, also include a sequence of in-course assessments (self-assessment tests and intermediate discussions) to verify acquired knowledge. Regarding written exams, the tools used may be:
1) multiple-choice or short written answers, organized around interdisciplinary issues, followed by exams to verify acquired competencies;
2) written reports on assigned topics, and analysis of activities and reports related to the final exam, as well as comments on field and laboratory exercises, and evaluation of the overall profile based on predefined criteria.
Particular attention is given during the educational path to acquiring practical and organizational skills through involvement in planning projects and research, optimizing participation in internships and stages, culminating in proposals for integrating the specialist graduate within SSN facilities, also for the purpose of preparing the thesis.
The Course organization includes a knowledge monitoring of the achievement of the above-mentioned knowledge and understanding, in terms of expected learning outcomes, through an articulated coordination, also set up for this purpose.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding The final second-level degree is awarded at the end of the educational path to students who are able to:
- demonstrate an applied approach to the knowledge and understanding acquired, and the ability to solve problems on new or unfamiliar topics within broader, also interdisciplinary contexts related to their field of study;
- exercise the necessary specific cultural competencies to address population health and care issues;
- use knowledge and understanding appropriately to analyze, design, and support arguments and solve problems, even complex ones, within their field of study, with particular attention to organizational and management issues of health professions and mastery of healthcare management techniques and procedures.
These competencies will be achieved through attention to the practical aspects of different courses and through practical sessions aimed at developing the ability to approach operational and professional problems individually.
In particular, regarding Population Health and Healthcare Systems, the graduate must be able to:
- consider the main determinants of health and disease in professional practice;
- undertake appropriate preventive and protective actions against diseases, injuries, and accidents, maintaining and promoting the health of the individual, family, and community;
- stay informed on the state of international health, global trends in morbidity and mortality of socially relevant chronic diseases, considering the impact of migration, market opening, environmental factors, and the role of international health organizations;
- accept roles and responsibilities of different healthcare personnel in providing care to individuals, populations, and communities;
- recognize the need for collective responsibility in health promotion interventions requiring close collaboration with the population, as well as the need for a multidisciplinary approach, including health professionals and inter-sectoral collaboration;
- know and apply appropriate techniques for individual and group communication to support the management of interpersonal relationships with public and private facilities, patients, and their families;
- refer to the basic organization of healthcare systems, including policies, organization, funding, cost-restrictive measures, and principles of efficient management in the correct delivery of healthcare.
The teaching methods include frontal lessons, conferences, seminars, discussion groups. The teaching process will utilize modern teaching tools. The ability to apply acquired knowledge will be acquired through guided laboratory and field activities, especially with interdisciplinary approaches.
The assessment of this learning is verified through exams, which, beyond traditional oral or written formats, also include a sequence of in-course assessments (self-assessment tests and intermediate discussions) to verify acquired knowledge. Regarding written exams, the tools used may be:
a) multiple-choice or short written answers, organized around interdisciplinary issues, followed by exams to verify acquired competencies;
b) written reports on assigned topics, in the analysis of activities and reports related to the final exam, as well as comments on field and laboratory exercises, and evaluation of the overall profile based on predefined criteria.
The Course organization includes a knowledge monitoring of the achievement of the above-mentioned ability to apply knowledge and understanding, in terms of expected learning outcomes, through an articulated coordination, also set up for this purpose.
III - Autonomy of Judgment The final second-level degree is awarded at the end of the educational path to students who have pursued the ability to integrate knowledge and manage complexity, as well as to form judgments based on limited or incomplete information, including reflection on the social and ethical responsibilities related to the application of their knowledge and judgments.
The student must also have developed awareness of their social responsibility linked to their profession, and consolidated the ability to acquire independent judgment, integrating knowledge in managing complex problems or forming independent judgments even based on essential, limited, or incomplete information, including reflection on the social and ethical responsibilities related to the application of knowledge and judgments, with particular reference to issues within the rehabilitation field, respecting their own and others' competencies.
To acquire the ability for critical thinking and scientific research aptitude, students must be able to:
- demonstrate in professional activities a critical approach, constructive skepticism, and an attitude potentially oriented towards research; formulate personal judgments to solve analytical and complex problems ("problem solving") and autonomously seek the best scientific evidence without waiting for it to be provided;
- demonstrate the ability to correctly apply the principles of moral reasoning and adopt appropriate decisions regarding possible conflicts in ethical, legal, and professional values, including those emerging from economic distress, commercialization of healthcare, and new scientific discoveries; respond with personal commitment to the need for continuous professional improvement, aware of their own limitations;
- respect colleagues and other health professionals, demonstrating the ability to establish collaborative relationships with them, coordinating with different professional figures operating in the field for the elaboration of integrated intervention projects;
- be able to design a research and intervention project within rehabilitation health professions, applying ethical and deontological principles in patient data treatment, avoiding plagiarism, confidentiality, and respect for intellectual property;
- effectively plan and efficiently manage their time and activities to face uncertain conditions, and exercise the ability to adapt to changes.
Autonomy of judgment will be stimulated and developed throughout the study course, both through guided internship moments connected to different courses, with attendance at characteristic educational activities, as well as in professionalized and related disciplinary fields specific to the class, and in other disciplinary fields, through continuous critical discussion of case histories, especially within the thesis preparation, where students will be required to develop a personal interpretation of data collected in complex situations, discussing alternative hypotheses according to models present in the literature or proposed by themselves under the guidance of a supervisor.
The assessment of this learning is verified through exams, which, beyond traditional oral or written formats, also include a sequence of in-course assessments (self-assessment tests and intermediate discussions) to verify acquired knowledge. Regarding written exams, the tools used may be: 1) multiple-choice or short written answers, organized around interdisciplinary issues, followed by exams to verify acquired competencies; 2) written reports on assigned topics, in the analysis of activities and reports related to the final exam, as well as comments on field and laboratory exercises, and evaluation of the overall profile based on predefined criteria.
The Course organization includes a knowledge monitoring of the achievement of the autonomy of judgment developed by students, in terms of expected learning outcomes and behavior, through an articulated coordination, also set up for this purpose.
IV - Communication Skills The final second-level degree will be awarded to students who can:
- communicate clearly and coherently both orally and in writing, without ambiguity, information, ideas, problems, and solutions, the conclusions of reasoning related to specific competencies applied, particularly within rehabilitation, as well as knowledge and rationale underlying them, to both specialist and non-specialist interlocutors;
- communicate with different professional figures working in the field using a common language derived from an interdisciplinary approach. demonstrate good sensitivity towards cultural and personal factors that improve interactions with facilities, patients, and communities;
- effectively summarize and present information appropriate to the audience's needs, and discuss achievable and acceptable action plans representing priorities for the individual and the community.
This competence will improve the graduate's opportunities for integration into various professional fields.
Graduates will be able to communicate effectively using computer and telecommunication tools.
These competencies will be acquired through activities related to characteristic, related, and integrative courses, some of which are oriented towards developing the ability for correct argumentative expression related to the field of study. The knowledge and application of appropriate techniques for individual and group communication represent one of the core specific objectives of the educational path. Communication skills are cultivated by encouraging students to present individual and group reports on rehabilitation topics orally, in writing, and using electronic and multimedia tools, as well as providing models for oral and written presentation of research results and more complex argumentation activities.
In the evaluation of reports, especially the final exam, the quality and effectiveness of the presentation will be considered for the overall assessment.
The Master's graduate is capable of designing communication strategies, recognizing different target populations for the communication project, realizing communications appropriate for different targets, choosing the most suitable communication tools for the purpose, the most effective communicator according to known qualities (empathy, honesty, clarity, authority, etc.), and monitoring and evaluating the result of the communication project itself.
The Course organization includes a knowledge monitoring of the achievement of communication skills by students, in terms of expected learning outcomes, through an articulated coordination, also set up for this purpose.
V - Learning Ability The final second-level degree is awarded at the end of the educational path to students who have developed learning abilities that allow them to continue studying mostly in an autonomous or self-directed manner (self-learning and self-updating), acquiring methodological knowledge to improve and update advanced professional skills in specific fields of interest, and evaluating the effectiveness of interventions within Rehabilitation and Health Promotion, also through critical analysis of scientific literature.
The Master's graduate must have acquired the ability to:
- listen to extract and synthesize relevant information on all issues, understanding their content;
- put into practice communication skills to facilitate understanding with different interlocutors;
- interact with other professional figures involved in their professional practice through integrated and efficient group work;
- demonstrate good sensitivity towards cultural and personal factors that improve interactions with patients and communities;
- demonstrate the ability for self-directed and autonomous learning and updating;
- access and use, also through computer tools, the scientific literature of the specific field and related fields, critically evaluating and elaborating it in a personal form.
These competencies will ensure the ability to effectively pursue a third-level study path (PhD) or enter the workforce with the capacity for updating in the field of application.
The ability to learn will be acquired during the academic career:
1) through specific seminars on computerized bibliographic research, refined during the preparation of the thesis, which will require consultation and critical analysis of relevant scientific publications;
2) through guided practical sessions, with attendance at specific class training activities, also in related and integrative disciplinary fields, organized in specific integrated courses, ensuring a unified and interdisciplinary view of the educational objectives;
3) through specific seminar moments of analysis of activities and reports related to the final exam, reaching maximum development in activities for preparing the final exam;
4) through Stages in healthcare management, training, and managerial fields, acquiring methods to refine the ability to manage work processes of a managerial type with progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy;
5) through the presentation of organizational and/or training projects within the scope of professional competence.
The teaching methods include frontal lessons, conferences, seminars, discussion groups.
The teaching process will also utilize modern teaching tools.
Assessment will take place concurrently with the evaluation of other training moments, as well as comprehensive evaluations related to the design, elaboration, presentation, and evaluation of the thesis.
Student assessment will therefore occur through formative in-course assessments (self-assessment tests and intermediate discussions), written reports on assigned topics, and evaluation of the overall profile based on predefined criteria.
Exam formats may include, beyond traditional oral or written exams, a sequence of items useful to verify acquired knowledge, such as multiple-choice tests or short written answers organized around interdisciplinary clinical cases or problems, followed by exams to verify clinical competencies.
The Course organization includes a knowledge monitoring of the achievement of the above-mentioned learning abilities by students, in terms of expected learning outcomes, through an articulated coordination, also set up for this purpose.
Workplace Function.
Workplace Function:
The main functions of the professional figure are expressed in the coordination and organization of healthcare services; design and implementation of training interventions for updating and continuous training within healthcare facilities, as well as contributing to the training of each specific professional figure through tutorial activities and internship coordination, and directly contributing to the updating of their professional profile and research.

Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Career Prospects:
Career opportunities are represented by service in SSN [hospital and/or ASL facilities and health professions departments] and in the organization of healthcare services; in the design and implementation of training interventions for updating and continuous training within healthcare facilities, as well as contributing to the training of each specific professional figure through tutorial activities and internship coordination, and directly contributing to the updating of their professional profile and research.
Professional activity can also be carried out in public and private healthcare facilities, also authorized according to current regulations, in dependent or self-employed relationships.
Master's graduates can access Research Doctorate courses, with objectives of deepening scientific investigation and research methodology, and University Master's courses of the second level, with objectives of scientific refinement and continuous training in specific intervention sectors.
