Master's Degree in SCIENCES OF PREVENTIVE HEALTH PROFESSIONS Specific Educational Objectives.
The educational path of the Master's Degree Course in Sciences of Preventive Health Professions has specific objectives including in-depth knowledge and application:
·- the essential methodological elements of epidemiology;
·- the essential elements of human resource management, with particular reference to issues in the healthcare sector;
·- the principles of Law, with acquisition of the main legislative norms regulating healthcare organization, as well as deontological and professional responsibility norms;
·- the basic notions of public and business economics, the essential elements and main techniques of business organization, with particular reference to the healthcare services sector and the optimization processes of human, information, and technological resource utilization.
Additionally, specific educational objectives of the course include:
·- appropriate use of effectiveness and efficiency indicators for healthcare services for specific diseases and disease groups;
·- verification of the application of research results to continuously improve the quality of care;
·- identifying the essential components of organizational and managerial problems of technical healthcare staff in medium to high complexity structures;
·- knowledge and application of appropriate techniques for individual and group communication and management of interpersonal relationships with patients and their families;
·- managing work groups and applying appropriate strategies to promote multi-professional and organizational integration processes;
·- acquiring the method for independent study and continuous education;
·- conducting systematic bibliographic research, also through databases, and periodic updates;
·- critically reading scientific articles;
·- developing research and teaching, as well as deepening personnel management strategies regarding the specific professional profile;
·- reaching a sufficient level of written and spoken English;
·- acquiring useful IT skills for managing information systems of services and self-education processes.
The educational activity, predominantly organized in "specific integrated courses," ensures a unified and interdisciplinary vision of the educational objectives, with in-depth knowledge derived from characteristic disciplinary fields, including those more specifically professionalizing, as well as related and integrative disciplinary fields.
Pursuant to DM 8 January 2009, each activated course provides a sufficient integer number of credit points to avoid fragmentation of information transmitted to students.
The teaching methods include lectures, conferences, seminars, and discussion groups aimed at achieving the educational objectives.
The teaching process will utilize modern teaching tools.
Traditional teaching is complemented by guided internship and training activities at public healthcare and specialized training services in Italy or abroad, linked by specific agreements. This training allows for progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy, within which students propose targeted simulations and their intervention projects, integrating with potential technical, evaluative, organizational, and managerial competencies in the Technical Prevention field within public management structures.
Laboratory and internship activities are conducted under the supervision and guidance of professional tutors specifically designated and assigned to each student, coordinated by a faculty member belonging to the highest educational level for the specific profile and corresponding.
The study plan allows a maximum of 12 exams and/or final assessments, organized as integrated exams for multiple courses or coordinated modules.
Assessment of this learning is verified through exams, which, beyond traditional oral or written formats, include interim assessments (self-assessment tests and intermediate discussions) to verify acquired knowledge. Written exams may use: (1) multiple-choice or short written responses on interdisciplinary issues, followed by exams to verify acquired competencies; (2) written reports on assigned topics and analysis of activities related to the final exam, as well as comments on field and laboratory exercises, evaluated based on predefined criteria.
The course's teaching regulations will define, within legal limits, the proportion of total weekly study time available to students for personal study or other individual training activities.
The educational path is structured, monitored, validated, and optimized continuously to acquire the abilities, technical skills, and knowledge specified in the curriculum profile established by current regulations and the specific objectives of the course.
These specific educational objectives are supported by a faculty aware of the need to utilize all institutional tools activated by competent bodies (NVF and NVA) for the accreditation of teaching quality. Through these tools, it is possible to measure improvements in teaching performance at all stages contributing to the attainment of the Master's Degree, in terms of educational path, exams, perceived quality evaluation by students, and acquisition of professional competencies aligned with the specific objectives of the educational path.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding
The graduate will have acquired specific basic knowledge in the healthcare and biological fields and will be able to identify environmental and occupational risk factors, assess their health effects, and plan appropriate protection and remediation measures in living and working environments. The graduate will have acquired specific knowledge on the human-environment relationship and environmental dynamics for implementing health promotion and risk prevention activities. The Master's graduate in Sciences of Preventive Health Professions will have acquired constitutional principles and organizational modalities of public administration, with particular reference to prevention services. The Master's graduate will have knowledge in labor law, environmental law, and healthcare organization within central and local public bodies. The graduate will be able to analyze healthcare organizations in terms of management, effectiveness, efficiency, and performance. The graduate will be able to identify the essential components of organizational and managerial problems of technical staff in preventive contexts.
The graduate will have achieved a high level of written and spoken knowledge of at least one European Union language and acquired specific IT skills regarding the management of service information systems and research methodology. The graduate will have acquired the necessary knowledge of methods and tools of research in the field of prevention service organization. The graduate knows the essential methodological elements of epidemiology, statistics, risk assessment, and systematic bibliographic research and will be able to read, critically evaluate, and produce scientific articles.
Knowledge and understanding are achieved and verified through the completion of the educational activities planned in the course program, particularly through lectures, group work sessions, internship and laboratory activities, aiming to strengthen the interaction between theoretical knowledge and practical experience over the two years to build a continuous updating path in prevention and related activities.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding
The Master's graduate in Sciences of Preventive Health Professions uses theoretical knowledge, skills, and attitudes to deliver and design safe, effective, evidence-based preventive interventions. They also use tools for evaluating public health interventions. The graduate will be able to use the theoretical and practical knowledge acquired over the two years to evaluate, design, organize, and implement appropriate preventive interventions within reference structures. The graduate will be able to assume responsibility for all prevention, verification, and control activities related to environmental and occupational hygiene in living and working places and environmental hygiene.
The graduate appropriately applies organizational analysis and management and expenditure control in affiliated structures. The graduate will be able to use effectiveness and efficiency indicators for services for specific intervention activities appropriately. The graduate will be able to integrate and apply ethical, legal, and management knowledge within the complex organization of the reference system, responsibly and consistently with national and international guidelines.
The graduate will be able to conduct systematic bibliographic research and apply the essential methodological elements of epidemiology. The graduate will be able to ensure continuous feedback on the work group from the most recent methods and tools provided by ongoing scientific and technological development in the sector. The graduate, using theoretical and practical knowledge acquired over the two years, will be able to design training interventions for updating and continuous education within reference structures, as well as university education.
Educational activities are carried out through courses that may correspond to different modules or types of activities (classroom lectures, exercises, seminars).
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is achieved and verified through group work sessions, internship and laboratory activities, and the preparation of the final exam.
III - Independent Judgment
The Master's graduate, having followed an educational path characterized by a preventive, promotional, and epidemiological approach to safeguard individual and collective health, will be able to make decisions in the field of their professional competence with a level of professional, cultural, and operational autonomy, demonstrating the ability to search for, use, and interpret data from services, territory, and specialized databases. The graduate must have developed awareness of their social responsibility linked to their profession and consolidated the ability to form independent judgments, integrating knowledge to manage complex problems and/or formulate independent judgments based on essential, limited, or incomplete information. The student must also demonstrate reflection on social and ethical responsibilities, particularly regarding issues related to the technical evaluative organizational managerial field of prevention, respecting their own and others' competencies.
Independent judgment will be progressively enhanced throughout the educational path through the completion of exams and all phases of preparation and writing of the Master's thesis. The evaluation of independent judgment will be conducted during the final thesis discussion.
IV - Communication Skills
The second-level degree will be awarded to students who can:
- communicate clearly and coherently both orally and in writing, without ambiguity, information, ideas, problems, and solutions related to specific applied competencies, particularly in the preventive technical field, as well as the knowledge and rationale underlying them, to both specialist and non-specialist interlocutors;
- communicate with different professional figures working in the territory using a common language derived from an interdisciplinary approach;
- demonstrate good sensitivity towards cultural and personal factors that improve interactions with structures, patients, and communities;
- summarize and present information effectively according to the audience's needs, and discuss achievable and acceptable action plans representing priorities for the individual and the community.
This competence will improve the Master's graduate's opportunities for professional integration in various fields.
Graduates will be able to communicate effectively using IT and telecommunication tools.
These competencies, acquired through activities related to characteristic, related, and integrative courses, some oriented towards developing the ability for correct argumentative expression, in relation to the study field content.
Knowledge and application of appropriate techniques for individual and group communication represent core specific objectives of the educational path.
Communication skills are cultivated by encouraging students to present individual and group work both orally, in writing, and using electronic and multimedia tools in the preventive technical field, as well as providing models for oral and written presentation of research results and more complex arguments.
In the evaluation of works, especially the final exam, the quality and effectiveness of the presentation will be considered in forming the overall judgment.
The Master's graduate must be able to design communication strategies, recognizing different target populations for the communication project, implementing appropriate communications for different targets, choosing the most suitable communication tools, selecting the most effective communicator according to the "good communicator" qualities (empathy, honesty, clarity, authority, etc.), and monitoring and evaluating the result of the communication project itself.
The course organization includes monitoring the achievement of communication skills in terms of expected learning outcomes through a structured coordination, also prepared for this purpose.
V - Learning Ability
The second-level degree is awarded at the end of the educational path to students who have developed learning abilities enabling them to continue studying mostly in an autonomous or self-directed manner (self-learning and self-updating), acquiring methodological knowledge to improve advanced skills in specific fields, continuously updating professional skills, and evaluating the effectiveness of interventions in the preventive technical and health promotion field, also through critical analysis of scientific literature.
The Master's graduate must have acquired the ability to:
- listen to extract and synthesize relevant information on all issues, understanding their content;
- apply communication skills to facilitate understanding with different interlocutors;
- interact with other professional figures involved in their professional practice through integrated and efficient group work;
- demonstrate good sensitivity towards cultural and personal factors that improve interactions with patients and communities;
- demonstrate the ability for self-directed and autonomous learning and updating;
- access and use, also through IT tools, the scientific literature of the specific field and related fields, critically evaluating and personalizing it.
These competencies will ensure the ability to effectively pursue a third-level study path (PhD) or enter the workforce with the capacity for continuous updating in the application field.
Learning ability will be acquired throughout the academic career through:
1) specific seminars on tools for computerized bibliographic research and evaluation of research quality, refined during the preparation of the thesis, which requires consultation and critical analysis of relevant scientific publications; (2) guided practical sessions, with attendance at specific training activities of the class, also in related and integrative disciplinary fields, organized in "specific integrated courses," ensuring a unified and interdisciplinary vision of the educational objectives; (3) specific seminar sessions on the analysis of activities and reports related to the final exam, reaching maximum development in preparation for the final exam; (4) Internships in healthcare management, training, and leadership areas, acquiring methods to refine the ability to manage directorial work processes with progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy; (5) presentation of organizational and/or training projects within the professional competence area.
The course organization includes monitoring the achievement of the above learning abilities by students in terms of expected learning outcomes through a structured coordination, also prepared for this purpose.
Workplace Function.
Workplace Function:
Master's graduates in Sciences of Preventive Health Professions, after acquiring the necessary scientific knowledge and professional competencies for the performance of health professions in the prevention field, as well as ethical values, at the end of the educational path, will be able to express advanced preventive and educational competencies in response to priority health problems of the population in living and working environments and environmental issues.
Competencies Associated with the Function.
Competencies Associated with the Function:
Master's graduates in Sciences of Preventive Health Professions who have acquired the necessary scientific knowledge, ethical values, and relevant professional abilities for professions in the prevention field, at the end of the educational path, will be able to express advanced assistive, educational, and preventive competencies in response to health problems of the pediatric, adult, and geriatric population and quality service issues in general living and working environments. Based on acquired knowledge, they will be able to consider, in the programming and management of healthcare personnel, both the needs of the community, the development of new work organization methods, technological and IT innovation (including tele-assistance or tele-education forms), and the planning and organization of pedagogical and training interventions, as well as harmonizing operational standards with those of the European Union.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Employment Opportunities:
Graduates of the Master's Degree in Sciences of Preventive Health Professions possess advanced cultural and professional training to intervene with high-level competencies in management, training, and research processes in one of the fields relevant to the various health professions included in the class. They may find employment in the programming and management of healthcare personnel, development of new work organization methods, coordination of technical practical activities of three-year degrees. The acquired methodological knowledge enables intervention in specific training and research processes of the class.

Degree Awarded.
Master's Degree in CHEMICAL SCIENCES
Specific Educational Objectives.
The Master's Degree Course in Chemical Sciences aims to integrate and strengthen the basic competencies acquired in the first cycle across various fields of chemistry, providing students with advanced preparation for engaging in activities focused on scientific and technological innovation in the chemical field. The Master's Degree Course also offers the opportunity to acquire specialized skills in specific areas of chemistry.
Subject to the general educational objectives of the degree class, the specialization areas of the Master's Degree in Chemical Sciences, which will correspond to specific orientations or alternative curricula within the master's degree program, aim to:
- provide advanced skills for understanding and predicting molecular reactivity and designing complex syntheses. In this context, students will consolidate their knowledge of reaction mechanisms to develop the ability to understand, design, and carry out syntheses of organic, inorganic, and organometallic molecules. Particular emphasis will be placed on the role of catalysis as an essential tool for preparing high-value-added compounds, considering the economic efficiency and environmental sustainability of synthetic processes.
- provide advanced skills enabling the Master's graduate to identify and apply the most suitable computational and experimental methods for characterizing a chemical system of interest or solving problems arising from various sectors of research and industry. In this context, students will acquire advanced knowledge of modern instrumental techniques while developing the ability to critically evaluate the quality parameters of experimental data based on the nature of the problem. It will also be essential to process data using statistical methods to identify and represent the information contained within, and apply computational methods to support experiments.
The proposed curriculum includes core courses in fundamental chemical disciplines (Physical Chemistry, Inorganic Chemistry, Organic Chemistry, Analytical Chemistry) and Industrial Chemistry, aiming to complete the foundational education acquired with the first-cycle degree and introduce more advanced specialized knowledge, as well as courses enabling students to acquire training relevant to their chosen path.
The common core courses applicable to all specialized paths, mostly concentrated in the first year, will enable students to:
- acquire advanced knowledge in coordination compound chemistry
- consolidate knowledge of the properties, mechanisms, and syntheses of organic compounds, as well as their structural characterization using advanced spectroscopic techniques
- acquire solid skills in quantum mechanical calculation methods and advanced chemical-physical investigation techniques
- understand the criteria for determining analytical data quality and procedures for developing, validating, and optimizing chemical analysis methods
- enrich knowledge regarding reactions and processes of industrial interest in organic and inorganic chemistry
The differentiation of the proposed paths will be implemented starting from the second semester of the first year through the inclusion of specific courses considered characteristic of a particular specialization area. Students may further personalize their training by selecting certain courses from a list of advanced courses considered consistent with the characteristics of their chosen path or capable of providing cross-cutting skills across different paths.
Students may opt for a specific specialization area by selecting one of the proposed paths and the corresponding optional courses through the submission of their study plan.
The Master's Degree Course in Chemical Sciences also includes a training internship to be carried out within the University, at Companies or Public Research Bodies in the national or international territory, under specific agreements, as an integral part of the educational path.
Ample space is dedicated to the thesis work, which concludes the training, where students, addressing an original research topic, learn to apply theoretical knowledge acquired and consolidate their experimental and/or computational skills, as well as their ability to present and discuss a scientific problem both in written and oral form.
Depending on the chosen path, while maintaining the general educational objectives of the degree class, the Master's graduate will have acquired specialized skills enabling them to design and study new chemical reactions and optimize the synthesis of new compounds and materials. Students will develop the ability to design and carry out syntheses of organic, inorganic, and organometallic molecules for various application types, prioritizing processes that meet the efficiency and environmental sustainability criteria imposed by social awareness and current international regulations. Students will also acquire the theoretical/mechanistic foundations necessary for rationalizing synthetic studies and will be able to apply advanced methods for structural characterization.
The Master's graduate will be able to develop and validate new analytical methods and make decisions regarding the most suitable sampling and analysis methods for characterizing complex systems. In this context, students will be able to identify and apply the most appropriate technologies for quality analysis and process control in various fields (clinical, toxicological, food, and environmental). These skills will enable the newly graduated to easily integrate into the workforce related to certification and quality analysis issues.
The Master's graduate will possess the skills to develop and validate statistical and computational models that can support experimental methods in characterizing chemical systems. To this end, students will become familiar with computational techniques aimed at solving structural and mechanistic problems, as well as statistical approaches for data processing and process optimization. They will also be able to use mathematical and computer tools for processing matrices obtained through the combination of experimental data and simulated quantities within the study of structure-property relationships.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding
The graduate must have acquired in-depth knowledge in various fields of inorganic chemistry, physical chemistry, organic chemistry, analytical chemistry, and industrial chemistry, as well as familiarity with the main methodologies and instrumental techniques for structural characterization and establishing structure-property relationships necessary for understanding molecular-level phenomena. They must also know the fundamental computational approaches to chemistry-related issues. Depending on the chosen path, the graduate will have the opportunity to consolidate their skills in a specific area of specialization. In particular, they may acquire advanced knowledge in organic and inorganic synthesis, emphasizing mechanistic aspects governing processes and the role of catalysis. They may consolidate knowledge in applying chemical analysis methods for studying systems of interest in biological, environmental, food, and quality control processes. They may acquire advanced knowledge in statistical treatment of data matrices to extract useful information and in simulating atomic and molecular properties.
To achieve these educational objectives, the study program provides a solid multidisciplinary preparation through the delivery of common courses, while the acquisition of specialized knowledge is entrusted to the courses characterizing the chosen path. A strong emphasis is placed on laboratory activities aimed at familiarizing students with modern measurement instruments for chemical compounds and materials, structural determination techniques, approaches for preparing and purifying scientific and technological interest compounds and materials, as well as methods for statistical processing of chemical data and simulation of experimental quantities.
The method of verifying the acquisition of knowledge and understanding, defined by each instructor, may consist of passing oral exams, in-course assessments, or the evaluation of brief reports on practical work carried out in the design and execution of laboratory experiments. This is complemented by the evaluation of the written thesis by the graduation committee, in which the student describes and discusses their thesis work, and their oral presentation.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding
Regardless of the chosen educational path, the graduate must be able to apply their knowledge across various fields of chemistry, demonstrating mastery of the scientific investigation method and possessing both the ability to formulate and support arguments and to solve chemical problems even in interdisciplinary contexts. They must be able to work correctly in the laboratory with autonomy and decision-making capacity, addressing and solving problems in various fields of chemical sciences, making motivated decisions and drawing conclusions based on available data and information. Depending on the chosen specialization area, the graduate may acquire the ability to carry out synthetic processes described in the literature in the laboratory, as well as design and carry out novel syntheses with the aim of obtaining products or materials with specific functions. They will be able to apply certified analytical methods or develop and validate new methods within the context of quality control of processes or materials, and use computational or chemometric methods competently for simulating or processing chemical data in specific scientific issues. To develop the ability to apply acquired knowledge, the study program emphasizes laboratory activities, provided for many courses, and includes a mandatory training internship in the second year, which can be carried out in a university laboratory or in external companies or bodies under specific agreements. An important formative role is played by the preparation of the thesis, where the student is required to carry out individual research under the guidance of one or more instructors in a university or non-university laboratory.
The verification of achieving the objectives in terms of the ability to apply knowledge and understanding is entrusted to passing the final exams, laboratory reports, evaluation of the mandatory training internship, and the final evaluation of the thesis.
III - Judgment Autonomy
Graduates must have acquired high-level critical reasoning abilities and be able to independently conduct scientific research in their chosen field, identifying the most appropriate methods to address issues within chemistry. They must be able to design and conduct experiments, interpret results, and plan subsequent experimentation to acquire knowledge and/or optimize methodologies or processes in a scientific and applied research context. They must also be able to appropriately use available bibliographic sources and electronic archives on the web. Based on the specialized training provided by the chosen path, the graduate must be able to evaluate the most suitable choices for synthesizing old and new materials or substances, taking into account the environmental and economic sustainability of the process, as well as the toxicity of reagents, solvents, and catalysts. In the context of applying analytical methods for quality control of materials and processes, the graduate must be able to evaluate the most appropriate analytical approach to meet the quality requirements specified by current legislation and present results in an adequate form. The graduate must be able to identify the most suitable and effective statistical or computational approaches to extract useful information from chemical systems while minimizing the use of human and instrumental resources in the laboratory.
IV - Communication Skills
The Chemical Sciences graduate must be able to communicate information, scientific data, and conclusions clearly and unambiguously to both specialist and non-specialist audiences, through the preparation of written reports, presenting experimental data in the form of diagrams, tables, and graphs, using also English and the necessary computer tools for presentation. They must be capable of working in teams, operating with high degrees of autonomy, and quickly integrating into work environments. Within the possible specializations provided in the study program, the graduate will have the opportunity to acquire specific languages and presentation methods for results. These specifics include describing stages, mechanisms, and conditions of synthesis processes, presenting quality parameters of analytical methods, representing results of multivariate statistical treatments and simulations of atomic-molecular properties. These objectives are achieved through laboratory training activities and the preparation of written and oral presentations for the final exam.
V - Learning Ability
Graduates must have developed the learning ability to effectively update themselves in all fields of chemistry and their applications. They must therefore be able to effectively integrate acquired knowledge by identifying textbooks, reference scientific literature, and other useful materials for deeper exploration. They must finally have the ability to read and learn in English. The development of general learning abilities, integrated with specialized training, must place the graduate in a position to continuously update their knowledge in specialized areas. In particular, they must take into account the continuous technological innovations in organic and inorganic synthesis, the evolution of instrumentation and analytical methods for quality control, and the development or implementation of computer tools for statistical and computational analysis.
The learning ability is monitored during the study program through profit assessments and exam exercises focusing on knowledge to be acquired through independent study.
Work Function.
Work Function:
The content of the Master's Degree course provides the necessary preparation to exercise the profession of chemist independently (self-employment with registration in the Professional Register of Chemists - Section A, following the passing of the State Exam) or to access research bodies, public administrations, professional companies, and consulting firms at national or international levels, companies, industrial and research laboratories, analysis, quality control, and environmental certification workplaces requiring in-depth knowledge in the fields of synthesis and characterization of new products and materials, health, food, and cosmetics.
Among the activities that Master's graduates may carry out, the following are particularly highlighted: promotion and development of scientific and technological innovation, management and design of technologies, and the exercise of high-responsibility functions in the fields of industry, environment, health, cultural heritage, and public administration.
The Master's Degree in Chemical Sciences constitutes a qualification for access to the Research Doctorate program in the area.
Skills Associated with the Function.
Skills Associated with the Function:
The Master's graduate can carry out highly specialized professional activities in the fields of industry, public and private research laboratories, synthesis and characterization of new materials, health, environment, energy, safety, food, and cultural heritage. They are able to work with broad autonomy, assuming responsibility for projects and structures, using the knowledge acquired in the fields of chemical sciences and materials, and applying disciplinary investigation methods independently. Graduates may carry out activities for promoting and developing scientific and technological innovation, managing and designing technologies. The Master's Degree Course allows access to third-level courses, such as Research Doctorates and Master's Programs in chemistry and other related scientific fields or interdisciplinary themes, as well as specialized courses for teaching in secondary schools.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Employment Prospects:
The employment prospects for the Master's graduate are offered by:
- Universities, Research Bodies, Agencies such as ARPA, ANPAT, Ministries, Civil Protection;
- Industrial and applied research centers, industrial production, certification companies, quality control;
- Scientific dissemination agencies.

Program, texts and objectives Official teaching and assessment languages.
ITALIAN Degree awarded.
Master's Degree in SPORT SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY Specific educational objectives.
The specific objective of the Course is to provide Master's graduates with advanced scientific and methodological knowledge in the field of high-level sports activities.
The Course acquires knowledge and skills to enable athletes to achieve optimal performance through advanced training techniques and optimization of the athlete's physiological and technical performance. These objectives are achieved through frontal lessons with a seminar approach and meetings with sector experts, case studies, technical-practical demonstrations on the field, and individual exercises using advanced performance analysis and functional assessment tools; through the compilation of individual bibliographic reviews and the preparation of original works on the disciplines and techniques studied; through internships at qualified institutions for different sports disciplines; finally, through the development of an experimental thesis on a topic related to the study curriculum, using recognized qualitative and quantitative criteria for writing a scientific report.
DESCRIPTION OF THE TRAINING PATH The two-year study path is organized into integrated courses, involving the defining disciplinary sectors as specified in the regulations table. The structure of the integrated courses and sectors allows the definition of two distinct curricula: the first oriented towards training methodology and assessment, the second towards physical preparation and management of motor and sports activities in mountainous areas.
The curriculum in training methodology and assessment is characterized as a systematic and professionalizing in-depth course of the methodological contents of applied research in sports training, where the assessment aspect assumes significant weight: the student thus applies all the knowledge acquired during the three-year path in motor sciences within a theoretical-practical assessment setting: from anatomical-functional and constitutional assessment to the study of limit adaptations; from the acquisition of quantitative modeling-biometric methods to the use of advanced assessment technologies for training and performance, both individual and team; from training programming and periodization to the programming of functional tests for verification and assessment of the athlete, with in-depth studies on endurance, strength, and artistic sports; from the study of nutritional integration needs to the consequences, including regulatory aspects, of doping; from the psychological components of competition to the study of chronic and acute overtraining pathology, up to the practice of BLS; the path finally includes advanced linguistic and computer science content.
The curriculum in physical trainer and expert manager of motor and sports activities in mountainous areas is characterized as a high-level specialized sectoral path, utilizing the natural and unique location of the campus in close proximity to mountain environments and structures. The educational core has a robust methodological foundation, similar to the previously described curriculum, but all professionalizing in-depth studies are thematic regarding mountains: for example, the study of limit adaptations is exemplified through high-altitude adaptations, similarly the analysis of psychological and medical aspects of training focuses on specific high-altitude issues; assessment and programming aspects are further explored in relation to the specificities of mountain sports, each of which is studied in great detail from a methodological and technical perspective.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding The Master's graduate knows the biological, biochemical, and physiological adaptations in high-performance sports, considering gender, age, and constitutional specifics. They also know different environmental conditions, principles of risk assessment and management, factors limiting the practice of various sports disciplines, interactions of pharmacological, therapeutic, or voluntary integrative treatments, including doping practices and related regulations, with sports performance and athlete health.
They know the principles of morphometric, functional assessment, and different motor abilities of athletes at various levels, with specific attention to high-level competition; methods of training programming and periodization; principles of using technological support for training and performance, even in team sports (with particular reference to match analysis); scientific methods underlying training for elite athletes in endurance, strength, artistic, and team sports.
II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding The Master's graduate:
- relates current and future physical condition to the performance model of various sports disciplines, determining personalized training loads based on desired outcomes;
- programs training in relation to the type of sport, competitive period characteristics, athlete level, and the load their organism can withstand, safeguarding health and preventing injuries and overtraining;
- verifies the athlete's condition and progress in relation to the implemented program through the most suitable functional assessment protocols;
- accordingly implements necessary corrections to achieve optimal adaptations;
- monitors current technical-tactical performance through the most advanced technologies for individual and team movement analysis, proposing specific corrections for individual and team training;
- analyzes different sports techniques using supporting technologies to improve technical performance and prevent risk conditions related to practice.
III - Making judgments The Master's graduate:
- is able to assess athletes' physical-metabolic conditions based on qualitative and quantitative instrumental functional assessment, and appropriately directs them to the most suitable disciplines and roles;
- is able to assess performance improvements through quantitative analytical tools, adapting and correcting training programs to achieve set goals;
- suggests the most appropriate psychological strategies for managing training, motivating athletes, and resolving conflicts within groups or teams.
IV - Communication skills The Master's graduate:
- communicates effectively with athletes and team collaborators to promote motivation and performance, both in training and competition;
- fosters interpersonal communication and communicates effectively with media, associations, and society.
- uses computer tools not only for improving performance and organizing training, but also for optimal information communication.
V - Learning ability The Master's graduate:
- applies methods and tools developed for deepening studied content, to be used in professional contexts or for further studies.
- autonomously updates and expands their high-level knowledge, in line with specific application and progress in sports sciences.
- acquires and uses necessary scientific information to evaluate the validity of their professional activities, in accordance with principles of evidence-based good practices.
Professional status conferred by the degree.
The Master's graduate can perform the following professional roles and functions in the indicated occupational areas: Coach and Physical Trainer Functions: - designs, coordinates, and directs technical-sports activities in competitive contexts at all levels, up to the highest competition, at sports associations, sports societies, promotion bodies, institutions, and specialized centers - programs, coordinates, and directs physical preparation activities in various sports and at all levels, up to the professional level, at sports associations, sports societies, promotion bodies, institutions, and specialized centers. - programs, coordinates, and directs physical preparation activities at Armed Forces Training Centers and bodies responsible for ensuring national security and defense. Employment opportunities Public and private structures in competitive sports at all levels, such as: gyms, swimming pools, sports facilities, multi-sport centers, Armed Forces training centers, and structures where sports activities are conducted under the regulations of national sports federations and CONI-recognized promotion bodies.

ITALIAN Specific educational objectives.
The Master's degree course in Psychology - class LM-51 enables the exercise of the profession of Psychologist (pursuant to Articles 1 and 3 of Law 8 November 2021, No. 163).
The Master's degree course in Clinical, Applied Psychology and Interventions aims to train a professional with a solid academic foundation and high levels of practical competence, capable of performing roles with responsibility within the scope of competence defined by current regulations, in clinical and neuropsychological psychological contexts, in settings such as public and private healthcare organizations, organizations, and institutions providing care and assistance to individuals.
The Master's degree in Clinical, Applied Psychology and Interventions also provides the necessary theoretical and methodological knowledge to design and conduct research activities, also in collaboration with other specialists, within the University and healthcare and scientific institutions.
The academic, theoretical, and practical profile of the Master's graduate in Clinical, Applied Psychology and Interventions is also suitable for access to higher levels of university and specialist training.
These educational objectives are achieved through advanced training in the disciplines characteristic of class LM-51 (general psychology, psychobiology and physiological psychology, psychometrics, developmental psychology, clinical and dynamic psychology), complemented by knowledge and skills acquired in related and integrative training activities, developing specialized aspects of some scientific fields not characteristic of class LM-51, but consistent with the proposed objectives.
In particular, the educational objectives are achieved through an advanced path that includes training based on different learning areas. These learning areas aim to acquire in-depth knowledge in the field of clinical and applied psychology in various contexts, in the methodological-statistical field, and in the field of the psychobiological foundations of cognition and behavior.
The learning areas are developed by considering both transversal training across curricula and more specific training for each curriculum. To this end, the learning areas are interpreted differently, assigning different weights to the scientific-disciplinary sectors characterizing the course. The different training paths also differ in the specificity of certain courses related to disciplines of related fields.
Common training will enable graduates to possess:
- knowledge of the main forms of psychopathological suffering and rehabilitation interventions;
- in-depth knowledge of the psychological interview tool and its applications and variations;
- knowledge of the theoretical and methodological foundations of psychotherapeutic approaches;
- knowledge of the main theoretical models of typical and atypical development and their applications;
- knowledge of the methodologies for diagnostic assessment and treatment evaluation;
- in-depth knowledge of cognitive function alterations caused by lesions or focal or diffuse dysfunctions of the central nervous system and their treatments, also in the context of normal and pathological aging.
Additionally, the differentiation of the Study Course into distinct paths (curricula) will allow for the deepening and integration of the professional aspects acquired in the common part, providing more specific knowledge and skills for certain application/occupational areas of the Clinical, Applied Psychology and Interventions graduate. This objective will be achieved both through scientific-disciplinary sectors of the class areas already characterizing the common path but contributing to the specificity of the curriculum, and through areas of the class assigned different weights based on the specific competencies proposed in the curricula. The specialist nature of related and integrative activities may also contribute to the different curricular paths.
In particular, the graduate in Clinical, Applied Psychology and Interventions acquires a solid scientific and professional preparation through training paths that have a more clinical character or are more oriented towards different application areas, including the neuroscientific one.
The more clinical character of the training will be predominantly characterized by cultural and methodological aspects of disciplines in the field of clinical and psychophysiological psychology (applied to the study of mental disorders, addictions, psychosomatics, sexology, deviance), developmental psychology, and group dynamic psychology.
Instead, the applied aspect of the psychobiological-neuroscientific training will be predominantly characterized by cultural and methodological aspects of disciplines in the field of general, physiological, and developmental psychology applied to the study of plasticity, cognitive, emotional, and developmental processes and states of consciousness, reserving adequate space for research methodology and data analysis.
The training path allows for a certain degree of flexibility in course selection among the activities included in the university's training offer, in order to integrate, in accordance with the educational objectives of the Study Course, knowledge of advanced topics and specialized skills.
Furthermore, the training path includes, in Additional Language Knowledge, an English course, at least at B2 level, which ensures that students without these competencies at entry reach an adequate level of understanding of the English language, with particular reference to the specific terminology of psychological sciences, essential for integrating communication skills in the language predominantly used in the international scientific field.
The educational objectives are enriched by the professional training activities of the Practical Assessment Internship (TPV), internal to the Study Course. The TPV consists of contextualized and supervised practical activities, involving direct observation and execution of activities aimed at situated learning and the development of fundamental procedural and relational competencies and skills for the exercise of professional activity. These competencies refer to typical and reserved acts, characteristic of the profession of psychologist, also pursuant to Article 1 of Law 18 February 1989, No. 56, and include the use of knowledge and intervention tools for prevention, diagnosis, rehabilitation, support activities in psychological contexts for individuals, groups, social organizations, and communities, as well as research, experimentation, and teaching activities.
Finally, the educational objectives are completed by the practical activities required for the completion of the Thesis, presented in the final exam. In preparing the Thesis, the graduate can contextualize the training experiences listed in the Study Course and the knowledge and skills acquired, in a laboratory/experimental/application setting or in the construction of an original bibliographic research project.
Frontal lectures, didactic laboratories, consultation of didactic materials, critical analysis and understanding of scientific literature, in-depth through bibliographic research (also independent) of articles and scientific texts with advanced content, open group discussions on topics of the Study Course as integral parts of learning methods, as well as intermediate and final verification tests and preparation/discussion of the Thesis, as verification methods, will contribute to the development/exercise/verification of the ability to learn and deepen, also independently, one's own knowledge, autonomy of judgment, aptitude for teamwork, acquisition of mastery and tools for communication and the ability to present/transfer/disseminate one's knowledge.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding The training path of the Master's degree course in Clinical, Applied Psychology and Interventions is structured in activities that enable graduates to acquire new knowledge, develop their understanding capabilities, and apply such knowledge to various professional contexts.
Graduates in Clinical, Applied Psychology and Interventions will possess in-depth knowledge regarding the psychobiological and functional bases of cognitive and emotional activity, and the mechanisms and processes of normal and pathological cognitive and linguistic development. They will also possess advanced knowledge regarding the genesis and dynamics of alterations and disorders of cognitive, communicative, emotional, and behavioral activity. Master's graduates will also have operational skills aimed at designing, conducting, and evaluating diagnostic, rehabilitative, and psychological support interventions in clinical contexts, as well as promoting psychophysical well-being and health. They will possess skills related to evidence-based psychological and psychotherapeutic intervention methodologies, according to various theoretical approaches. They will also be able to use psychological-clinical assessment tools (interview, systematic observation of behavior, use of tests) applied to the individual and group clinical process. Finally, they will have methodological skills enabling them to critically read, understand, and use the results of psychological and neuroscience research to plan and appropriately carry out clinical and research activities. Such knowledge and understanding capabilities are acquired through the study of advanced content texts, scientific articles/reviews, or didactic materials provided by the instructor, both in the disciplines characteristic of the course (general psychology, psychobiology and physiological psychology, psychometrics, developmental psychology, and educational psychology, clinical and dynamic psychology), and in those falling within the range of related disciplines, differentiated according to the path chosen by the student.
Knowledge acquisition will be guaranteed by specific and differentiated learning methods, based on frontal lectures (also with computer support); didactic laboratory activities with theoretical/practical lessons; seminar-type activities.
Knowledge acquisition will be verified through the final assessment exam for each training activity; the use of intermediate tests provided in some teaching units; the Practical Assessment Internship activity.
II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding Graduates in Clinical, Applied Psychology and Interventions must demonstrate the ability to apply acquired knowledge in designing and conducting person- or group-centered interventions, also in interdisciplinary contexts, for the promotion of health as well as for the prevention, diagnosis, psychological clinical and cognitive support and rehabilitation.
They will be able to take charge of, diagnose, and refer individuals with cognitive alterations due to atypical development, psychiatric disorders, brain injury, or cerebrovascular or degenerative diseases to rehabilitation treatment.
They must be able to work collaboratively with other specialists within multidisciplinary teams, providing a specific contribution to the design and conduct of person- or group-centered interventions. They will also have the ability to use acquired knowledge to critically analyze scientific literature in specific areas of interest, design and carry out research in the fields of clinical psychology, applied psychology, and neuroscience. The ability to translate acquired competencies into practical applications is reinforced through integrated practical activities with characteristic and related courses, allowing students to experiment with the application of psychological and clinical assessment tools; participate in research with tasks involving the administration of tasks and evaluation scales; engage with the main methods and techniques of behavioral and cognitive neuroscience research, and apply their understanding of specific, highly advanced scientific content.
The ability to apply acquired knowledge in the Master's degree is verified both through the approval of practical and/or laboratory activities and, in particular, through the individual work carried out by the student for the preparation of the final exam. Additionally, a particularly important moment at the educational and professional level will be the Practical Assessment Internship.
III - Autonomy of judgment The Psychologist is able to develop complex analyses and formulate independent reflections on topics related to specific areas of in-depth study. They are also able to form independent judgments regarding evaluations of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral functioning.
Autonomy of judgment is fostered by a teaching approach aimed at acquiring the ability to exercise full professional autonomy in any work context, assume responsibility for one's actions, even when working collaboratively in multidisciplinary teams, and evaluate the quality, effectiveness, and efficiency of implemented interventions.
The Psychologist will therefore be able to formulate evaluations based on observational or instrumental data related to individual or group situations, always considering the principles of professional ethics; be able to make choices regarding cognitive and clinical psychological support and rehabilitation interventions, also considering constraints derived from contextual factors (family, school, hospitals, rehabilitation services); possess critical judgment skills in reading and interpreting the relevant scientific literature.
These aspects are given great importance in both theoretical courses and methodological courses, as well as in those with a more pronounced practical and applied component. Courses present different theoretical and methodological approaches to each phenomenon examined, favoring a critical and open attitude oriented towards identifying the most suitable approach and tools for solving complex problems related to research, evaluation, and intervention.
The autonomy of judgment achieved by the student is evaluated in particular through: a) the ability to critically present, during profit exams, different theoretical positions related to specific topics treated, and provide multiple interpretative hypotheses of the phenomena under examination, proposing the most appropriate methodologies for evaluating such hypotheses; b) the level of independence and ability to work individually during the activity assigned for the preparation of the final exam; c) the suitability judgment of the Practical Assessment Internship.
IV - Communication skills The Psychologist must be able to communicate effectively with individuals in psychological distress and their families, always referring to the principles of professional ethics; possess communication skills that enable them to contribute with their competencies to teamwork within multidisciplinary teams; be able to present in written and oral form, effectively and with appropriate language for different interlocutors, their conclusions regarding studies and analyses, clearly explaining their reasoning; be able to communicate the results of their research activity both within the scientific community using discipline-specific terminology and outside through scientific dissemination channels.
These skills are reinforced through practical and applied activities that involve the realization, presentation, and discussion of clinical and psychometric reports or projects carried out individually or in small groups, role-playing, case discussions, reading and discussion of scientific articles, simulations, and the elaboration of a research project. Communication skills and synthesis abilities are evaluated through oral interviews and/or written tests with open questions in profit exams related to different courses, as well as through the presentation and discussion of the thesis.
V - Learning ability The Psychologist will be able to use analysis tools and apply learning methods developed to deepen and update their knowledge by independently following new scientific research acquisitions, using appropriate computer tools, including the use of bibliographic consultation tools. The acquisition of effective and flexible learning abilities will enable the graduate to continue their training and updating autonomously after obtaining the degree, knowing how to retrieve and evaluate different sources and materials useful for continuing education at a specialist level. These abilities can therefore form the basis for pursuing higher-level studies (master's, specialization schools, and doctoral programs).
This objective is achieved through the use and constant reference, within the curricular courses, to the most relevant and updated national and international literature on the topics treated, with the aim of developing the propensity for constant comparison between one's own knowledge and the latest developments in knowledge in various areas of psychology and neuroscience. This propensity is particularly evaluated in the individual work carried out by the student for the preparation of the final exam, through the evaluation of their ability to query databases, access international bibliographies on the proposed topics; illustrate the innovative aspects introduced by scientific research; identify which issues, in different areas of competence, pose further questions for the development of research and in which directions.
Function in work context.
Function in work context:
The acquired knowledge and skills enable the graduate to perform the following functions:
- Collect information and analyze the main forms of psychological distress and/or maladjustment through anamnestic interviews and behavioral data collection.
- Move from diagnostic evaluation to taking charge of the client/user, referring to different therapeutic models.
- Propose and negotiate with the client/user concrete and achievable goals.
- Select and apply tools aimed at assessing indices of psychobiological, behavioral, cognitive, and emotional functioning in consulting contexts.
- Select and apply tools for identifying modes of relationship of the individual with reference groups, with particular attention to the effects produced by such relationships.
- Select and apply tools for evaluating communication and relational skills in different social and environmental contexts.
- Design prevention and health promotion interventions for individuals, groups, or communities using integrated approaches, and analyze their results.
- Use techniques and tools derived from the most recent contributions of clinical and experimental research.
These tasks require synergistic collaboration with other professionals in the mental health field in various application contexts in public and private settings.
Competencies associated with the function.
Competencies associated with the function:
The psychologist possesses:
- advanced and up-to-date knowledge of the main models of normal and pathological psychological functioning, and the relationships between cognition and brain functions;
- the ability to administer and interpret tools for assessing cognitive and emotional functioning;
- the ability to conduct psychological assessment and support interviews, referring to different therapeutic models;
- the ability to administer and interpret the main psychological assessment tools;
- the ability to design prevention and health promotion interventions aimed at individuals, groups, or communities;
- the ability to collaborate with a critical spirit, autonomy of judgment, and recognition of specific professional competence with all other figures involved in psychological well-being interventions;
- the ability to continuously update their knowledge through critical reading of scientific texts, also in English;
- adequate transversal communication-relational, organizational-management, and planning competencies, in accordance with the level of autonomy and responsibility assigned, the organizational and work methods adopted, and the main interlocutors (colleagues, other professionals, and clients/users).
Professional status conferred by the title.
Career opportunities:
Pursuant to Articles 1 and 3 of Law 8 November 2021, No. 163, and in accordance with D.M. No. 654 of 05/07/2022, the final exam for the Master's degree in Clinical, Applied Psychology and Interventions (class LM-51) enables the exercise of the profession of Psychologist.
The graduate in Clinical, Applied Psychology and Interventions can apply the knowledge and skills acquired in the training path in public and private healthcare organizations related to the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of psychological distress (National Health Service, hospitals and clinics, territorial services, counseling centers, therapeutic communities, addiction services, family homes, communities for minors, Prevention Departments, Public Health Services, private third-sector agencies such as cooperatives or volunteer associations), in organizations and institutions providing care, rehabilitation, and assistance to individuals, public and private. Additional career opportunities may be identified in educational and school settings, universities, and other research-oriented institutions. The Psychologist can exercise the profession and related functions also as a self-employed professional and within private consultancy (including expert testimony) and training, with particular reference to evaluation processes in different contexts, identification and design of change strategies.

Program, Texts, and Objectives Official teaching and assessment languages.
ITALIAN Degree awarded.
Master's Degree in DESIGN AND MANAGEMENT OF SOCIAL AND EDUCATIONAL SERVICES AND INTERVENTIONS Specific Educational Objectives.
The selected educational path focuses on the complexity of the interdisciplinary approach, not limiting itself to the usual disciplinary proximity between professional subjects and sociological and pedagogical disciplines, but establishing, from the first year, a comparison on sociological and pedagogical subjects with a deliberately less theoretical approach, on political subjects, more attentive to local governments and intergovernmental relations. The common first-year path includes in-depth study of pedagogical themes through courses enabling the acquisition of educational research methodologies and the exploration of special pedagogy topics, alongside sociological themes complemented by the study of normative tools regulating planning in social and educational sectors. The path is completed through optional courses allowing graduates of the class to alternatively deepen demographic, ethnological, and anthropological themes or acquire the fundamentals of financial management for enterprises.
The course is structured in the second year into two educational curricula: the Specialist Social Assistant (recognized in Section A of the Professional Register of Social Assistants) and the Expert in Social Policy Design.
In addition to the ability to work with users of social services, the professional to be trained must acquire the necessary professional skills to exercise functions of programming, organization, and management of socio-health services, leadership of work groups, and coordination of services and personnel in such services; must acquire the necessary competencies for the specialist use of cognitive strategies, communication, and interpersonal relationships with professional interlocutors and users, as well as develop organizational skills within microsystems, regulation of educational interventions, and management of change. The curricular path also aims to enhance professional competencies in research, monitoring, health, and environmental protection.
For this reason, both curricular paths, despite having different content, require the acquisition of management tools focusing on the programming and evaluation of social services (Specialist Social Assistant Curriculum) and the management of training activities (Expert in Social Policy Design Curriculum), as well as tools for organizing human and economic resources, which presuppose a common foundation deepening the tools for planning and organizing social policies, a necessary prerequisite for social design. Additionally, an in-depth study of certain pedagogical themes is provided to enable graduates to acquire advanced tools for designing inclusion and cooperation.
The skills acquired and developed during the educational path can be applied in the sectors of health, training, family, immigration, and social exclusion. For this reason, graduates of this course must possess advanced knowledge regarding the organization and functioning of social and educational services.
They must also know and be able to refer to the organizational, social, and legislative framework within which intervention plans in the field of services are developed.
To this end, Master's graduates must develop skills for reading the territory, the ability to understand and interpret social phenomena and their evolutionary trends, in order to form the necessary competencies for experimenting with new programs and innovative approaches not only with users of social services and latent need situations, but also in diverse contexts expressing educational needs.
The acquisition of such skills will enable graduates to develop abilities that allow them to enhance and develop the networking of existing and potential resources, following innovative paths already used in other European experiences.
The verification of educational objectives is based on assessment tests, intermediate and/or final, written and/or oral, of the courses and integrated activities comprising the study plan, as well as the final exam.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding Social intervention in general and design in particular presuppose that graduates acquire the ability to know and interpret social phenomena in order to identify needs and consequently plan and design interventions through the networking of existing resources and activation of new resources. This interdisciplinarity characterizes the course, making the knowledge forming its core foundation acquired through courses belonging to sociological, social service, economic, statistical, legal, and psycho-pedagogical disciplines.
The acquisition of such abilities is verified through assessment tests, intermediate and/or final, written and/or oral, of the courses and integrated activities comprising the study plan, as well as the final exam.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding The Master's graduate will acquire methodological, organizational, and legal knowledge regarding the socio-health and educational services system, as well as knowledge of the most important forms of psychological and social distress. Such knowledge will enable them to achieve a high capacity for analyzing and interpreting social phenomena; advanced knowledge of the economic, historical, and political framework in relation to specific areas of sociological and applied educational analysis, reading territorial needs, and designing specific interventions. The ability to apply acquired knowledge is verified through assessment tests, intermediate and/or final, and integrated activities involving the practical application of theoretical knowledge, as well as the final exam, which must include an intervention project for the Specialist Social Assistant track, focusing on the thematic areas of social services under Law No. 328/2000.
III - Independent Judgment The sensitivity of professionals the Master's course aims to train must necessarily be built on a reflective habit regarding the application of professional methodology and that of others. They must be capable of positioning themselves at a higher level of complexity, indispensable for reconstructing and framing professional actions and strategies of colleagues, even in the role of case manager. This ability can only derive from a habit of concrete critical analysis applied to interventions. Capabilities that can be better developed through teaching and integrated teaching activities (seminars, indirect internship activities), within the Master's course, led by professionals with extensive experience in social and educational policy design (including European design), who are able to guide students in acquiring the theoretical-practical tools for identifying needs and elaborating appropriate project solutions.
In particular, the Master's graduate must be able to design and coordinate research in multiple areas of social and educational fields; must be able to analyze and read social problems independently, applying specific research methods or empirically verifying initial hypotheses; coordinate and design socio-health and educational services at the territorial level; design information, awareness, and prevention programs regarding various forms of psychosocial distress; design and plan services for the community based on territorial needs.
The verification of the acquisition of independent judgment occurs through the evaluation of the courses in the student's individual study plan and the evaluation of the degree of independence and ability to work, even in groups, during seminar activities, internships, and preparation for the final exam.
IV - Communication Skills The ability to communicate with very diverse interlocutors, belonging to institutions, the third sector, volunteering, and civil society, is crucial in the methodology of networking and project-based work: these remain key reference points of the course (in both its tracks), also based on its previous tradition. Additionally, communicating the results of impact assessments of interventions to citizens is an important ability necessary for all subjects involved in the design and management of social policies.
Internships, always a crucial point and strength of educational paths, in both tracks provide students the opportunity to engage with social reality, understood not only as the user of social operators but also as the coexistence and collaboration of different subjects (public and private) involved in the design and management of social and educational policies.
The verification of communication skills acquisition occurs through the evaluation of the student's presentation and argumentation abilities within training and seminar activities and the final exam, as well as through the evaluation of reports and documents prepared within the activities that require them.
V - Learning Ability Master's graduates are guided through a learning path where interdisciplinary references around the themes forming the skeleton of the educational path assume a central role.
Learning abilities are acquired throughout the study path, particularly through individual study, preparation of individual projects, internship experience, and activities carried out for the preparation of the final exam and project. The ability to learn is evaluated through continuous verification during training activities, requiring the presentation of autonomously gathered data, through tutoring activities during individual internship and project work, and through the evaluation of the ability to self-learn developed during the final exam activity.
Work Function.
Work Function:
- Specialist Social Assistant: Graduates can exercise functions of organization, management, and consultation for individuals, organizations, and institutions in the field of social policies and services in the following areas: relational dynamics, human resource management, organization of resources and structures, and economic management of entities, services, and organizations, as well as design of social and educational policies. Graduates may also exercise professional activities, even independently, in preventive-promotional, managerial, research, and support areas for inclusion and social cohesion processes.
- Expert in Social Policy Design: Graduates can exercise functions of design, organization, management, and consultation in the field of social and educational policies, from early childhood to adulthood, also referring to disadvantaged population groups.
Competencies Associated with the Function.
Competencies Associated with the Function:
- Specialist Social Assistant: Programming, organization, and management of social services, leadership of work groups, and coordination of services and personnel in such services.
- Expert in Social Policy Design: Design and consultation in the field of social and educational policies.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Employment Prospects:
- Specialist Social Assistant: Graduates can exercise their functions within public and private entities. Graduates may also exercise professional activities, even independently. As this is a regulated profession, the exercise of functions is subject to passing the qualification exam and registration in Register A of the Order of Social Assistants.
- Expert in Social Policy Design: Graduates can exercise their functions within public and private entities. Graduates may also exercise professional activities, even independently.
