Roles Chair PIER GIORGIO MASTROBERARDINO Program, textbooks and objectives Official teaching and assessment languages.
ENGLISH Specific educational objectives.
The educational objective is to provide students with a solid multidisciplinary preparation in neuroscience. To this end, many courses will involve collaboration between teachers with different expertise. Courses will cover areas including Molecular and Cellular Neurobiology, Developmental Neurobiology, Genetics and Neurogenetics, Neurobiochemistry, Neurophysiology, Anatomical Foundations of Neuroscience, Evolutionary Neuroscience, Neuropathology, Neuropharmacology, Neuroimaging. The training path will be completed by a selection of thematic courses taught by neuroscientists from Italian, European, and extra-European universities and professionals from the industry sector. Courses will be taught in English.
The training path requires acquisition of:
- in-depth knowledge of the general morphology of the nervous system and its developmental mechanisms; its connections and functional mechanisms; how it collects, encodes, processes, and integrates various sensory modalities to provide appropriate responses to the environment; how internally encoded information is stabilized, stored, and transformed into experience and self-awareness;
- in-depth knowledge of the biochemical-molecular and cellular processes of neural functions and the neurobiological, biochemical, and genetic bases of nervous system disorders;
- a solid cultural foundation in basic neuroscience and various applied neuroscience fields, along with high scientific and operational preparation in related disciplines;
- in-depth knowledge of methods for inferring the relationship between mind and brain in normal and pathological animal and human models;
- thorough knowledge of instrumental methodology, analytical tools, and techniques for data acquisition and analysis used in the study of excitable cells and the nervous system;
- mastery of the scientific investigation method to operate within neuroscience;
- knowledge and skills in experimental and statistical methodologies necessary to enable graduates to master the scientific investigation method and work with broad autonomy, including assuming project and structural responsibilities.
- ability to fluently use English, both written and oral, with specific reference to disciplinary terminology;
- ability to work with broad autonomy and in groups, including assuming responsibility for managing projects and structures.
To achieve these goals, the Master's Degree in Neurosciences provides:
- lectures and laboratory exercises dedicated to experimental methodologies and data processing;
- laboratory activities in university or non-university scientific structures, national and international;
- acquisition of experimental methodologies useful for understanding functional processes of the nervous system at the biomolecular, cellular, and organismal levels;
- study stays at other Italian and foreign universities, also within international agreements.
Dublin descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding The student acquires advanced knowledge related to neurobiology, cellular neurophysiology, and molecular and developmental neurobiology, enabling them to understand fundamental physiological functions such as communication between excitable cells and plasticity of the nervous system. The student acquires knowledge on the biophysical bases of excitable membrane functioning, ion channels, and receptors. Additionally, they learn the molecular mechanisms governing the main functions of neuronal and glial cells in vertebrates, synaptic transmission at central and peripheral levels, neuronal diversity, functional organization of nerve cells, and activities of neurotrophic molecules. Through the study of major stages of embryonic brain and spinal cord development, the graduate acquires knowledge of cellular mechanisms regulating nervous system formation and creation of complex neural networks.
II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding Each course includes classroom theory hours and laboratory practice hours. Thanks to the knowledge acquired in these subjects, Neuroscience students will be able to apply such knowledge to scientific experimentation on primary and stable cell cultures, cell lines, and nerve and muscle cells. They will be able to apply methods for morphometric analysis of nerve and glial cells and procedures for acquisition, recording, and analysis of electrophysiological signals in cellular preparations and fresh nervous system tissues.
Courses include assessment methods in written, oral, or both formats.
Graduates will also be able to critically read and understand scientific articles from journals in their field. Furthermore, they will be able to write scientific and project texts in English. They will be able to address scientific problems and work autonomously in a laboratory. They will have experience working in groups and thus be able to interact with others to achieve common goals. Graduates will be able to communicate scientific topics both in written and oral form.
III - Judgment autonomy Judgment autonomy will be developed through passing examinations, requiring individual re-elaboration of topics covered in class. This goal will also be achieved through reading, understanding, and re-elaborating scientific articles during classroom activities and invitations to attend expert webinars on neuroscience topics. In particular, students must be able to analyze and solve scientific problems within neuroscience and critically evaluate data from scientific literature. Judgment autonomy is verified through written or oral exams, as required for various courses, where the student's independent work is assessed.
A fundamental aspect is the experimental activity dedicated to the preparation of the thesis, strictly experimental as required by the final exam. This includes important laboratory activity in university or non-university scientific structures, national and international. This activity aims to develop autonomous work and critical judgment skills and to foster teamwork and the ability to organize and plan experimental protocols.
This activity is evaluated within the final exam, where the student must demonstrate having acquired the ability to operate with sufficient autonomy in collecting data and information and organizing them logically.
IV - Communication skills Lectures serve as the primary venue for fostering and developing communication skills, which are also expressed in the discussion of scientific articles, presentation of seminars on specific topics, and public defense of the thesis. Graduates will be able to communicate neurobiological problems, ideas, and solutions in English, both in written and oral form, to specialists and non-specialists. They will be encouraged to dialogue with experts in their and other fields, frequenting laboratories where they complete internships or with researchers invited to give specialized seminars and conferences.
The venue for verifying student achievements is the exams, conducted in written and oral formats, and the defense of the thesis.
V - Learning ability The Master's Degree strongly incentivizes learning ability, aiming for students to independently deepen or update their specific knowledge, address new topics, and learn innovative technologies. Students will be able to read and understand articles from high-quality journals in their field. Finally, learning abilities and the capacity to develop original ideas will be developed during the preparation of the experimental thesis, during which the candidate independently prepares an English manuscript under a faculty supervisor's guidance. The laboratory activity for thesis preparation will allow students to learn an approach to solving new problems within broader contexts than those offered by the degree course, including professional contexts.
Verification of learning abilities occurs in individual exam assessments and during the presentation and discussion of the experimental thesis.
Work context function.
Work context function:
Graduates of this class acquire all typical work context functions of a Master's Biology education.
The professional profile of a Master's graduate in Neurosciences is characterized by the ability to independently carry out basic and applied research activities in neurobiology and neuroscience, both in biochemical and biomolecular fields. Graduates of the class may also assume managerial roles requiring full responsibility for projects, structures, and personnel.
In particular, the Neurosciences graduate designs and manages laboratory experimental protocols in their field of competence involving the use of animal organisms and nerve cell cultures.
Within this context, the Master's graduate:
- designs and implements cellular and animal models to understand molecular mechanisms of Central Nervous System functioning;
- conducts and/or coordinates professional and project activities in research and industry sectors, particularly in neuroscience;
- drafts funding requests to public and private institutions;
- synthesizes results into scientific publications;
- is able to manage or contribute to managing neuroscience laboratories, as well as other laboratories typical of biology training, such as molecular and cellular biology laboratories.
The Master's graduate in Neurosciences also organizes scientific dissemination and technology transfer activities, particularly:
- acting as a communicator addressing the general public to promote scientific culture, especially in neurobiology, and the perception of science's importance in human activities;
- being able to carry out activities promoting and developing scientific and technological innovation in the same fields;
- operating in public and private institutions managing research funding acquisition and technology transfer, possessing multidisciplinary training;
- participating in activities promoting and developing scientific and technological innovation.
Function-associated competencies.
Function-associated competencies:
To perform their functions, Master's graduates in Neurosciences will have acquired the following specific knowledge:
- knowledge of cell biology, histology, anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, and pathology with particular reference to the nervous system;
- knowledge of major investigation methodologies used in neuroscience at cellular, organ, and system levels;
- knowledge of mathematical and statistical tools and computer programs used for data analysis;
- knowledge regarding protocols for developing new drugs and technology transfer;
- use of written and spoken English.
They will therefore possess the competencies necessary to:
- conduct practical experimentation in basic research laboratories as well as applied research laboratories;
- use methodologies and instrumentation for analyzing excitable cells and tissues;
- use specific experimental methodologies and instrumentation for analyzing electrical signals at single-cell, organ, and system levels;
- organize and coordinate research activities in the laboratory;
- propose and plan scientific development lines in their field of competence;
- write, present, and discuss scientific projects and reports in English;
- compete internationally and interact in group activities with colleagues possessing diverse competencies.
Professional status conferred by the degree.
Employment opportunities:
Master's graduates in Neurosciences can access a wide range of occupational and professional fields directly or through further training or qualification levels, particularly:
- at universities and other Public Research Institutes and Entities;
- at Private Research Institutes and Entities;
- at National Health System structures, Hospital Enterprises, public and private specialized laboratories;
- at pharmaceutical, chemical, and biotechnology companies;
- at public and private research and diagnostic centers;
- at structures dealing with scientific communication and dissemination services;
- after passing the state exam, they can register with the Register for the Profession of Biologist Section A and perform activities codified for the professional title of Biologist.
Master's graduates in Neurosciences who wish to assume a research coordination role need to acquire higher levels of responsibility and autonomy through a training path consisting of the third level of education, the Doctorate in Research.

Master's Degree in MATHEMATICAL MODELLING Specific Educational Objectives.
The proposed study program "Mathematical Modelling" (class LM-44) is of an international and interuniversity nature. It stems from the decade-long experience of the Erasmus Mundus Programme "MathMods - Mathematical Modelling in Engineering: Theory, Numerics, Applications". This experience continues in the new Erasmus Mundus Programme "InterMaths - Interdisciplinary Mathematics" for the four-year period 2021-2024. Starting from the Academic Year 2021-2022, the Master's Degree is offered by the Consortium composed of:
- University of L'Aquila
- Vienna University of Technology (Austria)
- University of Hamburg (Germany)
- University of Côte d'Azur (Nice, France)
- Autonomous University of Barcelona (Spain)
- Hamburg University of Technology (Germany)
The proposed study program awards a joint degree. The program duration is the standard 120 credits over two years. The study program is entirely taught in English.
The specific objective of the Master's Degree course "Mathematical Modelling" is to train an engineer particularly skilled in the design, development, and management of models and complex systems, understood both in the context of Engineering (complex control systems) and in the context of mathematical modeling (modeling, numerical simulation, and optimization of complex systems). To this end, students are first provided with in-depth mathematical competencies in areas such as mathematical analysis, numerical analysis, scientific computing, optimization, and control theory. These competencies are predominantly methodological and cover both the fields characteristic of Mathematical, Physical, and Computer Sciences and Engineering Sciences, with the latter primarily in the disciplinary sectors ING-INF/04 Automatic Control and ING-INF/05 Information Processing Systems. Subsequently, students specialize in the use of various methodological approaches aimed at modeling, simulation, and control of complex systems, touching upon other characteristic areas in both fields. These methodological approaches include
- Modeling and simulation of continuous media (fluid dynamics, including computational),
- Agent-based modeling (e.g., aimed at studying emergent behaviors in complex systems or robotics),
- Modeling and control on networks,
- Advanced optimization (understood both as optimization of control systems and in the strict sense of operations research),
with the aim of being able to formulate, analyze, and simulate models and complex systems in various application contexts typical of engineering.
Throughout their study path, students will develop not only a taste for studying and the ability to apply general principles and methods of Mathematics, but also sensitivity to adapt their application to the specific difficulties of the problem to be solved, the desired solution accuracy, even under technological aspects, and the sustainable investment of time and money.
DESCRIPTION OF STUDY PATH The teaching organization is structured as follows.
1) The first semester is held at the University of L'Aquila for all students. It provides common competencies for the various specializations students may pursue, primarily dedicated to advanced theoretical mathematics and, to a lesser extent, to engineering disciplines specific to the automatic control sector.
2) The second semester is held at Vienna (Austria) or Hamburg (Germany) for all students. It aims to unify knowledge of computer, computational, and numerical aspects. It predominantly includes content related to numerical analysis and information processing systems.
3) The second year focuses on extremely advanced fields in the international scientific-technological research world. Each partner institution offers pathways reflecting their own competencies and potential. The offered specializations are consistent with the background acquired during the first year and deepen some of the methodological approaches listed above. Various specializations are proposed, predominantly with applications in engineering. These include advanced control and optimization methods with industrial applications, modeling and simulation of complex systems, simulation of deterministic and stochastic models, both discrete and continuous.
At the end of the study path, students must write a thesis project with the help of their supervisor, which must then be approved by the degree committee. The local coordinator of the host institution during the thesis period is responsible for assigning a supervisor to the student; student proposals will also be accepted. The thesis topic may also address a problem proposed by a private company. In such cases, the company must designate a responsible person who will follow the student's work at the company, especially if the thesis activity takes place at their facilities; however, the local coordinator must also assign an academic supervisor to the student, who will be responsible for the progress, adequacy, and scientific quality of the thesis.
Finally, as an international interuniversity excellence program, individual study plan requests will be jointly reviewed by the three Consortium members to ensure that such plans comply with the regulations of the countries of the institutions awarding the degree, which must be verified by the Consortium itself.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding Regarding mathematical theory and modeling, students will acquire knowledge in the following areas:
- Advanced ordinary differential equations, with particular attention to nonlinear dynamic systems and bifurcation theory;
- Control theory, with particular focus on digital controls and, more generally, applications to automatic engineering;
- Functional analysis and partial differential equations, to prepare for the study of models and complex systems.
Additionally, students will acquire knowledge of the main numerical schemes used in the context of ordinary and partial differential equations.
Finally, students will deepen the above knowledge in methodological and application contexts consistent with their chosen specialization.
The verification of knowledge and understanding is conducted organically within all assessment methods provided during the study program. In particular, knowledge of mathematical theory and modeling in the three areas above is acquired through theoretical lectures and exercises, including in-course written tests and tutoring activities. Verification of these competencies involves written and oral exams. Knowledge of numerical schemes is acquired through lectures and laboratory activities, both group and individual. Learning verification involves written tests and project evaluation.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding The acquired mathematical theory constitutes a fundamental prerequisite for addressing the chosen specialization and opens students to an infinite-dimensional perspective, providing them with a new concept of "approximation" that potentially enables the study of advanced numerical computing, as well as the basic ingredients of calculus of variations. Moreover, control theory is applied and integrated within the context of more complex models, which may include stochastic phenomena or be distributed on networks.
In the context of numerical methods, students acquire sensitivity to adapt the use of learned methods to the specific difficulties of the problem to be solved, the desired solution accuracy, even under technological aspects, and the sustainable investment of time and money.
Students will develop the ability to apply learned methods in various contexts, including computational fluid dynamics, complex automatic control systems, agent-based systems modeling, and stochastic optimization. The methods learned include in particular the derivation, resolution, and simulation of partial differential equations, stochastic models, combinatorial optimization models, automatic control systems (also on networks), agent-based systems, and their emergent behaviors.
At the end of the training period, students will acquire the ability to formulate and manage complex systems and models with many variables, refining resolution methods and their accuracy according to the application context and current needs in the fields mentioned.
Students will also be able to plan a computational strategy for problem resolution, solve it numerically, interpret the results, and utilize them according to the problem's requirements.
The verification of the ability to apply knowledge and understanding is carried out through the exams provided for the study program. In particular, written and oral exams verify that students have understood the modeling techniques applied to the contexts considered according to the chosen study path. Project activities verify that students are able to apply acquired mathematical modeling competencies in solving problems not considered during classroom teaching. A fundamental role in verifying the student's ability to apply modeling and numerical simulation competencies in a concrete context is played by the final exam, which may also be conducted in collaboration with an industrial partner.
III - Judgment Autonomy At the end of the study path, graduates will have acquired a high level of advanced technical knowledge applicable to a wide range of professional contexts. This knowledge is inherently interdisciplinary and versatile. It allows approaching the resolution of concrete problems with a "new perspective" on the problem itself. This aspect commonly manifests in the application of mathematics to recently developed contexts not directly related to engineering applications, such as modeling of "multi-agent" systems, which uses techniques originating from the study of gas kinetics. This example is paradigmatic of the potential impact of a mathematical modeler in an interdisciplinary research team, given their ability to "see" problems abstractly, detached from their application field. Another important aspect characterizing the mathematical modeler is their ability to simplify and "disassemble" a complex problem to understand its deeper nature, even at the cost of temporarily making the model "less realistic."
In conclusion, graduates in "Mathematical Modelling" are characterized by strong independent thinking. At the same time, they contribute with their mathematical creativity to understanding phenomena "behind a problem" and resolving them using highly innovative and original techniques.
The verification of judgment autonomy is carried out through all exams provided for the study program. In particular, the final exam tests the student's ability to contextualize, as efficiently and effectively as possible, the various modeling approaches and numerical techniques learned to a problem never considered during the study program, even originating from an application context different from those considered in the courses attended. In this sense, the student's ability to self-organize in the design and implementation of the three fundamental steps of mathematical modeling in a concrete problem is tested: model formulation, numerical simulation, and result interpretation. The student's ability to simplify the model autonomously, stripping away non-fundamental components for result interpretation, is also tested.
IV - Communication Skills Graduates will have the ability to clearly and logically communicate process and design choices, as well as the underlying scientific orientations, to both mathematical and application-specialized interlocutors. Therefore, graduates will have the ability to manage relationships with the plurality of subjects (mathematicians and/or graduates in applied sciences) involved in the formulation, development, and application of models of interest.
Additionally, due to the strongly international nature of the study program, graduates will also have communication skills towards the international scientific community and different social components, even non-experts, and will be able to coordinate interdisciplinary teams, thanks to the diverse linguistic, cultural, and social knowledge acquired during the study path at various locations.
The verification of communication skills is carried out through all exams that include an oral component, particularly for courses that include individual projects discussed in seminars. In such cases, the student's ability to organize a presentation in a linear, simple, yet effective and comprehensive manner is tested. These aspects are particularly evident during the thesis discussion for degree completion in the final exam. Both public presentations and the final exam test the student's linguistic abilities in English, particularly speaking fluency and the ability to master technical English related to the studied context.
V - Learning Ability The proposed study path is strongly oriented towards research (including applied) and advanced training, so graduates will have acquired awareness of the need for continuous learning, to be pursued autonomously throughout their professional career.
Especially during thesis activities, students develop the ability to autonomously acquire new technical and scientific knowledge related to their interests from scientific and technical literature in the specific field.
In particular, students learn to document themselves on a specific topic through consultation of specialized literature.
The verification of learning abilities is carried out through all exams (written and/or oral) provided in the study path, with particular reference to those involving project activities. The final exam allows testing the student's ability to approach advanced scientific literature, case studies in literature, and innovative methods and models that may assist in implementing their thesis project.
Professional Role.
Professional Role:
Formulation and study (analytical and numerical) of mathematical models in applied sciences, with particular attention to the fields of optimization (including stochastic), fluid dynamics (including computational), and continuum mechanics, complex systems.
The professional role involves:
- Formalizing in mathematical terms problems of applied sciences (particularly in the fields mentioned) in collaboration with experts in research and development and production optimization;
- Developing and analyzing, also through numerical simulations, the corresponding mathematical models.
Graduates typically acquire additional competencies through post-graduate courses/research doctorates in mathematics and/or applied sciences.
Competencies Associated with the Role.
Competencies Associated with the Role:
- In-depth knowledge of mathematics and other basic sciences, as well as theoretical-scientific-modeling aspects of applied sciences
- Advanced competencies to address experimental, computational, and technological problems related to the formulation, validation, and use of mathematical models, particularly in the fields mentioned.
Degree Awarded.
Career Opportunities:
- Companies engaged in both consulting and research and development activities;
- Companies or public bodies managing services;
- Manufacturing companies producing and integrating complex systems;
- Research institutes and laboratories in the fields of mathematics and applied sciences.

ENGLISH Degree awarded.
Master's Degree in MATHEMATICS Specific educational objectives.
The study program aims to provide in-depth training in Mathematics while also offering students the opportunity to acquire applied and interdisciplinary preparation. It is structured over two-year pathways totaling 120 credits.
The first year is dedicated to deepening advanced mathematical topics and learning mathematical techniques applied to the study of various mathematical, physical, financial, biological, etc. problems.
In the second year, students can, through the selection of specific courses, direct their training towards theoretical or applied approaches in the aforementioned fields, facilitating easier entry into the job market through the specific skills acquired.
The study program falls under the category of international master's degrees, as the teaching language is English and there are various academic cooperation agreements with foreign institutions for the simultaneous award of the degree upon completion of the training path.
Details of the training pathways related to such agreements are approved annually and constitute an addendum to the didactic regulations of the relevant cohort.
Specifically, two pathways are provided:
1. PURE AND APPLIED MATHEMATICS (Applied General)
2. APPLIED AND INTERDISCIPLINARY MATHEMATICS (Applied Mathematics and Interdisciplinary)
The list of training activities provided in each pathway is indicated in the attached document. However, all training pathways are organized to acquire:
- all fundamental techniques in analysis, geometry, algebra, numerical analysis, and probability;
- in-depth knowledge of mathematical modeling;
- specific mathematical techniques and modeling approaches.
Achieving these objectives is designed to enable the Master's graduate in Mathematics to either pursue doctoral studies or enter the job market, with particular attention to teaching and sectors that heavily utilize quantitative methods, such as financial and insurance institutions, economic and statistical research bodies, information technology and communications companies.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding Master's graduates must have excellent understanding of mathematical techniques and good ability to apply them in modeling physical, biological, financial phenomena, etc.
They must have excellent inductive and deductive reasoning abilities.
More specifically, the training pathway is structured to acquire Knowledge:
- excellent knowledge and understanding of mathematical techniques in theoretical fields to be acquired in mandatory courses in Algebra, Mathematical Analysis, Geometry during the first year;
- in-depth knowledge of mathematical modeling: mechanics, analytical mechanics, classical mathematical models of physics to be acquired in Mathematical Physics and Physics courses;
- specific mathematical techniques and modeling approaches to be acquired in Probability and Mathematical Physics courses;
- knowledge of scientific computing techniques, to be acquired in Numerical Analysis course;
- advanced knowledge of models and demonstration and calculation techniques in specific areas, both theoretical and applied, through optional courses in the aforementioned areas, ranging from more theoretical fields to financial, engineering, and management contexts, according to student choice;
- knowledge of teaching techniques and mathematics learning processes.
Skills:
- ability to understand and master complex mathematical structures;
- ability to apply, develop, and conceive advanced calculation techniques;
- ability to abstract and rigorously deduce consequences from hypotheses;
- ability to translate real-world problems into mathematical models;
- ability to solve complex problems through equation solving and optimization techniques;
- ability to clearly and explicitly communicate results and reasoning to both specialists and non-specialists, in written and oral form;
- ability to formalize laws governing phenomena dynamics through interdisciplinary collaboration;
- ability to transfer mathematical knowledge to others.
Learning methods: Dedicated courses (characterizing and related).
Assessment methods: Individual exams with written and oral final exam, possible intermediate assessments for partial evaluation or feedback.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding Master's graduates must be able to apply their knowledge and understanding in a professional manner, possessing solid skills to design and support arguments and solve problems in their field of study.
They must be able to identify all essential elements of a problem and model it mathematically. They must also be able to understand, use, and design appropriate analytical and numerical methods for the topics addressed.
More specifically, they must acquire Specific Skills:
- Ability to solve complex problems logically and rigorously.
- Ability to calculate using advanced theoretical and practical mathematical tools.
- Ability to deduce decision-making strategies based on proposed and studied models.
- Ability and flexibility to apply these reasoning tools in any cognitive area.
- Ability to critically and rigorously analyze a decision-making problem.
- Ability to produce original rigorous proofs.
Learning methods: Courses with axiomatic treatments. Extensive practice of numerical exercises and calculation activities.
Assessment methods: All written assessments require application of knowledge to problems not previously addressed.
III - Judgment Autonomy Master's graduates must be able to critically analyze a proof and produce a standard one when necessary. They must also be able to conduct independent bibliographic research using mathematical content books, developing familiarity with sector scientific journals. Finally, they must be able to use available electronic archives for scientific research on the WEB, performing necessary information selection.
Learning methods: These abilities result from exercise activities.
Assessment methods: Intermediate and exam assessments require independent solution of theoretical and computational mathematical problems. A good degree of independence is also required in the elaboration and writing of the thesis.
IV - Communication Skills Master's graduates must be able to present their research or the results of a bibliographic research to both specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Learning methods: Training activities through group work and preparation of reports or essays. Preparation of written and oral presentation of the final exam.
Assessment methods: Evaluation of presentation ability during oral exam assessments. Thesis presentation.
V - Learning Ability Master's graduates must have understood the nature and methods of mathematical research and how it applies to many fields. They must also be able to construct complex proofs and modify standard proofs to adapt to new situations while studying scientific topics. Understanding the limits of their own knowledge and ability to identify textbooks and other useful materials for deepening.
Learning methods: Students are guided in improving study methods from the first year by professors and tutors. English, beyond being a requirement for intermediate level access, is refined through progressive use in training phases.
Assessment methods: Incorrect study methods prevent tackling the study program. Evaluation of learning of topics proposed for independent study.
Job context function.
Job context function:
High-responsibility functions in the construction and analysis of mathematical models of various natures and in the design and analysis of methods for their solution in various application areas, specifically in the fields of:
1. environment and meteorology;
2. banks, insurance, and finance;
3. publishing and scientific communication; logistics and transportation;
4. biomedical and healthcare; and any field requiring the use of mathematical models.
5. sectors of Mathematics and Science Communication.
6. teaching.
7. original research in Mathematics.
Associated job function skills.
Associated job function skills:
Flexible mindset, in-depth computational and computer skills, good familiarity with managing, analyzing, and processing numerical data, and ability to create, analyze, and manage mathematical models.
Ability to quickly integrate into diverse work environments and creatively learn and design new professional techniques.
Ability to communicate problems, ideas, and solutions regarding advanced Mathematics fields, both their own and others', to a specialized or general audience, in their language and in English, in both written and oral form.
Ability to produce rigorous proofs of mathematical results, even unrelated to known results.
Ability to theoretically solve complex problems in specialized Mathematics fields and construct and analyze appropriate explicit solution methods.
Professional status conferred by the degree.
Employment opportunities:
Companies and firms in applied, scientific, industrial, business, service, and public administration sectors.
Collaboration (continuous, contract, or freelance) with publishing houses, newspapers, journals, radio, television, websites, and generally multimedia communication and information companies.
Master's graduates possessing the credits required by current regulations may participate in entrance exams for teacher training programs for secondary schools of the first and second degree.
Entry into research through continuation of studies in Doctoral Programs in Mathematics or other scientific disciplines.

Program, texts, and objectives Official teaching and assessment languages.
ITALIAN
Degree awarded.
Master's Degree in LANGUAGES AND CULTURES FOR COMMUNICATION AND INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
Specific educational objectives.
The Master's Degree course in Languages and Cultures for Communication and International Cooperation offers students a solid foundation in two foreign languages (European and American), up to the C1 level according to the Common European Framework of Reference. Language courses are characterized by combining the objective of foreign language communication (oral and written) with the refinement of metalinguistic reflection, also considering sectoral languages and their specific terminology, to provide students with analytical tools for communication practices in professional contexts. Within language courses, translation courses are included that strengthen theoretical and practical skills in translating a wide variety of texts. Linguistic competence is complemented by good skills and understanding of the cultural and literary context of the studied languages. Additionally, the training path provides a basic preparation in the thematic areas of social sciences (history, geography, sociology), useful for professions in various sectors in national and supranational contexts. Classroom activities are integrated with seminar work, including external expert interventions (during teaching laboratories), from companies, European institutions, and language service companies, to bring students closer to the operational reality of different sectors. Particular attention is also given to enhancing skills and content aimed at research.

In the study plan, ECTS are allocated to the following sectors: L-LIN/04, L-LIN/07, L-LIN/12, L-LIN/14, L-FIL-LET/12, L-LIN/01, M-FIL/05, M-DEA/01, M-GGR/01, M-STO/04, SPS/07 L-LIN/03, L-LIN/10, L-LIN/11, L-LIN/05, L-LIN/13, L-FIL-LET/15, L-FIL-LET/09, L-FIL-LET/14, L-LIN/02. For the thesis, 30 ECTS are allocated, 6 ECTS for other activities.

The Course structures its training path through three core learning areas, to which a fourth area of applying acquired skills is added. The different areas combine the development of: 1 - [linguistic area] advanced practical, theoretical, and methodological skills in two modern foreign languages chosen by the student from French, English, Spanish, and German (12 ECTS each), complemented by 12 ECTS in Semiotic, Linguistic, and Computer Science disciplines. 2 - [economic-legal, social, and communication area] ability to critically understand issues related to professions connected to exchanges and international cooperation in the context of globalization; theoretical and methodological knowledge in sociology and communication within cultural and artistic contexts. (12 ECTS). 3 - [philological-literary area] in-depth knowledge related to the culture and civilization of the countries of the studied languages (12 ECTS). 4 - [area of applying acquired skills] skills in the context of didactic-training experiences (internships and other knowledge useful for entering the job market), aimed at expanding and reinforcing mastery of the aforementioned abilities, also with the aim of better employment prospects.

Dublin descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding At the end of the training path, students must have acquired advanced linguistic and metalinguistic knowledge and skills (C1 level of the Common European Framework of Reference) related to the two curricular languages studied, and be able to master the techniques of analysis and description of the different linguistic systems of the two studied languages. Advanced communication skills and analytical and relational abilities in two foreign languages and Italian enable effective interaction with a general audience as well as in public and private professional contexts. Graduates have acquired knowledge of the processes governing the planning and transmission of specialized discourse and have become familiar with textual conventions and communication dynamics governing the production of written and oral specialized texts. Specifically, graduates must demonstrate: - Rigorous and solid acquisition of knowledge and skills in general linguistics, and in linguistic and translation studies of languages A and B. - In-depth knowledge of the literary, historical (contemporary), and geographical culture of the areas where the studied languages are spoken. - Rigorous knowledge of the culture and institutions of the countries where the studied languages are spoken. The achievement of the C1 level in the two languages is verified concurrently with the first-year language exam. Learning outcomes, even for other disciplines, are verified not only through exams but also through constant interaction and dialogue with students during lectures, office hours, through the administration of partial tests, and the preparation of essays and reports by individuals and groups during the course.

II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding Upon completion of studies, graduates in Languages and Cultures for Communication and International Cooperation, thanks to the acquired linguistic, metalinguistic, and discourse knowledge, will be able to manage multicultural work realities in Italy and abroad and operate in communication and promotion for public and private companies and cultural institutions. Using a variety of communication channels, graduates will be able to analyze and optimize the processes governing interaction in specialized contexts, as well as produce, rework, summarize, and translate texts used in various professional practices. The ability to understand and apply the knowledge expected by the training path is achieved through: - participation in advanced lectures, linguistic exercises, and seminar activities; - participation in high-level scientific conferences and seminars held by national and international experts, possibly followed by a report prepared by students; - collective interactions during course delivery; - individual in-depth studies during professor office hours; - e-learning assisted teaching through a self-learning and self-assessment platform; - guided and individual personal study. The acquisition of these competencies is verified through: - final and ongoing written and/or oral exams and assessments; - production of individual and group essays, short papers, and reports; - final exam.

III - Judgment autonomy In-depth study of foreign languages, literatures, and cultures provides students with linguistic, philological, historical, and cultural tools that enable them to make hypotheses, recognize logical connections, argue, compare, and evaluate different interpretations and draw appropriate conclusions. In particular, with reference to their field of study, they are expected to become: a) capable of collecting, using, and interpreting data in the field of foreign languages and cultural and textual traditions, from both theoretical and applied perspectives, developing personal perspectives and reading keys capable of theoretically assessing the problematic nature of concrete situations (e.g., in the fields of teaching, cooperation, integration). Judgment autonomy develops in substantial seminar activities where students elaborate, document, and present their critical thinking, discussing it with peers and professors. Additionally, the deliberately convergent nature of linguistic and cultural disciplines promotes information transfer and thinking modes favorable to critical and creative activities across various disciplines. The study path also finds its most extensive and articulated expression in the final thesis, which aims to develop cross-disciplinary critical reflection skills in research, data collection, organization, and creative criticism of information. Verification of the acquisition of these competencies is carried out through final and ongoing written and/or oral exams, production of individual and group essays, short papers, and reports, and the final exam.

IV - Communication skills At the end of the training path, continuous written and oral practice in foreign languages, aiming for high levels of competence through reading, analysis, and translation practice, writing, and oral presentation, ensures graduates in Languages and Cultures for Communication and International Cooperation the competence and self-confidence in arguing and presenting scientific and cultural topics, both orally and in writing, with clarity in exposition, synthesis ability, and coherence in argumentation. The opportunity offered to students to spend periods at European and extra-European universities, through the extensive exchange network activated at the University, contributes to the development of solid communication skills. The convergence, outcome, and verification of these communication skills, in addition to final exams and the short papers prepared during the two years of study, is also the final thesis, in its requirements for exposition, speech organization, and argumentative and persuasive effectiveness.

V - Learning ability It is expected that, thanks to the knowledge acquired during lectures and exercises in the disciplines studied and generally during all moments of their training activities, students will enhance their learning abilities, especially developing: - metacognitive strategies (reflection on language and its learning process); - cognitive strategies (exploration of different learning styles and strategies, and recognition of individual needs); - communication and social-emotional strategies (through practice of the highest competencies achieved in L2). Additionally, self-learning activities that accompany traditional lectures aim to activate in students awareness of their own learning responsibility, encourage them to manage study planning, obtain in-depth materials, and become familiar with autonomous sources of documentation and training (Life Long Learning). All this allows students to acquire awareness of foreign language teaching/learning methods, making them capable of continuing to refine their linguistic competence in the future. In literature and culture courses, students are introduced to the use of critical and analytical tools necessary to define their learning path in future academic and professional contexts. Verification of the acquisition of these competencies includes: - final and ongoing written and/or oral exams and assessments; - production of individual and group essays, short papers, and reports; - final exam.

Work context function.
Work context function:
TRANSLATOR AND INTERPRETER Translators perform translation activities of written and oral texts in the contexts of productive and commercial activities, public institutions, and editorial contexts related to all media. Interpreters perform interpretation activities during conferences, negotiations, talks, interviews, interrogations, or judicial proceedings, ensuring that the correct meaning and spirit of the original speech are conveyed.

LINGUISTIC EXPERT Following a brief period of support and training in the specific context, graduates are able to collaborate on cooperation projects by applying the acquired linguistic and intercultural skills, enabling them to work in various contexts such as tourism, territorial development, trade, or find employment at cultural institutions, publishing houses, companies with continuous relations with foreign countries, multinational companies with offices in European and extra-European countries, public or private entities, volunteer organizations, and institutions operating in the fields of linguistic and cultural mediation, international cooperation, and development aid.

RESPONSIBLE FOR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS IN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ENTITIES AND COMPANIES Following a brief period of support and training in the specific context, graduates are able to collaborate on cooperation projects by applying the acquired linguistic and intercultural skills, enabling them to perform high-responsibility work in international relations within companies, public administration, European institutions, volunteer structures, local authorities, and entities promoting and valorizing the territory. The study path aims to build professional figures who interact with companies and international organizations in intercultural situations: linguistic and cultural mediators (communication area) in Italian and foreign companies, public administration, local authorities; leadership, responsibility, or consulting roles in international organizations and international cooperation projects.

TEXT REVISER Following a brief period of support and training in the specific context, graduates are able to work in the fields of publishing, information, communication, and entertainment. The main functions are related to the conception and/or supervision of editorial projects, coordinating the various phases of implementation; organization and control of translation services, editing of literary, technical-scientific, essay, or journalistic texts written in the two studied foreign languages and Italian; verification, based on their linguistic and metalinguistic skills, of the accuracy of lexical and linguistic choices in a broad sense for the various identified text genres.

Associated competencies.
Associated competencies:
TRANSLATOR AND INTERPRETER High-level translators are able to translate texts from one language to another, ensuring that the correct meaning of the original text is maintained, that the meaning of literary, scientific, technical-operational, and institutional texts is correctly rendered, and that the phraseology, terminology, spirit, and style of written and oral texts are transmitted to ensure comprehension and communicative effectiveness in the target language. They possess specialized linguistic preparation (in both the source and target language), based on a very extensive vocabulary and a good knowledge of foreign culture and traditions, complemented by specific skills in lexicons, phraseology, disciplines, and contexts as required. In the case of literary translators, in-depth knowledge of the culture and traditions of the languages involved in the translation process is required, specific skills in literature extending from individual authors to literary genres, as well as the current state of theoretical-critical studies on the same. In the role of interpreter, strong communication skills, adaptability, and flexibility in response to circumstances are required. These qualities are complemented by necessary knowledge of customs, cultural traditions, social and linguistic practices essential for correctly interpreting communication situations and ensuring successful interaction between the involved parties.

LINGUISTIC EXPERT - excellent mastery of at least two foreign languages among the four offered by the degree course (English, French, Spanish, German), enabling effective communication in multicultural and multilingual contexts, both written and oral; - interdisciplinary literary, historical, and geographical competencies related to the linguistic areas studied; - analytical skills and judgment autonomy that allow addressing complex issues in the communication field.

RESPONSIBLE FOR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS IN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ENTITIES AND COMPANIES Graduates of the Master's program possess high-level knowledge of two foreign languages and their use in the workplace for communication in intercultural situations, a cultural education and critical abilities that enable them to analyze and solve complex problems related to linguistic mediation in various professional fields.

TEXT REVISER In addition to excellent mastery of at least two foreign languages and Italian, the multilingual editor and reviser possesses excellent linguistic and metalinguistic skills, abilities related to managing communication activities with non-native Italian speakers, analytical skills, objectivity, and judgment autonomy, a solid general culture, and specific expertise in their field.

Graduates with sufficient credits in appropriate sector groups may, as per current legislation, participate in admission tests for secondary teaching training programs.

They can perform professional activities as experts and trainers at entities and institutions in the field of economic, social, and cultural integration; specialized consulting for public entities regarding the protection of languages used in migrant communities on the territory and, more generally, in relation to EU linguistic legislation, and regarding the valorization and promotion of the territory. They can finally continue their university studies by accessing research doctorates and second-level master's programs.

TEXT REVISER The text reviser performs editing and cross-checking activities at publishing houses and online journals, translation agencies, and reviser roles at the European Union.

ITALIAN Degree awarded.
Master's Degree in ENGINEERING FOR THE ENVIRONMENT AND TERRITORY Specific educational objectives.
The Master's Degree in Engineering for the Environment and Territory aims to train technicians with high-level university education, possessing skills related to pollution aspects of air, water, and soil matrices, with particular attention to identifying pollution sources and transport processes, and technologies aimed at preserving public health. It therefore seeks to build upon the foundational and engineering prerequisites required for admission to the course, providing a broad engineering education, with particular reference to civil engineering, and professional competence for solving complex engineering problems, such as:
- assessing the environmental sustainability of anthropogenic activities and the changes they may produce on the territory;
- managing water resources and optimizing their use;
- characterizing, remediating, and cleaning up polluted sites where active or abandoned production settlements have caused soil pollution;
- characterizing and restoring hydrogeological instability situations;
- promoting sustainable development through the rational use of environmental resources and their optimized utilization for final purposes.
The training offered provides a unified view of environmental problems, enabling Master's graduates, alongside specific professional skills, to understand the interdisciplinary nature of environmental issues, with attention also to the theoretical foundations of the fundamental principles of administrative and environmental law.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding At the end of the educational process, the student will have acquired in-depth knowledge and a clear understanding of the methodological and design foundations of Environmental and Territorial Engineering.
Master's graduates in Engineering for the Environment and Territory will have knowledge and understanding that extend and reinforce those of the basic sciences acquired in the first-level education, enabling them to develop original ideas and address complex engineering problems even in a research context.
The methodological training and necessary information for the student to acquire the above knowledge are distributed in a coordinated and progressive manner within the courses and other educational activities proposed by the study program.
The assessment of knowledge and understanding is conducted in an integrated manner within all the profit assessments provided during the study program (exams, written and oral, where both theoretical preparation and project development capabilities will be evaluated).
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding During the educational process, the student will acquire:
- the ability to apply their knowledge and understanding to identify, formulate, and solve engineering problems using established methods;
- the ability to apply their knowledge and understanding to analyze engineering products, processes, and methods;
- the ability to choose and apply appropriate analytical and modeling methods.
These abilities are acquired through exercises, typically monographic and project-based, which also stimulate the ability to interact in groups with other students, and through laboratory activities.
The assessment of the ability to apply knowledge and understanding is carried out through written and/or oral exams as part of the profit assessments, particularly through project-based exam exercises, and for other educational activities, through the final thesis.
III - Judgment Autonomy Master's graduates must possess, at the end of the study program, personal judgment autonomy regarding decisions to be made in the implementation phases of environmental engineering works. They will therefore be able to make autonomous decision-making responsibilities and actively participate in the design process in interdisciplinary contexts. Advanced critical reasoning skills will also be developed through progressive involvement in research activities, through the analysis and interpretation of experimental data, theoretical results, and models.
The evaluation of the achieved judgment autonomy will be conducted progressively through profit exams, project applications, and the preparation and discussion of the final thesis.
IV - Communication Skills At the end of the educational process, the student will have developed:
- the ability to clearly and logically communicate process and design choices, as well as the underlying scientific approaches, to both specialist and non-specialist interlocutors;
- the ability to manage relationships with a variety of stakeholders, specialists and non-specialists, involved in the development of systems of interest to Environmental and Territorial Engineering;
- communication skills both towards the scientific community (national and international) and towards different social components, even non-experts;
- both the ability to work independently and the ability to work as a member of a group with diverse competencies, depending on the project development needs;
- the ability to coordinate a group, even with an interdisciplinary character;
- knowledge of technical regulations;
- linguistic and IT skills enabling international openness;
- knowledge of the non-technical implications of professional practice.
These abilities are developed through regular educational activities and through various discussion and comparison moments in group work and various occasions of meeting with representatives of the business world (conferences, guided visits, etc.).
The assessment of communication skills is carried out through written and/or oral exams as part of the profit assessments and other educational activities, particularly through the final exam.
V - Learning Ability At the end of the educational process, the student will have acquired:
- awareness of the need for continuous learning, to be pursued autonomously throughout their working career;
- the ability to autonomously acquire new technical and scientific knowledge related to the course topics, starting from scientific and technical literature in the specific field and in the entire Environmental and Territorial Engineering.
These abilities develop primarily through individual study of the topics covered in lectures and exercises. The preparation of the thesis also typically involves consulting technical and scientific literature in the field.
The assessment of learning abilities is carried out through written and/or oral exams as part of the profit assessments and other educational activities, particularly through the final exam.
Workplace Function.
Workplace Function:
- assessing anthropogenic pressure in relation to the changes it can produce on the territory, aimed at protecting the territory itself and studying hydrogeological instability;
- rationally managing water resources as a non-inexhaustible asset throughout the entire cycle of processes and transformations related to water (water cycle);
- characterizing, remediating, and cleaning up polluted sites where intensified production activities have significantly disrupted biological balances in the territory;
- promoting sustainable development through the rational use of environmental resources and their optimized utilization for final purposes.
Associated Competencies.
Associated Competencies:
Innovation and development of production, advanced design, planning and programming, management of complex systems, both in free profession, manufacturing or service companies, and public administrations.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Employment Opportunities:
Employment in companies, public and private entities, and professional offices for the design, planning, implementation, and management of works and monitoring systems for the environment and territory, soil defense, waste management, raw materials and environmental, geological, and energy resources management, and environmental impact and compatibility assessment of plans and works.

ITALIAN, ENGLISH Degree Awarded.
Master's Degree in MECHANICAL ENGINEERING
Specific Educational Objectives.
The Master's Degree in Mechanical Engineering aims to train technicians with high-level university preparation, possessing skills to execute and manage complex activities related to the design and development of scientific and technological innovation, and the promotion of research with industrial purposes. It seeks to build upon the foundational engineering preparation required for admission to the program, providing a broad and advanced engineering education with particular reference to mechanical engineering, and professional competence focused on: solving complex engineering problems, designing advanced components, machines, energy systems, technologies, structures, and mechanical systems, designing and managing complex industrial production activities and their processes. Acquired knowledge must also be adaptable to evolving scenarios of methods, techniques, tools, and technologies.
The Master's Degree in Mechanical Engineering offers five curricula (Biomedical, Energy, Mechatronics, Design, and Vehicles) within which disciplinary content related to the core areas of Mechanical Engineering is addressed with varying emphasis.
- The Biomedical Curriculum provides a solid foundational education in Mechanical Engineering, oriented towards the analysis, modeling, design, and development of devices, equipment, systems, and procedures supporting medical imaging diagnostics; robotic systems for medical and industrial applications; prostheses, artificial organs, and devices supporting vital functions. It also imparts in-depth knowledge of thermofluid dynamics applied to the analysis and modeling of complex biological systems.
- The Energy Curriculum provides a solid foundational education in Mechanical Engineering aimed at imparting knowledge on heat transfer, thermodynamics, and fluid dynamics applied to machines and energy conversion systems. It also imparts knowledge on energy-related issues concerning power transmission. The educational objective is also oriented towards understanding combustion problems, dynamic models, control, environmental impact, and modern energy technologies from a sustainability perspective.
- The Mechatronics Curriculum provides a solid foundational education in Mechanical Engineering aimed at imparting knowledge related to the analysis and development of complex mechanical systems, such as robotic devices, automatic systems, and mechatronic systems in general. It also imparts knowledge on automation systems, electronics, and control of mechanical devices.
- The Design Curriculum provides a solid foundational education in Mechanical Engineering aimed at imparting knowledge on processes related to product development, process technologies, machines, and complex mechanical systems. It also imparts knowledge related to the analysis, conceptual development, functional and concrete design of complex mechanical groups and systems, including robotic devices and automatic systems. Additionally, it imparts in-depth knowledge of concurrent design methodologies and processes, considering known or to be identified requirements.
- The Vehicles Curriculum provides a solid foundational education in Mechanical Engineering aimed at imparting knowledge on the design and development of vehicles with specific reference to dynamic and fluid dynamic modeling, management of technological processes, and modern technologies. It also imparts knowledge related to propulsion systems with specific reference to the sustainable mobility sector.
The overarching educational objective across all curricula is to understand the methodologies and processes of non-routine design and development of innovative products, conducted under conditions of uncertainty, to address current and future complex challenges in Mechanical Engineering.
Upon completion of the educational process, regardless of the chosen curriculum, the student will have acquired:
- A deep understanding and clear comprehension of the methodological and design foundations of Mechanical Engineering;
- Knowledge and understanding of the most rigorous methodologies for the advanced design of components, machines, energy systems, technologies, structures, and mechanical systems, as well as for the design and management of complex industrial production activities and their processes and plants;
- Critical knowledge of the latest developments in modern technologies.
The final thesis, which is experimental, modeling, or design-oriented, constitutes an integral part of the preparation and is often accompanied by apprenticeship internships at national and international institutions, companies, and universities.
The shared educational objective across different curricula is ensured by common courses for all training paths and dedicated courses, but related to the same core disciplinary areas of the class. In this way, disciplinary content is combined with the specific industrial context to which the curriculum refers.
The educational path for obtaining the Master's Degree in Mechanical Engineering therefore involves balanced training activities distributed across disciplines related to completing the specific preparation in the core areas of Mechanical Engineering and integrating with related cultural areas. The disciplines covered focus on typical areas of Mechanical Engineering: machine construction, applied mechanics, machines, methods for industrial design, mechanical technologies, thermal measurements, and testing. These activities are complemented by the study of other transversal disciplines, such as fluid dynamics, control systems, electronics, drives, and electrical systems.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding Upon completion of the educational process, the student will have acquired:
- A deep understanding and clear comprehension of the methodological and design foundations of Mechanical Engineering;
- Knowledge and understanding of the most rigorous methodologies for the advanced design of components, machines, energy systems, technologies, structures, and mechanical systems, as well as for the design and management of complex industrial production activities and their processes and plants;
- Critical knowledge of the latest developments in modern technologies in the fields of mechanical design, energy, automation, biomedical, vehicles, integration of mechanical systems with electronic and information systems, and industrial production.
The methodological training and necessary information to enable the student to acquire the above knowledge are distributed in a coordinated and progressive manner within the courses and other training activities proposed by the study program. Verification of knowledge and understanding is conducted in an integrated manner within all profit assessments provided during the study program.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding Upon completion of the educational process, the student will have acquired:

- Critical knowledge of the latest developments in modern technologies in the fields of mechanical design, energy, automation, biomedical, vehicles, integration of mechanical systems with electronic and information systems, and industrial production.
The methodological training and necessary information to enable the student to acquire the above knowledge are distributed in a coordinated and progressive manner within the courses and other training activities proposed by the study program. Verification of knowledge and understanding is conducted in an integrated manner within all profit assessments provided during the study program.
III - Judgment Skills Upon completion of the educational process, the student will have acquired the ability to manage the complexity typical of Mechanical Engineering problems from the ideation and development phase through to the integration of all design and concrete realization activities of the product and processes. They will also have acquired the ability to independently manage complex systems and processes, assuming responsibility for them. They must therefore be able to formulate critical judgments and evaluations based on limited or incomplete information, taking into account the increasingly stringent issues of reliability, safety, environmental protection, and ethics related to the responsibility of using technologies and plants.
Specific skills must be developed in the field of design: ability to use knowledge to design solutions for complex, often unknown or interdisciplinary problems; creative ability for developing innovative and original approaches; ability to interact with social and cultural processes; ability to operate under conditions of uncertainty. In cases of lack of specific information about the system under study, graduates must also have the ability to conduct experimentation and simulation under conditions as close as possible to real operation of machines, technological processes, and plants under analysis.
Achieving this objective is particularly delegated to the preparation and writing of the final thesis, which must be the result of personal re-elaboration of the curricular content acquired.
Verification of judgment skills is carried out through written and/or oral exams provided for profit assessments, particularly through exam exercises for disciplines involving design activities, and for other training activities, through the final thesis.
IV - Communication Skills Upon completion of the educational process, the student will have developed:
- The ability to communicate clearly and substantively the process and design choices, as well as the underlying scientific approaches, to both specialist and non-specialist interlocutors;
- The ability to manage relationships with the plurality of subjects, specialists and non-specialists, involved in the development of systems of interest to Mechanical Engineering;
- Communication skills both towards the scientific community (national and international) and towards different social components, even non-experts;
- Both the ability to work independently and the ability to work as a member of a group with diverse competencies, depending on the project development needs;
- The ability to coordinate a group, even interdisciplinary;
- Language and IT skills enabling international openness;
- Knowledge of the non-technical implications of professional practice.
These skills are developed throughout regular training activities and through various discussion and comparison moments in group work and various occasions of meeting with representatives of the business world (conferences, guided visits, etc.).
Verification of communication skills is carried out through written and/or oral exams provided for profit assessments and other training activities, particularly through the final thesis.
V - Learning Ability Upon completion of the educational process, the student will have acquired the awareness of the need for continuous learning, to be pursued autonomously throughout their professional career.
They will also have acquired the ability to:
- Keep up-to-date with the technical regulatory framework relevant to their professional sector;
- Independently acquire new technical and scientific knowledge related to the topics of the course itself, starting from scientific and technical literature in the specific field.
These abilities develop primarily during individual study of the topics covered in lectures and exercises. The development of the thesis also, in most cases, requires independent consultation of technical and scientific literature in the field.
Verification of learning abilities is carried out through written and/or oral exams provided for profit assessments and other training activities, particularly through the final thesis.
Professional Role in Work Context.
Professional Role in Work Context:
The professional figure of the mechanical engineer requires the knowledge, skills, and technical-scientific competencies necessary to interpret, describe, formulate, and solve complex problems typically encountered in an industrial context.
Master's graduates in Mechanical Engineering acquire, through the educational path, knowledge of the main characteristics of the most advanced methods, techniques, systems, and tools used in industrial processes. These skills can be applied in both free professional practice or subordinate roles within manufacturing or service companies, or in public administration. The Master's graduate in Mechanical Engineering can also assume leadership and coordination roles.
The typical professional employment areas for Master's graduates in Mechanical Engineering, for which the study program provides directly applicable preparation in the workplace, include:
- Advanced design of industrial products and mechanical systems, even complex ones,
- Development of products integrating the typical capabilities of the mechanical engineer with the transversal competencies necessary for the realization of automatic and mechatronic systems,
- Applied and industrial research,
- Innovation in the development of industrial products and production processes,
- Innovation and development in the energy sector, also considering the environmental impact of related processes,
- Planning and programming of energy resource production,
- Planning, programming, and management of complex systems.
Associated Professional Competencies.
Associated Professional Competencies:
The Master's Mechanical Engineer is able to solve, often innovatively, complex and interdisciplinary problems where technical-functional and economic requirements interact. Sufficient cultural foundations are required to address and solve problems related to the design and development of products, mechanical systems, machines, energy systems, and technological processes. Additionally, the necessary competencies for conducting and managing complex production activities and their processes and plants are required.
The competencies associated with the role of the Master's Mechanical Engineer require the skills necessary to interact with professionals of different cultural backgrounds, lead group work, and operate within an organizational context with autonomy and flexibility while respecting professional ethics.
It is also required to manage professional relationships and business-related activities, even at an international level.
Master's graduates in Mechanical Engineering must therefore:
- Deeply understand the theoretical-scientific aspects of mathematics and other basic sciences and be able to use this knowledge to interpret and describe complex engineering problems or those requiring an interdisciplinary approach;
- Deeply understand the theoretical-scientific aspects of engineering, both in general and specifically in Mechanical Engineering;
- Be able to ideate, plan, design, and manage complex and/or innovative systems, processes, and services;
- Be able to design and manage highly complex experiments;
- Possess contextual knowledge and transversal skills;
- Have knowledge in the field of business organization (business culture) and professional ethics;
- Be able to fluently use at least one European Union language in addition to Italian, both in written and oral form, with reference to disciplinary terminology.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Employment Prospects:
The employment prospects for Master's graduates in Mechanical Engineering can be expected in manufacturing or service companies, public administrations, and research institutions, depending on the chosen areas of educational focus, as well as in free professional practice. The program prepares for the profession of engineer, Section A, Industrial Sector, Specialization Mechanical Engineering.
Considering the employment commitments that have affected Master's graduates in Mechanical Engineering in recent years, the following employment opportunities are identified in the industrial sector: mechanical and electromechanical industries; aerospace and automotive industries; public and private entities operating in the field of energy resource supply and management, both traditional and alternative; companies and enterprises producing industrial products and complex, innovative systems, including in the biomedical and mechatronic fields; enterprises involved in energy production and conversion; engineering companies; enterprises developing and producing systems for automation, robotics, and special machines; manufacturing companies and service companies for the design and development of capital and consumer goods; manufacturing companies where the graduate is employed in managerial roles for maintenance and management of complex machinery in production lines and departments; industries and research institutions operating in the automotive sector and related components; companies operating in the field of thermotechnology. More generally, the professional figure in question finds employment in numerous industrial sectors where the competencies of the mechanical engineer are applied.
