ITALIANO Degree Awarded.
Degree in MOTOR AND SPORTS SCIENCES Specific Educational Objectives.
The specific educational objectives of the Bachelor's Degree Course in Motor and Sports Sciences aim to train graduates with cultural and operational knowledge and skills for programming individual and group motor and sports activities with an educational, recreational, and sporting character. Such knowledge and skills are aimed at promoting and maintaining the psychophysical well-being of the individual as stated by the general principles of the WHO within a path of motor activities suitable to their needs. Motor activity is a practice linked to solid and proven scientific foundations, therefore the Bachelor's Degree Course in Motor and Sports Sciences identifies as its primary educational objective the development of knowledge and skills in the areas of motor-sport, biological-structural, and psycho-pedagogical, which contribute to promoting health, as listed below:
- biological and structural characteristics of the human body, also in relation to age and gender, expressed through movement and the adaptation processes related to physical exercise;
- biochemical and physiological foundations of the human body's functioning, as well as the functional modifications induced by motor, competitive, and non-competitive activities, and by the environmental conditions in which exercise is performed;
- main determinants of human health and hygienic-sanitary interventions for the protection of individual and collective health;
- motor techniques aimed at injury prevention and motor rehabilitation;
- programming and evaluation of motor activity for all age groups and in disability;
- measurement methodologies and evaluation of physical efficiency and motor/sporting abilities;
- applied biomechanics to human movement and various sports practices;
- scientific tools and methodologies necessary for programming effective motor and sports activity plans at the individual and group level;
- use of at least one European Union language to enable sufficient international communication;
- basic elements of psychology and sociological processes necessary for optimizing didactic programming in different educational contexts;
- pedagogical and didactic foundations for the effective transmission of motor and sports competencies combined with motivation, promotion of healthy lifestyles, respect for rules, fair play, and ethical values;
- data processing and communication tools, useful for the profession of a graduate in motor and sports sciences.
The finalization of the activities in the training path is oriented toward acquiring knowledge that can be divided into the following areas: Bio-Medical, Psycho-Pedagogical, Relational, and Educational, Functional Evaluation and Traumatological-Rehabilitative, and Technical-Sportive. To complete the training offer, from the second year, additional and integrative activities are provided, considered necessary for completing the curriculum for all students. Over the three years of the course, students have the opportunity to complete their technical training by following practical courses in the techniques and didactics of specific motor and sports disciplines. Starting from the second year, additional activities selected from the university's training offer must be coherent with the course's educational objectives. These activities will be integrated with internal training activities aimed at deepening specific disciplinary aspects in the fields MEDF/01 and MEDF/02.
Regarding the Bio-Medical Area, the training activities will include the study of the biochemical, biological, and anatomical foundations of the human body, biomechanics of movement, hygiene and prevention, principles of drug action, and particularly the impact of physical exercise and sport on health and well-being.
Regarding the Functional and Traumatological-Rehabilitative Evaluation Area, the training activities will include the study of morpho-functional and anthropometric characteristics of the human body, biomechanical foundations of human movement, methodologies, techniques, and didactics of motor activities, main methodologies for functional evaluation, and basic techniques of individual, team sports, and sports games.
Regarding the Psycho-Pedagogical, Relational, and Educational Area, the training activities will be carried out through the study of educational, didactic, and psychopedagogical aspects of motor and sports activities.
Regarding the Technical-Sportive Area, the training activities will be carried out through the study and practical application of methodologies, techniques, and didactics of sports activities, programming, implementation, and analysis methodologies of motor and sports activities, integrated with knowledge of the legal-economic and managerial principles governing sport.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding The Bachelor's Degree Course in Motor and Sports Sciences offers a training path with activities related to the relevant SSDs within the field of motor and sports activities, basic disciplines applied to the study of human movement, disciplines related to prevention and pharmacology for the study of biological and physical risks connected with the world of sport, as well as more transversal disciplines useful for students to apply acquired competencies to operate in the specific field of motor/sport activities for children and adolescents and adapted motor activities, particularly for disability.
At the end of the training path, graduates in Motor and Sports Sciences must:
- have acquired in-depth knowledge of the methodologies, techniques, and didactics of preventive, compensatory, recreational-motor, and adaptive motor activities, considering gender, age, and physical condition specificity, as well as the main methodologies for evaluating the different components of cardiorespiratory and muscular fitness and functional body composition for well-being and health;
- possess in-depth knowledge for programming, implementing, and analyzing the effects of physical exercise and sports programs at the individual and group level, with the aim of promoting active lifestyles and introducing sports in a school context and inclusive social populations to promote fair play and sports free from potentially harmful practices to health;
- have adequate knowledge of the principles of anatomy, biology, and physiology of movement, sport, and adaptation to physical exercise;
- additionally, have acquired adequate knowledge in related and integrative disciplines, including the legal-economic and managerial principles governing sport, which allow them to integrate motor and sports knowledge with those related to the work context.
Knowledge will be developed through frontal lectures and technical-practical and laboratory activities in the applied contexts of motor and sports disciplines. Assessment of knowledge and understanding will include oral exams and, where necessary, written and technical-practical tests.
Additionally, in the final exam (presentation and discussion of the thesis), the committee may recognize and evaluate the critical ability to apply acquired knowledge within an applied study specific to the field, judgment autonomy, and communication skills.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding The training path of the Bachelor's Degree Course in Motor and Sports Sciences consists of activities that will enable graduates to:
- operate in the field of Motor Sciences by applying the basic knowledge of the principles of anatomy, biology, and physiology of movement, sport, and adaptation to physical exercise to the didactic, biological, and functional aspects of human movement;
- integrate and apply, together with the methodologies, techniques, and didactics of motor and sports activities, basic psychopedagogical knowledge to conduct motor activity programs specific to age, gender, and individual characteristics, also operating with differently abled individuals;
- apply knowledge of the legal-economic principles governing sports societies and other public and private organizations operating in the sports sector to operate in the field of Motor Sciences;
- acquire the ability to exchange information efficiently in national and international contexts to maintain constant cultural and professional updating;
- apply knowledge of the main scientific tools and methodologies, as well as data processing and representation tools, to evaluate and program effective motor and sports activity plans at the individual and group level;
- apply knowledge in disciplines related to prevention and pharmacology for studying biological and physical risks connected with the world of sport to design and promote activities capable of stimulating a correct and active lifestyle and fitness, operating within the norms governing motor and sports activities in public and private contexts.
The learning methods used to ensure the acquisition of the ability to apply knowledge and understanding will be:
- Frontal lectures
- Didactic and technical-practical laboratories in classrooms and gyms
- Internships and technical-practical activities carried out within the university's motor/sports activity projects
- Thesis preparation.
The assessment of application abilities will be verified through the following methods:
- Intermediate tests and passing exams to verify the ability to integrate acquired knowledge for programming and conducting motor activity programs specific to age, gender, and individual characteristics, with processing and discussion of the results obtained.
- Final exam including a presentation and/or discussion of a written document on topics relevant to the qualifying and specific objectives of the Bachelor's Degree Course in Motor and Sports Sciences, contributing to the evaluation of critical ability, originality, and judgment autonomy.
III - Judgment Autonomy Graduates in Motor and Sports Sciences, thanks to a solid foundational knowledge of the technical-scientific and biological-functional aspects of movement, will be able to evaluate and interpret all parameters related to human movement. They will also be able to propose the most suitable solutions to individual practitioners to achieve their goals, satisfying the needs for maintaining a correct and healthy lifestyle. Graduates must have a pronounced judgment autonomy regarding the usefulness and specific modalities of implementing motor and/or sports activity programs, particularly considering the benefits and potential risks that may arise, especially in relation to the structural and hygienic conditions of outdoor and enclosed environments.
Graduates must also be able to recognize the severity of potential injuries or acute pathologies that may occur during activities and the need for timely medical assistance.
Judgment autonomy will be measurable not only through systematic assessments in various disciplines but particularly in technical-practical disciplines and especially during the internal training activities.
IV - Communication Skills Graduates must be able to:
- synthesize and report content acquired during the training path or through reading scientific texts and articles, independently;
- use correct and appropriate technical language when interacting with individuals of different ages, abilities, genders, and socio-cultural conditions;
- motivate, involve, and reassure in individual and personalized didactic phases throughout the motor and sports activity;
- use appropriate technical expressions for different types of motor activities and various sports disciplines;
- communicate and transfer the methodologies of motor activity and the technical, tactical, and regulatory characteristics of sports disciplines.
Expected outcomes will be verified using the following teaching tools and methods:
- internal internships supervised and evaluated by faculty members of the relevant area;
- written and oral exams (initial, in-progress, and final);
- discussion of the final written document at the conclusion of the training path.
V - Learning Ability At the end of the study course, graduates must have:
- acquired the ability to consult databases and bibliographic references;
- developed interest in acquiring knowledge as a means of enriching their professional expertise and critical awareness of fundamental issues in Motor Sciences;
- developed adequate curiosity and motivation to support the need for constant professional updating.
These abilities will be measurable throughout the entire curricular training activity, particularly starting from the second semester of the second year through the various evaluation phases applied by each discipline to achieve the educational objectives set by the degree class.
The Course also provides the fundamental basis for accessing the Master's Degree Classes in Preventive and Adapted Motor Activities Sciences (LM-67), Sports Sciences (LM-68), and Organization and Management of Services for Sport and Motor Activities (LM-47).
Work Context Function.
Work Context Function:
Graduates of the class will perform the role of basic kinesiologist as fitness instructor, personal trainer, athletic trainer, and sports facility manager. They can exercise these roles in both motor and sports education, in public and private structures, in sports federations, and in recreational and social associations. Graduates in Motor and Sports Sciences can collaborate with socio-health partners, CONI, schools, Sport and Health, Federations, and entities and associations dedicated to promoting health.
Function-Associated Competencies.
Function-Associated Competencies:
Graduates in Motor and Sports Sciences, with competencies acquired in the evaluation and programming of various motor and sports activities, will be able to operate as technical-practical instructors in sports, motor, and adaptive activities for all genders, ages, and physical conditions.
In particular, graduates in Motor and Sports Sciences:
- will be able to manage and evaluate individual and group motor activity plans specific to age, gender, and individual characteristics thanks to competencies acquired in motor, sports, adaptive, and disability activities;
- will be able to design and promote individualized motor activities capable of stimulating a correct and active lifestyle and fitness (personal trainer);
- will be able to use the most modern and sophisticated technologies for evaluating the physical efficiency of any subject and condition within any motor and sports activity (athletic trainer);
- through adequate communication-relational knowledge, also leveraging knowledge of a European Union language, will be able to interact with individuals, relate with sector professionals, and collaborate with national and international partners.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Employment Prospects:
Graduates in Motor and Sports Sciences will be able to exercise their professional activity in all structures where motor and sports activities are carried out, whether public or private, in sports organizations and recreational and social associations, particularly in:
a) Conducting, managing, and evaluating individual and group motor activities with compensatory, adaptive, educational, recreational, and sporting characteristics, aimed at maintaining psychophysical well-being through the promotion of healthy and active lifestyles.
b) Conducting, managing, and evaluating individual and group fitness activities.
The professional profile of a graduate in Motor and Sports Sciences currently does not have a well-defined legal profile but can be assimilated to the ISTAT codes below, which refer to the field of technical professions in public services and for people.

ITALIAN Degree awarded.
Bachelor's Degree in SCIENCES AND TECHNOLOGIES FOR THE ENVIRONMENT Specific educational objectives.
Considering the general objectives of the L-32 three-year degree class, the main educational objective is to prepare a graduate capable of conducting analysis and monitoring of environmental systems and processes from a sustainability and environmental risk prevention perspective, to promote environmental quality. The Bachelor's Degree aims to provide the necessary training for rapid integration into the job market or for continuing studies in Master's Degree courses offered by this University and other Italian Universities. The Course aims to ensure students acquire a solid foundation in the scientific method and specific professional skills through the use of innovative methodologies and complex equipment to operate on various fronts of the environmental context. In the educational path, general contents of animal and plant biology, chemistry, physics, earth sciences, and ecology are accompanied by a strong mathematical foundation, useful for understanding environmental modeling. Additionally, highly professionalizing courses strengthen the professional character of the Bachelor's Degree, such as Fundamentals of Geostatistics and Territorial Information Systems, and Principles of Sustainability for Environmental Systems and Processes.
The acquired skills enable the graduate to adapt to the evolution of various environmental disciplines and interact with culturally adjacent professions.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding The graduate will acquire the following knowledge and skills:
- Fundamental knowledge in mathematics, biology, chemistry, physics, geology, and ecology;
- Theoretical and practical abilities regarding all disciplines contributing to environmental sciences, in the analysis and evaluation of various biotic, abiotic, and process components;
- Knowledge of major environmental regulations.
Knowledge and understanding are verified through frontal teaching, laboratory teaching, and tutoring activities carried out by individual teachers for individual courses.
In particular, knowledge and understanding will be verified, besides through in-course assessments, through individual written and/or oral exams, aimed at evaluating detailed knowledge and the ability to conceptualize the issues discussed.
II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding The graduate must be able to apply knowledge and understanding by demonstrating the ability to:
- Conduct instrumental chemical, physical, ecological, biological, and geological analyses and process environmental matrix data;
- Acquire multidisciplinary practical skills for analyzing the state of ecological systems with reference to anthropogenic pressures and resulting impacts;
- Apply the scientific method and acquired knowledge to solve environmental problems.
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is verified through in-course assessments, classroom and laboratory interactions, and written and oral exams.
These skills will be developed particularly in courses with an experimental and laboratory approach and will be verified by assessing the ability to solve problems and write scientific reports.
III - Judgment autonomy The graduate must acquire:
- Judgment autonomy regarding the evaluation and integration of experimental and non-experimental data from different disciplines;
- Familiarity with the fundamentals of assessing anthropogenic impacts on the environment.
Judgment autonomy is assessed through tests where the student is placed in a position to express a reasoned opinion on one or more concepts presented in class or during exams.
Judgment autonomy acquired is also assessed during training activities such as field exercises and internships, through the resolution of "case studies" proposed.
Within these activities, the student must demonstrate, under the guidance of a responsible teacher, the ability to critically analyze problems and express independent judgments.
Verification of the achievement of this ability will be carried out through the preparation of concise reports (oral or written) aimed at evaluating the ability to interpret, re-elaborate, and present experimental results.
IV - Communication skills The graduate must be able to:
- Communicate in at least one European language other than Italian;
- Work in groups, transmit, and disseminate information on current environmental topics;
- Use computer tools and present data from different disciplines.
The use of computer classrooms and language laboratories with personalized and group exercises is provided.
Skills related to: ability to work in groups; transmission and dissemination of information on biological topics will be acquired mainly during the internship period (to be carried out at research laboratories, public and private structures, companies, bodies, and professional orders) and during the final exam period.
Communication skills are verified through assessment of the student's expressive ability during classroom, laboratory, and mainly by involving students in writing reports and oral presentations, also using audio-visual presentation software.
V - Learning ability The graduate must acquire:
- A scientific method and adequate abilities for information research, referring to consultation of bibliographic material, database consultation, and other online information;
- A study method, ability to work in groups, and independently.
These competencies will be acquired mainly during the internship period and during the final exam period.
Learning ability is assessed through practical tests or simulations where the student is invited to choose the approach to use to solve the posed issue and demonstrate the ability to address a study and research problem with a high degree of autonomy.
Work context function.
Work context function:
The function of the graduate in a work context involves junior environmental expert tasks, such as environmental monitoring under the direction of a senior environmental expert, preparation of relational databases on available knowledge of flora and fauna in protected areas, or databases assembling chemical and physical characteristics of specific environmental contexts or industrial processes under study, ability to retrieve information from Authorities and Offices for the employer regarding all environmental topics in any matrix (air, water, soil), compile obtained information into technical reports, ability to prepare synthetic sheets of plant and industrial process characteristics, direct collection of environmental data.
In detail, the main functions and associated competencies are listed below:
- Integrated sampling, monitoring, and analysis of environmental matrices in their abiotic and biotic components of ecosystems and connected environmental processes;
- Assessment of the health status of ecological-environmental systems;
- Biodiversity conservation;
- Management of environmental issues in the production system and impact assessment;
- Services in environmental systems of territorial bodies dealing with environment to support impact studies;
- Recovery and restoration of degraded environments;
- Analysis and monitoring of habitats and animal, plant, and microbial species aimed at applying European Environmental Directives.
Function-associated competencies.
Function-associated competencies:
The competencies associated with the function in a specific work context are those provided by the study plan, as structured, with teaching in the fields of basic physical and chemical disciplines, animal and plant biodiversity, conservation and management of flora and fauna, territorial information systems, knowledge of relational databases.
Professional status conferred by the degree.
Employment opportunities:
The junior environmental expert is able to operate, under the supervision of a senior environmental expert or an environmental biologist, in routine environmental monitoring activities of ARTA, the Ministry of Environment, industries, solid waste landfills, in the "Environment" sections of Municipalities, Provinces, Regions, private industries, and veterinary institutes.

Program, Texts, and Objectives Official Teaching and Assessment Languages. ITALIAN
Degree Awarded. Bachelor's Degree in CHEMICAL SCIENCES AND MATERIALS TECHNOLOGY
Specific Educational Objectives.
The Bachelor's Degree in Chemical Sciences and Materials Technology, which originates and develops within a strictly interdisciplinary environment such as the Department of Physical and Chemical Sciences of the University of L'Aquila, has as its primary objective to prepare graduates with solid knowledge and skills in various fields of chemistry, including (and with particular attention to) materials science, in both theoretical/computational and experimental aspects. The curriculum provides foundational knowledge in mathematics, physics, general chemistry, and analytical chemistry in the first year. In the second year, students deepen their understanding of essential chemistry areas, with particular emphasis on Organic Chemistry, Inorganic Chemistry, Analytical Chemistry, and Physical Chemistry. In the third year, students integrate their acquired chemical knowledge with a focus on inorganic, analytical-environmental, computational, and biochemical aspects. Additionally, students are expected to gain a solid foundation in Material Physics and Materials Science, particularly regarding the electronic and crystalline structure of solids, transport properties of solids, and the fundamental properties of basic electronic devices. To achieve the educational objectives, many courses include theoretical lectures, numerical exercises, and practical laboratory activities, enabling students to develop skills in laboratory safety, use of common laboratory equipment, handling of chemical safety data sheets, and proper disposal of chemical products. The Bachelor's Degree program also includes a training internship to be completed within the university or at cooperating public or private companies, as an integral part of the educational path. The seven learning areas outlined in the curriculum are:
Mathematical-Physical-Computational Area: Students must acquire foundational skills in mathematics, physics, and informatics suitable for a comprehensive understanding of their theoretical and practical applications in chemistry and materials science.
General Chemistry Area: Students will gain expertise in chemical terminology and nomenclature, principles of chemical equilibrium and reactions, atomic structure, classification of bond types, concepts of mole, concentration, pH, solubility, and knowledge of the characteristics and properties of main elements and their inorganic compounds.
Analytical Chemistry Area: Students will develop skills in using common analytical methodologies, atomic and molecular spectroscopic techniques, chromatographic and electrochemical techniques for qualitative and quantitative analysis.
Physical Chemistry Area: Students will acquire knowledge of thermodynamic principles, correlation between molecular properties and macroscopic behavior of matter, laws governing chemical equilibrium and reaction rates, fundamental physical principles of radiation-matter interaction, and conversion of chemical energy into electrical energy.
Organic and Biological Chemistry Area: Students will learn the fundamentals of nomenclature, three-dimensional structure, chemical and physical properties of molecules, and gain knowledge necessary to interpret and rationalize organic reactions in terms of reaction mechanisms and structure-reactivity relationships. They will be able to predict reaction outcomes, considering stereochemical aspects. Additionally, students will understand biochemical terminology, molecular foundations of biological systems and processes, and major metabolic pathways.
Materials Science Area: Students will acquire the basics of Material Physics and Materials Science for entering the workforce in the field of new materials, primarily but not exclusively in microelectronics, thin films, and optics. The acquired knowledge will also support further studies in materials science and applied physics.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding
Graduates must possess a broad scientific culture, solid preparation in mathematical and physical disciplines, and foundational training in core subjects, with particular reference to fundamental principles of general and inorganic chemistry, physical chemistry, organic chemistry, analytical chemistry, materials science, and biochemistry. Practical laboratory activities aim to develop aptitude for chemical experimentation, risk assessment related to chemical substances, and physical experimentation, particularly in materials studies. Graduates must know the main experimental methods for preparing chemical compounds or materials, conducting analytical and structural investigations, and acquiring skills for data processing. Graduates must also reach a standard of knowledge and competence enabling entry into the workforce or progression to second-cycle degree programs.
Learning Methods:
- Specific courses (Type A and Type B)
- Experimental laboratory courses
- Computational laboratory courses
A total of over 120 ECTS is dedicated to these activities.
Assessment Methods:
Assessments for each student through oral or written exams (for all basic courses) and practical and oral exams for experimental and computational laboratory courses. Intermediate assessments are conducted in all basic course types.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding
Ability to apply knowledge and understanding:
Upon completion of the program, graduates in Chemical Sciences and Materials Technology will be able to apply knowledge and understanding in professional contexts, operating both in chemical-technological fields and in related technical-scientific areas.
In particular, graduates will have acquired the following skills:
- Ability to approach inductive and deductive reasoning to solve problems;
- Ability to identify the most appropriate methodologies (experimental and/or computational) for problem-solving;
- Ability to critically sample and collect scientific data;
- Ability to process and interpret scientific data;
- Ability to set up and optimize simple experimental configurations where established methodologies and protocols are not available.
Learning Methods:
Theoretical courses; extensive numerical exercises; sufficiently extensive experimental and computational laboratory activities.
Assessment Methods:
Written assessments applying theoretical knowledge to original problems; laboratory practicals (experimental and/or computational) involving the setup and execution of an experimental or numerical design, followed by critical analysis of results.
III - Judgment Autonomy
Graduates in Chemical Sciences and Materials Technology must have acquired the ability to:
- Critical reasoning;
- Identify existing methods to address chemical problems through experimental design, data collection, and analysis;
- Improve processes (analytical, preparative, simulation);
- Understand the limits of their knowledge and fill any gaps.
Learning Methods:
In theoretical and laboratory courses, students are continuously presented with resolved problems, guiding them through the logical-deductive process to solve them, avoiding reliance on pre-digested formulas and automatic application. Students are then invited to independently solve original problems.
Assessment Methods:
Students are invited to solve original problems through written and oral exams. Additionally, through practical laboratory assessments, students are asked to evaluate the validity of an experimental design and subsequently implement it to solve a specific problem.
IV - Communication Skills
Upon completion of their studies, graduates must have acquired:
- The ability to present a scientific topic both orally and through a written scientific report, illustrating objectives, results, and critical interpretation;
- The ability to read and use precise and rigorous communication tools such as tables and graphs;
- The ability to communicate with the scientific community by supporting their arguments with appropriate evidence;
- The ability to integrate into research groups;
- The ability to use Italian and English languages appropriately and correctly.
Learning Methods:
Theoretical-practical activities and laboratory work for writing laboratory reports; language training courses for English; preparation of the final thesis (also in English) and oral presentation.
Assessment Methods:
Oral presentations are explicitly evaluated for communication skills; student-led seminar activities are organized and assessed; the final thesis presentation is given significant weight in evaluation.
V - Learning Ability
Graduates must have acquired the ability to study scientific topics and apply this knowledge in different contexts to effectively integrate received information. They must also be able to understand the limits of their knowledge and identify necessary textbooks and materials for further study. Finally, they must be able to read and learn in English.
To this end, students are guided in improving their study methods from the first year by instructors and tutors, and learning ability is continuously monitored through performance assessments and exams focusing on knowledge acquired through independent study. English is learned in dedicated courses and through progressive use of the foreign language in learning.
Workplace Function.
Workplace Function:
Graduates in Chemical Sciences and Materials Technology perform the following functions:
a) Use of measurement instruments for analysis and characterization of compounds and materials;
b) Application of established methodologies for synthesis and purification of compounds and materials;
c) Application of established methodologies for data processing;
d) Scientific support for industrial and healthcare activities concerning fine chemistry, formulation chemistry, pharmaceutical chemistry, environment, biochemical chemistry, merchandise science, materials science, energy, and cultural heritage;
e) Monitoring of chemical pollution within occupational safety professions;
f) Dissemination of scientific culture.
Therefore, graduates are expected to:
- Assist specialists in research activities or activities requiring the application of chemical procedures and protocols;
- Conduct chemical analyses, quality control, and preparative procedures requiring mastery of complex chemical and instrumental techniques;
- Prepare reports on analysis results;
- Use standardized methodologies such as chemical analysis of all species; material analysis (electronic, mechanical, optical, tribological);
- Manage chemical laboratories whose activities involve chemical analysis and quality control;
- Perform consultancy in pure and applied chemistry for implementing or improving quality systems in companies for chemical aspects, as well as achieving certifications or conformity declarations;
- Formulate judgments on the quality of goods or products and intervene to improve quality or eliminate defects;
- Be able to critically collect scientific literature and present scientific topics even at a popular level.
Skills Associated with the Function.
Skills Associated with the Function:
Graduates in Chemical Sciences and Materials Technology acquire knowledge and skills to collect and interpret data related to chemical problems or phenomena and apply well-established analysis and synthesis protocols. Their knowledge is aimed at supporting roles in industrial settings and in analysis and research laboratories across various sectors such as biochemical chemistry, pharmaceutical chemistry, fine chemistry, environment, merchandise science, materials science, energy, and cultural heritage.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Employment Prospects:
Graduates are offered employment opportunities by public and private research institutions, analysis laboratories, quality control and certification bodies, public and private entities and companies, as employees or independent consultants, by industries and work environments requiring basic knowledge in chemistry and materials science, and by all industries that use chemistry and new materials as an integral part of their activities for research and development of processes and products. Graduates must be able to interact with different components of the productive world.
In particular, based on their preparation and skills, graduates can perform their activities in the following types of companies:
- Public and private companies in the field of quality control and environment;
- Public and private companies in the field of pharmaceutical chemistry;
- Public and private companies in the field of formulation chemistry;
- Public and private companies in the field of materials science;
- Public and private companies in the field of chemical and biochemical analysis in healthcare;
- Public and private companies in the field of energy;
- Public and private companies in the field of protection and recovery of cultural heritage;
- Public and private companies for scientific literature and dissemination.

Program, Texts, and Objectives Official Teaching and Assessment Languages.
ITALIAN
Specific Educational Objectives.
The foundational training provided by the Bachelor's degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques includes activities aimed at acquiring the theoretical, methodological, and applied fundamentals of the main areas of Psychology and related disciplines. The educational offer also aims to equip students with a set of knowledge and skills necessary for continuing studies in a Master's degree in Psychology, where they will further develop their personal and professional training, and for carrying out various professional activities characteristic of the profile of a Psychologist registered in Section B of the Psychologists' Register.
The objective is therefore to train competent professionals capable of operating as technical collaborators in various psychological fields, focused on research, analysis, design, management, and evaluation of interventions. Graduates must possess knowledge and skills enabling them to interact with other professionals in the territory, with reference to services directed at individuals, families, groups, organizations, communities, and institutions. In any case, the Bachelor's degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques will provide the necessary tools to collaborate in psychological activities under the supervision of a mental health professional, or a psychologist or psychotherapist, within various social, organizational, and work contexts in public and private structures providing and managing home-based, residential, and territorial social and socio-health services.

Description of the Educational Path.
The general and specific educational objectives of the three-year Bachelor's degree are implemented through training modules (exams) and practical activities with training internship value, totaling 180 CFU.
The path is divided into three years, with courses progressively scheduled to optimize content delivery, increasing complexity, and coherence between different disciplinary areas.
In particular, the educational objectives achieved during the study path will enable graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques to acquire: knowledge of basic and characteristic psychological disciplines within general, physiological, social, and work psychology; biological and neurophysiological foundations of behavior; principles for defining scientific research designs and the ability to apply statistical methods and computer procedures for data processing in psychology; knowledge of individual differences in psychology and measurement of personality variables; adequate skills in using English for communicating psychological information and understanding international scientific sources.
Subsequently, specific psychological knowledge and skills will be further developed and integrated. In particular, advanced knowledge in psychometrics and testing will be acquired, along with adequate theoretical skills in studying human behavior from a physiological and evolutionary perspective. Cognitive, relational, and behavioral functions of humans across the lifespan in normal or pathological conditions will also be explored in depth.
Finally, more specific knowledge and skills will be provided, useful for the graduate in Psychological Sciences and Techniques in applied contexts. In particular, preparation will be provided for applying basic psychological knowledge in clinical and health psychology. These competencies will also be integrated through the specificity of related disciplines concerning psychopharmacological, psychopathological, and neurological aspects and their treatment methods.
During the final year, knowledge in the field of psychology is further enhanced through elective courses and participation in ethics and professional deontology seminars.
The curriculum includes 10 CFU for professional training internship activities (Practical Evaluation Internship, TPV), enabling the acquisition of practical skills in applying knowledge and competencies gained through courses. The final exam (4 CFU) will allow students to develop skills in writing a psychological report and discussing its content before a committee.
Agreements with other European universities ensure students the opportunity to complete an international psychological training during the three-year program, with recognition of the credits earned abroad.

Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding At the end of the educational path, graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques will:
- Have acquired adequate knowledge and understanding, analysis, and orientation regarding the theoretical and methodological foundations of the main and characteristic areas of psychology;
- Be able to integrate basic psychology knowledge with cognitive and psychobiological sciences;
- Have acquired skills in scientific research methods and application methodologies for interventions on individuals;
- Have also acquired adequate knowledge in related and integrative disciplines, enabling them to integrate psychological knowledge within a broader knowledge context.
Knowledge will be developed through frontal lectures and practical experiences with individual and group exercises. Assessment of knowledge and understanding will be conducted through oral exams and, where necessary, written tests.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding At the end of the educational path, the acquired knowledge will enable graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques to:
- Identify and analyze psychological risk factors and psychosocial protective factors in contexts of individual interaction with their environment;
- Use methods and techniques necessary for collecting, processing, and analyzing information quantitatively and qualitatively;
- Apply psychological knowledge also within related disciplines, in an integrated knowledge perspective;
- Access scientific literature to improve and expand their knowledge for the purpose of continuous professional updating.
To achieve these goals, students are guided by professors and tutors regarding study methods and verification of acquired knowledge in the various training activities. This part of the training will be achieved through frontal lectures and practical activities, exercises, and internships, allowing the application of knowledge acquired during the study program.
Assessment of learning outcomes is primarily conducted through written and/or oral exams. In-course assessments for each course may include tasks where students demonstrate theoretical mastery and the ability to apply acquired knowledge. The final exam, as specified in the study program regulations, consists of a written report and represents the final stage of the educational process, where the maturation and application of knowledge and understanding are completed.

II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding Graduates at the end of the educational path:
- Can use methods and techniques necessary for collecting, processing, and analyzing information quantitatively and qualitatively;
- Are able to apply psychological knowledge within related disciplines, in an integrated knowledge perspective;
- Are able to access scientific literature to improve and expand their knowledge for the purpose of continuous professional updating.
To achieve these goals, students are guided by professors and tutors regarding study methods and verification of acquired knowledge in the various training activities. This part of the training will be achieved through frontal lectures and more practical activities such as simulation of interventions, small evaluation exercises, or participation in experimental settings, where possible encouraging active student participation. As with basic knowledge, classroom work will be complemented by individual study, as required by current legislation.

III - Autonomy of Judgment Graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques must have acquired critical skills enabling them to evaluate different explanatory models and methodological and intervention approaches, and to formulate personal and independent judgments.
Graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques must also have acquired documentation, observation (structured or unstructured), empirical research, and textual analysis skills, along with an adequate technical-scientific and epistemological language. These skills must enable graduates to formulate independent judgments, as free as possible from prejudices and stereotypes, necessary for understanding and scientifically interpreting the social and cultural reality in which they live and work.
To develop and assess autonomy of judgment, guided activities and exercises will be provided within the curriculum courses, requiring students to exercise problem identification and solution processes, and evaluation of actions and processes. Critical ability will also be assessed during exams, in the preparation of written reports, and in the preparation and writing of the final report.

IV - Communication Skills For graduates in Applied Psychological Sciences, the acquisition of communication skills is central, as their professionalism is characterized by constant contact with users in various social and health contexts. Therefore, graduates in Applied Psychological Sciences must have acquired relational and communication skills enabling them to interact effectively at individual, professional, and institutional levels, and to engage with colleagues and other professionals. They must also have acquired knowledge of major information technology and telecommunication tools, as well as knowledge of the English language, including disciplinary terminology. The acquisition of the aforementioned communication skills is provided in different forms within training activities and is assessed through written or multimedia reports, oral presentations, participation in work groups, seminar interventions, and comprehension of foreign language texts.

V - Learning Ability Graduates in Applied Psychological Sciences must have acquired knowledge and skills enabling them to make autonomous choices for pursuing higher-level study paths (Master's degree, Master) and/or professional development paths.
To this end, students must develop during the educational path:
- Ability to study both independently and collaboratively;
- Ability to reflect on their learning processes and self-assess results;
- Ability to use scientific texts in psychology beyond mere manuals (such as essays or articles from scientific journals) and their bibliographic apparatus;
- Ability to use bibliographic databases in the field of psychology.
Assessment of the acquired ability to learn critically will be conducted through exams, particularly through the presentation of key topics from various disciplines in open-ended questions and the preparation of essays.
Additionally, the final exam, beyond thoroughly assessing the ability to present critical reflections in written and oral form in specific areas of student preparation, will evaluate the ability to use major bibliographic tools in an articulated manner.

Function in Work Context.
Function in Work Context:
The academic and professional profile of graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques, in line with educational objectives and expected outcomes, will enable graduates to perform professional functions focused on analyzing demand, psychological assessment, and designing interventions for risk reduction and prevention, rehabilitation, and promotion of psychological health for individuals and in community systems, schools, and workplaces.
The acquired knowledge and skills enable graduates to perform the following functions:
- Participate in empirical and experimental research activities and the planning of psychological and psychosocial interventions;
- Implement psychosocial and psychoeducational interventions for the development of individual and social potential;
- Use tools learned (interview, psychological tests, observation) in individual, family, and group settings under supervision, where required by regulations, by a professional psychologist or a psychologist registered in Section A of the Psychologists' Register;
- Carry out their activities in public, private, and third-sector structures in clinical, school, and social contexts.

Competencies Associated with the Function.
Competencies Associated with the Function:
Graduates possess:
- Ability to participate in the planning and evaluation of psychological and rehabilitative interventions;
- Ability to implement psychological interventions aimed at promoting the development of individual growth potential and social integration, facilitating communication processes, improving stress management, and quality of life;
- Ability to use interviews, questionnaires, observation, psychological tests, and other analytical tools for evaluating behavior, personality, cognitive processes, social interaction, opinions, attitudes, and psychological suitability for specific tasks and conditions;
- Ability to use psychological tools with disabled individuals to develop or recover functional cognitive, practical, emotional, and relational skills, and to halt functional regression in cases of degenerative neurological, psychiatric, and neuropsychiatric syndromes;
- Ability to use psychological tools for career guidance, human resource management, and development;
- Ability to manage the collection, uploading, and statistical processing of psychological data for clinical and research purposes.

Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Employment Prospects:
The three-year Bachelor's degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques naturally leads to pursuing a Master's degree in Psychology of any specialization for a complete definition of the professional profile of a Psychologist.
In accordance with current regulations, the Bachelor's degree prepares graduates to perform individual professional activities, subject to registration in Section B of the Psychologists' Register, and, where applicable, under the supervision of a mental health professional, or a psychologist or psychotherapist, within public and private sectors providing psychological services to individuals, families, and groups.
Coherent professional prospects with the proposed training are also found in employment centers and training centers, schools, and communities.
