Degree Awarded. Bachelor's Degree in Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance (qualifying for the health profession of Orthoptist and Ophthalmological Assistant)
Specific Educational Objectives.
The Bachelor's Degree program in Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance aims to prepare professionals who have acquired the foundational knowledge for understanding qualitative and quantitative biological and pathological phenomena, the principles of pathophysiology necessary to perform orthoptic rehabilitation treatments for disorders of eye movement and binocular vision, the principles of rehabilitation for visual function deficits, and the basics for performing instrumental ophthalmological semiotics techniques. Graduates in Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance, in addition to possessing the specific educational knowledge of the class, must acquire adequate competence in the field of visual prevention in neonatal, infant, and adult age (video terminal users, glaucoma, DMS), in techniques and methodologies for conducting screenings in childhood (preschool and school age), in the rehabilitation of visually impaired patients by acquiring evaluation skills, orthoptic rehabilitation of visual disorders, in the evaluation and rehabilitation of strabismus, amblyopia, and deficits of accommodation and convergence, and in performing instrumental ophthalmic examinations. In particular, at the end of the study program, the graduate in Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance must be able to:
- design and implement, in collaboration with professionals in the specific field, health promotion, screening, and prevention interventions for vision disorders, and early diagnosis targeting individuals and the community (particularly in visual prevention for infants, preschool, and school-age children, and prevention of asthenopia);
- plan, implement, and evaluate technical-diagnostic activities related to the psychophysical assessment of visual function, objective and subjective refractometry, quality and characteristics of sensory and motor aspects of normal and pathological binocular vision, electrophysiology, and static and dynamic imaging diagnostics of the eye;
- plan, implement, and evaluate visual rehabilitation activities and define rehabilitation goals considering the pathology, educational needs, and personal requirements;
- act consistently with the disciplinary, ethical, and deontological principles of the profession in various situations within the educational project;
- contribute to the programming and organization of diagnostic information collection, respecting the competencies of other healthcare professions as per Law 42/99, to ensure the best functionality of the diagnostic/therapeutic process.
Graduates must also acquire specific deontological and legislative knowledge to operate functionally in the areas of competence within public and private structures. Particular emphasis, as an integral and qualifying part of professional training, is placed on practical training and clinical internship acquired under the guidance of tutors belonging to the specific professional profile, coordinated by a faculty member belonging to the highest educational level for the Orthoptist and Ophthalmological Assistant profile, in accordance with the educational standards set by European Union regulations and directives.
The Bachelor's Degree program typically lasts three years, and educational activities can be divided into:
- Basic educational activities aimed at acquiring necessary knowledge in Anatomy, Physiology, Pathology, Psychology, and Binocular Vision Pathophysiology;
- Preparatory educational activities aimed at acquiring adequate knowledge in Pharmacology, Internal Medicine, Hygiene, Pediatrics, Oncology, Medical Genetics, and Radioprotection;
- Characteristic educational activities of the Bachelor's Degree program aimed at acquiring adequate knowledge in the field of Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance, including eye disorders, visual and neuro-ophthalmic rehabilitation methodologies and techniques, contactology, instrumental semiotics, and orthoptic rehabilitation methodologies and techniques;
- Other activities aimed at learning related or complementary subjects to basic and characteristic disciplines, including technical-scientific disciplines of the field of reference; foreign language, computer skills, training internship, and other student-selected activities to complete their education.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding The final degree of the first cycle (Bachelor's Degree in Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance) will be awarded to the student who has demonstrated, throughout the studies, the acquisition of adequate knowledge and understanding in the study of orthoptics and visual rehabilitation, utilizing multiple teaching tools such as advanced textbooks, specific handouts, scientific articles, computer materials, active tutoring, and other resources. Throughout the educational activities, there will be continuous updates regarding the use of the best advanced techniques in orthoptics and visual rehabilitation, surgical techniques, and major topics in the field of study. In particular, during the studies, students may achieve excellent knowledge in the fields of eye disorders, physiology and pathophysiology of binocular vision, visual and neuro-ophthalmic rehabilitation methodologies and techniques, contactology, instrumental semiotics, orthoptic rehabilitation methodologies and techniques, and legislative and deontological norms of the sector. Additionally, students may acquire knowledge of scientific English in their field for general information exchange and the main computer tools. The assessment of understanding and acquired knowledge will be evaluated through ongoing assessments, oral presentations of written work (using computer support), and final exams.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding Students in the Bachelor's Degree program in Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance will be able to demonstrate the knowledge and skills acquired through laboratory activities and during clinical internships at specialized facilities (public or private accredited), visual impairment rehabilitation centers, university clinics, optional activities, internships, and any other activities conducted for training purposes. Students will thus demonstrate the ability to approach work as an Orthoptist with a professional attitude and possess the necessary competencies to develop and support arguments and solve problems within their field of study, as well as apply acquired knowledge in diagnosis, therapy and rehabilitation planning, and evaluation of the therapeutic and rehabilitation process.
III - Independent Judgment Students in the Bachelor's Degree program in Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance will acquire the ability to collect and interpret information and data deemed useful for forming independent judgments (planning, implementation, and evaluation of technical-diagnostic activities related to the psychophysical assessment of visual function and planning of orthoptic rehabilitation interventions using available technological innovations), including reflection on social, scientific, or ethical issues related to them, while respecting pathology, educational needs, and personal requirements. Theoretical-practical activities during the three-year training period will be monitored and stimulated through ongoing assessments during teaching activities, particularly to develop reasoning and critical judgment skills.
IV - Communication Skills Students in the Bachelor's Degree program in Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance must be able to communicate information, ideas, problems, and solutions to healthcare professionals in ophthalmology, as well as specialists in other disciplines, and non-specialist interlocutors such as patients, educators, caregivers, etc. In particular, during the studies, interactive teaching methods with instructors and presentations of written work are provided, along with written and oral exam formats. During internship activities, group work will be encouraged to enhance relational and communication skills.
V - Learning Ability Students in the Bachelor's Degree program in Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance must develop the learning abilities necessary to pursue further studies (Master's Degree), acquire a high degree of autonomy and aptitude for professional updating, and perform work activities.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
The Orthoptist Ophthalmological Assistant is the healthcare professional who treats motor and sensory vision disorders and performs instrumental ophthalmological semiotics techniques. Graduates in Orthoptics and Ophthalmological Assistance, in reference to the diagnosis and prescriptions of the physician, within their scope of competence, also develop, in collaboration with multidisciplinary teams, the rehabilitation program aimed at identifying and overcoming the health needs of the person. They propose the adoption of aids, train users in their use, and verify their effectiveness; verify the alignment of the implemented rehabilitation methodology with functional recovery goals; conduct study and professional consultation activities in healthcare services and in those requiring their professional competencies; and perform their professional activities in healthcare facilities, public or private, in an employed or freelance capacity.

Bachelor's degree in BUSINESS LEGAL OPERATOR Specific educational objectives.
The Bachelor's degree in Business Legal Operator aims to provide a solid foundational cultural and legal preparation, inseparable from knowledge of economic and managerial nature. Within this context, the graduate in Business Legal Operator acquires secure mastery of specific areas of the legal system concerning, in particular, the legal disciplines of business and gains a methodology to effectively interpret and utilize legal instruments in public and private administrations and businesses, in all sectors requiring specific legal preparation in contractual activities, management of labor relations, labor conflicts, tax assistance, and issues related to administration.
To this end, the Bachelor's degree in Business Legal Operator includes basic activities of a legal and philosophical nature with particular attention to sectors related to business and the world of work, as well as typical issues of public administrations.
Characterizing activities focus on in-depth study of legal and economic-business disciplines concerning business and public administrations; related-integrative activities concern courses aimed at understanding managerial and economic-business profiles of companies and public administrations.
Two distinct study paths are provided:
- Generic profile (as above) open to all students intending to enroll in the Bachelor's degree program;
- Economic-Financial Study Plan profile (reserved for Financial Guard cadets of the Financial Guard Cadet School located in L'Aquila) which follows almost the entire generic path with minor modifications aimed at strengthening preparation in tax law and criminal law in relation to the specific professional profile of the graduate.
Dublin descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding The graduate in Business Legal Operator, as a result of the educational path followed, acquires, through the use of advanced textbooks (typical of a university study program), legal, economic, and economic-business knowledge that ensure understanding and ability to comprehend issues and questions related to the legal and economic-business dimension of business and its multiple connected issues, including knowledge of some cutting-edge topics related to current jurisprudential and regulatory phenomena. The teaching methods and tools through which the expected outcomes are achieved are those traditional to university teaching delivered through annual courses organized according to current regulations, and through the dissemination of course programs and recommended textbooks for exam preparation. Verification of achieving the expected outcomes consists of an exam for each individual course. The decision on exam format (written or oral) is left to the course instructor, who annually, in the exam program, also indicates the exam format aimed at verifying the achievement of the set objectives, including the assignment of the CFU credits for the individual course and the award of a grade out of thirty attesting to the quality level achieved by the individual student.
II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding The graduate in Business Legal Operator undertakes a study path that enables them to acquire the ability to apply both the knowledge gained and the acquired understanding, thus enabling them to address and solve practical and theoretical problems in the field of business dimension and legal regulation of the business phenomenon. The graduate in Business Legal Operator is therefore capable of addressing and solving concrete workplace issues, demonstrating also the acquisition of a professional approach to work, and is also capable of addressing and solving theoretical problems through structured and developed arguments by the graduate.
The teaching methods and tools through which the student acquires the ability to apply knowledge and understanding are those traditional to university teaching delivered through annual courses organized according to current regulations, and through the dissemination of course programs and recommended textbooks for exam preparation, but also include the provision of an internship experience. Verification of achieving the expected outcomes, also from the perspective of the ability to apply knowledge and understanding, consists of an exam for each individual course, the preparation of a final report at the end of the internship experience, and a pass test regarding foreign language knowledge. The decision on exam format (written or oral) is left to the course instructor, who annually, in the exam program, also indicates the exam format aimed at verifying the achievement of the set objectives, including the ability to apply knowledge and understanding. Passing the relevant test results in the student acquiring the CFU credits for the individual course and the award of a grade out of thirty attesting to the quality level achieved by the individual student.
III - Judgment autonomy The graduate in Business Legal Operator has the ability to collect and interpret legal and economic-business data in order to formulate autonomous judgments regarding theoretical and practical issues related to the actions of businesses and public and private entities, and the efficiency of both private and public administration.
The teaching methods and tools through which the graduate in Business Legal Operator acquires judgment autonomy regarding legal or economic-business issues consist in studying and deepening the individual disciplines of the educational path, and for this purpose, front-line teaching courses are structured in which the instructor illustrates to the student the individual objects of the study program, with references also to current events and recent developments in the individual disciplines. The acquisition of judgment autonomy is verified through a specific exam in which the instructor verifies possession of the knowledge outlined in the program and the ability to combine such knowledge with judgment autonomy.
The graduate in Business Legal Operator undertakes a study path that enables them to acquire the ability of judgment autonomy regarding practical and theoretical problems in the field of business dimension and legal regulation of the business phenomenon.
The teaching methods and tools through which the student acquires the ability of judgment autonomy are those traditional to university teaching delivered through annual courses organized according to current regulations, and through the dissemination of course programs and recommended textbooks for exam preparation, but also include the provision of an internship experience. Verification of achieving the expected outcomes, also from the perspective of the ability to apply judgment autonomy, consists of an exam for each individual course, the preparation of a final report at the end of the internship experience, and a pass test regarding foreign language knowledge. V - Learning ability The graduate in Business Legal Operator possesses learning abilities necessary to undertake and continue subsequent studies with a high degree of autonomy both within the strictly legal studies (jurisprudence), with an orientation towards typical legal professions, and within legal, legal-business, and economic-business studies with an orientation towards specialization studies in the management of public administrations, third-sector entities, and public and private entities.

Workplace role.
Workplace role:
Generic profile:
The functions the graduate in Business Legal Operator is called to perform are those related to providing legal and legal-business consultancy, as well as supporting the elaboration of solutions regarding legal and legal-business issues, or performing coordination management functions, as well as support functions regarding legal, accounting, and organizational issues, which may arise both within companies and private or public entities, as well as in the performance of consultancy and self-employed professional activities.
The competencies possessed by the graduate in Business Legal Operator relate to knowledge of legal phenomena, ability to navigate the regulatory and jurisprudential framework of issues related to business dimension and economic phenomenon, as well as ability to navigate economic-business issues of private and public companies and entities.
Economic-Financial Profile (reserved for Financial Guard Cadets):
The Economic-Financial Study Plan profile aims to train a professional figure capable of understanding and addressing issues related to legal and economic-financial problems of business, also for the purpose of controlling business activities for tax, criminal, administrative, and civil purposes. The functions the graduate in Business Legal Operator, Economic-Financial Study Plan profile, is called to perform are those related to processing legal and legal-business (accounting, tax) issues concerning the functional dimension of companies and private or public entities with specific regard to controlling compliance with current regulations.
The competencies possessed by the graduate in Business Legal Operator, Economic-Financial Study Plan profile, relate to knowledge of legal phenomena, ability to navigate the regulatory and jurisprudential framework of economic-business phenomena, with ability to navigate economic-business issues of private and public entities.

Associated competencies for the role:

The expected professional opportunities (beyond those listed in the Istat codes above) are those typical of public and private employment operating in legal and economic-management fields.
Economic-Financial Profile (reserved for Financial Guard Cadets):

The expected professional opportunities (beyond those listed in the Istat codes above) are those typical of public and private employment operating in legal and economic-management fields.
The graduate in this profile may access, in addition to all professional opportunities provided for the generic profile, those specific to the various activities of Financial Guard non-commissioned officers.

ITALIAN Awarded degree.
Bachelor's Degree in LINGUISTIC AND CULTURAL MEDIATION Specific educational objectives.
The Bachelor's Degree in Linguistic and Cultural Mediation provides students with a solid foundational preparation in foreign languages and literatures: the course offers a wide range of credits in SSD related to languages and modern literatures, enabling students to achieve a high level of competence, both written and oral (level B2 according to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages), in two foreign languages over the three years. Language courses aim at both foreign language communication and metalinguistic reflection. Literary courses aim at both foundational training in foreign literatures and cultures and critical reflection, also in a comparative direction. The training path deepens linguistic-technical preparation and initiates translation skills, with specific translation courses, including philological (SSD: L.FIL-LET/09, L.FIL-LET/15), comparative (SSD: L-FIL-LET/14), geographical (SSD: M-GGR/01), computer science (SSD: ING-INF/05), historical (SSD: M-STO/04) and demoethnoanthropological (SSD: M-DEA/01) courses.
The bachelor's degree also provides solid training in theoretical linguistics and Italian studies (SSD: L-LIN/01, L-FIL-LET/12).
Dublin descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding Through contact with texts from other European cultures, the student acquires adequate understanding of languages, literatures, and cultures in both historical dimension and contemporary manifestations, developing critical perspectives useful for refining analytical, synthetic, interpretative, and valorization skills for other languages and cultures. This is achieved through courses in basic and characteristic SSDs, which include frontal lessons, specific exercises, and seminars. Periodic assessments, both oral and written, are provided.
II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding The acquired linguistic and textual competence enables the student to analyze texts of various types, identifying their structural and thematic characteristics for the purposes of interpretation, mediation, and translation from a contrastive perspective. Practical exercises and seminar meetings are provided to facilitate the practice and enhancement of linguistic and cultural knowledge. Results are verified through periodic tests in the form of standardized tests, translations, and oral presentations in a foreign language for linguistic skills; through seminars on specific topics, essays, and guided theses for cultural and literary skills.
III - Judgment autonomy In-depth study of foreign languages, literatures, and cultures provides the student with linguistic, philological, historical, and cultural tools to formulate hypotheses, recognize logical connections, argue, compare, and evaluate different interpretations to draw appropriate conclusions. This is made possible through critical reflection on linguistic, literary, and cultural systems and their evolution and diffusion, as well as through supporting scientific and critical bibliographies.
IV - Communication skills In-depth study of the Italian language and continuous written and oral practice in foreign languages, aiming at high competence levels through translation, writing, and oral presentation practice, ensures the student's competence and confidence in arguing and presenting scientific and cultural topics. Opportunities for students of the Bachelor's Degree in Languages and Cultural Mediation to spend periods at major European and extra-European universities through the extensive exchange network activated by the university contribute to developing solid communication skills. For this purpose, a high number of CFU is specifically required in the two languages of study. Results are verified through standardized tests based on "Common European Framework" descriptors and other appropriate written and oral assessments.
V - Learning ability Learning foreign languages through both theoretical and practical lessons, laboratory exercises, and use of innovative information technologies enables the student to acquire awareness of teaching/learning methods for foreign languages, making them capable of continuing future improvement of their linguistic competence.
In literature and culture courses, the student is introduced to the use of critical and analytical tools necessary to define their learning path in future academic and professional contexts. In language and multimedia laboratories, the student is guided in the knowledge of information technology tools for dissemination and support in learning foreign literatures, cultures, and languages, useful also for lifelong learning. Within each cultural field of study, the student is encouraged to identify their interests and characteristics of their "learning style" to become aware of their abilities and possibilities for future learning contexts, including the potential choice of the field for master's studies. Self-assessment tools, such as various European Portfolios, are also used for linguistic competence.
Professional role in work context.
Professional role in work context:
The Bachelor's Degree in Linguistic and Cultural Mediation aims to provide mastery of written and oral communication in two modern languages and knowledge of their specific literary, artistic, and cultural manifestations; the training is completed with adequate knowledge of general linguistics and Italian literature and linguistics. Historical, philological, geographical, demoethnoanthropological, and computer science disciplines are also provided. These three-year studies contribute to forming graduates who, leveraging their competencies, can find professional opportunities in all public or private sectors of international relations where specialists in linguistic, literary, and documentary disciplines are required (archivists and librarians with foreign language skills, editors of foreign language texts). They may also find employment in any other linguistic assistance activities for businesses (domestic and international markets) and within institutions in various fields, including publishing, tourism, and journalism.
After the three-year Bachelor's Degree in Linguistic and Cultural Mediation, students may continue studies in Master's Degrees in Modern European and American Languages and Literatures (LM 37) and Modern Languages for Communication and International Cooperation (LM 38).
Associated professional competencies.
Associated professional competencies:
The course provides professional opportunities in multiple sectors requiring foreign language skills: international relations at public and corporate levels, translation activities, correspondence in foreign languages, linguistic assistance in private and public bodies operating in multilingual and multicultural contexts, cultural services, publishing, European and international institutions, cultural tourism, and multietnic and multicultural mediation.
After the three-year Bachelor's Degree in Linguistic and Cultural Mediation, students may continue studies in Master's Degrees in Modern European and American Languages and Literatures (LM 37) and Modern Languages for Communication and International Cooperation (LM 38).
Professional status conferred by the degree.
Employment opportunities:
- Editor, tourism, journalism, multimedia, and cultural sector operator;
- Linguistic assistance for businesses: commercial relations with international markets;
- Linguistic and cultural mediator in public services;
- Language experts in libraries, cultural foundations, superintendencies, archives, museums, private and public administrations, cultural institutions, international bodies, and national organizations for communication development in multietnic contexts;
- Language experts capable of managing relations with foreign and national institutions within cultural-touristic circuits and leisure organization.

ITALIAN Degree awarded.
Degree in MATHEMATICS Specific educational objectives.
Specific educational objectives:
The study program aims to provide a solid foundational preparation in Mathematics in both theoretical and applied contexts. Additionally, a basic preparation in Physics is provided along with an initial approach to Computer Science. More specifically, it aims to enable students to achieve:
- Basic mathematical knowledge (analysis and geometry, algebra)
- Basic knowledge of classical Physics: mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, optics;
- Basic knowledge of Computer Science;
- Knowledge of characteristic techniques of analysis, geometry, algebra, numerical analysis, and probability;
- Knowledge of the basics of mathematical modeling: mechanics, analytical mechanics, classic mathematical models of physics;
- Deepening of specific mathematical techniques.
Achieving these objectives is designed to allow the graduate in three-year Mathematics to access any Master's degree in Mathematics, and in other scientific fields with possible academic deficiencies, to specific training paths for teaching, and to intermediate positions in companies and organizations utilizing quantitative skills (banks and insurance companies, statistical agencies, computer companies).
The study program is structured over three years, with the first year focusing mainly on basic theoretical training and the second year on more characteristic training. The first two years do not allow for optional courses as they are considered indispensable in the formation of any mathematician. The third year allows for the selection of exams in characteristic and related fields that use mathematical tools to broaden the graduate's perspective on job opportunities.
Objective of the first year is the acquisition of basic knowledge and elementary techniques, which students will learn to apply to some simple but significant problems.
Objective of the second year is the acquisition of some more characteristic techniques as well as knowledge of some fundamental models in each of the above-mentioned fields.
Objective of the third year is the completion of preparation with more advanced material and the selection of courses in related and integrative subjects. Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding Graduates in Mathematics must have a good understanding of the most important mathematical techniques and a good knowledge of their applications in Physics, with brief references to other fields such as Biology and Finance. At the end of the program, they must be able to read an advanced text in a chosen mathematical field.
More specifically, they must have:
- Basic mathematical knowledge (analysis and geometry, algebra)
- Basic knowledge of classical Physics: mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, optics;
- Basic knowledge of Computer Science;
- Knowledge of characteristic techniques of analysis, geometry, algebra, numerical analysis, and probability;
- Knowledge of the basics of mathematical modeling: mechanics, analytical mechanics, classic mathematical models of physics;
- Deepening of specific mathematical techniques.
II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding Graduates must be able to apply their knowledge and understanding in a way that demonstrates a professional approach to their work, and must possess adequate skills to design and support arguments and solve problems in their field of study.
They must be able to identify the essential elements of a simple problem and model it mathematically. They must also be able to understand and use appropriate analytical and numerical methods for the topics addressed.
More specifically, they must acquire:
- Ability to pursue rigorous deductive logical reasoning and reproduce proofs;
- Ability to conceive simple proofs;
- Ability to understand relatively complex mathematical texts;
- Ability to mathematically model non-complex problems;
- Medium-high computational abilities;
- Ability to communicate and explain basic mathematical concepts and structures.
Specific skills:
- Ability to construct logical reasoning with identification of assumptions and conclusions even in non-mathematical contexts.
- Specific theoretical and practical calculation abilities
- Ability to formulate mathematical problems to facilitate their solution.
The expected results are achieved and verified as follows
- Learning methods: Courses with axiomatic treatments. Extensive practice of numerical exercises and calculation activities.
- Verification methods: All written verification tests require the application of knowledge to problems not previously addressed.
III - Judgment autonomy Graduates must be able to critically analyze a proof. Additionally, they must be able to conduct independent bibliographic research using mathematical content books, developing familiarity with sector scientific journals. Finally, they must be able to use available electronic archives for scientific research, performing the necessary information selection.
Learning methods: These abilities result from exercise courses and some theoretical courses Verification methods: In intermediate and exam tests, students are required to solve mathematical problems of theoretical and computational type independently. A good degree of independence is also required in the elaboration and writing of the thesis.
IV - Communication skills Graduates must be able to present their research or the results of a bibliographic research to both specialist and non-specialist audiences. For this purpose, it is important to have sufficient English knowledge for understanding scientific texts, through participation in English courses specific to the Faculty of Sciences.
Learning methods: Training activities carried out through group work and preparation of reports or short papers. Preparation of written and oral presentation of the final exam.
Verification methods: Evaluation of presentation ability during oral exam tests. Presentation of the thesis.
V - Learning ability Graduates must have acquired an understanding of the nature and methods of using mathematics and how it applies to many fields. They must also be able to construct simple proofs and modify standard proofs to adapt them to new situations.
Learning methods: Students are guided in improving their study methods from the first year by teachers and tutors. English is learned in specific courses and through progressive use of the foreign language in learning.
Verification methods: An incorrect study method does not allow students to undertake the degree program. Evaluation of learning of topics proposed for independent study.
Workplace function.
Workplace function:
The Mathematics graduate acquires knowledge and skills suitable for performing support professional activities in various fields and the qualification to continue studies in a Master's degree in Mathematics and Level I Master's. To achieve greater autonomy and responsibility in work, additional competencies must be acquired through a Master's degree.
In particular, the Mathematics graduate applies acquired knowledge to problems from technological, scientific, and economic-financial fields, developing mathematical models and creating the necessary software to solve real problems. Additionally, they can perform scientific dissemination activities.
Skills associated with the function.
Skills associated with the function:
- Specific theoretical and practical calculation abilities.
- Creativity and qualities of intuition and analysis.
- Project and planning abilities.
- Communication abilities to promote good dissemination of mathematical disciplines.
- Proficiency in using scientific software, particularly mathematical and statistical software.
Professional status conferred by the degree.
Employment opportunities:
One of the natural opportunities after a three-year Mathematics degree is to continue studies with a Master's degree in Mathematics, Mathematical Engineering, or possibly in other scientific disciplines, possibly with additional academic requirements to fill necessary prerequisites. Professional opportunities are also possible as support roles, for example in banks and credit institutions, insurance companies, survey institutes, software design and development companies.

Program, textbooks and objectives Official teaching and assessment languages.
ITALIAN
Degree awarded.
Degree in LOGOPEDIA
Specific educational objectives.
Within the health profession of logopedist, graduates are health professionals entitled to the responsibilities specified by the Ministry of Health Decree of September 14, 1994, No. 742 and subsequent amendments and integrations; or they carry out their activities in the prevention and rehabilitative treatment of language and communication disorders in developmental, adult, and geriatric age. The activities of logopedist graduates focus on the education and re-education of all conditions causing voice, speech, oral and written language, and communication disabilities. They, in reference to the diagnosis and prescription of the physician, within their scope of competence, develop, also in a multidisciplinary team, the logopedic assessment aimed at identifying and overcoming the health needs of the disabled; independently carry out therapeutic activities for the functional re-education of communication and cognitive disabilities, using logopedic rehabilitation and enabling therapies for communication and language, verbal and non-verbal; propose the adoption of aids, train users in their use, and verify their effectiveness; carry out study, teaching, and professional consulting activities in health services and in those requiring their professional skills; verify the alignment of the rehabilitation methodology implemented with the functional recovery goals; carry out their professional activities in health structures, public or private, in dependent or self-employed status. The academic curriculum must include teaching on radioprotection according to the contents of Annex IV of Legislative Decree No. 187 of May 26, 2000. The academic curriculum must include training activities as per Article 10, Paragraph 5, Letters a), c), d), e) of Ministerial Decree No. 270 of October 22, 2004, with the following ECTS credits: 6 chosen by the student; 9 for the final exam and English language; 6 for other activities such as computer science, seminars, etc.; and 3 for professional laboratories of the specific SSD of the profile (MED/50); finally, 60 ECTS, as per current regulations, are reserved for the training internship in the specific professional profile.
Graduates in Logopedics must possess:
- Good knowledge of the fundamentals of prerequisite disciplines (physics, statistics, computer science, sociology, and general pedagogy), molecular biology sciences, and integrated biological functions of human organs and systems (biochemistry, biology, general and specific anatomy and physiology);
- In-depth knowledge of disciplines characterizing the logopedist profession (medical and applied technical sciences, child neuropsychiatry, linguistics and phonology, theories and philosophy of language and communication, general and clinical psychology, otolaryngology, audiology and phoniatrics, neurology);
- In-depth knowledge of disciplines within the physiology, etiology, and pathology of language, communication, and swallowing in developmental, adult, and geriatric age, neurological and degenerative disorders of cognitive and language functions, linguistics, language development theories, philosophy of language, and methodologies for logopedic assessment and rehabilitation;
- Ability to independently carry out prevention, assessment, and functional rehabilitation activities for communication, linguistic, and cognitive disabilities, applying different assessment and intervention methodologies, planning timelines, and verifying outcomes, evaluating and preparing the appropriate rehabilitation setting for therapy or therapeutic exercises to ensure optimal conditions for both the patient and the therapist;
- Knowledge of human sciences and psycho-pedagogical sciences to understand, establish, and maintain relationships with the user, family, and social context;
- Ability to implement educational, preventive, care, and self-management activities for disability;
- Knowledge of health management sciences and business organization, as well as interdisciplinary and clinical sciences;
- Familiarity with the scientific method and ability to apply clinical recommendations in concrete situations with adequate knowledge of regulations and ethical and bioethical issues;
- Ability to work in a multidisciplinary team, interact with colleagues and other health professionals, operate with defined levels of autonomy, and integrate into work environments;
- Knowledge necessary to use methodologies and tools for quality control, assessment, and review;
- Knowledge to participate in various forms of professional updating, as well as to engage in research activities in different application areas, carry out teaching, and provide professional consulting;
- Ability to use English language within their specific area of competence and for general information exchange;
- Knowledge of communication and information management tools, as well as to propose the adoption of aids, train users in their use, and verify effectiveness, demonstrating ability to draft technical-scientific reports.
The Project prioritizes the theoretical/practical study of Logopedic Sciences, implemented through frontal lectures, exercises, and teaching laboratories, as well as professional internship in areas qualifying Logopedics, such as the assessment and functional recovery of communication, language, and swallowing in all age groups and rehabilitation contexts. The necessary relational competencies to interact with the user, family, institutional system, and professional environment are developed through human sciences, psycho-pedagogical courses, and personal training within the internship path aimed at acquiring essential behaviors and attitudes in therapeutic relationships and interaction with the multidisciplinary team.
Courses are structured into modules and delivered through frontal lectures, classroom or laboratory exercises. Learning outcomes are assessed through optional self-assessment tests for students and a final oral, practical, or written exam, which verifies the achievement of objectives, unique and simultaneous for each course, necessary for acquiring ECTS credits. All courses are evaluated with a grade out of thirty.
Regarding professional internship activities, objectives align with the Professional Profile and academic curriculum, as detailed in the Internship Form approved by the Course Council.
Students have access to 6 ECTS for preparing the final exam, which can be acquired at institutions dedicated to training.
Graduates in this class are health professionals whose specific field of activity and responsibility is determined by the contents of ministerial decrees establishing professional profiles and academic curricula of respective university courses and post-basic training, as well as specific ethical codes.
Upon completion of the training path, the logopedist must have acquired knowledge (knowing), competencies (knowing how), and relational abilities (knowing how to be), particularly in the following areas:
PROFESSIONAL RESPONSIBILITY: This area translates the professional logopedist's assumption of responsibility in all professional actions through the achievement of the following competencies: in professional conduct, learn to act respecting the professional profile, ethical code, and regulations related to the profession, develop specific competencies regarding the individual and family, learn to act in the patient's interest by recognizing their motivations, autonomy, and abilities, and independently practice clinical activities respecting the patient's interests and those of other professionals.
CARE AND REHABILITATION: This area refers to competencies students must possess to gather objective and subjective information through standardized tools, interviews, and observations to identify logopedic rehabilitation needs of individuals and communities. Collaborate in drafting the rehabilitation project, plan logopedic care and rehabilitation interventions, define the rehabilitation program, identify the most suitable therapeutic methods for the patient, identifying strategies for treating oral and written language, hearing, communicative-social, cognitive, praxic, and swallowing disorders in all age groups. Verify the need for aids to improve daily life. Implement rehabilitation interventions according to the project/program. Draft the rehabilitation program in writing with short, medium, and long-term goals, share it with the patient and family, establish the therapeutic contract. Evaluate outcomes and responses of the rehabilitation intervention, recording changes, prevent and address critical situations, implement targeted interventions for critical situations. Ensure patient safety and application of risk-free interventions in accordance with current regulations. Adapt and modify interventions during the rehabilitation process respecting the patient's needs. Evaluate logopedic interventions during the rehabilitation process.
THERAPEUTIC EDUCATION: This is the health activity of the logopedist aimed at developing awareness and responsibility in individuals or groups, realized through therapeutic education interventions, establishing a supportive relationship to assist the patient and family. Additionally, instruct the patient and family to learn self-care and functional recovery skills. Evaluate the educational needs of the patient and family and assess adherence to the educational project during the process.
PREVENTION: The logopedist must be able to identify health needs and disability prevention through: identifying potentially risky situations through targeted screenings for early detection of language and communication disorders, hearing, and oral functions in all age groups. In particular, this area is an integral part of the rehabilitation program, involving the logopedist in activities aimed at identifying and overcoming risks for the individual and community through investigations, screenings, and follow-ups.
MANAGEMENT: Includes all management tools (resources, information, economic aspects) necessary for the correct implementation of the logopedist's daily actions through the following actions: identify the nature of the problem, analyze, choose, and interpret, identify problem resolution through possible collaborations. In managing their work, recognize and respect roles and competencies, interact and collaborate with multidisciplinary teams, use General Guidelines and protocols to standardize operational methods. In clinical risk management, identify and report difficulties. Use information systems and computer tools to analyze data.
TRAINING/AUTOTRAINING: This is the context where the logopedist forms, develops, and consolidates their cultural foundations through the following competencies: identify learning and training objectives in the training path with coordinator and tutor, evaluate the achievement of objectives. Take responsibility for their own training and professional development, self-assess objective achievement, reflect and self-assess in implementing their knowledge and skills.
COMMUNICATION AND RELATIONSHIP: This area defines the relational substrate through which the logopedist applies their professional practice in rehabilitation and social/institutional contexts, through communication and relationship competencies with the user and their family, active listening, and management of relational dynamics. Interact with other professionals, coordinators, tutors, and operators from other structures.
TRAINING PATH: The set of knowledge acquired by the graduate, totaling 180 ECTS, will constitute the necessary cultural, scientific, and relational background to achieve full professional competence, understand, address, and manage pathological events requiring rehabilitation and/or therapeutic intervention, acquired through participation in frontal lectures, laboratory exercises, practical lessons in equipped classrooms with rehabilitation aids, guided by teachers and tutors, as well as personal study (library, databases) of the subjects offered by the CL. In particular, through biochemical, physical, statistical, anatomical, physiological, pathological, clinical, surgical, psychological, and sociological competencies, they will acquire a solid foundation of knowledge of the biological functions of human organs and systems, statistical methodology for detecting phenomena regulating individual and social human life, and concepts of emergency and first aid in close interaction with disciplines characterizing the CL. They will also build the professional construct through characterizing competencies in logopedic, linguistic, child neuropsychiatric, psychological, neurological, and neuropsychological sciences.
In relation to these specific training objectives, the training activity, predominantly organized in "Specific Courses," ensures a unified and at the same time interdisciplinary vision of the didactic objectives, with in-depth knowledge derived from characterizing disciplines, including those more specifically professionalizing and other disciplinary areas.
Pursuant to Ministerial Decree, February 19, 2009, each activated course provides an integer number of ECTS credits to avoid information fragmentation for students. The teaching methods include frontal lectures, seminars, group work, and discussions on relevant topics and simulations to pursue the training path objectives. The teaching process will utilize modern teaching tools. Traditional teaching activity is complemented by guided internship activity at specialized public health services and other scientifically significant structures, both in Italy and abroad through specific agreements. Laboratory and internship activities are conducted under the supervision and guidance of professional tutors specifically designated based on communication skills, specifically trained for this function, assigned to each student. Laboratory and internship activities are coordinated by a teacher with the highest educational level and belonging to the professional profile corresponding to the degree course.
The study plan provides a maximum of 20 exams, i.e., final profit assessments, organized as oral and written tests for modules and courses.
Exam procedures are structured not only in traditional final oral and written exams but also in a sequence of in-course assessments.
Written exams use:
1) Multiple-choice tests or short written answers;
2) Preparation of reports.
The training path is structured, monitored, validated, and optimized in a continuum to acquire the competencies, knowledge, and skills specified in the curriculum profile established by current regulations and the specific objectives of the Course. These specific educational objectives are supported by a faculty aware of the need to use all institutional tools activated by competent bodies (NVF and NVA) for the accreditation of teaching quality. Through these tools, it is possible to measure improvements in teaching performance in all different phases contributing to the acquisition of the first-level degree, in terms of training path, exams, perceived quality assessment by students, and acquisition of professional competencies specified in the training path objectives.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding At the end of the training path, logopedics graduates must demonstrate knowledge and understanding in the following fields:
- Biomedical sciences for understanding physiological and pathological processes related to the development and alterations of voice, speech, language, fluency, hearing, and swallowing across different life ages;
- Psycho-social and humanistic sciences for understanding cognitive and social aspects of communication, as well as psychological, relational, and cultural dynamics related to speech, language, hearing, and swallowing disorders; learning theories to improve understanding of educational processes for citizens or individual patients;
- General and specific logopedic sciences for understanding the fields of logopedic intervention, methods for assessing communicative and hearing functions, rehabilitation methodologies, and evidence guiding decision-making;
- Ethical, legal, and sociological sciences for understanding the organizational complexity of the Health System, the importance and utility of acting in compliance with regulations and guidelines, and respecting values and ethical dilemmas encountered in daily practice; aimed at fostering understanding of professional autonomy, areas of integration and interdependence with other members of the care team;
- Hygienic-preventive sciences for understanding health determinants, risk factors, individual and collective prevention strategies, and interventions to promote safety for health professionals and users;
- Computer and linguistic disciplines with particular emphasis on English language for understanding professional scientific literature, both printed and online.
Teaching methodologies and tools to develop expected outcomes:
- Lectures to introduce the topic;
- Guided reading and application;
- Videos, image demonstrations, diagrams, and materials.
Assessment tools to verify achievement of expected outcomes:
- Written and oral exams, practical tests.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding Logopedics graduates must demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the following processes:
- Use clinical knowledge and linguistic theories to assess alterations in language, cognitive, and swallowing functions, and the effects of hearing loss on communication development;
- Select and use appropriate assessment procedures, utilizing validated psychometric tools;
- Accurately analyze and interpret data collected through assessment, integrating with patient history information;
- Integrate knowledge, skills, and attitudes of logopedics to implement safe, effective, evidence-based rehabilitation interventions;
- Develop appropriate therapeutic and rehabilitation plans with measurable and achievable goals, adapted to different ages and considering cultural and linguistic differences;
- Measure and evaluate patient performance in collaboration with the interdisciplinary team;
- Modify the therapeutic plan based on the patient's needs;
- Assume responsibility for providing logopedic interventions in line with professional quality standards, considering legal, ethical implications, and the rights of the assisted person;
- Interpret and apply research results to logopedic practice;
- Use pedagogical and psychological knowledge to motivate patients to treatment and propose effective educational strategies.
Teaching methodologies and tools to develop expected outcomes:
- Lectures;
- Theoretical application exercises;
- Videos, use of images, diagrams, and materials;
- Case discussions in subgroups with presentations in plenary sessions;
- Internship with supervised experiences in various contexts and progressive assumption of autonomy and responsibility.
Assessment tools to verify achievement of expected outcomes:
- Written and oral exams, practical tests, project work, reports;
- Feedback during internship (through portfolio, structured evaluation forms, and clinical reports on professional practice).
III - Independent Judgment Logopedics graduates must demonstrate independent judgment through the following abilities:
- Practice logopedic rehabilitation treatments while recognizing and respecting the dignity, culture, values, and rights of individuals;
- Use critical thinking skills to deliver effective interventions to users across different ages;
- Assume responsibility and account for their professional practice in accordance with the profile, ethical code, and ethical and legal standards;
- Demonstrate awareness of the influence of personal feelings, values, and biases on the relationship with the patient and decision-making.
Teaching methodologies and tools to develop expected outcomes:
- Lectures;
- Guided reading and application exercises;
- Case discussions in subgroups with presentations in plenary sessions;
- Internship with supervised experiences in various contexts and progressive assumption of autonomy and responsibility.
Assessment tools to verify achievement of expected outcomes:
- Written and oral exams, staged case tests;
- Feedback during internship (through portfolio, structured evaluation forms, and clinical reports on professional practice).
IV - Communication Skills Logopedics graduates must develop the following communication skills:
- Listen, inform, and dialogue effectively with patients and families;
- Communicate, argue, and motivate their actions and decisions with colleagues and different professional figures;
- Adapt communication according to context while respecting cultural, ethnic differences, and values of the assisted persons;
- Implement logopedic counseling techniques for communication in complex situations to activate client resources and capabilities, involving family and caregivers in the rehabilitation process;
- Use documentation tools for clinical-rehabilitation activities.
Teaching methodologies and tools to develop expected outcomes:
- Lectures;
- Videos and critical analysis of films, simulations, narratives, testimonials;
- Case and relational situation discussions in subgroups with presentations in plenary sessions;
- Internship with supervised experiences in various contexts with debriefing sessions to reflect on and reprocess relational experiences with users and the team.
Assessment tools to verify achievement of expected outcomes:
- Observation of films or dialogues using structured grids;
- Feedback during internship (through portfolio, structured evaluation forms, and clinical reports).
V - Learning Ability Logopedics graduates must develop the following self-learning abilities:
- Develop independent study skills;
- Demonstrate ability and autonomy in seeking information necessary to resolve professional practice problems or uncertainties, consulting current literature and promoting its application in logopedic practice;
- Demonstrate knowledge of research methods related to language and cognitive therapy issues;
- Demonstrate continuous ability to seek self-learning opportunities;
- Demonstrate ability to self-assess their competencies and outline their needs for updating and learning.
Teaching tools, methodologies, and activities to develop expected outcomes:
- Use of learning contracts and self-training plans to empower students in planning their internship path and self-assessment;
- Research methodology workshops for printed and online literature;
- Guided reading for critical evaluation of scientific and professional literature in Italian and English.
Assessment tools to verify achievement of expected outcomes:
- Project work, reports on specific research mandates;
- Tutorial supervision of the internship path;
- Active participation in work and debriefing sessions.
Workplace Function.
Workplace Function:
Graduates in this class are health professionals whose specific field of activity and responsibility is determined by the contents of ministerial decrees establishing professional profiles and academic curricula of respective university courses and post-basic training, as well as specific ethical codes.
Upon completion of the training path, the logopedist must have acquired knowledge (knowing), competencies (knowing how), and relational abilities (knowing how to be), particularly in the following areas:
PROFESSIONAL RESPONSIBILITY: This area translates the professional logopedist's assumption of responsibility in all professional actions through the achievement of the following competencies: in professional conduct, learn to act respecting the professional profile, ethical code, and regulations related to the profession, develop specific competencies regarding the individual and family, learn to act in the patient's interest by recognizing their motivations, autonomy, and abilities, and independently practice clinical activities respecting the patient's interests and those of other professionals.
CARE AND REHABILITATION: This area refers to competencies students must possess to gather objective and subjective information through standardized tools, interviews, and observations to identify logopedic rehabilitation needs of individuals and communities. Collaborate in drafting the rehabilitation project, plan logopedic care and rehabilitation interventions, define the rehabilitation program, identify the most suitable therapeutic methods for the patient, identifying strategies for treating oral and written language, hearing, communicative-social, cognitive, praxic, and swallowing disorders in all age groups. Verify the need for aids to improve daily life. Implement rehabilitation interventions according to the project/program. Draft the rehabilitation program in writing with short, medium, and long-term goals, share it with the patient and family, establish the therapeutic contract. Evaluate outcomes and responses of the rehabilitation intervention, recording changes, prevent and address critical situations, implement targeted interventions for critical situations. Ensure patient safety and application of risk-free interventions in accordance with current regulations. Adapt and modify interventions during the rehabilitation process respecting the patient's needs. Evaluate logopedic interventions during the rehabilitation process.
THERAPEUTIC EDUCATION: This is the health activity of the logopedist aimed at developing awareness and responsibility in individuals or groups, realized through therapeutic education interventions, establishing a supportive relationship to assist the patient and family. Additionally, instruct the patient and family to learn self-care and functional recovery skills. Evaluate the educational needs of the patient and family and assess adherence to the educational project during the process.
PREVENTION: The logopedist must be able to identify health needs and disability prevention through: identifying potentially risky situations through targeted screenings for early detection of language and communication disorders, hearing, and oral functions in all age groups. In particular, this area is an integral part of the rehabilitation program, involving the logopedist in activities aimed at identifying and overcoming risks for the individual and community through investigations, screenings, and follow-ups.
MANAGEMENT: Includes all management tools (resources, information, economic aspects) necessary for the correct implementation of the logopedist's daily actions through the following actions: identify the nature of the problem, analyze, choose, and interpret, identify problem resolution through possible collaborations. In managing their work, recognize and respect roles and competencies, interact and collaborate with multidisciplinary teams, use General Guidelines and protocols to standardize operational methods. In clinical risk management, identify and report difficulties. Use information systems and computer tools to analyze data.
TRAINING/AUTOTRAINING: This is the context where the logopedist forms, develops, and consolidates their cultural foundations through the following competencies: identify learning and training objectives in the training path with coordinator and tutor, evaluate the achievement of objectives. Take responsibility for their own training and professional development, self-assess objective achievement, reflect and self-assess in implementing their knowledge and skills.
COMMUNICATION AND RELATIONSHIP: This area defines the relational substrate through which the logopedist applies their professional practice in rehabilitation and social/institutional contexts, through communication and relationship competencies with the user and their family, active listening, and management of relational dynamics. Interact with other professionals, coordinators, tutors, and operators from other structures.
Associated Competencies.
Associated Competencies:
The logopedist is placed within the National and Regional Health Service in dependent or self-employed form. Additionally, this figure finds opportunities in accredited private structures, clinics, rehabilitation centers, as well as in state educational structures or local authorities.
Professional status conferred by the degree.
Employment opportunities:
The logopedist is placed within the National and Regional Health Service in dependent or self-employed form. Additionally, this figure finds opportunities in accredited private structures, clinics, rehabilitation centers, as well as in state educational structures or local authorities.
