ITALIAN Degree Awarded.
Bachelor's Degree in INDUSTRIAL ENGINEERING Specific Educational Objectives.
The Bachelor's Degree Course in Industrial Engineering trains graduates with a solid foundation in basic disciplines, fundamental industrial engineering subjects, and transversal knowledge across different fields, emphasizing methodological aspects. The educational objectives can be summarized as follows:
- Knowledge of mathematical tools, fundamental physical and chemical sciences useful for understanding engineering applications. These subjects are taught in the first year across mathematics, computer science, and statistics, physics, and chemistry.
- Knowledge of the fundamentals of technical sciences and methodologies used in industrial engineering; operational knowledge and skills at a good level in cross-disciplinary engineering aspects: electrotechnics, applied mechanics, materials science, computer science, heat and mass transfer phenomena, thermo-fluid dynamics, machines, structural science, technical representation methods, economic and organizational aspects of companies. These subjects are primarily classified under "characterizing activities" and grouped into four distinct disciplinary areas. They are mainly delivered in the second year and form a homogeneous set of transversal content relative to the curriculum in which the study program is structured;
- Specialized knowledge for six industrial fields (better identified in the teaching regulations) delivered through corresponding curricula. These knowledge areas guide students toward roles as Junior Engineers or progression into master's programs in the following classes: LM22 Chemical Engineering; LM28 Electrical Engineering; LM31 Management Engineering; LM33 Mechanical Engineering; LM21 Biomedical Engineering. These subjects are primarily classified under "affine or integrative training activities" and grouped into affinity areas based on the curricula in which the study program is structured:
- Biomedical Engineering (affinity area A16);
- Chemical Engineering (affinity area A14);
- Electrical Engineering (affinity area A13);
- Industrial Electronics Engineering (affinity area A15);
- Management Engineering (affinity area A12);
- Mechanical Engineering (affinity area A11).
Additionally, the following are fundamental to the educational objectives:
- Knowledge of technical vocabulary, technical language properties (including English), and ability to interact with specialists in various industrial sectors;
- Ability to independently address complex problems and operate across diverse industrial sectors requiring interdisciplinary competencies;
- Ability to operate in rapidly evolving fields with operational versatility and a proactive attitude toward continuous knowledge and skill updates.
Achieving these objectives will qualify graduates for progression into master's studies and entry into the workforce. They will possess competencies suitable for initial technical roles and the ability to adapt their skills to the specific professional needs of their context.
The achievement of these objectives is planned across a common first year delivering basic scientific disciplines. A second year delivering a common core of industrial engineering disciplines alongside completion of basic scientific training. A third year focused on specialization in one of the reference industrial fields, completing engineering knowledge with differentiated content depending on the chosen curriculum. For this purpose, the bachelor's degree is structured into curricula.
Mandatory courses are complemented by free-choice courses allowing students to tailor their educational path to personal interests. While students retain freedom to make individual choices, suggested options are provided to integrate the general educational plan in a structured manner.
The achievement of objectives is pursued through a structured educational activity comprising modules involving lectures, laboratory exercises, and individual study, leading to credits earned through passing examinations. Activities are designed to stimulate teamwork, interpersonal relationships, and communication skills.
The program is delivered in Italian, though some courses may be offered in English.
At the time of entry assessment, English language proficiency will be verified. A B2 level (CEFR) or IELTS score of at least 6 or equivalent certification is required; such certification is recognized for 3 CFU. Students who do not meet this requirement will be provided with a dedicated course in the first year to reach the required English proficiency level.
Additional training credits (Article 10, Paragraph 5, Letter d) may be earned through specialized courses or internships, which can be conducted in university laboratories or (particularly for students not planning to pursue further studies) in companies under formal agreements.
Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and Understanding Upon completion of the program, students will have acquired:
- Knowledge and understanding of mathematical principles, basic sciences, and applied sciences underlying industrial engineering;
- Systematic understanding of key aspects and concepts in typical industrial engineering fields;
- Clear knowledge of the fundamental technical aspects of industrial engineering in general;
- Depending on the chosen educational path, knowledge of the technical content qualifying a specific industrial field, including some knowledge of the most recent applied developments;
- Awareness of the broader multidisciplinary context of engineering.
The methodological training and necessary information to acquire the above competencies are distributed in a coordinated and progressive manner across courses and other educational activities. Verification of knowledge and understanding is conducted organically through all assessment activities planned throughout the program, with careful attention to prerequisite planning.
II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding Upon completion of the program, students will have acquired:
- Ability to apply acquired knowledge and understanding to identify, formulate, and solve engineering problems using established methods;
- Ability to apply acquired knowledge and understanding to analyze products, processes, and methods of engineering;
- Ability to choose and apply analytical and modeling methods appropriately and consciously.
These abilities are developed through exercises, which also foster teamwork skills (group work within assignments and small projects) and technical-practical skills through laboratory activities.
Verification of the ability to apply knowledge is conducted through written and/or oral examinations, particularly through project-based assessments in relevant disciplines.
Alongside these intermediate assessments, the final thesis discussion represents the concluding moment to evaluate the candidate's ability to apply acquired knowledge and present results for a case study.
III - Independent Judgment Upon completion of the program, students will have acquired:
- Ability to evaluate, interpret, and reprocess literature data, select and use data and other information sources relevant to the assigned task;
- Ability to operate in an application context, select equipment, tools, and methods, and identify, design, and conduct experiments, interpret data, and draw conclusions;
- Ability to combine the right balance of theory and practice to solve engineering problems;
- Ability to interpret technical documentation of industrial products, plants, and processes, understand their techniques, applicable methods, and general feasibility;
- Ability to identify, consult, and interpret laws, regulations, and technical instructions applicable to industrial engineering problems;
- Knowledge of legal aspects of engineering practice;
- Knowledge of industrial activities' responsibilities regarding worker safety and well-being;
- Awareness of the social and environmental impact of engineering solutions;
- Full awareness of professional ethics in exercising responsibilities and respecting engineering practice norms;
- Awareness of non-technical implications of engineering practice.
The ability for independent judgment is verified during course delivery following lectures and exercises, and during the final assessment. Some courses include a project component and/or laboratory activities, allowing evaluation of the student's judgment when facing design choices or equipment selection during experimental procedures. The final thesis, with its preparation activities, aims to develop independent judgment within a specific assigned topic under the guidance of a thesis supervisor.
IV - Communication Skills The bachelor's degree aims to develop the following communication skills:
- Ability to communicate clearly and logically to both specialists and non-specialists;
- Ability to manage relationships with diverse stakeholders, specialists and non-specialists;
- Ability to work in teams, including interdisciplinary teams;
- Language knowledge enabling international openness.
Communication skills are exercised and assessed at various stages of the educational process:
- During teaching activities through presentation of exercise results;
- During examinations assessing not only acquired knowledge but also expression and correct use of technical language;
- During specialized courses organized by the program requiring students to prepare and present a report on interdisciplinary industrial engineering topics, possibly in collaboration with other students;
- During the preparation and presentation of the final thesis, where students engage in a full bachelor's thesis; completeness, synthesis ability, and language property will be evaluated.
The assessment of communication skills contributes to the final grade of examinations and the final thesis.
V - Learning Ability Upon completion of the program, students will have acquired:
- Awareness of the rapid evolution of technological and scientific knowledge and the consequent need to adapt their skills through continuous learning, to be pursued autonomously throughout their professional career;
- Ability to autonomously acquire new technical-scientific knowledge from scientific and technical literature in the specific field of industrial engineering and related disciplines.
This is achieved through a didactic approach focused on methodological rigor throughout the educational path, both in basic disciplines and in technical-scientific courses with practical applications. Teaching tools include traditional lectures and exercises, complemented by high-interaction student-teacher activities where students independently prepare project-related reports requiring autonomy in identifying required knowledge for assigned tasks. Individual study activities also include independent consultation of technical literature specific to the disciplinary areas.
Verification of learning ability is conducted through written and/or oral examinations, as well as other educational activities, particularly during the final thesis, which has the characteristics of a full bachelor's thesis conducted largely independently under the guidance of a tutor.
Workplace Function.
Workplace Function:
Graduates in Industrial Engineering from the University of L'Aquila are characterized by versatility derived from a training approach that prioritizes foundational industrial engineering and basic sciences over specialized content. The bachelor's degree is structured into distinct educational paths to align training with students' personal inclinations and employment expectations.
Industrial Engineers can exercise their operational capabilities across various sectors in the following roles:
- Operational functions related to a thorough understanding of mathematical tools and other basic sciences used to interpret and describe physical phenomena and typical industrial engineering problems;
- General functions related to foundational methodological and technological training accompanied by a solid cultural background in traditional industrial engineering disciplines, such as industrial technical drawing, economics and business organization, applied mechanics, structural science, applied thermodynamics and heat transfer, electrotechnics, materials science and technology, and machines;
- Complementary functions and ability to operate in initial responsibility roles, including coordination of business activities, thanks to knowledge of industrial contexts, processes, and associated economic, management, and organizational aspects;
- More specific functions depending on the chosen educational path among the six predefined for the sectors: Biomedical; Chemical; Electrical; Industrial Electronics; Management; Mechanical.
Skills Associated with the Role.
Skills Associated with the Role:
The skills developed for the Industrial Engineer role enable them to operate across various industrial engineering fields with competencies that make them immediately employable. Graduates can immediately work in areas requiring the use or production of technical product documentation, analysis, and understanding of content related to product or industrial plant systems, having acquired knowledge of recurring content. They possess knowledge of systems for energy production, transformation, and utilization. Skills related to momentum, energy, and mass transfer phenomena make Industrial Engineering graduates suitable for understanding and addressing various practical problems across different industrial applications, regardless of the specific sector.
Skills related to economic-management systems and typical process engineering aspects enable graduates to operate effectively in production and service provision contexts for companies.
The six educational paths within the bachelor's program allow for skill adaptation to target the Biomedical, Chemical, Electrical, Industrial Electronics, Management, and Mechanical sectors, as well as providing the necessary knowledge for progression into Master's programs in Chemical, Electrical, Electronics, Management, and Mechanical Engineering.
Professional Status Conferred by the Degree.
Employment Prospects:
Graduates in Industrial Engineering can pursue careers in manufacturing, process, or service companies, public administrations, or as independent professionals. After passing the state exam, graduates can register with the Engineers' Register Section B, Industrial Sector (Junior Engineer).
Industrial Engineering graduates, thanks to their solid foundational training and interdisciplinary technical and scientific culture, have broad and varied employment opportunities. The profile is open to roles requiring high flexibility and intervention areas such as design, energy, management, and industrial production. Graduates can also work in independent or subordinate consulting roles in manufacturing, service companies, technical areas of public administrations, or public enterprises. They can enter the workforce promptly and effectively or further develop their knowledge through progression into a Master's program.
Specific employment prospects vary depending on the chosen educational path:
Graduates in the Biomedical Engineering path are prepared for employment in industrial and healthcare sectors utilizing advanced technologies for treatment, diagnosis, prevention of diseases, or assistance for disabilities or enhancement of natural human capabilities. Potential employment areas include design, production, and marketing of diagnostic, treatment, rehabilitation, and monitoring equipment, electromedical devices, implantable and portable devices, prostheses/orthoses, robotic systems for biomedical applications, artificial organs, functional support systems, and assistive devices for disabilities or bionics. In technical service management, systems for health information (including biomedical data and images), they can work in hospitals, specialized clinical laboratories, and public or private healthcare institutions' biomedical engineering services. They can also work in technical roles in sports, physical exercise, and entertainment sectors, in service companies for development, marketing, and management of biomedical equipment and systems, and in pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies.
Graduates in the Chemical Engineering path are characterized by in-depth knowledge of chemistry and chemical processes, enabling work across a wide range of production contexts, environmental protection, and public administration. Preferred employment sectors include chemical, food, pharmaceutical, chemical and biotechnological process industries, production and transformation of materials (metallic, polymeric, ceramic, glassy, and composite), and industrial laboratories. Graduates in this path are also employable in areas requiring the role of energy and safety manager.
Graduates in the Electrical Engineering path are characterized by in-depth knowledge of electromagnetism and its applications across various industrial sectors. Graduates can be effectively employed in all operational areas involving electrical systems and equipment, power electronics systems. Specifically, their profile enables roles in design, production, testing, management, control, and maintenance of electrical equipment and power electronic devices. They can also perform technical-commercial activities in industrial companies generally and electrical companies specifically. Major employment areas include industries producing components, equipment, and machinery for electrical and industrial power electronics systems; companies producing, transmitting, distributing, and marketing electrical energy; electrical-mechanical, manufacturing, and process industries; industries for automation and robotics, measurement and testing equipment; companies managing technical and energy services.
Graduates in the Industrial Electronics Engineering path are characterized by qualified training in industrial engineering integrated with electronic engineering. This preparation enables graduates to enter the workforce in operational areas of design or production of electronic systems and equipment, with particular reference to industrial applications. Major expected employment areas include companies operating in the industrial electronics sector (production of microelectronic components, domestic, industrial, and telecommunications devices), aerospace and space companies, companies producing equipment and systems for industrial process automation (mechanical, metallurgical, chemical, pharmaceutical, food, etc.), and automotive and home automation companies. Additionally, employment opportunities exist in companies and entities for the design, planning, operation, control, and management of highly complex automated systems, assets, and services.
Graduates in the Management Engineering path naturally find employment in all companies and activity areas where technological, economic, and innovation elements coexist. They can perform professional activities in various business functions (logistics, production, commercial, administrative) and can also effectively pursue independent practice (as business consultants) or entrepreneurial activities. This profile is particularly relevant for small and medium-sized manufacturing enterprises increasingly needing to manage complex processes with interconnected technological, organizational, and economic requirements. More specifically, graduates in Management Engineering will find placement in typically operational contexts with different roles depending on the industrial sector (mechanical, electronic, textile-apparel, wood, steel, paper production, etc.) and intervention area (production, quality, maintenance, safety, logistics, commercial, administrative, etc.). The roles graduates can assume span key business functions such as procurement and material management, organizational and production management, automation of production systems, manufacturing and distribution logistics, project management, management control, and investment evaluation.
Graduates in the Mechanical Engineering path are characterized by in-depth knowledge of methods and tools for industrial engineering and metal-mechanical processes, enabling work across a wide range of production contexts in various industrial sectors. Major employment areas for graduates in Mechanical Engineering include mechanical and electro-mechanical industries; companies and entities for energy conversion; plant construction companies; automation and robotics industries; manufacturing companies generally for production, installation, testing, maintenance, and management of machines, production lines, and complex systems. Graduates in Mechanical Engineering are destined for typically operational roles with different responsibilities depending on the industrial sector (mechanical, electronic, textile, wood, steel, paper production, etc.) and intervention area (production, maintenance, production services, technical offices, execution design, quality, safety, logistics, etc.).

Program, Texts, and Objectives Official languages of instruction and assessment.
ITALIAN
Degree awarded.
Degree in LETTERS
Specific educational objectives.
The bachelor's degree in Letters aims to achieve, also through the use of advanced textbooks, a solid foundational, methodological, and historical education in the fields of linguistic, philological, literary, historical, geographical, archaeological, and historical-artistic studies, to address the study of humanistic disciplines. This education, which also includes knowledge and understanding of some cutting-edge topics in the respective fields of study, will broadly cover developments from classical antiquity to the contemporary era, and will provide specific expertise within the chosen curriculum.

To achieve the aforementioned objectives, the bachelor's degree in Letters offers four curricula focused on clearly differentiated cultural areas, but which share a common foundation in belonging to what in cultural debate and in historiographical and academic tradition has been qualified as humanistic culture.

The Bachelor's Degree in Letters aims to provide an adequate spectrum of knowledge and skills:
- In the disciplines of classical antiquity, offering also a solid foundation in historical and literary fields from the Middle Ages to the contemporary era;
- In geographical disciplines (with particular attention to territory, cartography, and the international context), anthropological disciplines, and cultural and environmental heritage, also offering a solid foundation in foreign languages;
- In Italian and European literature and linguistics, also offering a solid foundation in history, geography, and art history;
- In historical-artistic disciplines, also offering a foundation in literature, linguistics, and history.

The Course prioritizes targeted training for the acquisition of fundamental knowledge useful for the critical understanding of knowledge related to different paths, and while leaving ample room for individual choices through the curricula, deliberately avoids proposing to the student within each curriculum a fragmented and scattered educational offer, not functional to a first-level course.

Dublin Descriptors:
I - Knowledge and Understanding
The Bachelor's Degree in Letters, as a whole, aims to train graduates capable of demonstrating secure knowledge and correct understanding of the themes and issues of humanistic culture, acquiring an adequate foundational education in linguistic, philological, and literary classical and modern, historical, historical-artistic, and geographical fields. Depending on the curriculum, the Course allows for differentiated deepening of specific knowledge and understanding:
- Literary, philological, historical, historical-artistic, and geographical knowledge ranging from antiquity to the contemporary era;
- Knowledge and understanding of the main methodologies of linguistic, philological, literary, geographical, historical, and historical-artistic analysis;
- Ability to understand and contextualize fundamental themes and issues of humanistic culture in various contexts (languages and cultures of antiquity; civilization from the Middle Ages to the contemporary era in its philological-linguistic, literary, historical-cultural aspects; arts from the Middle Ages to the contemporary era in relation to archaeology, music, cinema, and theater; main contemporary geographical themes at local and global levels).

The Course also develops good written and oral proficiency in at least one of the European Union languages in addition to Italian and allows the acquisition of the main information technology and telematic communication tools.

- Knowledge and understanding are primarily acquired through basic, characteristic, and related courses, which, differently distributed according to the chosen curriculum, on one hand aim to broaden the spectrum of knowledge in as interdisciplinary a perspective as possible, on the other hand allow appreciation of the specificity of the research methodologies required in various study fields. Courses are conducted through frontal and interactive lessons, also using multimedia tools. During lessons, institutional and methodological themes are presented, and aspects and problems related to the most up-to-date research in various disciplinary sectors are also introduced.

In addition to courses, knowledge and understanding are also acquired through:
- Seminars, internships, and laboratory activities, diversified according to the chosen curriculum, complementing frontal lessons;
- Language modules for achieving at least B1 level in a European Union language;
- Student's autonomous choices for acquiring and/or recognizing credits in other training activities (selectable among additional courses, internships, additional linguistic knowledge, information technology and telematic skills, seminars, conferences, laboratories, excursions, etc.).

Finally, a final exam is required at the end of the course.

- The verification of acquired knowledge and understanding depends on the type of activity: initial assessment tests may be required at entry, which can lead to additional educational obligations; courses typically involve traditional examination methods (written, oral, or student-prepared works), integrated, depending on the course, with intermediate assessments, group work, etc.; other training activities are accredited based on suitability assessments (such as certification of B1 level in a foreign language, computer certification); finally, the final exam requires the preparation of a thesis to be discussed before a committee that issues a final judgment based on the student's academic record and the discussion itself.

II - Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding
The graduate in Letters is able to apply the knowledge, understanding, and various methodologies acquired, in a differentiated manner according to the chosen curriculum, for:
- Organizing, classifying, and analyzing everything related to texts and documents, whether verbal, visual, or cartographic;
- Contextualizing texts, documents, but also themes and issues in linguistic-literary, historical, historical-artistic, geographical-territorial contexts;
- Preparing texts (descriptive, argumentative, popularizing, journalistic, etc.) and oral interventions on topics in literary, philological-linguistic, historical, historical-artistic, geographical-territorial fields;
- Elaborating cartographic and geovisual representations;
- Approaching some initial research experiences;
- Applying classification, processing, contextualization, and analysis skills according to a professional approach in various work contexts of editorial and documentary services, cultural and tourist services, international cooperation, and local development.

The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is acquired through courses and internship, laboratory, seminar, and student involvement in organizational activities (conferences, excursions, field activities, etc.) and research experiences.

Verification of the acquisition of the ability to apply knowledge and understanding occurs mainly in profit exams but also in activities that provide suitability and/or credit recognition without a grade.

III - Judgment Autonomy
The overall objective of the Study Course is to enable students to collect, select, and critically interpret data useful for reconstructing cultural contexts of the present or past, reaching an autonomous evaluation that accompanies these competencies with reflection on social, territorial, epistemological, and ethical issues connected.

Students will be required to formulate independent analyses and evaluations on topics and problems presented by professors in lectures, seminars, and laboratories offered by the Department, encouraging them to develop greater judgment independence through personal collection of documents, data, and information related to course content.

Students' critical spirit will be tested by comparing them with differentiated teaching materials, such as texts (literary and non-literary), performing arts works, sets of linguistic data (Italian, Italo-Romance dialects, and other languages), maps, historical documents, statistical databases related to society and territory, artistic and architectural artifacts, cartographic representations, and image narratives (photographic, cinematic, pictorial, graphic, etc.).

Active student participation in themes addressed in courses will also be encouraged through the presentation of short reports (written or oral) during lectures and through their involvement in conferences and integration activities organized by the Bachelor's Degree Course.

Finally, special attention will be given to guiding students in the correct and critical use of primary and secondary sources (bibliographic, cartographic, multimedia) during individual meetings with students, exams, and thesis discussions.

To all these verification tools, through which the degree of acquisition of judgment autonomy by students can be recognized, paths will be added to encourage students to interact more directly with society and local, regional, and national cultures, without neglecting international dynamics and comparative aspects that, in characterizing contemporary global societies, provide students with opportunities to critically reflect on their educational journey and develop a more acute civic awareness.

IV - Communication Skills
The training path aims to ensure students achieve full mastery, written and oral, of Italian and another European Union language, as well as acquire skills in reading and using images (photographic, cartographic, pictorial, cinematic, etc.), so that they are able to communicate ideas, knowledge, skills, illustrate problems, and propose solutions in specialized and non-specialized contexts and in general in various social life circumstances (e.g., in the organization of exhibitions, in intercultural and territorial fields, in the field of performance, etc.). Mastery of at least one European Union language other than Italian will be documented by obtaining linguistic suitability. Mastery of Italian, analytical and problem-solving skills will be achieved and verified through various didactic tools: writing of written reports on seminar activities and study topics, oral presentations and discussions during lectures, individual meetings with professors during office hours, preparation of the final exam under the guidance of a professor and its public oral presentation, also with the aid of paper (handouts) or multimedia (PowerPoint presentations).

V - Learning Ability
The graduate in Letters, upon completion of the university path, will have developed the ability to autonomously use strategies for documentation, access to bibliographic, cartographic, documentary sources, and consultation tools, to undertake subsequent research and studies. In addition, the acquisition of the main information technology and telematic communication tools will provide graduates with the possibility to deepen all areas related to the course both in a theoretical direction and in a professional context, thus enriching and specializing the acquired knowledge and skills. The acquisition of the ability to move autonomously, which will be verified through intermediate checks, exams, and the thesis, can also be stimulated by participating in integrated didactic activities and training internships and orientation, diversified according to the chosen curriculum.

Professional Role:
EDITORIAL AND DOCUMENTARY SERVICES OPERATOR
Regarding this role, the graduate in Letters can perform functions such as:
- Editor, proofreader, collaborator for publishing houses, radio-television newsrooms, magazines and newspapers, both in print and online (eventually after passing professional suitability exams);
- Library and archive technician, document system technician, consultation and loan service technician.

CULTURAL AND TOURIST SERVICES OPERATOR
Regarding this role, the graduate in Letters can perform functions such as:
- Museum operator, tourist operator, tour guide, tourist companion (eventually after passing professional suitability exams), promoter and organizer of fairs, exhibitions, conferences, shows in public and private entities operating in the field of enjoyment of historical-artistic, environmental, cultural assets;
- Promoter and organizer of events in the field of arts and performance.

LOCAL DEVELOPMENT AND COOPERATION OPERATOR
Regarding this role, the graduate in Letters can perform functions such as:
- Cooperation operator, in the reception and territorial integration of migrants, in cultural mediation and communication in entities and institutions dealing with international cooperation, migration, inclusion, humanitarian aid; local development operator, territorial promotion for public and private entities.

ITALIAN Awarded degree.
Bachelor's degree in ENGINEERING OF INFORMATION Specific educational objectives.
The Bachelor's degree is structured into the following four study paths: Automatic Engineering; Electronic Engineering; Computer Engineering; Telecommunications Engineering.
The educational activity aims to provide future graduates with a solid foundational education and broad engineering preparation through the courses in the first and second years, which are common to all study paths of the Information Engineering degree, and specialized preparation in the third year.
The study program is structured around the following main activities:
- Basic educational activities in mathematical, physical and computer sciences, concentrated in the first year and partly in the second year;
- General educational activities in the field of Information Engineering, concentrated mainly in the second year and including circuit theory, electronic systems, signal analysis and telecommunication systems, system theory and automatic control, computer architectures and operating systems;
- Additional activities, including economic-organizational disciplines, related disciplines, professional courses and laboratories, internship activities, and consolidation of knowledge/practice of a foreign language;
- Specific educational activities for each study path.
The four study paths aim to provide students with specific competencies that may include practical and implementation experiences. Aspects related to research and complex design activities will be the objective of master-level training courses.
Specific educational activities for the Automatic Engineering path include further aspects of programming, robotics, and equipment for automation.
Specific educational activities for the Electronic Engineering path include electromagnetic fields, analog and digital electronics, and electronic measurements.
Specific educational activities for the Computer Engineering path include database studies, advanced programming, and computer networks.
Specific educational activities for the Telecommunications Engineering path include studies on transmission systems, telecommunication networks and internetworking, and electromagnetic fields.
Dublin descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding The graduate will acquire broad knowledge and understanding in the field of Information Engineering; will reach a level characterized by the use of advanced textbooks and technical documentation (also in languages other than Italian) and knowledge of cutting-edge topics specific to the different paths, as specified below:
1) Automatic Engineering: numerical control systems and advanced programming techniques, industrial automation systems, control system technology;
2) Electronic Engineering: analog and digital electronic circuits, complex electronic systems, methodologies and electronic measurements, microwave systems;
3) Computer Engineering: advanced programming techniques, databases and computer networks, software applications in web architecture;
4) Telecommunications Engineering: broadband networks and internetworking, wired and wireless transmission systems, security aspects, microwave systems, multimedia applications.
5) Verification of learning outcomes is primarily conducted through tests, written and/or oral exams concluding with a grade, exam or laboratory tests concluding with qualification.
II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding Consistent with educational objectives and the organization of the study path, the graduate will be able to apply their knowledge and understanding to solve concrete engineering problems in the Information field, demonstrating adequate competence to propose and support arguments regarding potential economic implications.
Achievement of the ability to apply knowledge and understanding occurs through critical reflection on texts proposed for individual study, stimulated by classroom activities, study of research and application cases presented by instructors, numerical and practical laboratory exercises, bibliographic research, home assignments, and small projects, as provided within certain courses belonging to the characteristic disciplinary sectors, as well as during preparation for the final exam. Verifications (written exams, oral exams, reports, exercises, "problem solving" activities) require the performance of specific tasks demonstrating mastery of tools, methodologies, and critical autonomy.
III - Judgment autonomy The graduate will be able to collect, filter, and interpret data both in the broader field of Information Engineering and in the specific aspects of their study path, sufficient to enable an autonomous judgment on the technical-scientific relevance of such data, while being aware of potential social or ethical implications.
Judgment autonomy is particularly developed through exercises, organized seminars, preparation of reports, and activities assigned by the supervisor for final exam preparation. Verification of acquired judgment autonomy occurs through evaluation of maturity demonstrated during exams and final exam preparation.
IV - Communication skills The graduate will be able to communicate data, information, ideas, problems, and solutions effectively to both specialists and non-specialists.
Written and oral communication skills are particularly stimulated during seminars, exercises, and generally in educational activities requiring preparation of reports and written documents and oral presentation of the same. Acquisition of the aforementioned communication skills is also provided through the preparation of a final report and its discussion. Verification of knowledge of basic and/or advanced foreign language constitutes an integral part of the communication skills acquisition process.
V - Learning ability The graduate will have developed the necessary learning abilities to pursue higher-level studies with a high degree of autonomy, as well as to continuously update and improve their competencies.
Achievement of the aforementioned abilities is supported by educational activities in the disciplinary fields identified in the current organization and, in particular, those carried out with partial autonomy. Specific teaching methodologies include tutoring activities. Verification of learning ability achievement is subject to the various exam procedures provided during the course.
Function in work context.
Function in a work context:
The educational profile of the Bachelor in Information Engineering enables operation in the fields of design, development, engineering, production, operation, and maintenance of automatic, electronic, computer, and telecommunication systems. Special attention is given to the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) scenario and the pervasive use of such technologies in all productive sectors and social life.
After passing the state exam, the Bachelor in Information Engineering can register with the Engineers' Register Section B Sector c - information (Junior Engineer).

Competencies associated with the function.
Competencies associated with the function:
The four study paths aim to provide students with specific competencies that may include practical and implementation experiences. Aspects related to research and complex design activities will be the objective of master-level training courses.
Specific educational activities for the Automatic Engineering path provide competencies in robotics and equipment for control systems and industrial automation.
Specific educational activities for the Electronic Engineering path provide competencies in electromagnetic fields, analog and digital electronics, and electronic measurements.
Specific educational activities for the Computer Engineering path provide competencies in computer architectures, operating systems, databases, advanced programming (web application development), and computer networks.
Specific educational activities for the Telecommunications Engineering path provide competencies in information transmission systems, telecommunication networks and internetworking, and electromagnetic fields.
Professional status conferred by the degree.
Employment opportunities:
The natural professional opportunity for the graduate consists of performing activities both in companies that design and/or produce systems and equipment, and in entities that provide services in the multiple fields of Information.
It is important to emphasize that the organization of the study path and the content of the teaching modules have been designed to provide the graduate with adequate and updated preparation in the field of modern information technologies.
This approach corresponds to the intention of providing the graduate with broad employment prospects throughout the national and community territory, satisfying also the recruitment needs of companies operating in the Abruzzo region. The insertion of the future graduate into the workforce is also facilitated through the offer of company internships, for which there is a consolidated tradition with a high number of companies.
The natural professional opportunity for the graduate in the Automatic Engineering path concerns companies, entities, and institutions providing services through the use of automation systems (e.g., in the fields of communications, transportation, distribution, maintenance, quality control, public administration, finance) or that produce products including computer components (such as dedicated systems, control systems, electronic products, integrated circuits). Some professional profiles corresponding to the above capabilities are listed below:
1) programmer of robotic systems;
2) designer of continuous or event-based automatic control systems;
3) quality control specialist.
The natural professional opportunity for the graduate in the Electronic Engineering study path consists of performing activities in companies that design or produce complex electronic components, systems, and equipment, and in companies and entities that provide services through the use of electronic systems. Numerous are the application fields, in the electronic, electromechanical, computer, aerospace, space, and telecommunications sectors. Given the vastness and diversity of possible applications of electronic equipment, the study path and teaching module content have been organized to provide the graduate with broad and diversified preparation, although naturally focused on electronics itself. In recent years, there has been an acceleration in the diffusion process of electronics and its application in both rapidly developing sectors, such as telecommunications, and more traditional sectors, such as industry. Some professional profiles corresponding to the above capabilities are listed below:
- designer of electronic systems;
- specialist in production control of components and systems;
- specialist in management of electronic systems.
The natural professional opportunity for the graduate with a Computer Engineering study path concerns software houses (product companies) developing software and information applications, companies, entities, and institutions providing services through the use of information processing systems (e.g., in the fields of public administration, finance, communications, transportation, distribution, maintenance, quality control), companies that use information products in production processes (e.g., robotic, steel, energy production industries), or that produce products including computer components (such as dedicated systems, control systems, electronic products, integrated circuits). Some professional profiles corresponding to the above capabilities are listed below:
1) programmer;
2) application analyst;
3) web application expert (design and development);
4) network system specialist;
5) application and database management expert;
6) consultant for sale and application of information technologies.
The graduate in the Telecommunications Engineering study path finds direct employment opportunities, with the ability to hold roles in design, development, testing, and management, in companies that design and/or produce components, systems, and equipment for telecommunications, in network operators managing complex telecommunication systems, and in companies and entities (public and private) providing services through the use of telecommunication and telematic systems. It is important to emphasize that the organization of the study path and the content of the specialized teaching modules have been designed to provide the graduate with adequate and updated preparation in the field of modern telecommunications technologies, with particular attention to the integration between telecommunications technologies and the Internet world. Some professional profiles (retrievable in various coding contexts) corresponding to the above capabilities are listed below:
1) telecommunications designer;
2) network manager.

Program, texts and objectives Official languages of teaching and assessment of preparation.
ITALIAN Specific educational objectives.

The three-year Bachelor's program in Civil Engineering aims to train technicians with a university education, who have a deep understanding of the theoretical-scientific and methodological-operational aspects of mathematics and other basic sciences, are capable of using this knowledge to interpret and describe engineering problems and systems, have a good grasp of the methodological-operational aspects of engineering sciences, and in particular those of Civil Engineering, where they are able to identify, formulate, and solve problems using updated methods, techniques, and tools, adapting to scientific and technological evolution.

In these areas, the professionals that the Study Program aims to train acquire the basic knowledge and tools for an integrated approach to problems concerning the mechanics of solids and structures, hydraulics, and geotechnics, possess solid foundational knowledge in mathematical disciplines, and have an adequate understanding of the models and methods of Civil Engineering, with the necessary requirements for subsequent full development of design autonomy and decision-making capabilities. Civil Engineering graduates apply existing knowledge in the field of structural design of buildings, hydraulic, and geotechnical works, in collaboration and contribution to design, construction, surveying, monitoring, maintenance, management, and commissioning of private and public buildings, in collaboration with construction supervision and commissioning of public and private buildings, and in coordination and execution of surveys on current and historical buildings.

The achievement of these objectives is pursued through a structured educational activity divided into teaching modules, which include classroom lectures, laboratory exercises, and individual study or exercises, leading to credits that the student earns by passing examinations. Activities are conducted to stimulate the ability to work in groups and communication.

The educational path for obtaining the three-year Bachelor's degree in Civil Engineering includes balanced educational activities between basic science disciplines and those characteristic of Civil Engineering and related cultural areas. In particular, it allows the acquisition of:
- an adequate knowledge of the tools of mathematics and other basic sciences;
- a basic methodological and technological preparation accompanied by solid knowledge in some disciplines traditionally characteristic of Civil Engineering fields;
- a deep understanding of the methodological and operational aspects of the fundamental sciences of Civil Engineering;
- an adequate knowledge of the English language as well as additional knowledge and freely chosen skills.

Therefore, two learning areas are provided:
- Basic Area: aimed at providing knowledge and tools of mathematics and other basic sciences in order to effectively use them to interpret, model, and analyze Civil Engineering problems.
- Engineering Area: aimed at providing methodological knowledge and tools in the field of design, construction, management, and monitoring of civil works.

The disciplines included in the educational path are also chronologically structured to first complete the basic and broad engineering preparation, and subsequently develop concepts and methods specific to the design, construction, management, and monitoring of civil works. The disciplines of the Basic Area focus on the typical sectors of Mathematical, Physical, and Natural Sciences, while those of the Engineering Area focus on the typical sectors of Civil Engineering such as Technical Drawing, Hydraulics, Science of Structures, Geotechnics, Technical Physics, Structures in reinforced concrete and prestressed concrete, Road, Railway, and Airport Construction, Science and Technology of Materials, Topography, supplemented by additional courses aimed at completing cultural training and knowledge of foreign languages. Finally, the selection of appropriate specific courses allows the acquisition of basic knowledge for the design of simple typical Civil Engineering works or for the technical and administrative management of construction processes.

Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding BASIC AREA Civil Engineering Bachelor's graduates, at the end of the educational path in the Basic Area, will have a solid knowledge of the essential mathematical and scientific tools for understanding and modeling Civil Engineering issues. This includes a deep understanding of the mathematical and scientific principles underlying engineering techniques, a systematic view of key sector aspects, and awareness of the multidisciplinary context. Methodological training is distributed in a coordinated and progressive manner through the courses and activities proposed by the study program, such as lectures, exercises, and participation in seminars held by university professors and visiting professors.

The educational path includes basic activities, predominantly in the fields of Mathematical, Physical, and Natural Sciences, particularly in the disciplinary sectors of Geometry (MAT/03), Mathematical Analysis (MAT/05), Chemistry (CHIM/07), and Physics (FIS/01).

The verification of knowledge and understanding capabilities is conducted in an integrated manner within all the assessment methods provided by the study program (exams, written and oral tests, in which both theoretical preparation and the ability to process theoretical-scientific and methodological-operational tools acquired are evaluated).

ENGINEERING AREA At the end of the educational path in the Engineering Area, Civil Engineering Bachelor's graduates will be equipped with a basic methodological and technological preparation, enriched by solid knowledge within Civil Engineering, where they will be able to identify, formulate, and solve problems using updated methods, techniques, and tools, adapting to scientific and technological evolution. This translates into a clear and solid understanding of the technical foundations of engineering disciplines, including a systematic understanding of key aspects and awareness of the multidisciplinary context. Methodological training is distributed in a coordinated and progressive manner through the courses and activities proposed by the study program, such as lectures, exercises, participation in seminars held by university professors, visiting professors, and professionals from the workplace, as well as guided visits to construction sites and sites of interest. The use of numerous departmental laboratories completes the study program's educational strategy.

The educational path includes characteristic activities of the Civil Engineering disciplinary field, particularly in the disciplinary sectors of Hydraulics and Hydraulic Structures (ICAR/01 and ICAR/02), Roads, Railways, and Airports (ICAR/04), Topography and Cartography (ICAR/06), Geotechnics (ICAR/07), and Science and Technology of Structures (ICAR/08 and ICAR/09).

The verification of knowledge and understanding capabilities is conducted in an integrated manner within all the assessment methods provided by the study program (exams, written and oral tests, in which both theoretical preparation and the ability to process even design-oriented aspects are evaluated).

II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding BASIC AREA As a result of the study program's teaching approach, Civil Engineering Bachelor's graduates, at the end of the educational path in the Basic Area, will be able to address the challenges and issues of Civil Engineering in a multidisciplinary and innovative context in both theoretical and practical ways. In particular, they will acquire the ability to apply acquired knowledge to identify and formulate problems, as well as the competence to appropriately understand the analytical methods and physical-mathematical modeling learned. These skills are developed through exercises, promoting group interaction and involving laboratory activities. Verification of these abilities occurs through written/oral tests, and for disciplines with design activities, also through examination tests.

ENGINEERING AREA As a result of the study program's teaching approach, Civil Engineering Bachelor's graduates, at the end of the educational path in the Engineering Area, will acquire a deep understanding of the regulatory framework governing verification and design activities of civil works, along with specific competencies. These competencies include the ability to appropriately understand analytical methods and physical-mathematical modeling, the application of consolidated knowledge to solve engineering problems, as well as the ability to identify, formulate, and solve technical problems within Civil Engineering. These skills are developed through exercises, promoting group interaction and involving laboratory activities. Verification of the ability to apply knowledge occurs through written/oral tests, including examination tests for disciplines with design activities, and for other educational activities, through the final examination.

III - Judgment autonomy Bachelor's graduates must possess, at the end of the study program, personal judgment autonomy regarding decisions to be made in the phases of civil works construction. They will therefore be able to assume autonomous decision-making responsibilities and actively participate in the design process in even interdisciplinary contexts. Critical reasoning capabilities will also be developed through the analysis and interpretation of experimental data, theoretical results, and models.

In particular, during the educational process, the student will acquire the ability to solve engineering problems through the development of technical and design applications, mainly within courses in the second and third years. He will acquire, without claiming completeness, judgment autonomy:
- in conducting bibliographic research and using databases and other information sources;
- in designing and conducting appropriate experiments and interpreting and synthesizing the obtained results;
- in laboratory operations and analysis methodology;
- in selecting appropriate equipment, tools, and methods;
- in understanding applicable techniques and methods and their limitations;
- in being aware of the non-technical implications of engineering practice.

The evaluation of the achieved ability and judgment autonomy will be conducted progressively in the course examinations, in the development of design applications, and in the preparation and discussion of the thesis.

IV - Communication skills The ability to communicate project objectives and implementation methods is essential for effective entry into the professional world. Therefore, it is important for the Bachelor's graduate to possess appropriate communication tools and have verified mastery through targeted simulations.

The study program will therefore provide all the tools to consolidate and further develop students' communication skills, both written and oral, and communication through graphical representation, as well as the use of computer and telecommunication tools.

At the end of the educational process, the student will have developed:
- the ability to clearly and logically communicate process and design choices, as well as the underlying scientific orientations, to both specialist and non-specialist interlocutors;
- the ability to manage relationships with the plurality of subjects, specialists and non-specialists, involved in the development of civil works (public bodies, companies, design studios, etc.);
- communication skills, also in English, both with the scientific community and with different social components, even non-experts;
- both the ability to work autonomously and the ability to work as a component of a group where diverse competencies are present, depending on development needs and the inherent complexity and interdisciplinarity in the design and construction of civil works.

These capabilities will be developed during the regular educational activities provided and through various discussion and comparison moments in group work and various occasions of meeting with representatives of the workplace (conferences, guided visits, etc.).

Communication skills verification is conducted through written and/or oral tests provided for the examinations and other educational activities, particularly through the final examination.

V - Learning ability The three-year Bachelor's course will provide students, in addition to specific knowledge, a methodological approach to study that will allow them to undertake subsequent studies (Master's degree) profitably and enable future professionals to independently embark on a continuous process of professional growth, updating, and learning.

The study program's objective, among others, is to offer a work method, as well as specific knowledge. This objective will be pursued through the alternation of traditional educational moments (lectures) with other moments more dedicated to developing self-organization, critical synthesis, and personal research abilities (internships, thesis).

Assessments will be conducted through examinations and the discussion of the final thesis examination.

Professional role in the workplace.

Professional role in the workplace:
The professional profile of graduates is, in particular, characterized by the following functions, without claiming completeness, in a workplace context:
- structural design of buildings, hydraulic, and geotechnical works within the limits set by current regulations, or design of simple buildings using standardized methodologies;
- design of water supply and disposal systems;
- design of building systems;
- surveying of areas and structures;
- control during the execution of civil works;
- collaboration and contribution to design, construction, surveying, monitoring, maintenance, management, and commissioning of private and public buildings;
- collaboration in construction supervision and commissioning of public and private buildings;
- coordination and execution of surveys on current and historical buildings.

Competencies associated with the function.

Competencies associated with the function:
In order to perform the functions and activities associated with the professional profile, the Civil Engineering student will acquire specific knowledge, skills, and competencies. In particular, as an example, they include:
- adequate knowledge of the methodological-operational aspects of mathematics and other basic sciences and the ability to use this knowledge to interpret and describe Civil Engineering problems;
- the ability to identify, formulate, and solve typical Civil Engineering problems using updated methods, techniques, and tools;
- the ability and skill in using techniques and tools for the design, verification, and maintenance of components, systems, and processes, even using integrated digital modeling tools;
- knowledge of methods for evaluating the resilience of civil systems and structures with respect to phenomena resulting from changes in usage conditions as well as aging and degradation of materials and components;
- knowledge of methods, techniques, and tools for monitoring and surveying civil works as well as the associated data processing;
- the ability to conduct experiments and analyze and interpret their data;
- the ability to understand the impact of engineering solutions in the social and physical-environmental context;
- knowledge of one's own professional and ethical responsibilities;
- knowledge of business contexts and corporate culture in its economic, managerial, and organizational aspects;
- knowledge of contemporary contexts;
- the ability to interact with other professional figures involved in the Civil Engineering supply chain, in relational and decisional terms;
- the ability to adapt one's actions according to the evolution of methods, techniques, tools, and technologies;
- the ability to communicate effectively, in written and oral form, both in Italian and English, with the engineering community and generally with society, both in national contexts and in international settings;
- knowledge of basic cognitive tools for continuous updating of one's education.

Professional status conferred by the degree.

Employment opportunities:

The professional profile and the expected employment and professional opportunities for Civil Engineering graduates are a direct consequence of consultation with stakeholders and analysis of sector studies.

The study program's objective is to train Civil Engineers who can practice the profession in the fields of design and construction of civil works and capable of receiving and following innovation by adapting to scientific and technological evolution. It is consistent with the University's Strategic Plan 2020-2025, which, among its objectives, aims to promote the quality of the educational offer with paths aligned with the needs of the individual and society. The profession is classified, according to ISTAT, in the category "Civil Engineers and similar professions".

It is emphasized that access to the profession, as indicated by current regulations, is subject to passing the State exam for authorization to practice the profession of Junior Engineer, Civil and Environmental Sector.

Professional opportunities cover the typical sectors of Civil Engineering and range from the classic figure of the freelance engineer employed in medium/large companies to employment with managerial functions at design companies, construction companies, central and peripheral bodies of the State, Regions, and Municipalities. The professional opportunities for graduates can be listed, without claiming completeness, as follows:
- Civil Engineering area: construction and maintenance companies for civil works, civil plants and infrastructure; professional studios and design companies for works, plants, and infrastructure; public offices for design, management, and control of urban and territorial systems; companies, bodies, consortia, and agencies for management and control of works and service systems; service companies for feasibility studies of urban and territorial impact of infrastructure;
- Safety and Civil Protection and Territory Engineering area: large infrastructure, construction sites, workplaces, industrial environments, local authorities, public and private bodies where prevention and safety management activities are developed and where the responsibility profiles required by current regulations for safety condition verification are held.

Additionally, Civil Engineering graduates possess the curricular requirements for access to Master's degrees in Civil Engineering, Environmental Engineering, and equivalent programs.

ITALIAN Degree awarded.
Bachelor's Degree in INFORMATICS Specific educational objectives.
The Bachelor's Degree in Informatics provides the necessary skills to operate in the fields of specification, design, development, management, and maintenance of software systems and computer networks. Graduates are prepared to join software development and integrated systems projects; configure and manage network services; start and manage data processing centers; provide support for management decisions regarding automation, informatization, and modeling of problems; design, lead, and test facilities and systems for generation, transmission, and processing of information. Additionally, the Bachelor's Degree provides the theoretical and methodological knowledge necessary to: integrate skills in interdisciplinary fields; follow the evolution of new technologies; identify new application areas for computer science disciplines.
The Bachelor's Degree in Informatics is characterized by a strong presence of laboratory courses, which constitute a fundamental, defining, and indispensable element, and also provides the possibility of completing internships and traineeships at companies, as an integral part of the educational path, facilitating the transfer of skills from the University to companies.
Regarding the quality of the educational process, it is noted that the Bachelor's Degree holds the "GRIN Badge".
The GRIN Badge, issued annually since 2004 in collaboration between GRIN (Group of Computer Science - the association of university professors of computer science) and AICA (Italian Association for Computer Science and Automatic Computing), certifies the quality of the content of three-year and master's degrees in computer science (classes L-31 and LM-18).
The results of the quality certification process for content are available online at the site http://grin.informatica.uniroma2.it/certificazione This certification is based on a set of criteria defining how much and which computer science is taught, how much mathematics from relevant areas for computer science is taught, and how many permanent computer science faculty members are present. The details of the certification rules for 2012 are available at the URL http://www.grin-informatica.it/opencms/export/sites/default/grin/files/RegoleCertificazione2012.pdf Dublin Descriptors: I - Knowledge and understanding Graduates must have a solid knowledge and understanding of the fundamentals of mathematics and, in general, of the sciences, essential to meet the other learning objectives of the study program; these fundamentals include integral and differential calculus, discrete mathematics, mathematical logic, probability calculus, and basic physics.
They must also possess adequate knowledge of computer science and its main related fields, and in particular of the theoretical, computational, methodological, logical, and semantic foundations, of system architecture, algorithms and data structures, programming languages and paradigms, operating systems, databases, distributed systems, and communication networks.
The graduate must finally acquire fundamental knowledge in related fields, with particular reference to operations research and combinatorial optimization.
Based on such knowledge, the graduate must be able to independently understand the principles and solutions related to information technology applications and technologies, even if not considered during the study program due to a high degree of innovation or related to specific contexts.
In summary, graduates must have:
- knowledge and understanding of the mathematical and scientific principles underlying computer science;
- a clear general knowledge of computer science and a systematic understanding of key aspects and concepts related to it;
- the ability to independently understand the latest developments in the field and innovative and specific applications.
These objectives are primarily achieved through dedicated courses (basic, characteristic, related, and integrative) for over 100 ECTS, each requiring the successful completion of an individual final exam consisting of a written and oral examination.
II - Ability to apply knowledge and understanding Graduates must be able to apply their knowledge and understanding to the analysis and development of information systems and solutions.
In particular, they must be able to analyze computer problems, evaluate corresponding solutions, and propose new solutions appropriate to their level of knowledge and understanding, which may involve considerations beyond their field of specialization. Analysis may involve identifying the problem, clearly defining specifications, examining possible solution methods, selecting the most appropriate method, and correctly applying it.
Graduates must be able to use a variety of methods, including mathematical analysis, computational modeling, or practical experimentation, to design and implement information solutions appropriate to their level of knowledge and understanding, whether working independently or in collaboration with computer science graduates and professionals.
In summary, graduates must have:
- the ability to apply their knowledge and understanding to identify, formulate, and solve computer problems using established methods;
- the ability to apply their knowledge and understanding to analyze information products, processes, and methods;
- the ability to apply their knowledge and understanding to develop and implement solutions and projects that meet defined and specified requirements;
- an understanding of design methodologies and the ability to use them.
These objectives are achieved both through dedicated courses and through a significant number of laboratory courses, which allow practical application of acquired knowledge and require the completion of projects either independently or through participation in work groups.
III - Judgment autonomy Graduates must have developed critical reasoning skills, the ability to identify the most appropriate methods for analyzing and solving computer problems and designing systems, to understand the limits of their knowledge, and to independently conduct investigations appropriate to their level of knowledge and understanding. Such investigations may involve bibliographic research, the design and conduct of experiments, data interpretation, and computer simulation. They may also require consultation of databases and regulations.
Regarding the computer profession, graduates must be able to apply their knowledge and understanding to develop practical skills for solving problems, conducting investigations, and designing information solutions. These skills may include knowledge, use, and awareness of hardware and software processes and equipment, experimentation, use of technical literature and information sources.
Graduates must also be able to recognize the broader non-technical implications of computer practice, of an ethical, commercial, and industrial nature.
In summary, graduates must have:
- the ability to use appropriate methods to conduct research activities with a predominantly applied character or other complex investigations on suitable technical topics, leveraging bibliographic references, databases, and other information sources;
- the ability to design and conduct appropriate experiments, interpret data, and draw conclusions;
- the ability to choose and use appropriate equipment, tools, and methods, combining theoretical and practical aspects - an understanding of applicable techniques and methods and their limitations;
- awareness of the non-technical implications of computer practice.
In addition to dedicated courses and laboratory courses, these objectives are also achieved through internships and direct placements in work contexts and through training activities related to the final exam.
IV - Communication skills Graduates must:
- be able to effectively operate individually and as members of a group;
- be able to use methods to communicate effectively with the computer community and, in general, with society;
- have the necessary skills to integrate and organize activities within collaborative projects;
- have the necessary skills to acquire problem requirements through interaction with clients;
- have the necessary skills for the effective presentation and communication of results;
- be able to appropriately use, in addition to Italian, English both in technical-scientific contexts and for general information exchange.
These objectives are achieved through laboratory training activities carried out through group work, the preparation of project and laboratory reports, language learning activities, and finally through the preparation of the written and oral presentation of the final exam.
V - Learning ability Graduates must have acquired the ability to study scientific topics, even in relation to different contexts, to effectively integrate received knowledge. They must also be able to understand the limits of their knowledge and have skills in identifying textbooks, other sources, and useful materials for in-depth study. They must finally have the ability to read and learn in English.
To this end, students are guided in improving their study methods from the first year by teachers and tutors, to enable them to best face the planned educational path. The learning ability is continuously monitored through profit assessments and exam tests focusing on the knowledge to be acquired, especially through independent study.
English is learned in specific courses and through the progressive use of the foreign language in learning.
Work context function.
Work context function:
Considering the pervasive role of Computer Science and information technologies in modern society, the roles that a Basic Graduate in Computer Science can hold are numerous. We list only the main ones.
Programmer: knowledge of the main algorithmic methods and programming languages, and their application domains.
Web Programmer: knowledge of the main languages related to Internet and mobile applications.
System Administrator: knowledge of the main operating systems and their application in different fields.
Network Manager: knowledge of the main network systems and protocols.
Software Designer: knowledge of the elements and methods of Software Engineering.
Database and DBMS Designer: knowledge of the main formalisms and languages for defining databases, knowledge of the computational mechanisms of DBMS even in concurrent environments.
Database Administrator: knowledge of the main DBMS.
Training Technician: general knowledge acquired in the basic degree.
Marketing Specialist: knowledge of the main information systems and their applicability.
Small entrepreneur in the computer field: general knowledge acquired in the basic degree also in relation to the development of the discipline.
Function-associated skills.
Function-associated skills:
The skills of a Computer Science graduate relate to the design, organization, implementation, management, maintenance, and application of information systems, also regarding computer networks, the web, and mobile devices. The graduate will be able to define and manage aspects related to completeness, adequacy, reliability, performance, and security of systems. They can apply the acquired skills both in producer companies in the areas of information systems and networks, and more generally in companies, public administrations, or any organizations that use information systems. They can also access higher study levels in the Computer Science field, thus having career opportunities in more advanced professions related to innovation, teaching at secondary school level, or in research and development and continuing education training in public or private centers.
Professional status conferred by the degree.
Career opportunities:
The reference occupational and professional fields for graduates of the class are as follows. Employee in a Private Computer, ICT (Information and Communication Technology), or other sector company where Computer Science finds application (virtually all sectors). Employee in a training company.
Employee in a Public Administration with a role in developing or managing information systems. Entrepreneur in the computer or ICT field or in sectors where computer science and/or ICT play a significant role. ICT Consultant.
